Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tunix and Gemma 4 on Google TPUs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In our previous posts - Easy FunctionGemma finetuning with Tunix on Google TPUs and Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs - we showed how Google Tunix streamlines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and single-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Cloud TPUs.
  • We will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host.

In our previous posts - Easy FunctionGemma finetuning with Tunix on Google TPUs and Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs - we showed how Google Tunix streamlines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and single-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Cloud TPUs. Real-world AI agents, however, rarely finish their job in a single turn. They have to reason over partial observations, invoke tools, observe environment feedback, and adapt their strategy across multiple steps. So in this post, we will walk through how to train a multi-turn, tool-using LLM agent using Tunix's agentic reinforcement learning pipeline on Cloud TPU v6e-8. You can find the complete code in this GitHub repository.

We will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host. Plane Strike is played on a 6x6 grid (A1 to F6) where one 8-cell plane is hidden in one of 4 orientations. Each turn, the agent sees the result of its previous strike and the raw visible board (. untried, X hit, O miss), thinks through candidate placements, and calls the strike(cell="...") tool to strike one cell. The game ends when all 8 plane cells are hit, or after 23 strikes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, MGM Resorts and BetMGM have canceled their memberships in the National Council on Problem Gambling because the group accepted Kalshi. Their exit brings licensed operators into a split over prediction markets that had so far involved regulators and state problem-gambling councils.

In a recent development, the companies’ letter to the council is dated Nov. 18. Stephen Martino, MGM Resorts’ senior vice president and chief compliance officer, signed it alongside Rhea Loney, BetMGM’s chief compliance officer. It went to interim executive director Charles Jeffers and board president Derek Longmeier.

The companies wrote that they no longer hold the principles the group once stood for. They argued that promoting gambling as a way out of financial trouble runs against responsible gaming principles. The letter also charged that Kalshi disregards state gambling laws when it sells sports event contracts in states whose regulators consider them unlicensed gambling.

Industry observers note that MGM and BetMGM are the first gambling operators to confirm they left specifically over the council’s work with Kalshi, SBC Americas reported. The Ohio Casino Control Commission had already ended its membership. The Michigan Gaming Control Board withdrew its membership in a July 1, 2026 letter. The Nevada Council on Problem Gambling and Washington’s Evergreen Council on Problem Gambling also left.

Industry observers note that the council confirmed the deal at the center of the dispute on May 18, 2026. Besides its funding commitment, Kalshi received a seat in the NCPG’s Leadership Circle. That group is made up of top partners that help fund the organization.

The Nov. 18 letter sets out the main grievances licensed operators hold against prediction markets. Kalshi lets 18-year-olds trade. Most licensed sportsbooks require bettors to be 21. Prediction markets pay little in state taxes, which leaves less money for problem-gambling programs. They also sit outside state self-exclusion programs.

Recent findings suggest that each of those points touches the core work of a harm-reduction body. The fight over whether prediction markets count as gambling has now reached the main US problem-gambling group.

“No organization should understand the risks Kalshi and other prediction markets pose to responsible gaming more clearly and urgently than NCPG,”– MGM/BetMGM while ending membership in the National Council on Problem Gambling.https://t.co/7A0Wi2AIFo via @reviewjournal.

— David Danzis (@AC2Vegas_Danzis) November 22, 2026.

The NCPG has not backed down. The group describes its prediction-market work as a way to tackle fresh sources of gambling harm. It claims that work does not endorse particular companies or how they do business. In a Friday statement, the NCPG mentioned the risks of prediction markets will not go away when organizations refuse to engage. It added that leaving over this work may send a political message but does nothing to prevent gambling-related harm.

Sources indicate that A long form can feel like a chore before anyone types a word. Splitting it into smaller steps lets people focus on a few related questions at a time.

The code looks simple: show one section, hide the rest and add a button. The difficult parts are validation, keyboard use, focus and what happens when JavaScript doesn't run. This guide builds an accessible multi step form with HTML and plain JavaScript. It also reproduces a bug that can leave visitors stuck on the first step.

It has been revealed that multiple steps make sense when questions fall into clear groups, such as project details, timing and contact information. A form with only an email address and a message usually doesn't need them.

Splitting a form doesn't make unnecessary questions useful. Remove those first. More steps also aren't a guarantee of more completed forms, so test the change with your own audience.

It has been revealed that the W3C tutorial on multiple page forms advises dividing long forms into logical stages and telling consumers about their progress. Our example applies those ideas within a single page.

In a recent development, without JavaScript, all three groups remain visible and Send works as an ordinary submit button. The Back button stays hidden because it has no job in that view. This approach is called progressive enhancement: start with a working form, then add the step behavior.

The action value is a placeholder. Point it to a real server endpoint in your project. If your stylesheet sets a display value on fieldsets, check that it doesn't override the hidden attribute.

Save the following code as form.js in the same folder:.

Recent findings suggest that the form has one submit button. Its label reads Continue until the last step. The submit handler decides whether to show an error, open the next step or let the browser send the data. Pressing Enter in a text field follows the same path.

It has been revealed that back is a regular button, so it never submits anything. The answers remain in their fields because the code only hides each step. It doesn't remove or rebuild it.

Here is the line that is easy to miss:.

To test its purpose, I removed only this line, filled in the first field and pressed Enter in headless Chromium 158. The form stayed on step 1. The console reported messages like these:.

Before firing the submit event, the browser checked the entire form. The empty required fields on later steps were invalid, but they were hidden. Submission was blocked, so our handler never had a chance to open step 2.

According to recent reports, setting noValidate stops that automatic check during submission. It doesn't disable checkValidity() or reportValidity(), so our code can validate only the visible step. Because the line lives in JavaScript, the browser's normal validation still applies if the script never loads.

For more detail on native validation rules and methods, see SitePoint's Complete Guide to HTML Forms and Constraint Validation.

According to recent reports, the test intercepted the request, so it checked what the browser sent rather than a real server. It also doesn't show how other browsers behave.

Industry observers note that each legend includes the current step number, and the page title changes with it. After someone moves to another step, focus goes to the new legend. This gives keyboard users a clear starting point. The code doesn't move focus during the first page load.

The negative tabindex lets JavaScript focus a legend without adding it to the normal Tab order. Keep the focus outline visible, or replace it with an equally clear style. Screen reader behavior varies, so test with the browser and screen reader combinations your visitors use.

Native validation messages are useful for a small example. A production form may need persistent error text beside each field. If so, connect each message to its field with aria-describedby, set aria-invalid when needed and clear both after the error is fixed.

In a recent development, also avoid asking for the same information twice. WCAG 2.2 Redundant Entry requires previously entered information needed again in the same process to be filled in or available to select. There are exceptions, including certain security needs and information that is no longer valid. This example alone doesn't make a whole website WCAG compliant.

Recent findings suggest that browser checks can be changed or bypassed. Your server should validate required fields, allowed choices, lengths and formats again. It should also handle spam, protect against cross site request forgery where relevant and escape stored values when displaying them.

Be careful with automatic draft saving. If you send answers before the final submission, explain this clearly and check which privacy or consent rules apply. Saving a draft only in the browser also needs care, especially on shared devices.

Before release, try the complete form with only a keyboard. Check mobile layouts, zoom, browser autofill, Back and Forward navigation, slow connections and server errors. Make sure repeated clicks don't create duplicate records.

SitePoint's practical workflow for testing JavaScript forms is a helpful next step when you're preparing a broader test blueprint.

The example also leaves out conditional questions. If one answer can remove a later step, calculate the active steps before updating the progress label. Decide how to handle old answers from inactive branches, and enforce the same rules on the server.

In a recent development, custom code gives you control over the markup and behavior, but your team must maintain validation, delivery, security and testing. A form builder can reduce the amount of interface code you manage. For example, LeadGen App lists multi step forms, conditional logic and website embedding among its features.

Whichever route you choose, test the finished form instead of relying on a feature list.

Recent findings suggest that an accessible multi step form needs more than a few hidden sections. Start with semantic HTML, validate each visible step and keep progress and focus clear.

According to recent reports, pay special attention to required fields that appear later. A single hidden field can stop the first button from working, even when the visible answer is correct. Test that case, then check the whole journey with real users and a real server before launch.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that great news from the OGs of open source LLMs! Muse Glimmer, released today, is Meta’s upcoming multimodal model, especially designed for local agentic use cases. Distilled from Muse to 30B parameters, and released under the Apache 2.0 license, it’s ideal deploying locally for privacy, reducing costs, or just hacking around. It’s intended for privacy-aware applications such as coding, document analysis, personal assistants, Claw- or Hermes-like setups.

Recent findings suggest that to celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Recent findings suggest that scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:.

In addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:.

According to recent reports, muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

According to recent reports, after transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as moviebox a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

In a recent development, muse Glimmer looks like a really exciting step for practical open-source AI, especially with its focus on local, agentic, and multimodal workloads. A 30B-parameter model combining a 2B vision encoder with a 28B text decoder gives developers a strong foundation for coding, document analysis, personal assistants, and other privacy-sensitive applications. 🔥🤖.

It has been revealed that the Apache 2.0 license is another major highlight because it makes the model much more approachable for developers who want to experiment, customize, and deploy without relying entirely on hosted inference. Local deployment can also bring meaningful benefits around privacy, latency, and infrastructure costs, which makes this especially interesting for personal and enterprise workflows. 🚀.

I also like the architectural choices here, particularly the hybrid attention pattern, grouped-query attention, and Q-K normalization. Alternating sliding-window and full-attention layers seems like a thoughtful way to balance long-context capability with efficiency, while sharing KV heads across query heads can significantly reduce memory requirements during generation.

The day-zero ecosystem support makes the release even more compelling. Having integrations across Transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, and other tools means developers can start testing real-world workflows immediately instead of waiting for the surrounding ecosystem to catch up. Open multimodal models that are genuinely practical to run locally could be a huge part of where AI development goes next. 💡👏.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A bill now sponsored by Wyoming's Legislative Management Council would make running a dual-currency sweepstakes casino a felony. The draft also targets the vendors behind these sites, which raises the legal risk for payment processors and B2B suppliers.

Wyoming is moving to outlaw dual-currency sweepstakes casinos. Its bill reaches past operators to the companies that keep them running. The draft reached the Legislative Management Council through Sen. John Kolb, co-chair of the Select Committee on Gaming. The council also agreed to sponsor two other gaming bills, one on pari-mutuel wagering breakage and one on background checks.

In a recent development, the gaming committee claims casino-style sweepstakes games are already available in Wyoming. These games let players wager with currency redeemable for money or prizes. The draft would state that the state’s prize-promotion laws do not authorize them. People who take part only as players are exempt.

It has been revealed that working draft 0.4 widens the definition of professional gambling. It covers anyone who knowingly provides services to an online sweepstakes game. Those services include geolocation, payment processing, hosting, game content and advertising. Vendors and processors would carry legal risk, not only the brands that face players.

It has been revealed that the approach follows Oklahoma. Under SB 1589, companies that provide geolocation or payment services to a sweepstakes operator after November 1 face the same felony charges as the operator. Oklahoma lawmakers overrode Gov. Kevin Stitt’s veto of that bill. The votes were 34-10 in the Senate and 68-19 in the House.

Complaints to the regulator help explain the push. Wyoming Gaming Commission Executive Director Nick Larramendy described his office’s complaint load to lawmakers. Sweepstakes complaints arrive each week in greater numbers than complaints about any regulated form of gaming. Most come from players whose accounts were shut down when they tried to cash out a jackpot. The operators are often offshore, where the commission cannot reach them.

Recent findings suggest that taking such sites down would be easier with the ban in place, in Larramendy’s view, because the commission would have firmer ground for working with the Department of Justice and internet service providers. His testimony also pointed to a well-known payment processor. It serves offshore sweepstakes sites while holding a Wyoming online sports betting permit.

Sources indicate that the bill has drawn broad support at each step. At its October 5-6 meeting, the gaming committee voted 6-0 in a roll call to recommend the amended draft. It also renamed the bill ‘Online sweepstakes prohibited.’ Lawmakers weighed a rival draft, 27LSO-0200, which would have regulated sweepstakes rather than banned them. Only the prohibition draft went to the council.

A sweepstakes ban bill in Pennsylvania has stalled. Rep. Russ Diamond introduced HB 2801 on September 24. The bill has had no hearing or vote in the House Gaming Oversight Committee. The state’s legislative session ends November 30.

Sources indicate that wyoming’s draft is written as a Senate File. It now goes to the 2027 General Session, which is scheduled to begin January 12, 2027. A general session can last no more than 40 legislative days. If passed, the ban would take effect July 1, 2027.

Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

📅 10 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1182 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning.
  • It has been revealed that the distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline.
  • The standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

It has been revealed that the distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a new, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

The standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

As a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

Dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

Offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

Sources indicate that A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:.

The GIF below indicates the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss.

The table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

Sources indicate that the loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only reveals up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

To see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

It has been revealed that distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

Industry observers note that the efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

Industry observers note that the student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

Want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

By the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one customers notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

Sources indicate that voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

Recent findings suggest that NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Supporting more languages is only part of the challenge. Developers also need the ability to:.

Open models change what's possible on every one of these.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:.

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (fresh) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new).

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

In conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before users hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most important latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

Recent findings suggest that at 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

The table above shows Magpie served as the NVIDIA NIM, measured on-prem — the optimized container running on your own GPU. The open Hugging Face checkpoint is the same model and your path for research and fine-tuning; the NIM is the tuned serving stack that produces these production latencies. Both run on hardware you control.

Because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

Low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

Local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

Together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

According to recent reports, this release doesn't only add languages — it also improves synthesis quality across many existing ones. Compared to the previous release, Magpie shows reduced character error rates (CER) and higher speaker similarity (SSIM) on several languages, with the clearest gains on French and Spanish:.

The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

While objective metrics help measure progress, speech quality is ultimately perceptual. You can hear the difference yourself on NVIDIA Build or the Hugging Face demo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming York State Senator Jeremy Cooney has filed a bill that would bring prediction markets into the state's tax base instead of banning them. The proposal puts a state lawmaker at odds with New York's own lawsuit against Kalshi.

Revenue raised under Jeremy Cooney’s FUTURES Act would flow into a Futures Fund for Early Education to pay for universal pre-K.

The timing gives the bill extra weight. Attorney General Letitia James had sought to stop Kalshi at a virtual hearing held the day the bill was filed. Governor Hochul and James announced on July 31, 2026, that Fresh York had sued KalshiEX LLC for running an illegal gambling operation through its prediction market.

Cooney’s bill states that CFTC-registered markets “may operate within the state of New York lawfully.” That language sets it against the state’s executive branch. It also marks a shift from his earlier bill, S8889, introduced in January. That version would have required operators to get a license from the Department of Financial Services. “I’m placing a bet on the future of UPK in New York,” Cooney said in his release.

Licensed mobile sportsbooks face a far heavier tax than the bill proposes. The gap could widen in practice. Operators would be allowed to deduct some operating expenses from taxable revenue, which sportsbooks cannot do.

The scope is narrow. The bill covers sports contracts only, so election, economic and culture markets fall outside it. Its official summary also covers the use of prediction markets in election violations. Elected officials and some state employees would be barred from trading.

In a recent development, the consumer rules borrow from regulated betting. Operators would have to verify identity and age, run self-exclusion programs, and offer deposit limits and cooling-off periods. They would also file a yearly consumer-protection audit with the attorney general. The minimum trading age, however, would be left to federal authorities instead of New York’s sports-betting minimum of 21.

Age also came up in court. The state argued that Kalshi lets younger users bet. Justice Crane asked the organization to consider safeguards for users aged 18 to 20. Kalshi’s lawyers said the company could look at limiting access to its contracts for those users in New York.

Newly introduced York is not alone in treating prediction markets as a taxable business. North Carolina’s new law recognizes the CFTC’s exclusive federal authority over prediction markets. It taxes platforms at 6% of net trading-fee revenue from state residents.

Sources indicate that A judge denied Newly introduced York's TRO against Kalshi. Hours later, New York introduced a bill to regulate and tax prediction markets.

The judge denied the State's request for a temporary restraining order against Kalshi. According to Kalshi, the judge… https://t.co/1T7RAZh7j6.

Oregon may go higher. Senate Majority Leader Anthony Broadman told OPB he will probably seek a rate above North Carolina’s, perhaps 8%, in the 2027 session. That money would go toward wildfire costs. If more states follow, platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket, along with their licensed sportsbook rivals, would face higher costs.

In Upcoming York, S10748 was sent to the Senate Rules Committee on the day it was introduced, and it remains pending there.

It has been revealed that the first sign of trouble is rarely a crash. It is the invoice.

Sources indicate that A small team ships a Node.js app on a serverless platform because it is quick to set up. Traffic grows, and the bill grows with it, in ways that are hard to forecast. Some visitors also wait a beat longer for their first response, because the function has to start up before it can answer.

In a recent development, the usual alternative is a virtual private server (VPS). The price is fixed, but the work is not. Someone has to patch the operating system (OS), configure the web server, renew SSL certificates and keep backups running.

Recent findings suggest that between the two sits a third option: managed hosting for Node.js. Here is how the three compare, and how to choose.

Recent findings suggest that platforms such as AWS Lambda charge for what runs. Lambda's event functions are priced on the number of requests and on duration, measured in GB-seconds, and the memory you choose sets the CPU and the cost per second.

Industry observers note that that suits small or spiky workloads. A newly introduced app with little traffic can sit inside the free tier, which covers one million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds a month.

Industry observers note that the surprises come with growth. Billed duration is multiplied by the number of requests, so even small inefficiencies in a handler can turn into significant costs at scale.

Then there is the cold start. When the platform has to create a new execution environment, the first request waits. AWS's own decision guide puts Lambda cold starts at roughly 100 milliseconds to over 1 second.

Since August 2025, AWS bills for that initialization (INIT) phase across all function configurations, so a cold start now demonstrates up on the invoice as well as in the response time.

Industry observers note that AWS's own analysis found they occur in under 1% of invocations, so steady traffic makes them far less. For a checkout page that does hit one, it is still a pause the customer feels.

There are fixes. Provisioned concurrency keeps functions initialized and ready, but it is billed for the time it is enabled. Newer options let one execution environment handle several requests at once, which means fewer cold starts.

Limits matter, too. A Lambda function can run for 15 minutes at most, and accounts start with a default of 1,000 concurrent executions. Long-running jobs need a different home.

A VPS fixes the pricing problem. A blueprint costs the same every month, whatever traffic does.

Industry observers note that on an unmanaged VPS, the team owns everything above the hardware. That means operating system updates, a firewall, a web server such as NGINX in front of the app, a process manager such as PM2 to restart it if it crashes, SSL certificate renewals and backups that someone has to test.

Industry observers note that none of it is exotic. All of it is a job. Left undone, it is how small teams end up with unpatched servers and no way to restore one.

For a team without a sysadmin, the real price of a VPS is the hours.

Recent findings suggest that managed Node.js hosting sits between the two. The app runs on a persistent infrastructure, so there is no scale-to-zero and no cold start between requests. The price is a flat monthly plan. The provider handles the work around it.

Cloudways Velocity is one example. It patches the OS, manages SSL and domain mapping, and runs backups automatically.

The stack is NGINX and PM2, pre-configured with caching, and PostgreSQL is provisioned on all looks. Deployment is by Git push with built-in CI/CD, and a WAF, malware protection, DDoS mitigation and Cloudflare Enterprise CDN are included.

It ships presets for 12 project types, including Next.js, Remix, Express, Fastify, Astro, Nuxt, Angular and n8n. Anything that builds to SSR or a static bundle and starts with a Node command can run under "Other". Runtime versions are selectable, with Node.js LTS 22.x and 24.x listed.

In a recent development, the trade-off is scaling. Velocity scales vertically: you pick a server size and move up when the app outgrows it. A traffic spike beyond that server's capacity is a capacity problem, not something the platform absorbs by adding instances.

Look at the traffic first. If it comes in bursts with long quiet gaps, serverless often wins. If it is steady, a server is usually simpler to reason about.

Take one handler and keep the assumptions the same throughout. Each request runs for half a second on 1 GB of memory. The rates are AWS's published x86 prices: $0.20 per million requests and $0.0000166667 per GB-second, after the free tier, as shown earlier.

Recent findings suggest that now compare Velocity's aims, which use a pay-as-you-go model billed on an hourly basis according to the selected blueprint, ranging from Starter at $20 a month (2 GB RAM, 2 vCPU, 5 apps) to Business at $400 (64 GB RAM, 16 vCPU, 150 apps). More importantly billing is strictly tied to the server plan rather than incoming traffic, a sudden spike in visits will not automatically raise your hourly compute rate.

The Lambda figures leave out API gateway charges, data transfer and logging. A single server has a ceiling, so load-test before assuming one strategy carries 100 million requests.

And Velocity has metered extras: $0.033/GB for offsite backup storage, $0.02/GB for CDN bandwidth beyond the blueprint's allocation, and $1 per 10 GB of extra disk.

If you want to test managed hosting, you can try Cloudways Velocity during Black Friday with the promo code BFCM802 for 80% off for 2 months plus unlimited migrations, valid through December 4, 2026.

The point is the shape, not a winner. Serverless cost tracks usage. A server's cost tracks its size. Choose the one you can forecast.

The strongest case is also the most common one: steady traffic, a small team and a budget that has to be forecast.

According to recent reports, when cloud hosting costs have to fit a budget, a flat monthly blueprint beats a meter. Velocity's aims give you Node.js hosting with predictable pricing, so finance can see the number in advance and it does not move with every spike.

Because the server stays on, there is no cold start between requests, and the first visitor after a quiet spell is not left waiting.

Cloudways claims Velocity patches the operating system, manages SSL and domain mapping, and runs backups automatically. The people who built the product keep building it.

APIs, full-stack apps and automation workflows such as n8n need a process that stays up. A persistent server is built for exactly that.

When the app outgrows its server, you move up a size, and you can move back down if you don't need it.

For most small teams, that adds up to a simple choice. Velocity trades the theoretical ceiling of serverless for something many teams value more: costs they can forecast and an app that stays ready, without a DevOps hire.

Teams whose traffic is extreme, or who need code running at the edge, may still prefer a specialist platform, but that is the exception.

In a recent development, when using the out-of-the-box Gemini Enterprise web application, identity and access management happen behind the scenes. Employees sign in through Google Identity or Workforce Identity Federation (such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta), search results automatically respect per-user access controls (ACLs), and third-party login prompts for Federated Connectors or custom agents appear automatically in the chat UI.

According to recent reports, in practice, however, many enterprises build their own Customer UI to embed Gemini Enterprise into an internal portal, intranet, or line-of-business application. To do this, Customer BE calls the Gemini Enterprise StreamAssist API.

The moment an application builds a custom UI and calls the StreamAssist API directly, the three authentication flows that the built-in web app handled automatically become the responsibility of Customer UI and Customer BE:.

#161374. Thinking of ACE? We Can Do It with Fewer Tokens

📅 11 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1320 w)

Thinking of ACE? We Can Do It with Fewer Tokens

📅 11 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1320 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories.
  • It has been revealed that give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge.
  • Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories. The difference is what they do with what they learn — and that decides the token bill.

It has been revealed that give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge. It mis-paginates an API, resolves the wrong person, or returns a value when none was asked for. The model knows the APIs; what it hasn't internalized is how to use them reliably. That's learnable from the agent's own history.

Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here). Both are a form of agentic memory — turning an agent's past trajectories into reusable lessons and feeding them back at inference time, no weight updates, no human labels. They even agree on the hard part. Where they part ways is delivery.

A note on words, because the two systems name things differently: we'll call the raw thing an agent learns a lesson. ACE organizes its lessons into one comprehensive, evolving playbook; we consolidate ours into individually retrievable guidelines. Same lessons, two containers.

Both systems refuse to compress.

ACE names the failure modes precisely: brevity bias — optimization collapsing toward short, generic instructions — and context collapse — a model asked to rewrite its whole context each step summarizing the detail away. Its answer is to keep a rich, itemized playbook, with a helpful/harmful counter on every bullet, and let the model distill relevance at read time.

We reach the same conclusion from the other direction. Every distinct guideline keeps a support count — how many independent episodes produced it — and we never summarize the store down to a handful of rules. A lesson five different tasks discovered is a different object from one that appeared once, and both are worth keeping.

It has been revealed that so on the core question — should you compress an agent's hard-won lessons into a tidy summary? — ACE and ALTK-Evolve give the same answer: no. Count them, don't collapse them. ACE's per-bullet counters and our support counts are two spellings of the same idea.

Two places: how the memory is built, and how it's delivered — and it's the delivery difference that shows up in the token bill.

In a recent development, consolidation (how the store is built). ACE grows one playbook through a Generator → Reflector → Curator loop, applying incremental delta updates and de-duplicating by embedding. We cluster near-duplicate lessons and merge within a cluster, support-conserving — when several lessons merge, the survivor inherits their combined count, so the store shrinks without losing the record of how much experience backs each guideline. We also extract typed guidelines — strategy, recovery, and optimization — with causal attribution and provenance back to the source trajectory, and at subtask granularity, so a lesson learned on one app can transfer to another.

Sources indicate that delivery (what reaches the model at inference). This is the one that drives the numbers. ACE injects the comprehensive playbook on every step, the same way regardless of model or task. We treat delivery as a dial, not a constant: a small fixed core of high-support guidelines, extended per task with a handful selected for the task at hand (cosine or LLM-guided, priority-weighted) — or, when a model has the headroom to use it, the full consolidated set. The same lessons are available to both agents; the difference is that ACE always sends all of them, and we send however many a given model can actually use.

On AppWorld, with the same base ReAct agent, running both systems in-house:.

On the strong model we're better on both metrics at ~40% of ACE's inference cost. On the weak model we edge ACE 56.0 to 54.8 — close enough that we call it a tie on accuracy (a repeat run of ours landed at 54.8, matching ACE almost exactly, which is within this benchmark's run-to-run noise) — at about one-seventh the cost.

A fair word on cost: ACE's own efficiency story is about building its context cheaply. Ours is on a different axis — serving it. Retrieving a few guidelines per task instead of injecting the whole playbook on every step is where the tokens go, and it's the direct consequence of the delivery difference above.

Where does the accuracy come from? The by-difficulty breakdown tells two different stories:.

Figure 1. Post-memory Task Goal Completion by difficulty, ours vs. ACE. On DeepSeek-V3.2 (right) we win Easy, Hard, and Overall; ACE only edges Medium. On gpt-oss-120b (left) ACE leads easy and medium, but per-task selection wins the hard tasks — and the aggregate. Each system improves from its own no-memory baseline (see the by-difficulty reference tables under Method notes below).

Industry observers note that the two models tell different stories. On gpt-oss-120b, ACE's full playbook has the edge on Easy and Medium — there's enough of the task solved by generic instruction-following that a comprehensive prompt helps more than it distracts. But on Hard tasks, where the model has to pick the right lesson rather than wade through all of them, curated retrieval pulls ahead — and that's the tier that decides the aggregate. On DeepSeek-V3.2 the story flips: the stronger model absorbs ACE's full playbook well enough to edge us on Medium, but we lead Easy, Hard, and Overall — with more capacity to spare, more lessons (delivered our way) keep helping instead of crowding each other out.

Sources indicate that we give each model its best configuration — the full consolidated set for the strong model, selective retrieval for the weaker one, because a large context overwhelms a weaker model rather than helping it. (Exactly how much to inject, and how it scales across the capability spectrum, is the focus of our follow-up post.).

Industry observers note that both systems refuse to compress an agent's hard-won experience into a tidy summary — that part, we agree on. The difference is whether delivery is fixed or calibrated: ACE sends the whole playbook every step no matter what; we send however much of the guideline set a given model can actually use. That calibration is what bought the numbers above — same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of ACE's inference cost — and on the weaker model, it was the difference between guidance that helped and guidance that got in the way.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

According to recent reports, appWorld test_normal, 168 tasks. A ReAct code agent (each step writes Python; the environment returns the output). TGC = Task Goal Completion; SGC = Scenario Goal Completion, which requires every variant of a scenario to pass. Memory is mined from train/dev only; results are single runs (pass@1), as is standard on this benchmark.

Recent findings suggest that the ACE numbers are our own runs of the ACE agent, evaluated in-house on the same AppWorld splits and the same base models as ALTK-Evolve (DeepSeek-V3.2 and gpt-oss-120b). The ACE paper reports on a different base model (DeepSeek-V3.1), so running it ourselves keeps the comparison controlled for model and harness. Both systems are the same ReAct agent and differ only in the prompt template — which is why the two no-memory baselines differ (72.0 vs 79.8 TGC); we don't rest the comparison on that baseline gap, only on the claims a prompt tweak can't touch: same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of the tokens.

  • According to recent reports, olmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models.
  • It has been revealed that embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth | 📊 Documentation: https://docs.olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings | 💻 Learn more about OlmoEarth: https://allenai.org/olmoearth.

According to recent reports, olmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models. The source code and model weights are publicly available alongside the research paper, so the community can inspect exactly how these embeddings are generated.

It has been revealed that embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration. Locations with similar surface characteristics end up with similar vectors; locations that differ land far apart. OlmoEarth embeddings have shown strong performance in our own benchmarking and in independent evaluations. The exported Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) are lightweight and easy to share. Choose your area of interest, time range, encoder variant, resolution, and imagery sources via the Studio UI or API, and get back a COG you can use however you like. If your application requires higher performance, Studio also supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

In a recent development, custom-computed embeddings are now available for users of OlmoEarth Studio. Reach out if you're interested in gaining access. Instructions for using the publicly available OlmoEarth models to compute your own embeddings are available here.

Industry observers note that global structure in OlmoEarth embeddings from seasonal Sentinel-2 imagery across 1.1M samples. Colors indicate 15 k-means clusters in a PCA-reduced embedding space.

Industry observers note that computing embeddings follows the same workflow as any other prediction in Studio. First configure a model and run it, and then download the results. Several parameters tailor the output:.

Different visualization options applied to the same embedding raster.

Studio delivers a COG with one band per embedding dimension. Vectors are stored as signed 8-bit integers (int8). Values range from -127 to +127, with -128 reserved for nodata. To recover floating-point vectors, see dequantize_embeddings in olmoearth_pretrain.

Because everything is computed on demand rather than pulled from a pre-computed global archive, your embeddings reflect exactly the conditions you care about. You can generate monthly embeddings to capture seasonal dynamics, not just annual snapshots.

The examples below all use OlmoEarth-v1-Tiny (192-dim) embeddings at 40-meter resolution with Sentinel-2 L2A composites (annual for most examples; monthly for change detection). Tiny is a lightweight encoder but still highly performant; for your own applications, you can swap it for a larger variant at the cost of higher compute and storage.

Industry observers note that pick a query pixel, extract its embedding, and compute cosine similarity against every other pixel. The result is a heatmap showing where the landscape looks most and least like your query pixel.

It has been revealed that this query sits near the Merced urban center in California. Urban fabric and road corridors light up coherently while agricultural parcels stay dark. The model distinguishes built-up surfaces from cropland without any labels.

Switching the query to a small agricultural window, we define the query vector as the mean of the embedding vectors over that window, then pull Sentinel-2 imagery at the highest- and lowest-similarity locations to see what the model treats as similar and dissimilar.

Sources indicate that the most similar patches (0.89 and above) are all agricultural parcels with irrigated fields. The least similar (around zero) are an airport with surrounding bare ground, a reservoir with dry terrain, and arid rangeland. No training data, no labels, just a dot product in embedding space.

According to recent reports, similarity search tells you "where is it like this?" but sometimes you need discrete labels across a region. Because the representations are already rich, a simple linear classifier can produce a wall-to-wall land-cover map from very few labeled pixels.

Industry observers note that to test this, we labeled just 60 pixels (20 per class) over Ca Mau, Vietnam, a coastal mangrove region. Using ESA WorldCover 2021 as the label source for three classes (mangrove, water, other), we randomly sampled 20 pixels per class, trained a logistic regression with per-feature standardization, and predicted every pixel in the region.

From 60 labeled pixels, the classifier produces a coherent map with weighted F1 = 0.84. Mangrove stands, tidal channels, and open water are delineated across the entire region. The classifier saturates promptly: increasing from 30 to 300 labels barely changes accuracy, because the embeddings are doing most of the heavy lifting.

The core of the analysis is a few lines of Python:.

This is a linear probe, a standard evaluation for foundation models. The fact that a logistic regression over 192 dimensions recovers land-cover boundaries from so few labels means the Tiny encoder has organized these ecological distinctions during pretraining. Larger variants (Base, 768-dim) encode even richer representations.

If you have ground-truth polygons, field survey points, or a coarse existing map, you can train a similar classifier and produce a wall-to-wall map for your own region of interest.

According to recent reports, because Studio can generate embeddings at any temporal resolution (monthly through annual), you can compare two time periods directly to identify where surface conditions have changed. Below, we computed monthly Sentinel-2 embeddings for the same region in September 2023 and September 2024 and measured per-pixel cosine distance. The Park Fire (July-September 2024) burn scar in Butte County, California lights up immediately.

No labels or training required—just two embedding COGs and a few lines of Python.

In a recent development, sometimes you have no query location or reference labels. You just want to understand what structure exists in the embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a clean way to do this: reduce to three dimensions, map to R/G/B, and display as a false-color image. Similar embeddings get similar colors automatically.

Flevoland, in the Netherlands, is a reclaimed polder landscape with a regular grid of agricultural parcels. The PCA false-color image reproduces those boundaries with high fidelity. Different crop types, water bodies, and urban areas each get distinct hues. The embedding has internalized landscape structure without ever being told what a parcel or crop is.

This kind of unsupervised view is a quick way to see what structure the model has picked up across your area of interest.

Similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA exploration are simple operations on standard raster data that run in seconds. The power comes from the embeddings: learned representations that compress earth observation data into vectors capturing rich information about each location from many sensors and millions of training examples.

Custom embedding exports are available now. Create a project, configure an embeddings model, and compute your embeddings. The exported GeoTIFF works with any geospatial tool: QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, or your own scripts. For end-to-end code reproducing the examples in this post, see the embeddings tutorial, which includes working code for similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA visualization. To get hands-on without any local setup, try the Colab notebook.

The examples in this post all use frozen embeddings with no task-specific training. Embeddings are a great entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they enable fast, cost-effective generation of results, work well in resource-constrained environments, and are easy to share. For applications that require higher performance, OlmoEarth Studio also supports SFT, training a task-specific model head on your own labels, which typically outperforms linear probes on frozen features.

Sources indicate that while we are always working to improve our pretraining approaches, it's notable to check the quality of the embeddings for your use case using some of the techniques described above. Performance also depends on the quality of the input imagery—persistent cloud cover, atmospheric artifacts, or missing observations in the composite period can affect the resulting vectors.

According to recent reports, sentinel-2 L2A imagery from the European Space Agency, accessed via Microsoft Planetary Computer. ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 for mangrove reference. The global clustering visualization uses OlmoEarth-v1-Base (768-dim) with seasonal Sentinel-2 composites at patch size 8, instance-level embeddings over 1.1M pretraining samples.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A federal judge in Upcoming Mexico has blocked Kalshi's sports-event contracts on the lands of four tribes and ruled that the Commodity Exchange Act does not override tribal gaming law.
  • Kalshi has lost a key round against four New Mexico tribes.
  • Recent findings suggest that the tribes filed suit in May.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A federal judge in Upcoming Mexico has blocked Kalshi's sports-event contracts on the lands of four tribes and ruled that the Commodity Exchange Act does not override tribal gaming law. The order requires geographic restrictions just as the CFTC is telling exchanges to drop them.

Kalshi has lost a key round against four New Mexico tribes. On November 23, U.S. District Judge Margaret Strickland granted the Mescalero Apache Tribe and the Pueblos of Isleta, Pojoaque and Sandia a preliminary injunction that gives Kalshi 14 days to stop offering sports-event contracts on their lands. Strickland also denied its motion to dismiss, so the lawsuit now goes forward.

Recent findings suggest that the tribes filed suit in May. They argue that Kalshi’s sports contracts violate the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (IGRA) and the tribes’ gaming compacts with Fresh Mexico. In their view, the contracts allow unauthorized wagering on tribal lands. Under IGRA, only tribes can authorize gaming on Indian lands.

Kalshi argued that the Commodity Exchange Act overrides both IGRA and the tribal-state compacts. Strickland disagreed. In her reading, that statute leaves the federal regulator without sole authority over the contracts, Tribal Business News reported. She also rejected Kalshi’s claim that IGRA’s injunction provision only allows suits against parties to a tribal-state compact.

Recent findings suggest that location was central to the ruling. To Strickland, a Kalshi user taking a sports position from a reservation is like a casino patron placing a bet. In her reasoning, the wager takes place wherever the bettor is physically located. The order cites a declaration from a Mescalero Apache Tribal Gaming Commission agent. She opened Kalshi’s app at several places on the reservation and found sports contracts on offer.

Kalshi cited the CFTC’s impartial-access requirements in opposing the injunction. Strickland ruled that the harm to tribal sovereignty outweighed the compliance burden. She also noted that Kalshi already uses geofencing elsewhere.

That reasoning runs straight into the CFTC’s upcoming directive on Regulation 38.151(b). The interpretation was published in the Federal Register on November 10, 2026, as document 2026-22863. The exchange therefore faces a court order to geofence alongside a regulatory push to remove such limits.

Recent findings suggest that the legal theory also matters beyond Newly introduced Mexico. The tribes rely on IGRA and their compacts, not state gambling law. As a result, CFTC preemption arguments may not protect Kalshi on tribal lands. If other tribes copy the approach, prediction-market operators could face geofencing obligations on reservations nationwide.

NEWLY INTRODUCED: Kalshi asserts that Native American Tribes have no regulatory authority over the activities of non-members, seeks the dismissal of the New Mexico Tribes' federal lawsuit asserting that Kalshi's offering of online sports-event contracts on Indian lands violates IGRA pic.twitter.com/gkLkM1x2KD.

— Daniel Wallach (@WALLACHLEGAL) June 25, 2026.

Tribal results have been mixed so far. Earlier in 2026, a federal judge in Wisconsin refused a similar injunction sought by the Ho-Chunk Nation. He did so even though he found the tribe likely to succeed on the merits. In California, District Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley granted two tribes a preliminary injunction after a Ninth Circuit ruling in September. It was the first injunction any tribe had won against Kalshi.

The timing leaves little room. The CFTC’s deadline for exchanges to drop domestic geographic restrictions lands only days before Kalshi must comply in Newly introduced Mexico, SBC Americas reported.

Amazon S3 Vectors now supports metadata pre-filtering for higher recall on filtered searches

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today, we’re announcing metadata pre-filtering for Amazon S3 Vectors, which delivers higher recall on filtered queries by evaluating your metadata filter before the similarity search.
  • Most applications never search a whole index.
  • Common use cases Pre-filtering applies wherever results have to be both relevant and correctly scoped:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today, we’re announcing metadata pre-filtering for Amazon S3 Vectors, which delivers higher recall on filtered queries by evaluating your metadata filter before the similarity search. You can filter on attributes such as tenant, category, status, or time, and pre-filtering adds prefix matching with $startsWith for paths, URLs, and hierarchical keys. Each vector carries up to 2 KB of filterable metadata, and a single query supports up to 100 filter constraints. There is no additional cost, no re-ingestion, and no change to your queries.

Most applications never search a whole index. They search the part of it that belongs to a particular user, account, or category, and they express that scope as a metadata filter. Semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and agentic applications all need the same thing from a filtered query: a similarity search that covers the vectors matching the filter, and returns the closest of them. With pre-filtering, a filtered query returns more of the relevant matches your index contains, giving you higher recall on filtered searches.

Common use cases Pre-filtering applies wherever results have to be both relevant and correctly scoped:.

How pre-filtering works Each vector in an S3 Vectors index can carry application-defined metadata, and a query can filter on those fields.

It has been revealed that every vector index has an index mode. On an index whose index mode is ENHANCED, S3 Vectors resolves your filter first, then searches only the vectors that match. On an index whose index mode is CLASSIC, S3 Vectors performs the vector search and filter evaluation in tandem, validating each candidate vector against your filter as it searches. Existing indexes use CLASSIC until you revision them.

In a recent development, consider a support knowledge base of 8 million tickets, where an agent searches one customer’s history for a recurring error. If that customer accounts for 400 of those tickets, resolving customer_id first means the similarity search runs across all 400 of them, so the agent sees that customer’s prior occurrences. Before the index was updated, the same query drew its candidates from the full 8 million, and the result set contained fewer of that customer’s matching tickets.

On highly selective filters, pre-filtering returns up to 5x more of the matching vectors than the same query returned before on CLASSIC indexes.

Getting started Before you start, make sure your IAM policy grants permissions for the fresh actions.

The dimension must match the output size of your embedding model, and distance-metric should match how that model was trained (cosine is common for text embeddings). Second, write vectors with the PutVectors API, attaching up to 2 KB of filterable metadata to each vector:.

Each vector carries the attributes your application filters on. In this example, tenant_id scopes results to a single customer, category narrows by document type, created_date records when the document was created, and active is a boolean flag. By default every metadata field is filterable, so you can query on any of them without declaring a schema up front.

In a recent development, third, run a filtered similarity query with the QueryVectors API. The filter uses a compact JSON syntax where a bare key-value pair is an equality match, and operators such as $and, $or, and $gt combine or refine conditions. Pass --return-metadata so the query returns each vector’s metadata:.

The expected result is a single vector, doc-001, the only one matching all three filter conditions (tenant_id, category, and active):.

According to recent reports, S3 Vectors first narrows the search space to vectors matching all three filter conditions, then returns the 50 most similar vectors from that subset. Because the filter is applied before the search, those results are drawn from across all the vectors that match it.

Prefix matching with $startsWith Pre-filtering adds a prefix match operator for filtering on paths, URLs, and hierarchical keys. A document store that encodes case and folder structure into a document ID can scope a search to a subtree in one condition:.

$startsWith joins the existing operators: equality, numeric range, set membership, existence checks, and boolean logic with $and and $or.

Turning on pre-filtering for existing indexes Call UpdateIndexMode on an existing index to turn on pre-filtering:.

Pre-filtering takes effect in place. Your existing vectors are not re-ingested, your queries do not change, and the fresh filter operators are available immediately.

Here is the difference on the same index and the same query. Before the update, a query scoped to one tenant returns two of the ten results requested:.

After the update, the same query returns a full result set drawn from across that tenant’s documents:.

Rolling out across your indexes Once you have validated pre-filtering on an index, set the default index mode on the vector bucket so that new indexes use ENHANCED without a follow-up call:.

To bring the rest of your existing indexes across, list them and check the index mode on each one, then call UpdateIndexMode on the ones still using CLASSIC:.

In a recent development, now available Metadata pre-filtering is available at no additional cost in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available, and in the AWS China Regions. You pay standard S3 Vectors pricing for storage, PUT requests, and queries. For full pricing details, visit the Amazon S3 pricing page. For regional availability, visit Amazon S3 Vectors Regions and quotas.

Recent findings suggest that whether you’re scoping a RAG application to one tenant, scoping an agent’s searches to one user’s documents, or narrowing a catalog search to a licensing window, pre-filtering lets you apply those filters without trading away recall. To learn more and get started, visit the Amazon S3 Vectors documentation. Send feedback to AWS re:Post for S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts.
