Latest Update: What We Learned by Reproducing 2,200 papers from ICML

📅 13 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2242 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Back in July, we ran a hackathon where more than 1,200 community members brought their own coding agents and tried to reproduce the papers published at ICML 2026, claim by claim.
  • In this post, we're sharing what we learned from running this hackathon, and what it suggests about the role humans will play when agents are doing the research experiments.
  • It has been revealed that questions about how reproducible AI research really is are older than the current AI wave.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back in July, we ran a hackathon where more than 1,200 community members brought their own coding agents and tried to reproduce the papers published at ICML 2026, claim by claim. In 19 days, participants published 6,816 Trackio logbooks reproducing 2,226 papers, about a third of the conference 🤯.

In this post, we're sharing what we learned from running this hackathon, and what it suggests about the role humans will play when agents are doing the research experiments.

It has been revealed that questions about how reproducible AI research really is are older than the current AI wave. But these questions are exacerbated by scale. ICML 2026 received 23,918 submissions and accepted 6,352 papers, roughly double the previous year, continuing an exponential trend that is at least partly driven by AI agents making it faster to run experiments and write them up.

Reviewing capacity has not doubled along with it. Reviewers at most conferences are volunteers who may not have the time or expertise to fully review a paper. Here is a review of one accepted ICML 2026 spotlight paper, in the reviewer's own words:.

"My low confidence score is because I did not check all the proofs carefully.".

Note that this paper got strong scores and a spotlight. Keep it in mind, because we will come back to this exact paper later in the post, and to what happened when we finally did check the proofs carefully.

It has been revealed that what has changed, though, is that the same technology driving the flood of submissions can also help us keep up with it. Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Pi can now read a paper, write the code, launch the experiments, and report back on what they found. Checking a paper carefully used to cost a reviewer a weekend; an agent can attempt it in an afternoon, in parallel, thousands of times over.

So the question we wanted to ask was: if we actually re-examined a major conference at scale, and tried to reproduce every paper, what would we find?

Rather than audit papers ourselves, we opened it up to the whole community, with all the diversity of agent frameworks, compute budgets, and scientific taste that brings. From July 15 to August 2, 2026, the ICML 2026 Open Reproductions challenge worked like this:.

According to recent reports, participants received $20 in Hugging Face compute credits to run experiments on HF Jobs; across the challenge, participants launched 2,962 cloud jobs. Where a full reproduction was impossible, for example when a paper's dataset was proprietary or its checkpoints unreleased, participants ran toy reproductions on synthetic data mimicking the original's properties.

Here is what a finished reproduction looks like:.

By the numbers, this hackathon was probably the largest attempted reproduction of a scientific conference:.

Aggregating the claim-level verdicts per paper:.

51% of examined papers (1,103) had at least one claim independently verified. Of those, 266 papers were fully reproduced, with every extracted claim verified, and 632 more were partially reproduced with nothing falsified. In total, 3,978 individual claims were confirmed with real experiments.

23% of examined papers (496) had at least one claim falsified or contested. That includes 49 papers where all claims were falsified and nothing could be verified, and, maybe most interestingly, 242 papers where independent reproduction teams reached opposite verdicts on the same claims. Reproducibility is not binary; it is adversarial.

The remainder sat in the middle: 502 papers with toy-scale evidence only, and 280 where nothing could be established either way (missing artifacts were the most common cause).

Some papers came through the gauntlet looking great, and the community's best logbooks are worth reading in their own right:.

35 participants formally claimed they had falsified something. We adversarially re-verified every claimed falsification: re-reading the paper, re-reading the logbook, and re-deriving the math or re-implementing the experiment from the paper's own text.

A few of the confirmed falsifications, linking to the logbook that found it:.

The paging paper from the introduction. The reviewer who did not check the proofs carefully? The paper, "Towards Optimal Robustness in Learning-Augmented Paging," claims its algorithm achieves robustness Hk+O(1)H_k + O(1)Hk​+O(1). One participant's logbook measured the additive term growing like 0.38ln⁡k0.38 \ln k0.38lnk and located the exact step of the proof that breaks. Our own re-implementation extended the sweep to k = 1,024 and confirmed the growth at roughly nine sigma. The true robustness is Hk+Θ(log⁡k)H_k + \Theta(\log k)Hk​+Θ(logk).

Sources indicate that A theorem that falls after step 224. "Attention's forward pass and Frank-Wolfe" proves that token particles collapse to the origin whenever the origin starts inside their convex hull. Three independent teams found counterexamples, with violations first appearing at t = 224, ~3,800, and 6,416 steps, which neatly explains why everyone else "verified" the claim: finite-horizon checks stop too early. The cleanest counterexample is stated in exact rational arithmetic, so there is no floating-point ambiguity to hide behind. The authors confirmed the same day and are working on a fix.

Industry observers note that theory written for one loss, results produced by another. In "Self-Distillation Enables Continual Learning," the paper's central equation and its entire theory section analyze reverse KL divergence, but the released code's default, which per the authors produced all the paper's results, computes forward KL. The logbook that caught it also failed to reproduce the paper's headline +4pp result under the authors' own code and data. The authors have already uploaded a clarified version to arXiv.

An evaluation diluted by padding. In "Do Transformers Need Three Projections?", a participant discovered that ~66% of evaluated label positions were EOS padding tokens that train to near-zero loss, deflating perplexity roughly threefold. The abstract's "3.1% quality cost for 50% cache reduction" becomes roughly 9.4% once corrected.

Recent findings suggest that 🚨 False falsifications. Sometimes we found flaws in an attempted reproduction. One logboook claimed dramatically, "the paper's method is 2x slower than the baseline"; this turned out to be an arithmetic bug in the reproduction: per-trajectory time compared against per-batch-of-50 time. Correctly normalized, the participant's own data confirms the paper's claimed 8x speedup.

It has been revealed that we have begun writing to the authors of every confirmed finding, with a simple framing: here is what we found, here is all the evidence, do you agree or is our analysis wrong? The early responses have been very positive:.

So far authors have confirmed findings on multiple papers, two arXiv corrections are in flight, and in one case an author had quietly fixed the error in a upcoming arXiv version a month before the challenge found it, which we count as independent convergence 🤗.

Sources indicate that the most interesting question that this hackathon raises is: do humans still have a role in reviewing papers? We think so, for several reasons:.

Pure agent execution hits real limits. Agents got stuck in local loops, misread scale-dependent behavior (several "verified" verdicts on the paging paper came from checks that stopped before the log-k growth became visible), and occasionally built an entire falsification on top of a units mismatch. The challenge's most reliable results came from workflows where a human was steering: re-pointing the agent, questioning an assumption, or deciding that an experiment's premise was wrong before burning a week of compute on it.

Some evaluation is irreducibly human, for now. Our human-in-the-loop winner is the clearest example. The paper claimed stable image generation under extreme quantization. Numerical metrics stated "no collapse"; whether the images were actually usable was a perceptual question. The agent built a purpose-built review UI, and the human personally judged all 128 image pairs, with the annotations committed to the repo and the agent validating their consistency afterward. The published agent trace captures the whole exchange, down to the participant asking how the review tool works and coming back with "I have gone over the pairs and put the csv in the repo, please check.".

So what are our roles as human reviewers? We think it is to manage intelligence effectively. Much like a professor or principal investigator (PI) sets up an environment where grad students can do good work, with compute, harnesses, data access, and targeted feedback at the right moments, the participants who got the most out of their agents were the ones who built the right environment and asked the right questions, then let the agents do the running.

Recent findings suggest that to the 1,221 people who joined, the winners, the authors who responded with grace, and our organizers at Hugging Face and alphaXiv: thank you. Every logbook, verdict, trace, and artifact from the challenge is public, starting from the challenge Space. We think this is the largest open, claim-by-claim audit of a machine learning conference to date, and we would love for it not to hold that record for long.

According to recent reports, stay tuned for future reproduction events. 🤗.

It could also serve as a valuable pathway toward refining autonomous scientific discovery, revealing not only where agents succeed, but also where they fail, providing important insights into their limitations and how human-agent collaboration can be improved.

The scale of this experiment is honestly incredible 🤯... Reproducing 2,226 ICML papers in just 19 days shows how promptly coding agents are changing the research workflow. What once took researchers days or even weeks can now be tested in parallel, giving us a much larger picture of what actually holds up when the claims are checked carefully. 🔬💻.

Sources indicate that what I find especially interesting is the human side of this shift... Agents can read papers, write code, run experiments, and generate reports, but deciding what the results actually mean still requires strong human judgment. A successful reproduction is not automatically proof that every claim is correct, and a failed reproduction can have many possible explanations. 🤔📊.

According to recent reports, the point about reviewing capacity is particularly vital... When thousands of papers are being submitted and reviewers simply cannot examine every proof, experiment, or implementation in depth, scalable reproduction could become an important second layer of scientific scrutiny. It could help researchers focus their limited time on the most meaningful questions instead of spending every hour on repetitive experimental work. 🔎⚙️.

Industry observers note that most importantly, this experiment suggests that AI agents may not replace researchers so much as change where researchers add the most value... Humans may increasingly become the people who design better questions, evaluate evidence, investigate unexpected results, and decide which findings deserve attention. That combination of human curiosity + agent-powered experimentation could make scientific research far more rigorous and scalable. 🚀🧠✨.

Recent findings suggest that every deploy, autoscaling event and node drain ends the same way for a running Node.js process: the platform sends it SIGTERM and waits. What happens next decides whether your consumers notice the deploy.

If the process has no handler for that signal, it exits on the spot. Any request that was halfway through, say a report that takes three seconds of database work, never gets a response. Here is what that looks like with a plain Express app and no signal handling:.

It has been revealed that exit code 143 is 128 plus 15, the number of SIGTERM: the process was killed by the signal rather than exiting on its own. The client gets an empty reply, and if that request was writing data, nobody knows whether the write finished.

A graceful shutdown fixes this by draining the process: it stops taking upcoming work, finishes what it already started, closes its connections and then exits. This tutorial builds that sequence for an Express 5 API backed by PostgreSQL, tests it against a real database, and covers the container and Kubernetes details that decide whether the signal ever reaches your code.

The order of operations matters more than any single line of code. A process that receives SIGTERM should go through four steps:.

According to recent reports, the first step is the one most implementations skip. If the server closes immediately, requests that the load balancer routes in the next second or two get connection errors, which is exactly what graceful shutdown was supposed to prevent.

Create an ES module project and install Express 5 and node-postgres:.

Industry observers note that two timings drive the whole sequence. DRAIN_DELAY_MS is how long the process keeps serving after it fails readiness. It should be longer than your load balancer's health-check interval multiplied by its failure threshold. SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS is the hard deadline for the whole shutdown, and it must be shorter than the time your platform waits before sending SIGKILL.

The sleep helper comes from Node's promise-based timers API, so the shutdown code can await a delay without wrapping setTimeout by hand.

According to recent reports, the middleware handles a detail that is easy to miss. HTTP clients reuse connections with keep-alive, so a client that already has a socket open to this instance would keep sending requests down it. A Connection: close header on the response tells the client to close that socket and open a newly introduced one, which the load balancer will route to a healthy instance.

Liveness stays green during shutdown. The process isn't broken; it's leaving on purpose, and a failing liveness probe could get it restarted in the middle of draining.

A few choices here are deliberate:.

Shutdown code rarely gets tested, because it only runs on deploys. You can test it locally with curl and kill. Start the server with a short drain delay, start the slow request, and send SIGTERM while it is running:.

Here is the timeline from a run against PostgreSQL 16 on Node.js 22:.

Everything the sequence promised highlights up in order. Readiness failed within a third of a second, the instance kept answering during the drain delay, newly introduced connections were refused once the server closed, and the request that was already running finished with a 200 before the process exited cleanly. Compare that with the empty reply and exit code 143 at the start of this article.

Two more cases are worth running once:.

Recent findings suggest that all of this only works if SIGTERM actually arrives at the Node.js process. In containers, that is not a given.

It has been revealed that the Dockerfile reference explains the difference between the shell and exec forms. With the shell form, CMD node server.js, Docker starts /bin/sh -c as the main process, and the shell does not pass SIGTERM on to Node.js. Your handler never runs, docker stop waits out its grace period (10 seconds by default), and then the container is killed. For the same reason, start node directly rather than through an npm script or a shell wrapper, so there is no extra process between the platform and your code.

Recent findings suggest that the first process in a container runs as PID 1, which the Linux kernel treats specially: signals whose default action is to terminate are ignored unless the process installs a handler. The code above installs handlers, so Node.js shuts down correctly as PID 1. But any code path that relies on default signal behavior won't, and PID 1 also has to reap orphaned child processes. Running the container with docker run --init puts a tiny init process in front of Node.js that forwards signals and reaps zombies, and it costs nothing to add.

Sources indicate that when Kubernetes deletes a pod, it removes the pod from Service endpoints and sends SIGTERM at roughly the same time, not one after the other. That race is the reason for the drain delay: for a few seconds after the signal, traffic can still arrive. After the grace period, 30 seconds by default, the kubelet sends SIGKILL. The pod termination documentation describes the full sequence, including preStop hooks, which run before SIGTERM and count toward the same grace period.

The timings need to nest inside each other:.

In a recent development, with a 2-second readiness period and a failure threshold of 1, a 5-second drain delay leaves a comfortable margin for the pod to leave rotation. The 20-second shutdown deadline sits well inside the 30-second grace period, so the process exits on its own terms instead of being killed. If your slowest legitimate request takes longer than about 15 seconds, raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds along with the deadline rather than letting those requests be cut off.

Recent findings suggest that graceful shutdown is about forty lines of code, and it runs on every single deploy. Getting it right means a release is something your customers never notice, which is exactly how a release should feel.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon S3 Tables now support all data types in the Apache Iceberg V3 specification.
  • In a recent development, apache Iceberg has become the open standard for managing large analytics datasets.
  • Teams running analytics on Apache Iceberg V2 tables often hit the same limits as their data grows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon S3 Tables now support all data types in the Apache Iceberg V3 specification. You can create V3 tables or upgrade existing V2 tables to take advantage of V3 features like deletion vectors, row lineage, and new data types such as variant, nanosecond timestamps, unknown, geometry, and geography.

In a recent development, apache Iceberg has become the open standard for managing large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data in open Parquet files in data lakes on object storage like Amazon S3. Amazon S3 Tables offer storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with fully managed features like automatic compaction, maintenance, replication, and Intelligent-Tiering.

Teams running analytics on Apache Iceberg V2 tables often hit the same limits as their data grows. A compliance request to delete 50,000 user records from a 2-billion-row table leaves behind positional delete files that slow queries until compaction runs. Semi-structured events land as JSON strings that every query has to parse. Geospatial coordinates and nanosecond-precision timestamps get encoded as strings or integers. Each workaround adds storage cost, query latency, and pipeline code. With V3, Iceberg solves these challenges by offering native support for semi-structured and geospatial data, faster row-level operations, and built-in row lineage for data governance.

Starting today, Amazon S3 Tables support all V3 data types, including variant, nanosecond timestamps, geometry, geography, and unknown, along with deletion vectors and row lineage. You can create latest V3 tables or upgrade existing V2 tables in place, and S3 Tables continue to run compaction and maintenance for you.

Apache Iceberg V3 V3 is the latest version of the Iceberg specification. Among its many improvements, V3 introduces capabilities that address the most common pain points in V2. This includes:.

Recent findings suggest that deletion vectors replace V2’s positional delete files with a compact binary format. That 50,000-row compliance delete now writes a single deletion vector file instead of thousands of small deletes, significantly reducing compaction time and delete file overhead.

Row lineage adds _row_id and _last_updated_sequence_number to each record automatically. Your downstream pipelines can query these fields to find changed rows without scanning the full table.

Fresh data types let you store semi-structured, geospatial, and nanosecond-precision data natively instead of encoding it as strings or integers:.

Sources indicate that variant data type stores semi-structured data in columnar format. During writes, the engine shreds variant data into hidden columns and collects statistics. At query time, those statistics enable file pruning that significantly reduces I/O compared to parsing JSON strings.

The following sections walk through how to use these V3 capabilities in practice, with examples that show how to create tables, work with the new data types, and manage data at scale.

Getting started A retail analytics team tracks user behavior across web and mobile apps. Each event has a different structure: page views include URLs and duration, purchases include items and amounts, and searches include query terms and result counts. With V3’s variant type, you store all event shapes in one table without predefined schemas:.

Insert events with different payload shapes without worrying about schema evolution:.

In a recent development, now query the variant column directly, without PARSE_JSON at read time. With Amazon EMR Spark, use variant_get:.

To enable deletion vectors for write operations, configure merge-on-read mode:.

Now when you run a compliance delete, V3 writes a small deletion vector instead of rewriting data files:.

S3 Tables compaction handles these deletion vector files automatically on the next maintenance cycle.

Upgrading from V2 AWS provides backwards compatibility for both versions to minimize disruption during migration to V3. Existing V2 readers continue to work on upgraded tables until you’re ready to fully adopt V3 features. For more details, see the S3 Tables Iceberg V3 documentation. Upgrade an existing table atomically without rewriting data:.

On the next compaction cycle, S3 Tables remove old V2 delete files. Newly introduced modifications use deletion vectors automatically. Row lineage fields initialize on the first data modification after the upgrade.

This is a one-way operation. The Apache Iceberg specification does not support downgrading from V3 to V2. Verify that all engines accessing the table support V3 before upgrading.

Using row lineage for incremental pipelines After your table has V3 data, use row lineage to build efficient incremental pipelines:.

Sources indicate that this returns only rows modified after sequence number 42. Your downstream jobs can checkpoint this value and process only latest changes on each run, instead of scanning the full table.

Compatibility across AWS analytics services AWS offers the broadest native Apache Iceberg support of any major cloud provider, with Iceberg-compatible services at every layer of the data stack: ingestion, storage, catalog, and analytics. You can store and automatically optimize V3 tables in Amazon S3 Tables, write data with Amazon EMR Spark, integrate and manage data with AWS Glue, and run analytics with Amazon Redshift. To learn more about AWS analytics support for V3, see the Apache Iceberg on AWS prescriptive guidance.

Both S3 Tables and AWS Glue Data Catalog support the Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) API, enabling interoperability across engines regardless of the catalog endpoint.

According to recent reports, now available Amazon S3 Tables support for all Apache Iceberg V3 data types is now available in all AWS Regions where S3 Tables are supported. Apache Iceberg V3 support is available at no additional charge; standard S3 Tables pricing applies.

To get started, visit the Amazon S3 Tables documentation or create a table bucket from the Amazon S3 console. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. Send feedback to AWS re:Post or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A walkthrough of the streaming data loop in Strands Robots, one loop that records robot demonstrations, trains on them by reading straight from the Hub, and deploys the policy back to hardware, with the dataset in the same on-disk LeRobot format the whole way through.

Updated for Strands Robots 0.6 and LeRobot 0.7.

Industry observers note that you have an agent that can already drive a robot while your code records a demonstration and pushes it to the Hugging Face Hub. Now you want to run that loop continuously: collect episodes through the day, train a policy on the growing dataset, deploy it, and pull the next batch back to improve it. Run that loop once and every piece works. Run it every day and you start paying for the same byte transfers over and over. The recordings you upload keep growing, each training run copies the whole dataset to the GPUs before it starts, and every new checkpoint ships out while the next batch of recordings comes back.

It has been revealed that the first post in this series introduced Strands Robots, an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools you compose into a single Strands agent. That post followed the agent loop in one direction, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot. This one follows the data the other way, from the first recorded frame back to the deployed policy, over Hugging Face Storage Buckets - a mutable, non-versioned, Xet-backed object-storage repository type declared in March 2026. A bucket sits beside your dataset repositories in the same hf:// namespace and uses the hf CLI you already have, so it becomes the working layer that holds your data between the day you record it and the day you train on it.

Someone has to decide which episodes to keep, when the scene has drifted far enough to re-record, whether today's batch is enough to train on, and which checkpoint replaces the one on the arm. Each of those decisions comes up dozens of times over a collection campaign, and each one needs a look at what came back before the next command goes out. That is the work an agent is for: it drives the robot and reads the results, while the recording itself stays one line of your code. This post walks you through the data loop: record a demonstration into a Storage Bucket, store it so that each sync uploads only the bytes that changed, train by streaming the dataset straight from the Hub instead of downloading it, and deploy the checkpoint back to hardware with one keyword argument change. The runnable companion to this post lives at notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb.

According to recent reports, where the first post recorded a dataset and pushed it to the Hub, the loop you build here records a LeRobotDataset with one run(record=...) call, syncs it into a Storage Bucket, and streams that same dataset back frame by frame, decoding camera video on the fly, with no local copy. You read it back with LeRobot's own streaming reader, so the dataset Robot() recorded is exactly the one LeRobot trains on. Your trained checkpoint then deploys to that same Robot() with one keyword argument change, and the demonstrations it records on hardware return to the same bucket.

According to recent reports, figure 1. The four stages share one backend. Robot("so101") records a LeRobotDataset with run(record=...); hf sync syncs it into a Storage Bucket; lerobot-train reads it back over the Hub through LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset with no full download; and the trained checkpoint deploys to the same Robot with a port=. The on-disk format stays exactly as LeRobot wrote it.

It has been revealed that when the agent runs an episode, it invokes one tool, and the rollout then proceeds at the robot's control frequency until the episode ends, with the policy producing every action. Stripped down to the code, the whole loop is a handful of lines:.

What follows is what's actually happening inside that loop, step by step.

In a recent development, that's it. Every stage in this post runs on a laptop with these three, plus the bucket and training items under Advanced. What runs is the loop, not a working policy: the default path uses a placeholder wave function, which records a valid dataset but not a useful one.

Industry observers note that you record upcoming episodes through the day, each a continuous run of camera frames and joint state-action telemetry. LeRobot writes that as a small set of large files that grow as you record. Push them into a versioned dataset repository and every append becomes a commit, and every revision is retained. Collection wants the reverse: somewhere to write bytes and overwrite them in place. That is a Storage Bucket, which lives inside your Hugging Face workspace and uses the permissions you already have. There are no identity and access management (IAM) roles to configure, no cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) rules, and no upload service to maintain.

It has been revealed that strands Robots records a LeRobotDataset in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware: pass record= to run(), and each run adds one episode. Record the episodes, then sync the finished dataset into a bucket. The wave function is a placeholder that produces joint targets without a trained model, so you can run the whole loop before you have a checkpoint to run:.

The sync writes to hf://buckets/{bucket}/{run_id}, where run_id is the folder name that follows the bucket, cube_pick here. The streaming read in Step 3 names the run too: the first two segments of the id are the bucket, and everything after them is the path inside it.

Sources indicate that each sync uploads only the files that changed. Write to the bucket through the day, and publish a versioned copy to a dataset repository when you want one: record="hf://my_user/cube_picking", push=True does that at the end of a run. The placeholder episodes are not useful training data. Pass a trained Policy("") to run() instead.

To record on a physical SO-101, LeRobot's record CLI handles the leader-follower bring-up:.

The dataset lands on disk in the same format as the simulation recording, so the same sync takes it to a bucket: hf sync ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/my_user/cube_picking hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. Collection runs append into one place, and your published repositories only get the versions you choose to publish.

Industry observers note that now that a dataset is in the bucket, the question is what the next sync costs you. Point two fixed cameras at an arm clearing the same table for eight hours and most of what you record is pixels you already have: the same lighting, the same chassis, the same background, across thousands of episodes. On a versioned repository it gets worse, because changing one frame in a multi-gigabyte video shard re-uploads the whole file.

Industry observers note that buckets are backed by Xet, which deduplicates your uploads at the byte level using content-defined chunking. Chunk boundaries follow the content, so inserting a few bytes changes only the chunk it lands in instead of shifting every boundary after it. In Hugging Face's own measurements (HF Storage), content-defined chunking reduces data transferred per upload by about four times across the Hub, and on Enterprise prepares billing is on the deduplicated footprint. Their bucket benchmarks show what that looks like on a single file. Starting from a 500 MB upload, changing 1% of the bytes and re-uploading moved 5.5 MB, changing 5% moved 27.5 MB, and changing 10% moved 55 MB. Without chunk-level deduplication, overwriting an object means sending all of its bytes again, whether or not they changed.

In a recent development, how much that saves you depends on the file layout, and the Strands Robots recorder uses LeRobot's. Episodes go into Parquet shards (data/chunk-000/file-000.parquet) and per-camera MP4 shards (videos/observation.images.front/chunk-000/file-000.mp4), rolling to a new file when the current one fills, at LeRobot's defaults of 100 MB for data Parquet and 200 MB for video MP4. Each run(record=...) starts its own shards, and a lerobot-record session grows its open shard until it fills. Either way, a sync after a day of recording uploads the new trailing shards plus, at most, the one partially-filled shard that grew, rather than the whole dataset. Sync the same bucket again tomorrow and Xet handles the deduplication.

Figure 2. A sync uploads only what changed. The first sync of a fresh dataset uploads every chunk; after recording more episodes, Xet's content-defined chunking means the next sync uploads only the new chunks and skips the ones already stored.

Industry observers note that to train, you point GPUs at your dataset. Download it first and those GPUs sit idle until hundreds of gigabytes finish copying. Streaming straight from the Hub works here because of the shard layout from Step 2: a batch becomes a few byte-range reads over large shards rather than thousands of small fetches. LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset turns that into a drop-in torch iterable, and it opens a bucket with repo_type="bucket":.

Figure 3. Stream, don't download. The download path copies the whole dataset to local disk first, so the GPU waits; StreamingLeRobotDataset reads batches straight from the bucket with only metadata on local disk, so the GPU trains from the first batch.

According to recent reports, nothing lands on local disk except the small meta/ folder of schema, statistics, and episode index, plus a seek index for the video shards: a full streaming read of the 86 MB lerobot/svla_so101_pickplace dataset left under 1 MB on disk. Camera frames are decoded from the remote MP4 shards as you iterate; state and action come from the Parquet shards. That loop reads one frame at a time, which suits inspecting an episode. To train, pass the reader to a DataLoader and iterate batches instead. The streaming dataset shuffles internally through a bounded reservoir buffer, so video decoding parallelizes across worker processes:.

On macOS, run that from a script with an if __name__ == "__main__": guard, because DataLoader workers start by re-importing the script.

Recent findings suggest that if you would rather not write the loop at all, LeRobot's own trainer reads through the same engine, so the dataset you collected trains without a line of new code. It takes a bucket through the same keyword argument the in-process reader uses:.

It has been revealed that buckets are streaming-only, so --dataset.repo_type=bucket requires --dataset.streaming=true and the config rejects the combination otherwise. --policy.push_to_hub=false keeps the checkpoint local; name a --policy.repo_id to publish it instead. Reach for StreamingLeRobotDataset directly when you want the loop in your own process: validating an episode, replaying it in simulation, or feeding a custom evaluation loop.

The checkpoint lerobot-train writes loads straight back through the same entry point used to run any other policy, so the record-train-deploy loop closes in a few lines:.

A 20-step CPU run of ACT over the two-episode dataset above, streamed from a private bucket, wrote a checkpoint that Policy() loaded and ran on the simulated arm. Twenty steps over placeholder episodes check that the loop connects; it does not train a policy that grasps. Training time scales with dataset size, batch size, and step count, and a useful ACT policy needs real demonstrations and a GPU.

Hugging Face's pre-warming caches bucket data at edge locations near the cloud and region where your jobs run, so your cluster reads locally and the dataloader stays ahead of the GPU. In Hugging Face's own bucket benchmarks, a warm content delivery network (CDN) read hit about 1,086 MB/s on a 10 GB payload against 780 MB/s cold, and roughly 1,124 MB/s warm at 100 GB, measured on an m5dn.24xlarge in us-east-1. The full comparison against plain object storage, upload as well as download, is on that dashboard. Choosing where that data lives is a Storage Regions setting on Team and Enterprise intends, as of this writing US and EU, with Asia-Pacific and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) regions confirmed as coming; outside those plans repositories are stored in the US.

In this step you take the checkpoint you just trained, run it on a physical robot, and record the next round of demonstrations with it. This is the same agent code from the first post. The keyword argument that changes is port=, which selects the physical arm; id= names its LeRobot calibration, cameras= names the image keys the policy was trained on, and operator= approves its moves.

Sources indicate that nothing moves on the real arm until operator= approves it. The demonstrations it records with record= are in the same LeRobot format you started with, ready to sync back to the bucket for the next training run.

Sources indicate that if your data already lives on Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), nothing in this post changes: a LeRobotDataset is a directory of Parquet and MP4 shards, and every step reads it wherever it sits. A bucket adds the Hub-native path, the sync and the streaming read, with no storage to provision first.

It has been revealed that run the loop again tomorrow and you record into the same bucket, sync only what changed, and stream it to the GPUs without waiting for a download. The data never leaves the LeRobot format.

The full Strands Robots sample is on GitHub at strands-labs/robots in notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb. It walks you through the full loop cell by cell: record, sync to a bucket, stream back, train, and load the checkpoint. Every cell runs in simulation on the placeholder policy, so no GPU and no Docker are needed, and without a bucket set it needs no Hugging Face credentials either.

Run the cells top to bottom. To sync to a bucket, set HF_BUCKET=my-org/robot-fave before starting Jupyter (after hf auth login); each run syncs under its own folder, nb12-, and the notebook streams back from it. Without HF_BUCKET it trains from the local folder instead. To train on a GPU, raise --steps and drop --policy.device=cpu in the training cell.

The snippets here are a "hello world" of the Strands Robots data loop. Five things change once you run it against real data.

Prompt injection. Supplying untrusted data to an agent can lead to prompt injection, where untrustworthy context is treated as LLM instructions. These agents actuate robots, so this is an important risk to track. Feed the agent only data from trusted sources. If not all input can be trusted, restrict the tools available to the agent so it cannot take safety-critical actions. In Strands Robots an agent cannot record, push, or calibrate, and on a real robot operator= answers every move and every policy run's proposal before anything moves.

Training data is a trust boundary. Anything that can write into the collection bucket can also write episodes that a policy later trains on, and that policy drives a physical arm. Keep the credential that writes collection data separate from the one a training job reads with, sync each run under its own run_id so an episode can be traced to the run that produced it and removed on its own, and treat the versioned dataset repository as the reviewed artifact, because the bucket keeps no revisions to audit against.

Sources indicate that bucket credentials and scope. hf sync and StreamingLeRobotDataset use the token from hf auth login. Use a token scoped to the specific namespace you are writing to, prefer --private buckets for collection data, and keep the bucket distinct from the versioned dataset repository you publish and share.

Sources indicate that overwrite in place keeps no revisions. A bucket overwrites in place and retains no revisions, which is what makes it a working layer and also means a repeated run_id replaces the run already stored there. Sync each collection run to its own path, as in hf sync ./recordings hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. For anything you need to be able to return to, push to a versioned dataset repository, where every revision is retained.

Industry observers note that only use trusted Hugging Face orgs. Loading a checkpoint runs code its publisher chose. A Policy your own code builds loads directly; a Hub checkpoint the agent asks for by name loads only if the operator lists it in STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS (for example STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS=lerobot/smolvla_base,my_user/*). Only load checkpoints from organizations you trust. Model weights can contain arbitrary code (pickle-based checkpoints). Prefer safetensors-format checkpoints where available.

Sources indicate that the loop leaves a bucket, datasets under /tmp, and a checkpoint on disk. Bucket contents count toward your stored volume, so remove what you no longer need:.

Recent findings suggest that stop any training process still on a GPU instance, and stop the instance. If you ran the notebook, its last cell prints the command that removes its run. Anything you published to a dataset repository is versioned and is untouched.

The Strands Robots documentation covers the robot catalog, simulation, policies, recording, and the mesh in depth. The recording guide documents run(record=...) and reading a dataset back with LeRobot.

If you collect from more than one robot, give each one its own run_id and they write into the same bucket in parallel. The multi-robot mesh fans one agent out across those robots, so the same loop becomes a fleet collecting through the day into shared storage. A streaming reader reads one run at a time, so point each training run at the run_id it should learn from.

If you want a larger policy than ACT, lerobot-train fine-tunes LeRobot's vision-language-action (VLA) policies, such as SmolVLA and pi0, on the dataset you just streamed, and the checkpoint loads as a Policy the same way. For heavier simulation to generate that data, the Newton (newton) and Isaac Sim (isaac) backends sit behind the same Robot(), so the agent code does not change as you scale up.

Bucket streaming reached LeRobot through contributions from both the Strands Robots and LeRobot teams, upstream in LeRobot itself, so the datasets your agent collects are readable by every tool in that ecosystem. That runs both ways: the reader in Step 3 opens any of the LeRobot datasets already published on the Hub, so you can replay and evaluate against existing demonstrations before you record any of your own.

Contributions are welcome under Apache 2.0. If you build something with this loop, open an problem with what worked and what didn't.

It has been revealed that what makes this architecture particularly compelling is that the agent isn’t just executing a task—it’s sitting inside a continuous data, learning, and deployment loop. Connecting data collection, streaming, training, evaluation, and deployment through one agent workflow opens up some fascinating possibilities for adaptive systems. At the same time, the trust boundaries around data, credentials, and agent actions become critical. This is where custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions need to be designed as complete systems rather than isolated agent features. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that agent Anomaly Detection is in Private Preview, including monitoring for agents that run outside Google Cloud. To request access, see the Agent Anomaly Detection overview.

Our launch post introduced Agent Anomaly Detection, which helps you understand and act on agent behavior that drifts outside its intended boundaries. It covered agents on Google Cloud, such as Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Many teams also run agents on other clouds: on AWS Lambda next to an inventory database, as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry, or on-premises next to a system that can't move. Those agents carry the same behavioral risks, and until now Agent Anomaly Detection couldn't review them.

It has been revealed that agent Anomaly Detection works from an agent's traces and logs, so it doesn't need access to the agent's runtime. If those traces and logs reach your Google Cloud project, it can detect anomalous behavior wherever the agent runs. In this post, we explain what Agent Anomaly Detection needs from an agent on other cloud, then show what it found for an agent on AWS Lambda and an agent on Microsoft Foundry.

Agent Anomaly Detection reads the logging and observability buckets that you choose when you enable it. Telemetry from anywhere works when:.

Agents built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) for Python, version 2.12.0 or later, can produce this telemetry with ADK's Google Cloud exporters and a few environment variables, which the next section highlights.

  • The demand from Arm lawyers to Jon Palmisciano concern Jon’s Arm Reference, a site that provides the same arm Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) info available on Arm’s site, but with what Palmisciano describes as “without a million popups and all of the bloat” that Arm provides on its own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that easy-to-use, popular, not collecting data for us, or serving our ads? Down with you!

Arm is swinging the hammer at an enthusiast’s site hosting a bloat-free version of its instruction reference documentation, demanding it be taken offline after several years of availability.

The demand from Arm lawyers to Jon Palmisciano concern Jon’s Arm Reference, a site that provides the same arm Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) info available on Arm’s site, but with what Palmisciano describes as “without a million popups and all of the bloat” that Arm provides on its own.

Recent findings suggest that according to Palmisciano, his copy of the Arm ISA was culled from machine-readable XML files and stripped of the bloat. He built his version in 2022 with fresh CSS on top of it, and the addition of a quick search feature that, according to his comments on Hacker News, isn’t available in the official version.

“The aim has always been to make it the most comfortable and bullshit-free browsing experience for people who need these docs daily,” Palmisciano wrote in HN. Based on the responses the site seems to have plenty of fans.

Arm doesn’t care if Palmisciano’s project is well intentioned or for the benefit of the many software developers that write code for its chipsets, either: They want it offline by December 4 – 10 days from the publication of this story – or else.

As for what is going to happen, it seems like Jon’s Arm Reference will likely cease to exist in a little over a week – at least in its current form.

According to recent reports, “Ideally I'd love to just get permission from Arm to keep the site up, but I'm pretty pessimistic about that,” Palmisciano told us. That mentioned, Palmisciano has “already seen a few archives and mirrors already.” The HN thread discussing the takedown order includes links to several versions, and Palmisciano has another trick up his sleeve that he’s considering playing: Open-sourcing the software he used to build his ISA page.

“I'd also consider open-sourcing my tooling so that people can (for their own private use) turn the original XML downloads from Arm into an identical site they can host locally,” Palmisciano told us. He noted that he'll likely tweet about opening the tooling if he does do so. He's also considered directing the URL for Jon's Arm reference to point to the open-source tool, but Arm wants the subdomain it's hosted on removed from his site as well, so that may not happen.

Arm has been in touch to defend itself as well, saying that Arm appreciates the efforts of people like Palmisciano, but that it still has to protect its brand, and documentation.

In other words, if you’re an Arm dev worried about losing a valuable resource and having to turn to a website that bombards you with junk just to look up a few simple opcodes and operands you’d better find a backup host before next month.

That said, Arm is willing to work something out with Palmisciano, the company told us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that today, we’re announcing the public preview of AWS Well-Architected Agent, an AI-powered service that analyzes your AWS environment to deliver targeted, contextual recommendations for improving your applications’ cost, security, performance, and resilience. The AWS Well-Architected Agent analyzes your infrastructure, understands unique business goals, and delivers contextual recommendations with ready-to-implement fixes. It delivers context-aware optimization without relying on manual audits or generic checklists.

The agent evaluates your environment as an experienced cloud architect would. It automatically correlates utilization metrics, resource configurations, and application topology, and analyzes against Well-Architected best practices across 65+ AWS services. It generates recommendations aligned to your declared business goals, delivers implementation packages with every finding, and surfaces cross-pillar trade-offs making it simpler to remediate the findings.

Here are the three main features of this service:.

AWS Well-Architected Agent in action To get started, create an agent profile to define the scope of what Well-Architected Agent can access and provide recommendations on, complete the IAM role setup to access resources, conduct architecture review, and remediate recommendations.

According to recent reports, create an agent profile In the AWS Well-Architected console, choose Get started with Well-Architected Agent. You can define an agent profile that specifies which AWS accounts and applications to monitor, which optimization pillars to focus on, and the permissions required.

In a recent development, you can choose AWS accounts or AWS Regions to monitor and optimization pillars that matter most to your business. You can also set goals for each pillar: cost optimization, performance, resilience, and security.

To give access to the agent for your AWS environment, provision customer-managed IAM roles the agent uses to read resource configurations, utilization metrics, and application topology. To learn more, visit the IAM prerequisite for AWS Well-Architected Agent.

Recent findings suggest that when you choose Get Started, the agent creates your agent profile. Resource and application recommendations will be generated within 24 hours after profile creation.

According to recent reports, you can conduct an architecture review on pre-deployment workloads by uploading an IaC project in Terraform, AWS CloudFormation, or AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) to be analyzed. Choose Conduct architecture review in the dashboard, upload a.zip file containing IaC project or repository file, and select which Well-Architected lens to use for reviewing your infrastructure.

Sources indicate that you can define your applications to add context which will enhance the relevancy and further contextualize recommendations. Choose Add application context in the dashboard, add your applications with AWS accounts, AWS Regions, AWS services, tags if you want to narrow the scope to specific resources, and the details of applications.

Review prioritized recommendations and start remediating Now you can see generated prioritized recommendations generated by the agent across your resources and applications, selected pillars, ranked against your declared goals, with automation-ready remediation included.

When you choose the specific recommendation, you can see the details, insights into why the agent are suggesting the recommendation, impacts and trade-off, and recommended fixes across affected AWS resources.

Sources indicate that choose Start remediation to address recommended fixes. You can choose the console, updated IaC template, CLI commands to remediate by the resolution type. It provides detailed step-by-step instructions and you can roll out this instruction and verify the result.

When you choose Using updated IaC template, the agent provides the code changes needed to update your existing IaC templates such as the CDK function shown above which you can copy directly into your codebase.

You can also configure API access to integrate recommendations directly into your existing development and operations workflows. To interact with the agent programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the AWS Well-Architected Agent documentation.

Things to know Here are some things that you should know about the Well-Architected Agent.

You can still use existing AWS Well-Architected Tool to manually evaluate your cloud architecture with user-defined lenses that measure your workload using your own best practices.

In a recent development, join the preview Access to the AWS Well-Architected Agent and its recommendations is available in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon). You can onboard workloads from any AWS commercial Region. AWS Well-Architected Agent is delivered by AWS Support and available to AWS customers with an AWS Support plan.

Give it a try today in the AWS Well-Architected console and send feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

  • Models and datasets on HF hub are growing on a daily basis.
  • In a recent development, there used to be a clear progression path: labs would start by releasing smaller models and gradually work their way toward the top end of the scale.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the AI world, time feels compressed. A few months after our spring report in our biannual analysis worked through the ecosystem, there are quite a few findings that we have observed until this summer. This report lays out these observations from January to August 2026 and presents the data behind each one.

Models and datasets on HF hub are growing on a daily basis. Public model repositories grew from 2.43 to 2.96 million over the period, datasets from 711,000 to 1 million, Spaces from 1.00 to 1.44 million. The distribution underneath stays extreme, roughly 85.6% of models have fewer than 200 lifetime downloads, and 1.5% of repositories account for 99.2% of all downloads. Everything below happens inside that shape.

In a recent development, there used to be a clear progression path: labs would start by releasing smaller models and gradually work their way toward the top end of the scale. In 2026, several Chinese labs skipped this progression entirely.

In almost every month of 2026, the largest and most performant open model from a Chinese lab was larger than any model an American lab released. China's monthly ceiling ran between 754B and 2.78 trillion parameters; U.S. models stayed under 130B in five of seven months, the exception being NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 561B in May and June, and Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab.

Recent findings suggest that the chart splits the labs into two camps. Moonshot, MiniMax, Xiaomi and Z.ai publish almost nothing below 70B, so a developer's first encounter with them is a model too large to run on anything they own. Tencent and Alibaba Qwen cover the whole range instead, from under 1B upward.

According to recent reports, two things made the first camp possible. Building large stopped being a differentiator. Xiaomi, Ant Group and Meituan all cleared a trillion parameters this year, and neither was a household name in open weights twelve months ago. And a lab no longer has to ship a small model to be reachable, because the community's quantization layer will make a large one runnable within days, a dependency we return to below.

Sources indicate that that leaves the size profile as a statement of intent rather than of capability. A frontier only portfolio stakes everything on benchmark position and API demand. A full spectrum portfolio is a bid to be the family developers standardise on. Both are rational, they are playing for different prizes.

The United States is not absent from open source.

The two organizations publishing the most new open models this year are also the companies making the hardware: AMD and NVIDIA. Each released more than 200 new model repositories, far ahead of the rest of the field, with LiquidAI ranking third at around 100. Hardware vendors have realized that open models are a way to sell chips: a model optimized for your hardware and freely available is the clearest proof that the hardware works.

When smaller models and embedding models are included, where Google, Microsoft, IBM Granite, and OpenAI’s older vision and speech models generate hundreds of millions of downloads annually, U.S. open source AI is growing.

It has been revealed that more hardware and infrastructure organizations such as NVIDIA are training and open-weighting competitive models. NVIDIA's Nemotron model family boasts high performance. Long-time leaders such as Meta reignite open roots with Meta's Muse Glimmer.

Industry observers note that at the frontier scale, some U.S. model releases above 100B parameters this year are built on top of Chinese models or leverage artifacts from Chinese labs, such as Thinking Machines’ Inkling (952B). Major original American models include NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Ultra (561B), Nemotron 3 Super (124B), and Arcee AI’s Trinity-Large (399B).

Industry observers note that AMD contributed many conversions. This work is notable: it enables trillion-parameter models to run efficiently on U.S. hardware. This represents a distribution and optimization layer.

Meanwhile, Chinese open models are increasingly optimized for domestic chips in China, the same competition in reverse, where models are designed around specific hardware ecosystems.

We took the top 25 model repositories by downloads accumulated this year and the top 25 by likes. Exactly one repository appears in both lists.

According to recent reports, we counted downloads inside the window rather than lifetime, so nothing is credited for merely having existed longer, and controlling for age makes the split sharper. Not one model published in 2026 reaches the download top 25, while thirteen of the twenty-five date from 2022. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 was pulled 1.55 billion times in seven months against 5,156 likes; Kimi-K3 was pulled about 60 times per like it received.

Industry observers note that the two numbers record different acts. A like states a release matters, and goes to frontier models in the weeks after they ship. A download says something is wired into a pipeline that runs on a schedule, and accrues to small, stable models over years. Likes are the right instrument for reading what the field is excited about, downloads for reading what it currently depends on. Treating either as a proxy for the other is the most common mistake we see in coverage of the Hub, including our own earlier work. The same split appears at the level of the publisher.

Sources indicate that china's frontier labs are the only accounts on the Hub where the heavy band carries the volume. Effectively all of MiniMax's 2026 downloads are of models above 70B, along with 88% of Moonshot's, 55% of DeepSeek's and 39% of Z.ai's. No large American account looks like this: Google, Microsoft and IBM Granite record essentially none of their 2026 downloads above 70B, and NVIDIA and Meta only 14% and 9%.

Recent findings suggest that the difference becomes clearer in total downloads. Moonshot’s frontier-only portfolio recorded 37M downloads over the year, while Qwen’s broader release strategy across model sizes reached 2,045M (across repositories with declared parameter counts, 2,061M including all repositories) , about 55 times more. The continued expansion of the family, from the 2.4T-parameter Qwen 3.8 Max to smaller variants such as 27B, shows the same focus on coverage across different use cases.

Time also plays an key role. Most models experience a sharp decline in usage after release, followed by a long tail of steady activity. A model’s adoption is largely determined within its first few months.

This helps explain why today’s download volume is often driven not by the newest releases, but by a smaller group of models that have become established infrastructure over time.

Sources indicate that if frontier models were a licensing business, you would expect the biggest releases to carry the tightest terms. However, the data below reveals a different story.

Of 178 Chinese releases above 20B parameters this year, 59% carry Apache 2.0 and 22% carry MIT, and almost none carry non-commercial restrictions. However, in the last few weeks, we started to see a change on this trend for the really large models, with Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 2.4T starting to include some non-commercial restrictions and revenue share requirements to their licenses.

It has been revealed that deepSeek and Z.ai ship models between 700 billion and 1.65 trillion parameters under plain MIT. Chinese labs license their largest models about as permissively as their smallest, and more permissively than American labs license theirs: on the American side of the same size band, 29% is Apache or MIT, 41% sits under custom terms and 30% declares nothing at all.

In a recent development, whatever these releases are for, it is not licence revenue. The weights are given away on the most permissive terms available. The return has to come from somewhere else: API and cloud business, hardware and platform positioning, or the ecosystem position itself. For instance, the valuations of Z.ai and Kimi point to an effective open source strategy, getting traction and growth opportunities in the community. Going forward, however, the industry is likely to shift toward clearer monetization paths from open-source adoption.

In a recent development, A model’s ecosystem position is not defined only by its own releases, but by how much the community builds on top of it. As mentioned above, Qwen is one exception which is getting attention and adoption.

By this measure, Qwen has become one of the largest foundations in the open model ecosystem. Qwen-based models now account for 151,448 derivatives on the Hub, 2.6× Meta’s total footprint and 4.7× the Llama repositories specifically. Google follows with 82,506 derivatives. The third-largest source is Unsloth, a community account publishing quantized and fine-tuning-ready builds, many of which further extend the Qwen ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that qwen derivatives have increased at roughly 180–210 new repositories per day throughout the first seven months of 2026, showing that adoption is not driven only by individual introduces. Qwen has become part of the default workflow for developers deciding what models to fine-tune and deploy.

Several factors contributed to this position. First, consistency. Qwen has maintained a regular release cadence, continuously updating its model family rather than relying on occasional flagship releases. Second, coverage. It publishes models across a wide range of sizes and use cases, allowing developers to stay within the same ecosystem whether they need a small local model or a larger deployment model. Third, openness. Apache 2.0 licensing reduces friction for modification, redistribution, and commercial use.

These factors reinforce each other. A broad model family attracts more developers; more developers create more derivatives; and those derivatives make the ecosystem more attractive to future customers.

Industry observers note that this position was built largely by the community. The 151,448 derivatives represent downstream work created by other developers, not releases produced by Qwen itself. Even among the 28,531 GGUF conversions of Qwen models on the Hub, Qwen published only 54.

Among models that declare a parameter count, those under 1B take 83% of all-time downloads and everything above 100B takes 1%. Restricting to downloads accumulated in 2026 changes nothing: 3% of the volume goes to models above 70B. This is the March finding that has held up most cleanly, for the same reason as before, small models are the only ones that run on the hardware most developers actually have.

Industry observers note that so how does a trillion-parameter model reach anyone at all? Through llama.cpp.

Recent findings suggest that in February the ggml team joined Hugging Face, with the project remaining fully open-source, community-governed and in the same technical direction. What changed is that the most vital project in local inference now has durable resources behind it.

Industry observers note that the ceiling moved with llama.cpp. The July snapshot carries GGUF builds of DeepSeek-V4-Flash at roughly 284B parameters and Kimi-K3 at roughly 2.8 trillion. Local inference used to mean an 8B model on a laptop. It now means a trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts spread across a few consumer machines, which is the alternative route the frontier did not have a year ago, and the reason a frontier-first release strategy is viable at all.

And that route runs on Qwen: 39.6 million GGUF downloads a month, nearly twice Gemma's 20.8 million and more than five times Llama's 7.5 million. The Llama gap is not a supply problem, Llama-derived GGUF repositories slightly outnumber Qwen's. Same shelf space, a fifth of the traffic.

In a recent development, model repositories grew 21.5% over these seven months. Several things around them grew several times faster.

Repositories declaring the gguf library rose 464%, lerobot 194% and Apple's mlx148%, against 16% for transformers and peft and 21% for diffusers. The modelling core is growing at roughly the platform average. The layer that decides where a model can physically run local inference formats, Apple silicon, robot control stacks, is growing three to seven times faster than that.

In a recent development, across the ten largest model families, the labs behind these models publish very few official GGUF conversions. Yet GGUF versions are often the ones used by developers running models locally. Providing an official conversion at release, documenting quantization choices, and signing the artifacts would require limited additional effort. Rather than maintaining this workflow internally, labs could collaborate with existing ecosystem contributors such as Unsloth. Doing so would narrow the gap between the weights tested by model creators and the versions adopted by the broader community.

Recent findings suggest that we could not have written this section in March, because the instrument did not exist. The agent-usage dataset, published in July, records the agent/ token that coding agents send when they call the Hub through huggingface_hub or the hf CLI — searching for models, pushing datasets, running Jobs, creating Spaces. For the first time we can see how much agent traffic the Hub receives and which harnesses it comes from.

Claude Code led July with 44.4%, but a single month conceals the real finding: it held 67.8% in April and 64% in May, while Codex climbed steadily from 10.4% to 20.8%. This is a market with no incumbent, where one release or one changed default can move half the traffic in a month.

The second finding is the unregistered row. Nearly a quarter of agent-tagged traffic in July came from harnesses not yet named in the dataset, and in May that figure was 59.8%. Between April and July more than a dozen new client identifiers appeared. New entrants are arriving faster than any registry can name them — which is itself the finding.

According to recent reports, we spent much of the year building for this reader rather than only for human browsers. Papers began serving machine-readable Markdown in March. April brought agent traces as a first-class dataset type and an agents.md endpoint on every Gradio Space, so an agent can read a Space's API and call it directly. July brought the hf_fs tool on our MCP server, exposing repositories, storage, docs and papers through a single interface in just over a thousand tokens, alongside attachable sandboxes for secure execution. The same consolidation happened at the protocol layer, with MCP moving into the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

Then, in July, an agent stopped being a reader and became an intruder. What appears to be the first documented case of an autonomous agent running a sustained intrusion on its own initiative happened to us. While our team tried to use frontier closed models to analyze the captured attack code, their safety guardrails declined the work. The analysis was completed in the end on a quantized open model GLM-5.2 running on our own infrastructure. We published a disclosure and a full technical timeline.

Industry observers note that compared to the spring report, the geographical rebalancing of power continues to accelerate. While U.S. open source models continue to be competitive, the race between several Chinese frontier model labs draws strong attention. Many likes on these frontier models point to what excites the community the most, and growth opportunity for companies leveraging the attention for valuations.

Recent findings suggest that however, the AI race is not only sprints, but also a marathon; tools like llama.cpp helps deploying the massive models locally, but a broad model family and its adoption is still the key, to build a positive feedback loop between developers, publisher and future consumers. Models to be embedded in the infrastructure and being part of the ecosystem, may lead to a commercially sound exit at the end of the tunnel.

In the end, with agents being the number 1 user on HF Hub for the first time, the next report may look very different.

In AI, a few months can reshape the ecosystem.

This analysis is based on activity observed on the Hugging Face Hub during the first seven months of 2026.

The metrics used in this report, including downloads, likes, derivatives, and model releases, represent different aspects of ecosystem activity. They should not be interpreted as direct measures of model quality, commercial adoption, or overall market share.

Downloads indicate usage within the Hub ecosystem, but they do not capture API usage, private deployments, or models distributed through other channels.

Likes reflect community attention and interest, while derivative models provide a signal of how much developers build on top of an existing model.

Because open-source AI adoption happens across many channels, Hub activity should be viewed as one perspective on ecosystem development rather than a complete measurement of the AI market.

This article was edited to include latest releases in early August.

According to recent reports, "Of 178 Chinese releases above 20B parameters this year, 59% carry Apache 2.0 and 22% carry MIT, and exactly none carry a non-commercial restriction.Not true. Kimi models cannot be served by companies that make more than $20M/year unless explicit authorisation by Moonshot.

According to recent reports, smartphones have defined personal computing for nearly two decades. They changed how people communicate, work, navigate and find information. They also still depend on screens, app switching and a lot of manual effort.

Industry observers note that artificial intelligence is starting to change that relationship. Emerging personal devices can respond to natural language, use context and offer help when it is needed instead of waiting for constant input. For developers, that raises practical questions: where should a model run, what should an interface look like without a large screen, and how much data should leave the device? This article walks through those questions and includes a small, tested helper for one of them. Product details change promptly, so check each platform's current documentation.

Sources indicate that the smartphone interaction model is screen-centered: open an app, navigate menus, enter a command. AI-powered devices combine machine learning, sensors and conversational interfaces to interpret a request with fewer manual steps.

Sources indicate that navigation is a simple example. On a phone, you check the map or listen to directions. A wearable could give timely audio instructions or a visual cue based on location and movement. That does not mean the phone goes away. Personal computing may instead spread across interconnected devices, with the phone continuing to supply connectivity and processing.

Contextual computing means a system uses relevant information about the environment, user activity or earlier interactions. A traditional app responds to explicit commands. An AI-assisted one can also interpret natural-language requests and combine several inputs. A personal assistant might use calendar and location data, with permission, to suggest when someone should leave for an appointment.

Multimodal AI, which McKinsey describes as AI that can handle several kinds of data at once, including text, images, audio and video, makes interactions feel more natural than touch controls alone.

Sources indicate that context only helps when the underlying information is reliable. Developers need to manage permissions, data accuracy and user expectations, or the feature will feel intrusive or wrong.

Smartwatches and fitness trackers already showed the value of getting information without pulling out a phone. AI extends this to other products, including smart eyewear, earbuds and connected accessories.

Smart glasses are one example of familiar accessories gaining intelligent features without a conventional screen. Depending on the model, they can support voice assistance, hands-free photography, audio playback and interaction with AI assistants. Several makers sell them, and guide pages such as ai glasses describes how the category is presented to buyers. Capabilities differ widely, so compare sensors, battery life, privacy controls and the software platform before building for or buying any one device.

For interaction design, the point is to deliver help while the user keeps doing something else. That changes what an app should show, say and ask.

Many AI features rely on cloud infrastructure. The cloud offers large models and plenty of compute, but adds network delay and requires sending data off the device. On-device AI runs supported models on personal hardware. It can reduce latency, support some offline features and limit how much sensitive information is transmitted.

Sources indicate that local processing has costs. Small devices have limited memory, battery and thermal headroom, so teams balance model size, compute demand and response quality. Hybrid architectures split the work between local hardware and cloud services, and are a practical answer for many applications.

A hybrid app needs a rule for where each request runs. The Python module below is a deliberately simple example. It takes the task (model size, whether the data is sensitive, the latency the user will tolerate) and the device state (free memory, battery, connectivity, measured round-trip time) and returns device, cloud, ask_user or unavailable.

The tests cover the main cases: a live caption on glasses stays on the device when the network is too slow, a large model that does not fit goes to the cloud, sensitive data stays local or triggers a question to the user when the model will not fit, an offline device runs only what fits, and low battery pushes a heavy job to the cloud.

Run it with python3 test_route-py.

In a recent development, ambient computing describes technology that blends into everyday environments instead of demanding continuous attention. Users may reach connected services through speakers, watches, glasses and other devices. Someone could start a task with a voice assistant, get a reminder on a watch and continue on a laptop without recreating the context.

Sources indicate that that requires reliable synchronization, interoperable services and consistent identity across devices. AI can help interpret requests and coordinate interactions, but a seamless experience still depends on well-designed software architecture. Developers should decide how information moves between devices, what happens when connectivity fails and how customers stay in control of automated actions.

Apps built around large screens and touch navigation may not translate well to devices that rely on speech, audio feedback or compact visual displays. Google's Android XR developer documentation describes building for several device types, including XR headsets, audio glasses and display glasses, and lists tools such as the Jetpack XR SDK, Unity, OpenXR and WebXR.

Whatever the platform, a few priorities recur:.

It has been revealed that not every interaction benefits from AI. Predictable tasks may be better served by a conventional interface, so use intelligent features where they measurably improve usability.

Industry observers note that probably not soon. Phones are likely to remain a hub for connectivity and processing, while wearables and ambient devices handle some everyday interactions.

Running a machine learning model directly on personal hardware, so a task can run without sending each request to a remote server.

When the model is too large for the device, the data is not sensitive and the network is fast enough. Many apps use a hybrid, as in the routing helper above.

Interaction relies more on voice and audio, displays are small or absent, and messages must be short and timely because the user is busy doing something else.

Industry observers note that personal computing is moving toward a connected, context-aware ecosystem of wearables, on-device processing and ambient interfaces. That transition needs careful attention to privacy, security, accessibility and usability. The products that last will be defined less by the hardware people carry and more by how naturally and responsibly technology supports what they are trying to do.
