Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck.
  • Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.
  • ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every fresh service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs), AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, revision, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization.

Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.

ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.

ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes.

A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console, platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later.

In a recent development, choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings, you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation.

According to recent reports, using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector.

Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters.

Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters.

Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster:.

Industry observers note that to create and manage the ECS Gateway programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Gateway documentation.

Sources indicate that ECS Gateway:Behind the scenesA gateway can be associated with up to 10,000 clusters, and a single cluster supports up to five gateway associations. This many-to-many relationship gives platform teams the flexibility to share a gateway across environments or assign multiple gateways (for example, public and private) to a single cluster.

Sources indicate that platform teams can control access by choosing which gateways to associate with which clusters. For additional control, use IAM policies to restrict who can deploy services to specific clusters.

According to recent reports, application teams add the gateway connector to each service definition in CreateService or UpdateService. If you have an existing ECS service with its own load balancer, you can adopt ECS Gateway incrementally by calling UpdateService to add a gateway connector. Both ingress paths remain available, allowing you to validate the gateway connection before removing the existing load balancer configuration.

At deployment time, Amazon ECS evaluates the gateways associated with the cluster and connects the service to every compatible gateway. A gateway is compatible when its access type matches the service’s connector filter, it is in the same VPC as the service, and it covers all Availability Zones used by the service’s configured subnets.

Sources indicate that for each connection, Amazon ECS assigns the service to an ALB with available capacity and provisions the per-service resources: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, a listener rule routing traffic for that hostname to the service target group, and a service security group allowing inbound traffic only from the ALB security group. If no existing ALB has capacity, ECS creates a new one (up to maxAlbCount referring to quota limit). Once provisioning completes, the gateway route becomes ACTIVE, and the service URL is ready to receive traffic.

ECS Gateway handles common operational scenarios automatically:.

Things to Know Here are a few important details to keep in mind:.

Sources indicate that now available Amazon ECS Gateway is available now in all commercial AWS Regions where ECS is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when services connect to a gateway, including applicable ALB charges, CloudWatch logs and metrics, ACM certificates, and data transfer charges. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Pricing page.

To get started, create your first gateway today in the ECS console, and send feedback to AWS re:Post for ECS or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Tech Report: Where should your code live in a Docker Sandbox?

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1204 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on.
  • Industry observers note that you might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results.
  • Industry observers note that sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on. You can share a checkout from your host, give it a separate working directory for a task, or keep the repository entirely inside the sandbox. Each arrangement changes how you, the human, participate in the work.

Industry observers note that you might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results. sbx supports both. The way you organize the checkout can change as you ask the agent to take on more of the work.

Industry observers note that sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use. Run sbx run from your project directory, and it mounts that directory at the same absolute path inside the sandbox:.

In a recent development, open a file in your local editor while the agent works on it, and you’ll see changes as they happen. Git works from either side, so you choose whether you want to let the agent make commits or you do it yourself. Development servers on your host can pick up the edits through hot reload, using the runtime and dependencies installed on your host.

Sources indicate that this fits close collaboration on one task. The coordination cost comes from sharing that working tree: switching branches changes the files the agent sees, and your edits become part of its ongoing work. If you want to switch to something unrelated while the agent continues, you’ll need another checkout.

NOTE: Dependencies written into the shared checkout are shared too. Packages with native binaries, such as esbuild, may work in the Linux sandbox and fail on a macOS or Windows host. Reinstalling on the host can reverse the problem. Keep separate dependency installations, or run the app consistently in one environment.

Git worktrees give each task a directory and branch. You can mount each worktree in its own sandbox, while your original checkout remains available for other work. The agent’s edits appear in the worktree. You can inspect either with your local editor and development tools. Each task also gets its own running environment, with tools to prepare and a sandbox and worktree to clean up afterward.

There is a Git limitation with mounting only a linked worktree. Its .git file points to metadata outside the mount, which the agent can’t reach. It can edit files, but checking status, branching, and committing have to happen on the host. The future of software development still needs you to run git status.

sbx supports a clone mode that gives the agent a separate checkout with Git available inside the sandbox. You keep your local project, but sbx mounts the host source as read-only and creates an independent clone for the agent. Its branch changes and dependency installations stay in its checkout.

Bringing the result back becomes a handoff. While the sandbox is running, you can fetch committed branches through the Git remote sbx adds on your host. Or the agent can push to the repository’s remote and you can retrieve the branch through your usual Git workflow. Your local editor and development server see the changes after you bring them into your checkout.

A mountless sandbox has no host workspace directory attached. Clone the repository inside it, and the sandbox holds the checkout and its development environment. Your host copy of the project shares no connection with the sandbox checkout.

It has been revealed that this workflow resembles working on a remote development machine. Agents connect to the project environment, and you can open a shell with sbx exec or connect an editor to the sandbox over SSH. Changes and dependency installations stay separate from your host. To bring work back, you push a branch to the Git remote.

In a recent development, one sandbox per project can be a useful mental model here. The project and its tools persist across agent sessions and sandbox restarts. An agent can create worktrees per feature it’s working on, push branches, and create pull requests for review. Starting another task doesn’t require you to prepare another host worktree and sandbox, and the agent has Git access in each working directory. Clone mode supports this internal-worktree approach too.

Those tasks share tools and services, so running servers or changing the environment still needs coordination. Separate sandboxes are useful when tasks need independent environments as well as separate files. Branches alone don’t isolate simultaneous edits in one working directory.

Industry observers note that that independence adds some distance when you want to try the result. Your usual local editor isn’t looking at these files, and a development server running inside the sandbox needs a published port to reach it from your browser.

For a web app preview, ask the agent:.

Start the development server on port 8080, bound to 0.0.0.0.

Then publish the port from another terminal on the host:.

It has been revealed that open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. It’s possible to work interactively this way, but there’s more ceremony than opening a project already on your filesystem.

According to recent reports, an environment file can make setup repeatable, selecting tools and cloning the repository at creation with something like the community github-clone kit. Recreating the sandbox then gives you a fresh environment. Push or copy out work you want to retain first: removing a sandbox deletes files held only there.

Sources indicate that an API change might need a corresponding frontend change, or another repository might provide useful reference material. You can mount several directories into one sandbox, with read-only access for reference repositories. Local editing and previews remain available, but each writable checkout needs branch and change coordination. Task-specific checkouts also leave directories to clean up afterward.

A workspace manager such as jganoff/wsp can assemble selected repositories for a task. Mounting that workspace gives the agent the projects it needs together. These are standard clones with their own Git metadata, so the agent retains Git access, unlike a mounted linked worktree.

In a recent development, the same scope fits inside a mountless sandbox: clone the repositories needed there and keep the whole workspace in the sandbox. The number of repositories and where their files live are separate choices.

According to recent reports, the checkout’s location, the sandbox’s lifetime, and the repositories it contains are choices you can combine. You can keep a project sandbox around for many tasks, or mount a workspace assembled for one job. What suits you may change when you want to work more closely with the agent, or give it more room to manage the work itself.

The Git workflows documentation covers the mechanics of direct mounts, clone mode, and host worktrees.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Win4Wine runs the genuine Explorer shell atop Linux.
  • Industry observers note that win4Wine is one of the more remarkable and creative hacks we've read about in recent years.
  • As its GitHub repository explains: "The taskbar, Start menu, desktop and folder windows are XP's real ones, and Linux applications get XP's frames and taskbar buttons.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Win4Wine runs the genuine Explorer shell atop Linux.

Industry observers note that win4Wine is one of the more remarkable and creative hacks we've read about in recent years. It runs Windows XP's genuine Explorer shell through patched Wine on Debian 13, with a custom window manager integrating Linux applications into the desktop.

As its GitHub repository explains: "The taskbar, Start menu, desktop and folder windows are XP's real ones, and Linux applications get XP's frames and taskbar buttons.".

In a recent development, this impressive, possibly demented project has English installation instructions and a README, although its design documents are in Japanese. We found Mozilla's built-in translation handled those pretty well.

Its developer goes by miKuta0407 on GitHub, their homepage, and X.

In a recent development, also note, you're going to need some Windows installation media for the full experience. The README states: "No Microsoft files are included. Only the files that are needed are extracted locally from your own ISO.".

It supports Windows XP Professional SP3 installation images in 32-bit Japanese or English editions, with an experimental option for Windows 7 SP1 x64. Without either Windows image, it can download and use ReactOS's free software shell instead, for what it terms "a Windows 2000-like classic look." In our view, that sounds much better anyway.

Before any former Windows users cry hurray and reach for an optical drive, this is not some ready-to-run project. The top of the README warns: "This is a personal, experimental project, not a finished product for daily use." The developer has tested it only on a fresh Debian 13 installation and recommends a VM or spare machine, rather than an existing working desktop, which sounds like an excellent precaution to us.

Also, before you ask, yes, it was vibe-coded with Claude.

We found ourselves reminded of another crazy-but-is-it project that we wrote about back in January: What if Linux ran Windows... and meant it? Meet Loss32. The Loss32 proposal was even more extreme. It suggested replacing essentially the entire Linux userland, so it would be a Linux kernel running Wine with a Windows desktop and Windows apps.

However, Mikuta-san was way ahead of us – lower down, the README mentions and even links to Loss32. Saying that, since it launched at the end of 2025, the bottom of the Loss32 web page indicates a couple of updates, reporting on delays in getting it working. That, to be honest, did not shock us, but we still admire the let's-do-this spirit. The developer also seems to have got slightly distracted by a previous project, touchHLE: high-level emulator for early iOS apps.

Recent findings suggest that loss32, in turn, reminded us of Neptune OS, an attempt to give seL4 a Windows personality transplant. We wrote about that back in 2022, and work on it has continued: the project page indicates updates in recent months. The team has also pushed out preview releases in 2022, 2024, 2025, and most recently in September.

In a recent development, this OS face transplant also reminded us of our article, Classic 7 is Windows 10 LTSC cosplaying as Windows 7. Some people really miss the look and feel of vintage Windows. Can someone do Windows NT 4 next, please? ®.

#161336. Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

📅 25 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2497 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

📅 25 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2497 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost.
  • Our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it?
  • Sources indicate that most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it? We introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), and applied to a GPT-OSS 120B model compressed to 60B parameters and quantized to MXFP4, it produces a model that beats its own full-precision (bfloat16) version on 7 of 9 benchmarks. The 4-bit model ends up smaller, cheaper to run, and more accurate than the checkpoint it was quantized from. This inverts the usual relationship between a 4-bit model and the 16-bit model it came from.

Sources indicate that most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage. The difference between methods is entirely in that last step.

The dominant healing recipe is quantization-aware training (QAT). It inserts fake-quantization operators into the forward pass and keeps fine-tuning the model on a task loss, so the weights learn to tolerate the low-precision representation. In practice this means re-running an already expensive multi-stage post-training process, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, agentic tuning, through a noisier, lower-precision forward pass. It is costly, and as our results show, it can also become unstable if training continues too long past its best point.

An alternative, quantization-aware distillation (QAD), avoids re-running that history. Instead of a task loss, it distills a frozen full-precision teacher directly into the quantized student through a KL-divergence loss on the output logits. This works well when the only change is quantization, because a genuine full-precision version of the exact same model exists to act as teacher. But once a model has gone through structural compression, fewer layers, heads, or neurons, and not just fewer bits, that assumption breaks. There is no independently trained full-precision version of the smaller architecture. The only candidate teacher is the recovered bfloat16 checkpoint, which is itself a distilled approximation of the original model. Distilling from it anchors the quantized student to a degraded target and caps its accuracy at that recovered checkpoint's own ceiling.

So the question of how to heal a model that has been both structurally compressed and quantized was, until now, genuinely open.

It has been revealed that QAH removes that ceiling with one change: it distills directly from the original, pre-compression model rather than from the recovered one. Teacher and student do not even share an architecture. The teacher is full-size and full-precision, the student is half the size and running in MXFP4. Because a teacher's output distribution is architecture-agnostic, nothing about the size or shape mismatch prevents the transfer. The student never sees hard labels, only the teacher's output distribution, matched through KL divergence on the logits.

This reframes what the quantization stage is doing. Under QAH it is no longer a lossy postprocessing step applied after healing is finished. It is a second, full pass of distillation against the original teacher, supervision that the bfloat16 checkpoint never received. The 4-bit student is not compensating for information lost to quantization; it is picking up information the earlier recovery stage did not have the time or data to transfer.

Industry observers note that there is also a stability benefit that falls out of the loss itself. Because KL distillation ties the student to a fixed teacher distribution, once the student catches up there is no further pressure for it to drift. A cross-entropy task loss, by contrast, keeps pushing the student toward hard labels indefinitely. That difference turns out to matter for both accuracy and training stability, as the comparison below shows.

It has been revealed that to make QAH work at long context, where the healing corpus includes documents up to 32k tokens, we reuse the memory-efficient chunked KL-divergence loss from our companion paper on efficient distillation. That loss computes the KL one slice of the sequence at a time and never materializes the full vocabulary-by-sequence grid, which is what makes 32k-token healing fit inside a fixed GPU memory budget. We covered the mechanics of that loss in a previous post.

Sources indicate that QAH overview. After structural compression and quantization, capabilities drop sharply. QAH distills from the original model, a frozen teacher whose logits are precomputed offline, rather than from the recovered checkpoint. Source: paper Figure 1.

Sources indicate that we applied QAH to a GPT-OSS 120B model, compressed to 60B parameters and recovered in bfloat16, then re-quantized to MXFP4 under QAH. The natural comparison is against that same 60B model's bfloat16 checkpoint, the best full-precision version of this architecture that exists. The QAH model wins on 7 of the 9 benchmarks.

In a recent development, the two benchmarks where QAH trails, MMLU-Pro and SciCode, lose by less than a point and a half. Everywhere else the 4-bit model is ahead of its own 16-bit source, and the largest gains land on exactly the capabilities compression usually damages most: long-context reasoning (+7.4 on AA-LCR) and math (+5.6 on AIME 2025).

The comparison against the original 120B teacher is just as telling. Despite running at half the teacher's parameter count and roughly a quarter of its weight memory, the QAH model surpasses the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench (66.5 vs. 66.0) and comes within 1.6 points on GPQA Diamond (67.4 vs. 69.0). The largest remaining gap against the teacher is on AA-LCR, an extreme long-context benchmark where the capacity lost to compression is intrinsically the hardest to recover.

Sources indicate that the 4-bit QAH model matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, and beats the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench. Source: paper Figure 2.

To isolate the effect of the loss function from everything else, we also compared QAH directly against QAT under matched conditions, quantizing a GPT-OSS 9B model to MXFP4 and tracking average performance across MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond as training progresses.

Sources indicate that both methods reach a similar peak, 54.9 for QAH against 54.6 for QAT, so on best-case accuracy they are effectively tied. The difference is in how they get there and what happens afterwards. QAH reaches its peak in about 100 steps, roughly 7 times faster than QAT's 700, and then stays within about two points of that peak for the rest of training. QAT collapses sharply once past its peak, shedding nearly 19 points by step 1,200.

According to recent reports, the practical consequence is a real deployment risk difference. A QAT checkpoint needs careful early stopping against a held-out signal to avoid shipping a model that has already started to degrade, whereas a sufficiently trained QAH checkpoint can be served safely because it simply does not drift. This is consistent with the mechanism: KL distillation against a frozen teacher gives the student no incentive to move once it matches the teacher, while a cross-entropy objective keeps pushing on hard labels and eventually erodes capabilities the model inherited from the original.

Sources indicate that QAH peaks at 54.9 in roughly 100 steps and holds; QAT reaches 54.6 only around step 700, then loses nearly 19 points by step 1,200. Source: paper Figure 3.

The accuracy story comes paired with the efficiency story that motivated compression in the first place. At 4-bit precision the QAH model uses roughly 4 times less weight memory than the bfloat16 student, and at half the parameter count of the 120B teacher it roughly halves compute per token, which is what lets it run on substantially smaller hardware. For model families that ship in bfloat16 rather than 4-bit, the combined parameter and precision reduction would be closer to 8 times less compute per token.

Sources indicate that the takeaway is that a compressed, 4-bit model does not have to be a lower-accuracy version of its full-precision counterpart. With this healing recipe it can be smaller, cheaper to serve, and more accurate at the same time, and it reaches that point in a fraction of the training a QAT recipe would need. Quantization stops being a tax you pay for efficiency and becomes an extra opportunity to teach the model.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making large models smaller and cheaper to run without giving up the capabilities that make them useful. It sits alongside our companion work on efficient distillation, which supplies the long-context training machinery QAH depends on.

According to recent reports, want the full technical details, including the healing pipeline, the chunked KL implementation for long-context healing, and the distributed-training findings? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying compression and healing to your own models.

Industry observers note that making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as rbtv77 gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

This is a really fascinating take on model compression 🤯🔥. The idea that a 4-bit model can actually outperform the full-precision version turns the usual assumption about quantization completely upside down.... Instead of simply accepting the accuracy loss that comes with compression, QAH seems to show how targeted recovery can bring back—and even improve—important capabilities like reasoning, math, and coding. 🧠⚡.

It has been revealed that what really caught my attention is the result with the compressed GPT-OSS 120B → 60B model.... Getting a smaller MXFP4 model to beat its own bfloat16 checkpoint on 7 of 9 benchmarks is pretty impressive. 📊🚀 It makes the whole compress-then-heal pipeline feel much more practical for real-world deployment, especially when memory usage and inference costs matter.

I also like the broader implication here.... Quantization doesn't necessarily have to mean sacrificing model quality if the recovery process is designed with the quantized model in mind. 💡🔧 A smaller model that costs less to operate while still delivering stronger benchmark performance could be a huge advantage for teams trying to deploy capable LLMs efficiently.

Definitely an interesting direction for efficient AI deployment.... Turning a heavily compressed 4-bit model into something that can outperform its larger full-precision counterpart is the kind of result that makes you rethink what "compression" actually means. 👏🔥 Really curious to see how far Quantization-Aware Healing can go across other architectures and workloads.... 🚀🧠.

According to recent reports, A bit of context on what the paper is: it's an applied case study, not a theoretical claim. The result we stand behind is narrow and reproducible: the shipped 4-bit checkpoint scores above the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, rather than below it, which is the usual outcome of direct post-training quantization. The Ecosystem is the Answer: Docker, the Blueprint Alliance, and the Importance of Collaboration in the Agentic Era

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1310 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, the average global Fortune 500 enterprise had fewer than 15 AI agents in use.
  • Today, most security leaders face an agentic Sophie’s choice: allow AI adoption without the right controls and hope for the best, or block it and become the obstacle to a priority the business has already set (while adoption continues in the shadows, anyway).
  • It has been revealed that but there is a third option, one in which organizations fully tap into the transformative power of agentic agents without having to live in fear of a catastrophic security failure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, the average global Fortune 500 enterprise had fewer than 15 AI agents in use. Gartner expects that number to explode to more than 150,000 by 2028. Only 13 percent of organizations think they have the right governance for today, and AI is evolving and moving faster than any other technology paradigm in our history.

Today, most security leaders face an agentic Sophie’s choice: allow AI adoption without the right controls and hope for the best, or block it and become the obstacle to a priority the business has already set (while adoption continues in the shadows, anyway).

It has been revealed that but there is a third option, one in which organizations fully tap into the transformative power of agentic agents without having to live in fear of a catastrophic security failure. The good news is history has already shown how to get there.

Recent findings suggest that historically, technology adoption has followed a reliable pattern. A capability spreads, each vendor and team builds its own approach, the inconsistency becomes expensive and ineffective, leading the industry to agree to a shared baseline. Adoption then accelerates.

Industry observers note that take the credit card industry, for example. The big credit brands each ran their own security programs, and merchants had to satisfy every one. This was, of course, cumbersome for the vendors, but also for the customers, too. Every time a customer wanted to adopt a new technology, they had to manually build out security and adoption aims, adding significant adoption and procurement delays.

Rather than continue on their own, the credit card companies came together to create PCI DSS 1.0 in December 2004 and formed the PCI Security Standards Council in 2006. Buyers now had one thing to ask for, and auditors had one thing to check. Collaboration overcame complexity, and everyone benefited.

In a recent development, security-minded technologists can find another example closer to home in the Center for Internet Security (CIS). In the early days of the internet, cybersecurity was a veritable wild west. Enter the CIS, which was founded in 2000 because the industry lacked prescriptive, recognized hardening standards. To this day, each CIS Benchmark is built by consensus among volunteer experts, vendors, and academics.

Docker itself is no stranger to the development and furthering of shared standards. As just one example, in 2015, Docker contributed its image format and runC runtime to the Open Container Initiative. A shared baseline at the runtime layer let registries, runtimes, and clouds interoperate.

Each of these examples played a different role: PCI mandated, CIS guided, and OCI standardized.

Agents will need elements of all three.

Industry observers note that agents are in the everyone-builds-their-own phase. Each product solves a real piece of the problem, but which piece, and how the pieces fit, is rarely clear. “Agent governance” or even “AI governance” can mean almost anything.

It has been revealed that adoption is incremental. A developer allows common commands, widens filesystem access, then connects GitHub, a cloud tool and an MCP server, each through a prompt that makes sense on its own. The logs mostly record that the developer acted. Security is often the last to know.

Much of the risk is familiar. Shadow adoption looks a lot like early SaaS and cloud. Credential sprawl and supply chain exposure are old problems. Inventory, least privilege, audit, and joiner-mover-leaver discipline still apply.

Several things are new, however:.

Existing controls still matter, but they were not built for this mix of programmability, access, and autonomy.

Recent findings suggest that as with the credit industry and PCI, cybersecurity and the CIS, and containerization and OCI, collaboration offers the answer to this new era of complexity. That’s why Docker is not just focused on building tools like Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance, but in taking an ecosystem-centric approach to problem solving for our customers. Docker is already a founding participant in multiple initiatives aimed at developing valuable reference architectures for AI security workflows, including the Blueprint Alliance and Agent Baseline.

Both start from the same premise: no single vendor or enforcement point can solve this.

The Blueprint Alliance sets out how the pieces fit together. Okta, AWS, CrowdStrike, Databricks, Docker, Google Cloud, Lovable, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Wiz and Zscaler are founding members, with GE Appliances and World Central Kitchen as strategic advisors. The open, multi-vendor reference architecture answers four questions: Where are my agents? What can they do? What are they doing? How do I respond? Members have committed to interoperability testing over MCP, OCSF, SSF and CAEP, and to publishing reference integrations.

In a recent development, agent Baseline sets out what each piece must do and how to verify it. It fills the gap between threat lists, which say what can go wrong, and the capabilities an enterprise needs in place. It defines six outcomes (Discover, Constrain, Authorize, Observe, Validate and Respond) and 35 open, versioned controls, each with a permanent identifier you can cite in an audit finding or RFP response. Docker, Snyk and Keycard drafted it, and the current release is v1.0-draft. Controls stay where they already live, in the identity provider, the sandbox and the SIEM.

According to recent reports, blueprint says how the pieces connect. Agent Baseline says what must be true and can be checked. Both advise starting with discovery before policy, and testing the kill switch before you need it.

According to recent reports, for partners, the roles are defined. The Alliance whitepaper assigns integrators the operating model: assessing a customer’s current stack against the architecture, assigning ownership across the pillars, tiering risk, and running lifecycle and compliance over time. Technology partners get a published target to integrate against, and the reference integrations cross vendor lines by design. The partners who can design, integrate and operate across those lines are the ones customers keep.

Most Alliance members govern agents from the outside: who the agent is, what it can reach, and what it is observed doing. Docker governs the inside: the environment where the agent executes. As agents move from suggesting actions to taking them, trust has to extend beyond the model to the places where they run. Docker has helped define a shared baseline for the runtime before, and now we’re working with the Alliance and our partners to make that baseline concrete, open, and testable in the age of agents.

The execution environment is where policy gets enforced and evidence gets produced.

According to recent reports, that boundary is where policy gets enforced and evidence gets produced. The Alliance whitepaper notes that without runtime support to pause an agent without collateral impact, API-driven containment “provides a false sense of security.” Agent Baseline’s CON-03 calls for isolated, confined execution, which is the job of Docker Sandboxes, while Docker MCP Gateway and Docker Hardened Images cover tool access and the supply chain.The Secure Software Factory reference architecture, drafted in part by Docker authors, applies Agent Baseline to agents that ship code.

In a recent development, baselines let adoption move faster, not slower. Security and platform leaders can assess against the baseline today. Agent Baseline controls are citable, and Okta offers an AI Blueprint Assessment Tool. Partners can start with the Docker Navigator Partner Program, which rewards AI governance work, and with the reference integrations the Alliance publishes. Docker’s VP of Partners Leon Jones explains the program here. Download the blueprint at blueprintalliance.ai and read the controls at agentbaseline.org.

According to recent reports, docker launches a upcoming brand built on trust. Learn why Docker is evolving for AI agents, what stays the same, and how to run agents securely with Docker.

Docker publishes fixed images for both Java4Shell and the NGINX HTTP/2 in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog.

Learn how Docker AI Governance secures agentic AI with sandbox policies, MCP tool governance, and audit visibility to support controlled AI agent workflows.

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1247 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities.
  • Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process.
  • Continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting problems by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define.

Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes.

Continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems.

It has been revealed that continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path.

For each confirmed problem, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate.

It has been revealed that AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in actionTo show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide.

The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context.

I open one of my environments. The Issues tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues.

According to recent reports, the Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other people in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict.

In a recent development, the Remediation section shows a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the issue is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from.

The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow.

The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that challenges are built from.

The Scans tab shows the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context.

Recent findings suggest that in a single workflow, I work through the validated issues in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships.

Recent findings suggest that now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page.

In a recent development, to learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

JetBrains finds agents may cheat with open source

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI coding agents caught peeking at GitHub answers, stumble when JetBrains hides the crib sheet.
  • JetBrains has revamped a benchmark for evaluating large language models after suspecting too many agents gamed their tasks the first time round.
  • The company labelled this agentic practice "reward hacking" in a post summarizing the results of its revised evaluation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI coding agents caught peeking at GitHub answers, stumble when JetBrains hides the crib sheet.

JetBrains has revamped a benchmark for evaluating large language models after suspecting too many agents gamed their tasks the first time round.

The company labelled this agentic practice "reward hacking" in a post summarizing the results of its revised evaluation.

Sources indicate that like its predecessor, Kotlin Benchmark 2.0 is a collection of tasks that evaluates how well AI coding agents work with the Kotlin programming language, in order to help Kotlin programmers decide which agent-model configurations to use. The tasks include fixing tricky problems in Kotlin code across different domains, and making corrections to multiple files.

The revised benchmark now includes 30 Kotlin multi-file code problems that have not been exposed to the public in any way before. The revised test all but guarantees that the agents have not encountered this set of problems, or potential solutions, before. Another 70 tasks are based on code that resides in public repositories.

The test also blocked all network access for the open source tasks, except for what was needed to communicate with the model itself. This minimized the possibility that the agent could look for an existing answer already posted, perhaps through a patch or pull request.

A 30-minute limit was set for each task.

Overall, the agents were significantly less accurate when solving problems on codebases they had never encountered. Top resolution rates dropped rather suspiciously from 86.2 percent on tasks based on open source repositories to 60  percent on those based on closed source repositories.

Although the agents lacked network access, JetBrains boffins theorized that they might have benefited from encountering and internalizing these open source repositories during training. Only the private repositories were completely new to them.

Also curious was how a different set of models excelled at the closed source problems, compared to those models that usually did better on the open source tasks.

When restricted to closed source tasks, two dark horse models rose to the top: Gemini 3.8 Flash, via Antigravity CLI, topped the list with a 60  percent success rate, closely followed by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (running on OpenCode) at 58.9 percent.

Of the two, the open weight DeepSeek was far cheaper (at $0.08 per task) than the closed weight Gemini ($1.74 per task), however.

In a recent development, in contrast, Opus 5.5 completed only 53.3 percent of the tasks at $1.21 per task, and Fable 5.1 completed only 44.4 percent of the tasks, at a luxurious $3.27 per task. Claude Code harnessed both of these models.

Claude’s lackluster completion rates on closed source tasks are somewhat sus given how both of these Anthropic models scored significantly higher on tasks using open source materials.

In fact Claude ran the table when it came to open source: Fable 5.1 topped the charts with 86.2 percent accuracy, closely followed by Opus 5.5 at 84.8 percent accuracy.

(Kotlin people will pay dearly for the extra sliver of Anthropic accuracy: The average cost of Fable completing a Kotlin cleanup task runs $2.38, while Opus could do the job for $0.68.).

One possible interpretation of these disparate numbers is that models are drawing from their own knowledge bases instead of reasoning from scratch. Whether this is cheating or the models simply working as intended might be more a matter of philosophical debate.

Mark Hinkle, founder of the AIE Network consultancy, suspects the concern of integrity may go deeper.

"Private code doesn't stop reward hacking, it changes the shortcut," he wrote to The Register on LinkedIn.

Industry observers note that "On public code the agent goes and finds the answer somebody has already published. On private code there's no answer to find, so it satisfies whatever is checking it. I treat these things like entry-level employees, and a sharp latest hire figures out fast what the boss actually looks at.".

According to recent reports, jetBrains did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but concluded in its post that more investigation is needed. It promises that its people will pore over the open source results to see if any have been contaminated by the LLMs' own memory. It also looks to run its own static analysis tool, Qodana, against the results to check for errors.

Sireesha Pulipati, a staff data engineer and AI observer, suggested, also by LinkedIn, that JetBrains may have needed more specificity in its agent instructions.

Industry observers note that "Out of the box [an agent] tends to reach for generic patterns. But when we give it instructions and skills that tell it where to look for our patterns and context, it follows them. A well-controlled harness, with those standards built in, is what makes the agent useful," Pulipati wrote.

In a recent development, so good on JetBrains for providing Kotlin consumers some information about working with AI, but, as always, AI benchmarks should be approached with extreme side-eye. ®.

Granite 4.2 LLMs: How They're Built

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A technical walkthrough of how we built the Granite 4.2 reasoning model family.
  • Industry observers note that TL;DR: Granite 4.2 is our first family of dense, decoder-only reasoning LLMs, released in three sizes: 3B, 8B, and 30B.
  • It has been revealed that granite 4.2 is the reasoning-focused release of the Granite language-model family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A technical walkthrough of how we built the Granite 4.2 reasoning model family.

Industry observers note that TL;DR: Granite 4.2 is our first family of dense, decoder-only reasoning LLMs, released in three sizes: 3B, 8B, and 30B. These models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were pre-trained from scratch on roughly 15T tokens with a five-phase strategy that extends the context window to 512K tokens, supervised fine-tuned on chain-of-thought, reasoning, and agentic-trajectory data, then post-trained with a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline. That pipeline includes agentic RL, where the 8B and 30B models learn to act with tools inside real sandboxed environments. Every model has a thinking / non-thinking switch, a low-effort thinking mode that spends a short reasoning budget on easy questions, and native tool calling. All Granite 4.2 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

It has been revealed that granite 4.2 is the reasoning-focused release of the Granite language-model family. Earlier Granite releases were strong instruction-following assistants; Granite 4.2 adds explicit reasoning. Every model can produce a chain of thought before its answer and can run in thinking or non-thinking mode depending on how much deliberation a task needs. A low-effort mode falls between the two, spending a short reasoning budget on easy questions.

According to recent reports, the three sizes (3B, 8B, and 30B) share the same architectural design and follow the same training pipeline (base model, SFT, then multi-stage RL), each at its own scale. All three are strong reasoners and instruction followers. The clearest capability split highlights up in post-training. The 8B and 30B models additionally go through an agentic RL block that teaches them to operate as agents: calling tools, editing and running code, driving a terminal, and searching the web inside real environments. Every model supports native tool calling. Served through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (for example, with vLLM), it emits tool calls in the OpenAI function-calling format and plugs into agentic harnesses without extra glue. Granite 4.2 is also supported in SGLang, see the SGLang cookbook for a ready-to-serve recipe.

The rest of this post walks through the build: architecture, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, the multi-stage RL pipeline, and results.

Granite 4.2 models are built on a decoder-only dense transformer architecture with the following core components:.

Granite 4.2 models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five-phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre-training, phases 3–4 perform mid-training with progressively higher-quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long-context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase uses a distinct data mixture and learning-rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web-scale data toward more curated, high-quality sources.

The pre-training recipe closely follows the previous generation; for a detailed treatment of the data blend, phase schedule, and long-context extension, see the Granite 4.1 blog.

In a recent development, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) turns the base model into a reliable instruction-following, reasoning, and tool-using assistant. The SFT data mixture combines agentic (31.6%) and non-agentic (68.4%) data, totaling approximately 7.2 million samples, or roughly 100B tokens, of which about 65B are trainable.

The agentic corpus covers a broad range of domains, including software engineering (SWE, 69%), tool calling (12.1%), terminal use (8.0%), math (3.5%), search (0.8%), and action (0.2%). These samples and trajectories are generated using a diverse set of agent scaffolds and harnesses, including OpenHands, OpenCode, Terminus-2, SWE-agent, OpenResearcher, MiniSWE, OpenSeeker, EnvScaler, Gemini CLI, Hermes, Codex, and Goose. The agentic data combines samples from both open-source datasets and our own synthetically generated RL environments, spanning a variety of agent–harness combinations.

The non-agentic corpus consists of several major categories: instruction following (18.8%), coding (18.8%), math (14.6%), multilingual (7.0%), science (5.4%), reasoning (3.0%), and safety (0.8%).

It has been revealed that we apply multiple stages of quality control before a sample enters the final SFT mixture. First, data from different sources is normalized and reformatted into a consistent OpenAI Chat format, making the conversation structure and tool interactions uniform across datasets and scaffolds.

We then use GPT-OSS-120B and Gemma 4 as LLM-based judges to assess sample quality. Low-scoring samples are removed, as are samples containing hallucinated or fabricated information, invalid tool interactions, or tool calls to functions that are not defined in the corresponding tool list. Several targeted, dataset-specific heuristic rules are also applied where appropriate to further improve quality and remove known sources of noise.

In a recent development, finally, we perform both local and global deduplication. Deduplication is based on SHA-256 hashes computed over the combination of the tools and messages fields, removing duplicate samples both within individual data sources and across the overall SFT mixture.

The complete corpus is first globally shuffled to reduce ordering effects and ensure that samples from different domains are well mixed during training. The shuffled corpus is then partitioned into equally sized .parquet shards, which are tokenized using the model's tokenizer and chat template and prepared for large-scale distributed training.

Before launching the final large-scale runs, we tune hyperparameters on representative configurations, sweeping learning-rate schedules, initial learning rates, and warm-up ratios to find settings that train stably across model sizes. The final training configuration is summarized below:.

For the 30B model, we additionally perform a second phase of SFT focused specifically on agentic coding. In this phase, agentic, SWE, and coding data are upsampled to increase their effective contribution to the training distribution, while approximately 16% of the mixture is retained as replay data from the original SFT corpus.

Sources indicate that the 30B model is then fine-tuned for roughly one additional epoch at a lower learning rate of 3.0e-6. This targeted second phase increases the model's exposure to agentic coding trajectories without discarding the capabilities acquired during the initial SFT phase.

Industry observers note that after SFT, we apply a multi-stage, multi-environment reinforcement learning pipeline. Rather than a single RL pass, we run a chain of focused stages spanning many environments: math, code, science, instruction following, tool use, and structured output, then software engineering, terminal use, and web search. Each stage is an independent RL run that targets one capability and warm-starts from the previous stage's checkpoint.

Figure 1. The staged RL curriculum. Foundational RL (verifiable rewards + skill boosters) runs for all sizes; the agentic RL block (SWE → Terminal → Search) runs for 8B and 30B only. Every model finishes with RLHF. Each stage is a separate GRPO run that warm-starts from the previous checkpoint.

Every stage trains with asynchronous GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), so the generator and trainer halves of the loop never block on each other. A pool of generation workers keeps sampling responses and dropping the finished trajectories into a shared buffer; once the buffer holds a full step's worth, the trainer pulls that batch, takes an optimizer step, and streams the updated parameters back to the generator workers without pausing them. A refresh can land partway through a rollout, leaving a single trajectory stitched together from two adjacent policy versions. We allow this instead of paying to prevent it: the workers reuse their existing KV cache rather than rebuilding it after each refresh, and the one guardrail is a limit that keeps them from drifting more than a single enhancement behind the trainer, which bounds how off-policy any sample can get. Whatever mismatch survives that limit is handled in the objective by truncated importance sampling, which clamps the train-versus-generation log-probability ratio to a fixed ceiling so a handful of stale tokens cannot dominate an update.

Advantages are group-relative with a leave-one-out baseline: each response is judged against the mean reward of the other samples drawn for the same prompt, which removes the need for a separate value network. To make this concrete, take RLVR, the first and longest-running stage: each step pairs 256 prompts with 16 sampled responses apiece for a 4,096-example batch, which the trainer consumes in a single optimizer step before the next rollout begins. Later stages keep this machinery unchanged and adjust only the per-stage shape, shown next.

Sources indicate that the pipeline keeps a common backbone of hyperparameters across every stage, which makes the curriculum easier to run and compare. A handful of knobs are fixed everywhere:.

Recent findings suggest that what changes from stage to stage is the shape of each run: how many prompts and generations per step, how long the context is, whether the agent loop runs, and how hard we pull back toward the reference policy. The table below gives the exact settings for the 30B chain, stage by stage:.

Parameters shown for the 30B model. Global batch size = prompts/step × generations/prompt (e.g. 256 × 16 = 4096 for RLVR). The 3B and 8B models use the same recipe and hyperparameters with fewer stages (see How the Three Sizes Differ); the stage list is what changes, not the knobs.

Recent findings suggest that the KL schedule follows the reward type: explore freely where the reward is objective and verifiable (RLVR and SWE 2 run at KL 0), and stay close to the reference where the objective is preference, safety, or a narrow skill graft (RLHF and the code booster use KL 0.05). The rollout-turns column counts the environment interactions GRPO itself sees per rollout. In every case the model is trained on complete, real-environment trajectories.

Each stage is a separate RL run with a single objective and its own reward signal. When it finishes, its policy is exported to Hugging Face format and becomes the base model for the next stage, so the pipeline is a sequence of warm-starts:.

Recent findings suggest that the 8B and 30B models follow the full ladder. The 3B model takes a shortened path: foundational RL and alignment, without the agentic block.

A stage is defined mostly by how it is rewarded. Across the pipeline there are three reward types, and a single stage can use more than one:.

Verifiable rewards are objective and hard to game, so the pipeline front-loads them. Judge- and preference-based rewards handle open-ended qualities that no checker can express. Agentic-outcome rewards are the sparsest: often a single bit at the end of a long tool-use trajectory.

RLVR is the foundational stage and the broadest data mix in the pipeline: a single blended dataset spanning many verifiable domains.

Each task type carries its own verifier, so the reward is grounded per example. RLVR runs for two rounds on 3B and 8B, and three on 30B. Each round is a fresh warm-started run on a re-weighted mix of public and internally curated RL data.

After RLVR, a few short booster stages sharpen specific capabilities that benefit from concentrated training focusing on the following domains:.

Sources indicate that boosters are small, focused runs. A light KL penalty keeps the model close to its current behavior while nudging one skill.

It has been revealed that in the agentic stages the model learns to act: call tools, observe results, and iterate inside a real environment, rewarded on whether the task was actually solved. These stages share the same shape: multi-turn tool use, real (not simulated) environments, sparse outcome rewards, and GRPO, warm-started from the coding-boosted checkpoint. They run in order: SWE → Terminal → Search.

It has been revealed that figure 2. The three agentic-RL environments. Each pairs a real harness with a real environment and a sparse, outcome-based reward. The 3B model runs none of these.

The final stage of every model is RLHF for human preference and safety. It optimizes against a generative reward model (GenRM) for preference, plus a safety reward covering jailbreak resistance and appropriate refusals. This stage uses the highest KL penalty in the pipeline, aligning tone and safety without eroding the capabilities the earlier stages built. In addition to human preference and safety alignment, this stage also applies a reasoning-length penalty to discourage overly verbose reasoning behavior acquired during earlier stages.

Same method and infrastructure; the difference is how far up the ladder each model goes.

3B is a strong foundational-RL model; 8B and 30B add the agentic-RL block on top, learning to act with tools in real environments.

It has been revealed that reinforcement learning at this scale needs infrastructure that can drive a training loop and a fleet of live environments at the same time. This matters most in the agentic stages, where every training example is a multi-turn rollout that edits code, runs commands, or browses the web. Granite 4.2's RL runs on two open components: NeMo-RL on the training side and NeMo-Gym on the rollout side.

According to recent reports, figure 3. The RL system. NeMo-RL drives the GRPO loop (Megatron-Core training backend, vLLM generation, and Megatron-Bridge for HF⇄Megatron weight conversion). NeMo-Gym orchestrates rollouts and hosts the tools, sandboxes, and reward/verifier calls as pluggable Resources.

That uniformity is what makes the staged curriculum above practical: a booster's rule-based checker and a full SWE sandbox present the same interface to GRPO.

This split is also what makes the asynchronous training loop described above physically possible: generation and policy updates live on separate GPU pools, so the expensive generation fleet — including the live agentic environments — stays busy instead of idling through optimizer steps.

Granite 4.2 was evaluated across agentic coding, general agentic and tool use, reasoning, chat and instruction following, and long context. The full benchmark table is below, followed by charts that break out the headline results by model size.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

The charts below break these results out by capability area.

Sources indicate that figure 4. Reasoning (pass@1). Scores rise consistently with model size across math (AIME25, HMMT), science (GPQA), and code reasoning (LiveCodeBench, SciCode).

It has been revealed that figure 5. Agentic coding resolve rates. The agentic-RL block is trained only for 8B and 30B; the 30B model leads across SWE-Bench variants and Terminal-Bench.

According to recent reports, figure 6. General agentic and tool-use benchmarks, reported for all three sizes.

According to recent reports, we also released four quantized variants of the Granite 4.2 models for inference with vLLM. The models are converted to FP8, NVFP4, and MXFP4 using LLM Compressor, and to the GGUF format using the llama.cpp framework for reduced-memory deployment.

It has been revealed that the FP8 version is quantized with dynamic per-channel weights and per-token activations. No calibration is used.

The NVFP4 and MXFP4 versions are quantized using GPTQ calibrated on 2K samples drawn from the SFT dataset. Max context length is 2K during calibration.

Conversion of the Granite 4.2 models to GGUF is done with the canonical llama.cpp tool as described in https://github.com/IBM/gguf#gguf-conversion--quantization.

Several GGUF formats are provided:.

We trained the Granite 4.2 language models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted by CoreWeave, featuring:.

This infrastructure delivers the high-bandwidth, low-latency communication required for efficient large-scale distributed training.

In a recent development, the training software stack is packaged into .sqsh container images, each giving a run a reproducible, portable environment with its SBSA-compatible CUDA targets, Linux aarch64 Python wheels, and GPU-specific binaries pinned. The large-scale SFT runs build on an NGC PyTorch base image (Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.8, Python 3.12); the RL stack runs in its own NeMo-RL container.

Sources indicate that granite models support tool calling with integrated reasoning: the model reasons about which tool to call and why before calling it. Tools are defined with the OpenAI function definition schema.

Sources indicate that granite models can serve as the backbone for agentic coding tools. Because they support reasoning and tool calling through the OpenAI-compatible API, they integrate with popular agentic harnesses without extra adapters. Start the vLLM server, then follow the harness-specific instructions below.

Configure ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json:.

Configure ~/.pi/agent/models.json:.
