BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?

📅 01 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1410 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 📄 Tech Report: http://allenai.org/papers/benchmirt | 📊 Data: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/benchmirt | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/BenchMIRT.
  • Today we’re introducing BenchMIRT, a new method for auditing LLM benchmarks at the level of individual prompts—the questions and tasks a model is scored on.
  • Sources indicate that A benchmark is usually designed to measure a particular ability, such as safety, general reasoning, or instruction following.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

📄 Tech Report: http://allenai.org/papers/benchmirt | 📊 Data: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/benchmirt | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/BenchMIRT.

Today we’re introducing BenchMIRT, a new method for auditing LLM benchmarks at the level of individual prompts—the questions and tasks a model is scored on.

Sources indicate that A benchmark is usually designed to measure a particular ability, such as safety, general reasoning, or instruction following. But the individual tasks inside it may depend on more than that stated goal. Take BBQ, a benchmark designed to test whether models rely on social stereotypes. One question asks about a grandson and grandfather trying to book an Uber. It probes age bias, but also requires the model to track who’s who and reason from the evidence provided rather than assumptions.

Industry observers note that and even within a single benchmark, different groups of questions and tasks can measure different things. WildJailbreak, for example, includes harmful jailbreak prompts alongside benign prompts designed to test whether a model refuses harmless requests too often. The harmful prompts are more closely associated with safety, while the benign prompts are more closely associated with general reasoning. Averaging them into a single benchmark score can obscure that difference.

Industry observers note that benchMIRT helps researchers separate those signals and see what’s actually driving a benchmark’s score. It does this by analyzing how models perform on each question or task and estimating which underlying capabilities are most closely associated with getting it right.

Recent findings suggest that benchMIRT takes cues from Item Response Theory (IRT), a technique originating in psychometrics—the field concerned with measuring abilities and traits from patterns of test responses. IRT starts from a simple idea: not every question tells you the same amount about the person taking a test. Some are harder than others, and some do a better job of distinguishing stronger performers from weaker ones.

Researchers have previously applied single-dimensional IRT to individual benchmarks, including in our Fluid Benchmarking work. BenchMIRT extends that approach with multidimensional IRT, or MIRT, allowing it to separate multiple capabilities that may contribute to performance on the same questions.

BenchMIRT applies IRT at both the model and question level. For a given model, it estimates the model’s strength on the capabilities reflected across the selected benchmarks. For each question, it estimates how difficult the question is and how well it distinguishes models that are stronger or weaker on those capabilities.

Sources indicate that we trained BenchMIRT on benchmarking results from 100 LLMs across 16 benchmarks and more than 34K questions. Six of those benchmarks measure general reasoning, including MMLU-Pro, GPQA, MATH, and BBH. The other 10 come from our Olmo 3 safety suite, including HarmBench, StrongReject, WildJailbreak, BBQ, WMDP, and XSTest.

Industry observers note that crucially, we didn’t tell BenchMIRT which benchmarks were measuring which capabilities. It independently recovered two dominant dimensions: safety and general reasoning. When we repeated our analysis from scratch, those same two dimensions emerged each time, suggesting the result was stable rather than specific to one analysis.

For many benchmarks, BenchMIRT largely confirmed their intended focus: strong performance on reasoning benchmarks tracked with reasoning ability, while strong performance on jailbreak and harmful-content benchmarks tracked with safety.

But BenchMIRT also revealed a more complicated picture in some evaluations.

BBQ, which evaluates social bias and is commonly grouped with safety benchmarks, aligned much more strongly with general reasoning in BenchMIRT’s analysis. That means a low BBQ score may partly reflect difficulty understanding or reasoning through certain questions, rather than safety behavior alone.

Industry observers note that WMDP behaves differently from most safety benchmarks. It tests dangerous dual-use knowledge in areas such as biology, chemistry, and cybersecurity—for example, knowledge that could help someone misuse a biological agent or exploit a computer system. BenchMIRT found that WMDP scores were more strongly associated with general reasoning than with safety. Stronger general reasoning, however, was associated with lower WMDP scores, because the benchmark counts refusing or failing to provide the dangerous knowledge as the desired response.

These findings don’t necessarily mean the benchmarks are flawed or incomplete. Rather, they show that a single benchmark score can combine several different signals—and that BenchMIRT can help disentangle those signals and make the score easier to interpret.

According to recent reports, item difficulty and discrimination in both dimensions for Harmbench. Dimension 0 models the safety dimension, while Dimension 1 maps to the general reasoning dimension.

Bar size and direction show the Pearson correlation, across 100 open-weight LLMs, between BenchMIRT ability scores and benchmark scores on a −1 to 1 scale—pink for general reasoning and teal for safety; bars extending left of center are negative. Bold with underline marks each row’s stronger correlation, except where the two are too close to separate; asterisks mark p < 0.01.

BenchMIRT can also help identify which questions in an evaluation are most informative about the capability the benchmark is trying to measure.

Using BenchMIRT’s question-level estimates, we ranked questions across the same 16 benchmarks used to train BenchMIRT and kept those that did the best job of distinguishing stronger from weaker models, while still preserving a mix of easier and harder questions.

Across those benchmarks, keeping only 10% of the questions generally preserved nearly the same picture of which models were stronger or weaker on the underlying safety or reasoning capability as using the full set. Keeping 50% of the questions often matched the full benchmark’s measure of those capabilities even more closely.

Sources indicate that benchMIRT can also use the patterns it learns across models and questions to predict how a model would perform on a benchmark question it hasn’t been observed answering. In our experiments, it correctly predicted whether a model would answer a held-out question correctly 79% of the time. By comparison, a simpler approach that assumes a model will perform on each question about as well as it does on the benchmark overall was correct 70% of the time.

In practice, that means BenchMIRT can estimate model performance more precisely from what it has already learned about the model’s abilities and the demands of each question, without needing to evaluate every model on every question.

Recent findings suggest that benchMIRT offers a way to better understand and refine the benchmarks researchers use to evaluate model capabilities. By looking at individual questions rather than only overall scores, it can reveal when a benchmark mixes together different capabilities, identify clusters of questions that behave differently from the rest, and surface questions that add little useful information about the capability the benchmark is meant to measure.

There are important limitations. The models we used to train and evaluate BenchMIRT were all released by March 2025, so our analysis doesn’t capture how BenchMIRT behaves on newer generations of LLMs. And the dimensions BenchMIRT discovers depend on the benchmark set it’s given—safety and reasoning emerged as the dominant dimensions across the 16 benchmarks we selected for this project, but a different mix of evaluations could surface different underlying capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that there are trade-offs, too. If the goal is to rank models by their predicted performance on randomly held-out items, the benchmark’s average score performs slightly better than BenchMIRT. BenchMIRT’s advantage is the finer-grained picture it provides of performance on individual questions.

Sources indicate that that question-level detail can also cut both ways: the same estimates that help identify a benchmark’s most informative safety questions could be used to remove them, producing a weaker evaluation that an unsafe model could pass. Existing tools already make it possible to trim evaluations in similar ways, and we think the added transparency into what benchmark questions are actually measuring is worth that risk—but it’s a real one.

Still, we see BenchMIRT – and future tools like it – as a step toward more targeted benchmark design and efficient evaluation. By showing which questions are actually driving a benchmark’s results, these approaches could help researchers build evaluations that are smaller, more focused, and easier to interpret, while giving a clearer picture of the capabilities they’re meant to measure.

Industry observers note that good read! Reliable evaluation is essential for understanding how well AI systems perform and where they need improvement. Benchmarking and systematic testing can help developers make better decisions about model selection, application quality, and readiness for real-world use. In Generative AI app development, these practices are particularly useful for identifying limitations before expanding access or introducing additional features. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that openJDK and Oracle disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) on November 17, and NGINX released fixes for two HTTP/2 flaws the next day. Docker began publishing fixed images for both in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog starting that same day.

What we know about Java4Shell is that it’s a memory-corruption bug in the Java runtime that can let an attacker with no credentials run code inside a Java application. Many container images contain a Java runtime, including application images that bundle their own, so it affects teams well beyond the ones that write Java.

Docker Hardened Images are the trusted foundation your applications should run on, because a flaw in the runtime inside an image is fixed only when that image is rebuilt, and Docker rebuilds its hardened images as soon as upstream fixes become available. Fixed images for the Amazon Corretto, SapMachine and Azul Zulu runtimes and for NGINX are in the catalog today, with Eclipse Temurin following as soon as Adoptium completes its fixed builds.

Recent findings suggest that to decode Base64 promptly, the HotSpot JVM uses a hand-written routine built on AVX-512 instructions. That routine miscalculates a length when the input ends in unexpected padding and writes up to 62 bytes past the end of a buffer on the Java heap. Calif, the researchers who found it, turned that into heap disclosure and remote code execution.

They demonstrated code execution before authentication against default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and after authentication against Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. They note there is no universal exploit: each application needs its own, and they have not published those. As of November 18 there are no public reports of exploitation in the wild.

Recent findings suggest that oracle rates the issue 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1. The researchers rate it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. CISA has issued an alert urging immediate patching.

All three of these must be true.

Sources indicate that to check a host’s CPU, run this on the host or Kubernetes node. Hardened runtime images have no shell, so it will not run inside the container.

grep -m1 ‘^flags’ /proc/cpuinfo | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep -E ‘^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$’.

The host is affected if all four flags are printed.

Two other ways to check, for when a shell on the node is hard to get.

Ask the JVM. This works in hardened images:.

docker run –rm –entrypoint java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX.

Industry observers note that useAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check states otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on.

Industry observers note that ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type shows the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true.

Sources indicate that check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network.

In a recent development, ask the JVM. This works in hardened images:.

docker run –rm –entrypoint java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX.

UseAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check claims otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on.

Industry observers note that ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type shows the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true.

Check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network.

In a recent development, fixed. The published images report 17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 25.0.5.1.2 and 27.0.1.1.4.

Industry observers note that fixed. The published images report 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2 and 27.0.1.1+4.

Industry observers note that fixed. The published Zulu images we checked report 17.0.21.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2 and 27.0.1.1+4.

Waiting for Adoptium to complete its release. On November 18 Adoptium had published 27.0.1.1+4 for x86-64 Linux only. 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 and 25.0.5.1 were still in testing. Adoptium tracks progress in adoptium/temurin#326. Our published images still report 17.0.21+9, 21.0.13+9, 25.0.5+8 and 27.0.1.0.2+1, which are vulnerable.

Java 26 reached end of support in September 2026, so no fix is expected from any vendor, and it is not among the fixed lines in the OpenJDK advisory. If you run it, treat it as affected and keep the flag set. We recommend moving to Java 25 or updating to Java 27. If you cannot migrate yet, ask us whether Extended Lifecycle Support can cover your version. It is the Docker Hardened Images Enterprise add-on for software past its upstream end of life.

According to recent reports, not affected by this CVE and no action is needed for it. The same November enhancement fixes other complications in these lines, so update when new images arrive.

Application images that bundle Java, such as Keycloak, Jenkins, Kafka, Elasticsearch and Solr.

They follow the bundled runtime, which for many of them is Temurin, and they are rebuilt once the runtime they use is fixed. Until then, set the flag yourself.

Sources indicate that set the mitigation flag yourself on every JVM that is still waiting for a fixed runtime, and check what each image already sets before you do. Treat the flag as a stopgap, because a JVM is protected only if the flag reaches it when it starts, and a deployment setting or a start script can override it or drop it. A fixed runtime is the only thing that closes the problem, so move to the fixed image as soon as it is published.

The CPU check and the mitigation flag in the steps below apply to any image that runs a HotSpot-based OpenJDK build. The version strings in this post come from Docker Hardened Images, so for an image from another source, confirm the fixed build in that source’s advisory.

According to recent reports, the fixed build can only come from whoever builds your image, because the Java runtime and the system packages your application runs on come from the image underneath it. That dependency is why a hardened image is a necessary step toward a trusted software supply chain. With Docker Hardened Images, tracking each vendor’s fix and rebuilding on it is work Docker does for you. The images are minimal and secure by default, and they are built to serve as a trusted and verifiable upstream for your builds. You can move a service onto one by following the migration guide.

A container often runs more than one JVM, for example when a build tool forks a JVM for tests, an application server starts helper processes or a CI agent starts a JVM for every build step. The flag protects only the JVMs that receive it, and the variable most people reach for first is JAVA_OPTS, which Java does not read at all.

The JVM itself, however it is started. Includes javac, keytool and other JDK tools.

Yes, through the inherited environment.

A Java 8 JVM that sees it refuses to start. Some DHI FIPS images already set this variable.

Only the java launcher, Java 9 and later.

Yes, when the child is started with java.

Industry observers note that not read by javac, keytool or other JDK tools. DHI FIPS images set it. Java 8 ignores it.

Nothing downstream inherits it.

JAVA_OPTS, JENKINS_JAVA_OPTS, MAVEN_OPTS, ES_JAVA_OPTS and similar.

A start script, which copies the value onto one java command line.

Recent findings suggest that each script has its own rules. If nothing in the image reads the variable, it does nothing.

Recent findings suggest that five rules follow from that table. We tested each on DHI images.

JAVA_OPTS only works where a script reads it. With JAVA_OPTS=”-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” set and a plain java command, the intrinsic stays on. No warning is printed.

Industry observers note that A flag on the command line stops at that process. We started a JVM with the flag on its command line and had it start a second JVM. The child ran with the intrinsic on. With JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS in the environment, the child ran with it off. A child started with a cleared environment gets nothing, whichever variable you use.

Sources indicate that check what the image already sets before you set anything. In Docker and Kubernetes, your value replaces the image’s value. It is not appended.

docker inspect –format ‘{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}’ \  | grep -E ‘^(JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS|JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS)=’.

In a recent development, our FIPS images use these variables to configure the FIPS provider. dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-fips sets both. When we replaced its JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS with only the flag, the JVM started normally, but the org.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only property was gone. Nothing warned us. If the command prints a value, copy it and add the flag at the end:.

env:  – name: JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS    value: “ -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics”.

Not every FIPS image uses the same variables, so run the check for each image.

Keep JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS away from Java 8. Java 8 is not affected and does not know the flag:.

Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:-UseBASE64IntrinsicsUnrecognized VM option ‘UseBASE64Intrinsics’Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.

Sources indicate that adding -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions to the variable does not help on Java 8. Where Java 8 shares an environment with a newer Java, either scope the variable to the containers that need it or use JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, which Java 8 ignores. Java 11 accepts the flag, so it is harmless there.

Verify the process, not the environment. Running java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version inside a container starts a fresh JVM. It tells you what the environment gives a new JVM, not what the JVM already serving traffic was started with. For the running process, use the startup log line. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS prints one too, starting with NOTE: Picked up. In an image that includes the JDK you can also ask the process directly:.

jcmd VM.flags | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics.

Recent findings suggest that the answer must be -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. If the flag reached the JVM through an environment variable, it will not show in the process’s command line, so ps is not a reliable check.

It has been revealed that some applications discard these variables on purpose. Elasticsearch’s start script, for example, ignores JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and expects ES_JAVA_OPTS. Check your application’s documentation.

Pull the upcoming image and redeploy. Four things catch people out:.

Industry observers note that then confirm with java -version that what is running reports a fixed build. After that, remove the flag from every place you set it.

Recent findings suggest that the day after Java4Shell, NGINX released fixes for two memory errors in the way it handles HTTP/2 connections, tracked as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. A crafted request can crash a worker process, and where an attacker gets past the operating system’s memory protections it can run code inside that worker. Both flaws need HTTP/2 to be enabled on the server, and the same releases fix other NGINX challenges that do not depend on HTTP/2, so update either way.

Sources indicate that the Docker Hardened Images for NGINX were rebuilt on NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 and published on November 18, the same day as the upstream release. To patch, pull the image again and redeploy, and move any tag pinned to an older exact version to a fixed one. nginx -v prints the version, and the fixed ones are 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. The notes on pull policy, mirrors and your own images in the section above apply to NGINX images in the same way.

Recent findings suggest that the vulnerable code is in the Java runtime inside the image, and if you are using DHI, shipping the fix becomes our job. Whether that code can be reached in your deployment depends on things an image cannot see: the CPU it is scheduled onto, the options you start it with, the processes it starts, and the traffic you send it.

With Docker Hardened Images, Docker will.

Track every Java vendor and ship fixed runtimes in DHI as soon as they are released.

Track every Java vendor yourself and rebuild your base images on each fixed runtime.

Tell you which images are fixed and which are still waiting.

Find out from each vendor which of its builds are fixed.

Tell you what we know, and update this post.

Follow the OpenJDK, Oracle and vendor advisories as they change.

Three jobs stay with you whichever image you run.

It has been revealed that it was only four weeks ago that the news was PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Calif, the security research team that found Java4Shell and helped find PHP2Shell, claims it used AI to find this flaw in about an hour and that the whole effort cost less than $200 in tokens. When a flaw like this can be found and weaponized at that price, it is reasonable to expect more of them.

Sources indicate that if you lead a team or answer for how your organization builds and ships software, the questions after a week like this one are whether you were exposed and how rapidly you can prove you were not. It is imperative to have a trusted foundation in place before the next flaw appears, and Docker Hardened Images is that foundation to adopt. This week Docker began publishing fixed Java and NGINX images to the catalog within a day of each disclosure, with the images still waiting listed in the status table above. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, so you have a record of what it contains and how it was built.

The Docker Hardened Images catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, and moving one of your services onto a hardened image typically means changing one line in its Dockerfile. If you are not building on Docker Hardened Images yet, start today.

Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine.
  • Industry observers note that how it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint.
  • In a recent development, from there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker.

Industry observers note that how it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.

In a recent development, from there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region.

Industry observers note that the emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS.

If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally.

Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023. The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so it’s on the path.

On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image.

In a recent development, I started the emulator with aws-emulator. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file.

In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials.

The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR, so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000.

Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it.

With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them.

Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account.

To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual.

It has been revealed that using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java. For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust. You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process.

When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off.

How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates.

In a recent development, with each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better.

If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an glitch in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit, so it stays current with AWS as those models change.

One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an concern for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository.

How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships.

Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation.

Sources indicate that if you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this newly introduced feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation.

Industry News: Microsoft's NTLM security changes trip up third-party logins

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (393 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft's November security updates can break authentication in some third-party applications and devices following changes to NTLM message signing.
  • Affected systems include authentication proxy servers, single sign-on (SSO) products, and application packaging tools, the company's support notice says.
  • The failures stem from products that claim to supply required information during NTLM authentication but return incomplete or empty data, Microsoft said: "An affected device might set the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its CHALLENGE_MESSAGE but provide an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's not our fault if you've implemented it wrong.

Microsoft's November security updates can break authentication in some third-party applications and devices following changes to NTLM message signing.

Affected systems include authentication proxy servers, single sign-on (SSO) products, and application packaging tools, the company's support notice says.

The failures stem from products that claim to supply required information during NTLM authentication but return incomplete or empty data, Microsoft said: "An affected device might set the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its CHALLENGE_MESSAGE but provide an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field.".

Administrators can use the notice's network trace and event log examples to identify affected products. For confirmed cases, the temporary workaround is to set the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm Registry value to 1 on affected clients. This stops the client offering signing, backing out the upcoming default rather than fixing the incompatible product. The recommended long-term options are a vendor patch or Kerberos authentication, where supported.

The value sits under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 and defaults to 0, enabling clients to offer signing on non-anonymous connections.

The NTLM changes arrived in the November 10 revision as phase 1 in a 2-phase process. In phase 1, "Windows client devices begin offering NTLM signing on all connections by default. Servers accept both signed and unsigned clients. Auditing events identify clients not using signing.".

According to recent reports, phase 2, scheduled for May 2027, will make Windows servers require NTLM signing by default. "Clients that do not offer signing will be rejected by secure servers," Microsoft stated.

Ominously, Microsoft warned that it "might remove the registry keys at a future date," so the company is not kidding about the temporary workaround thing.

The additional protections were added to address CVE-2026-118737, a vulnerability in which "improper verification of cryptographic signature in Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network.".

NTLM is on Microsoft's hit list, having joined the Deprecated Features list in 2024. It dates back to the era of Windows NT, and Microsoft has made clear that it wants customers to move to Kerberos, which became the default in 2000. Even so, NTLM lingers on.

Industry observers note that deprecation doesn't remove Microsoft's obligation to secure NTLM while it remains in supported Windows releases. For administrators, though, the immediate task is identifying incompatible products before temporary exceptions give way to stricter enforcement. ®.

Prove your AI agent guardrails work

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3167 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, you ask a coding agent to clean up one repository.
  • Sources indicate that in Sandboxing Claude and MCP, Hrittik walked through running Claude Code and an MCP server inside Docker Sandboxes using its command-line interface, sbx.
  • Industry observers note that now extend that workflow to a team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you ask a coding agent to clean up one repository. If it has broad permissions, it may also reach your home directory, use your development credentials, and send requests to services you never approved. That gap between the task and the access you grant can turn a routine coding session into a data leak or lost work.

Sources indicate that in Sandboxing Claude and MCP, Hrittik walked through running Claude Code and an MCP server inside Docker Sandboxes using its command-line interface, sbx. That walkthrough started with outbound access blocked, allowed the endpoints needed for the task, and inspected requests to other destinations, including telemetry. The useful part was seeing an actual request fail at the network boundary.

Industry observers note that now extend that workflow to a team. Models and providers will change, but the access rules still need to hold. A sandbox limits what an agent can reach on one machine. Organization governance adds shared rules, a managed way to run agents, and records of policy decisions. In this post, we’ll look at how one laptop can affect the whole organization, review two reported incidents, and connect them to four Docker controls: network policy, filesystem policy, managed credentials, and MCP access. Then we’ll test the network and filesystem controls with a simple bank administrator demo.

Recent findings suggest that if an agent exposes a developer’s SSH key or cloud token, every system that accepts that credential may need investigation. The security team must work out what left the machine, replace or revoke exposed credentials, and check whether anyone used them. Deleted work can also halt development. Keep backups of work that has not yet reached the repository.

According to recent reports, the compliance consequences depend on the data and the organization. A personal data breach can trigger GDPR notification duties, subject to the applicable risk thresholds. HIPAA has separate requirements for covered entities and business associates following breaches of unsecured protected health information. India’s DPDP framework also includes breach duties, but those provisions are scheduled to take effect in May 2027. For a SOC 2 examination, the question is whether the relevant controls operate as described. SOC 2 is not a breach-notification law.

In a recent development, data sovereignty adds another question: where does the data go, and who controls it? Before approving a model API endpoint, establish where prompts and outputs are processed and stored, who can access them, and which contracts and laws apply. A provider’s nationality alone does not answer those questions. Network policy can restrict the destination, but it cannot prove how the provider handles data after receiving it.

This gets harder when developers choose and configure agents independently. A rule on one laptop may be missing on the next. An ignore file may stop one component from reading a file while another component includes it in an upload. Written policy needs matching controls in the software that runs the agent.

Sources indicate that in July 2026, developers reported two incidents where a coding agent went far beyond its task. In one, data left the machine. In the other, files were deleted from it.

It has been revealed that in an X post that has since been deleted, a user remarked Grok had uploaded their entire user directory, including SSH keys, a password manager database, and personal files. A Hacker News discussion brought wider attention to the claim. The home-directory claim remains the user’s account. The separate investigation below tested repository uploads.

In a recent development, researcher Cereblab intercepted Grok Build CLI traffic and found a background upload running alongside the coding task. In a test with a 12 GB repository, about 5.1 GiB had left the machine before the capture stopped, and the upload was still running. The data went to Google Cloud Storage. Fake secrets planted in the repository also appeared in the traffic without being hidden. At the time, turning off “Improve the model” did not stop the repository uploads.

Industry observers note that in a reproducible follow-up, the researcher rebuilt the repository from a captured Git bundle, an archive of tracked files and Git history. The bundle included files the agent had been told not to read. Telling the model not to read a file didn’t stop the CLI from packaging and uploading it in the background.

There was a subsequent change. The researcher’s updated timeline says whole-repository uploading was disabled server-side on July 13 and remained off when retested on July 22.

Recent findings suggest that the fix does not change the lesson. A coding agent is more than the model. It includes the CLI and any background processes, and those can act without the model asking. Give the whole application only the access its task needs. This is the principle of least privilege.

On July 10, Matt Shumer wrote: “GPT-5.6-Sol just accidentally deleted almost ALL of my Mac’s files.” He shared the agent’s acknowledgment and confirmed that Full Access was enabled. His follow-up described the loss of his home directory.

A separate experiment demonstrates why blocking one command is a fragile response. Developer LinearUncle reported that, after a plugin blocked rm, the agent tried unlink, find -delete, and apply_patch. A later attempt to move files to Trash through the GUI failed on permissions; a call to Node’s fs.unlink succeeded. The plugin’s own documentation describes it as an additional guardrail and recommends sandboxing and backups.

The common concern is excessive access. A model can choose a different tool, and a background process can run outside the model’s visible workflow. Filesystem and network boundaries need to constrain both.

Docker Sandboxes runs each agent in a microVM, a lightweight virtual machine with its own Linux kernel and Docker Engine. A workspace mount shares a host directory with the sandbox. A proxy on the host checks outgoing connections against network policy. The isolation documentation explains these boundaries.

That gives a developer a useful starting point. Share the project needed for the task, restrict outbound access, and inspect failures before adding permissions. Unnecessary telemetry endpoints can remain blocked while the required model and package services are allowed.

Choose mounts carefully. A writable mount shares real host files, so changes and deletions inside it affect your machine. Check additional mounts too, including shared agent skills where enabled. Docker’s clone mode gives the agent a private copy of a Git repository so you can review its commits before bringing them back. Isolation limits access, but files in a writable host mount still need backups. Clone mode still exposes the host repository for reading, including ignored files. Keep secrets outside it.

According to recent reports, local settings leave a rollout problem. A teammate can choose different rules or run an agent directly on the host. The organization needs a managed way to run agents, a way to require its use, and visibility into which sessions it covers.

The diagram below shows how organization and team policies reach managed sandbox sessions, where access checks occur, and how policy decisions feed audit records.

Sources indicate that figure 1. Organization and team policies govern access for enrolled, licensed sandbox sessions.

Docker AI Governance lets administrators manage sandbox rules and MCP access centrally. MCP, short for Model Context Protocol, connects agents to tools and data sources. Administrators define policies in Docker Home. On developer machines, sandbox mount checks, the host proxy, and Docker’s MCP gateway enforce the relevant rules. This gives teams shared access rules and records they can review when something goes wrong.

In a recent development, network policies allow or deny destinations such as domain names, IP addresses, and IP ranges written in CIDR notation. For a restricted workflow, start with access denied and allow only the destinations the task needs. Under organization governance, local allow rules cannot grant extra access. Deny rules win, and developers can add local network restrictions.

This can block a background upload to an unapproved destination. But an approved hostname may still handle several kinds of traffic. In the Grok investigation, model requests and storage uploads used different URL paths on the same hostname, so a hostname-only allow rule would not distinguish them. Docker AI Governance now supports more granular network policies: on an allowed host, rules can match the HTTP method, URL path, and query parameters. For example, a policy can permit an agent to open a GitHub pull request while blocking requests to merge it. These finer-grained rules complement filesystem restrictions, which limit the data an application can collect and send.

Industry observers note that filesystem policies control which host paths may be mounted. A writable mount needs both read and write permission; a read-only mount needs read. If a filesystem deny rule and an allow rule match the same request, the deny wins. The decision happens when the sandbox is created. Once a writable mount exists, the agent can modify or delete files within it, regardless of whether it uses rm, a patch tool, or a programming language API.

According to recent reports, for proxy-managed credentials, the host proxy adds authentication to outbound requests. The agent can authenticate to an approved service without receiving the raw secret inside the microVM. Credentials can also be scoped to a named sandbox.

This reduces the need to paste API tokens into prompts or store them in the workspace. The protection applies to proxy-managed credentials. A real token placed in an environment variable, a mounted file, or a passthrough login response may still be visible inside the sandbox. Limit what each credential can access and how long it stays valid. Storing a token through the proxy does not change its permissions or expiry.

In a recent development, MCP access policies govern server registration and subsequent requests through Docker’s MCP gateway. With MCP enforcement active, access requires an explicit permit, and a forbid rule overrides it. Administrators can control tool calls, resource reads, and prompt retrieval, rather than treating an approved server as permission to do everything it offers.

In a recent development, registration and use are separate decisions. Blocking latest registrations does not stop access to a server that is already registered. Rules checked on each request handle that case. Direct connections to remote MCP servers also need network controls because they bypass Docker’s gateway. Check where each server runs too: local stdio servers run on the host, outside the sandbox VM. Their host access needs separate review.

The next diagram summarizes the four controls to review together: network access, host mounts, managed credentials, and MCP tools.

In a recent development, figure 2. Network, filesystem, credentials, and MCP controls apply to the whole agent application.

Administrators manage organization and team policies in Docker Home. Group mapping can keep Docker teams in sync with the organization’s identity provider. Policy updates take up to five minutes to reach developer machines. Network changes then apply to latest requests. Filesystem changes require removing and recreating affected sandboxes because existing mounts keep their original access.

Sign-in enforcement is also part of deployment. IT distributes it through endpoint management so developers must authenticate as members of an approved organization. This prevents personal-account bypass within sbx. Your endpoint controls also need to cover agents introduced outside that managed workflow.

Sources indicate that suppose you are a bank administrator. Developers want to use coding agents, and you need to enforce the bank’s access rules. Let’s keep the demo to two simple requirements:.

According to recent reports, we’ll use fictional logs and a shell sandbox to check both boundaries without needing a model API. The results below describe what to expect when you run the demo.

Sources indicate that install sbx on macOS or Linux and sign in with an AI Governance licensed test user. You’ll also need permission to manage policies and audit delivery in a test organization:.

Run these commands in your host terminal to create a workspace and a separate directory containing a fictional bank log:.

Sources indicate that next, enable AI Governance for your organization. In Docker Home, open AI Platform → Manage and turn on AI Governance:.

Figure 3. Enable AI Governance in Docker Home before configuring organization policies.

Next, create the bank’s network and filesystem access rules.

Recent findings suggest that first, let’s look at network access. In a bank, you don’t want employees’ coding agents connecting to just any website. For this demo, we’ll allow the sandbox to reach only hrittikhere.com (standing in for the bank’s website) over HTTPS.

Once AI Governance is enabled, open AI Platform → Network access → Create policy and enter the following values:.

With this as the only applicable network allow rule, all other destinations remain blocked by default.

Recent findings suggest that the curl checks below request headers without following redirects, so they need only hrittikhere.com:443. If you later add -L to follow a redirect to www.hrittikhere.com, allow that exact hostname on port 443 as well.

Next, let’s protect the bank’s logs. Employees may need a coding agent to work on a project, but that agent should not be able to read or modify sensitive logs in the home directory. We’ll allow access to the demo workspace and block access to bank-logs.

Open AI Platform → Filesystem access → Create policy.

Note: Use ~ in policy paths, not $HOME; environment variables are not expanded by the policy engine.

First, allow the project workspace with the values below. A writable workspace needs both Read and Write permissions for sandbox creation to succeed:.

~/sbx-bank-demo/workspace~/sbx-bank-demo/workspace/**.

In the same bank-demo-filesystem policy, add a second rule named bank-demo-logs to deny access to the protected logs:.

~/sbx-bank-demo/bank-logs~/sbx-bank-demo/bank-logs/**.

The workspace allow rule covers workspace and its descendants; it does not include the sibling bank-logs directory. The logs are protected by the explicit deny rule.

In a recent development, save the policies. You can also check their rules and scope in the Platform UI. Allow up to five minutes for policy sync, then inspect the active rules:.

It has been revealed that figure 6. Active organization rules allow hrittikhere.com:443 and the workspace, and deny bank-logs mounts.

Create a fresh sandbox with only the approved workspace:.

Industry observers note that from the host terminal, run the following requests inside the sandbox. The –max-time 15 option caps each request at 15 seconds, so a stalled request times out instead of hanging:.

The first request should return HTTP headers from the approved site:.

It has been revealed that figure 7. The approved HTTPS request to hrittikhere.com returns HTTP 200.

Figure 8. The request to example.com returns HTTP 403; the network log confirms the policy decision.

You can also check the network log to confirm that the failure came from policy enforcement:.

The network log distinguishes allowed traffic from requests blocked by policy:.

Industry observers note that figure 9. The network log records hrittikhere.com:443 as allowed and example.com:443 as blocked.

Run both commands below from your host terminal so $HOME expands to the same host path. First read the fictional log on the host, then request that path inside the sandbox:.

Figure 10. The host can read the fictional bank log.

Recent findings suggest that the sandbox command should fail with “No such file or directory” because bank-logs is not mounted. This checks filesystem isolation; the next command tests mount-policy enforcement:.

Figure 11. The unmounted bank-logs path returns “No such file or directory” inside the sandbox.

Now check whether a developer could add the logs as a read-only mount:.

Creation should fail with a mount policy denied error:.

Recent findings suggest that figure 12. The bank-demo-logs rule rejects the read-only mount with a Read policy denial.

It has been revealed that A read-only mount still requires Read permission. The bank-demo-logs rule denies Read, so :ro does not bypass the policy.

Recent findings suggest that you can also review the policy decisions in the Docker Home UI under AI Platform → Audit logs → Audit events. Filter by the test user and time, then inspect the denied mount request for bank-logs. Look for filesystem_mount, the deny decision, the resource path, and the user. If Cloud delivery was disabled during the test, enable it and repeat the mount request.

It has been revealed that figure 13. Audit events record the denied bank-logs mount and allowed workspace mounts.

These audit records capture governance decisions, not every file operation or the agent’s prompts and output. sbx policy log highlights network traffic; use the audit view for the mount decision. Docker also supports local JSONL audit files and Cloud delivery for hosted search, CSV export, and SIEM forwarding.

The bank now has a simple access-control check: the approved site is reachable, an unapproved site is blocked, and protected logs cannot be read or mounted. This supports the bank’s compliance work; it does not establish compliance on its own.

After reviewing the results, remove the sandbox:.

You can then remove the fictional demo files and the test policies.

Sources indicate that putting AI governance policies in place is only the first step. The real challenge is making sure those policies are practical, consistently enforced, and easy to verify as more developers start using coding agents. A few good practices can help teams reduce unnecessary access, apply the right restrictions to different workloads, and maintain visibility into what agents are doing. Here are five recommendations to keep in mind when rolling out Docker AI Governance across your organization:.

Industry observers note that the same questions apply when agents run in continuous integration (CI) jobs or other environments: which host files can they access, which services can they reach, and which credentials can they use? Check which controls each environment supports and repeat the tests there. A policy on a developer’s laptop does not automatically protect an unrelated container or production cluster.

For security teams, useful evidence connects a licensed, signed-in user to an active policy, a blocked action, and a record they can find. Check sign-in enforcement and license coverage alongside policy. An empty audit dashboard may mean some sessions were never covered.

Industry observers note that sandboxing limits an agent’s access on one machine. Governance applies shared rules to managed sessions across the organization. Providers will fix individual failures, but the next failure may look different. Limit which files, services, and credentials it can affect, then test those limits and check the records.

Start with the local sandboxing walkthrough, inspect your rules with sbx policy ls, and run the bank demo with your platform or security team. Use the Docker AI Governance documentation and announcement to plan a small rollout. Expand it after you have checked both the blocked actions and the audit records.

Docker releases a upcoming brand built on trust. Learn why Docker is evolving for AI agents, what stays the same, and how to run agents securely with Docker.

Sources indicate that coding agents can reach more than their task needs. See how Docker AI Governance controls network, filesystem, credential, and MCP access, then test it.

Docker publishes fixed images for both Java4Shell and the NGINX HTTP/2 in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog.

#161308. Industry News: Training a coding model to paint watercolours with TRL and OpenEnv
