Industry News: Training a coding model to paint watercolours with TRL and OpenEnv

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model.
  • The video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet.
  • Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model. The model writes JavaScript through p5.brush, a library that "adds natural drawing tools to p5.js". The video went viral fast, over 1.5M views at the time of writing.

The video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet. His site says a full technical report is coming, so ensure you follow him. The original idea is his, coming from the art and design side, where his skills are way beyond mine. My attempt is on the engineering side, reproducing the recipe in the open with every piece published.

Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.

It has been revealed that in this article I try and reproduce his idea with TRL and OpenEnv. The reference pool dataset, the RL environment, the training scripts and the trained models, all open.

The whole pipeline runs on Hugging Face, end to end:.

It has been revealed that once the two Spaces are up, the recipe is one command. Duplicate the environment and the scorer model, set two environment variables for the reward mix, and launch:.

The rest of this article is the story of getting there, and every piece is in the repo.

In a recent development, I have followed the original blog step by step, and only changed something when strictly needed. Every idea of my own went into a list instead of into the experiment, and that list became "What I would try next" at the end, next to the full list of published artifacts. If you have already read his post, the framing and the reward design will be familiar. The latest material is the open implementation, the hand-rated pool, and three reward mixes trained and compared, and it starts at The RL environment you need to build.

The paintings look loose, imperfect, handmade, at a moment when image models produce perfect (statistically average) pictures. My guess is that this contrast is a massive part of why the video went viral. It reminded me of the early days of generative AI art, when the point was to explore the medium. DeepDream (2015) was a debugging tool that people turned into art, works like Edmond de Belamy (2018) came from artists probing what a GAN could do, and artists like Mario Klingemann spent those years making dreamy portraits with neural networks.

Industry observers note that this project feels closer to those early days. In his thesis, Surya describes the path that led here. He started by prompting text-to-image models, where the prompt is the only lever you can pull, and more detail buys more control only up to a point. Training the model itself goes further. The other half of the idea is the medium. The model writes a program of about 150 lines of JavaScript that paints the image. That model output is code. You can read it, edit it and run it again, and the decision behind each brushstroke is visible. And the style comes from a restriction where the model is only allowed ten of the library's methods. More on that below.

Industry observers note that in that same period, Anna Ridler photographed thousands of tulips, hand-labelled every one, exhibited the dataset itself as the artwork, and later trained a model on it. I found her work through the references AI agents brought back while building this project and loved it because this project does something very similar by curating a set of images by hand, and then training against them.

It has been revealed that most of the recent RL work on language models uses rewards you can verify. For example, math problems with a known answer, code that passes tests, or graders that are right or wrong and cheap to run. This project is closer to the older exception, RLHF, where the model learns a reward model from human preferences.

Here the reward is aesthetic preference. There is no correct answer. The real question of the project is whether you can do RL over taste.

The reward, as his blog defines it and as the RL environment I built implements it:.

HPSv3 is an open 7B preference model. Give it an image and a text description, and it returns a score for how much a person would prefer that image. It was trained on a large set of human choices between pairs of images, so its score is an average of many people's taste. The pairwise judge is Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, a general vision model called through HF Inference Providers. The pairwise judge sees the candidate painting next to four references randomly selected from the pool, guided by a written description of what to weigh (bleeds, translucent washes, soft edges), each comparison in both presentation orders, and its score is the share of comparisons the candidate wins. Its only standard is the pool, so its score is my taste, as encoded in those ratings.

Recent findings suggest that those are the weights Narreddi converged on. The pool defines taste here. That moves the work from tuning hyperparameters to building the set that decides what is beautiful.

I trained three runs with this reward. They differ only in how the weight splits between the two model judges:.

It has been revealed that I started with hps-only to validate that the pipeline could learn at all. Once the reward was going up and the metrics were healthy, there was no reason to run it longer, so I launched the two longer runs instead. The question that the longer runs ask is how much of HPSv3's power can you hand to the pairwise judge? The more weight the judge carries, the more the reward means my taste instead of everyone's, and the harder it should be to climb. Incidentally, if you push it far enough or your style is too far from the average, the model could stop entirely.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, it did not stop and both runs with the pairwise judge on learned too. The hand-rated pool can steer the policy, at least as far as the metrics and the final paintings show. The numbers are below.

In a recent development, disclaimer. If we use a frontier model, it can already generate the JavaScript code that paints watercolour from a prompt. That's the starting point. The work here is about teaching a smaller model to do it combined with a person's own artistic preferences.

The environment wraps everything that sits between the model and the reward, including the JavaScript library that the model uses for painting, the system prompt that restricts it, the headless Chromium that renders each sketch, and the gate that rejects cheats.

It has been revealed that the library does more of the work than it seems. p5.brush, by @acamposuribe, simulates a medium rather than drawing shapes: pigment bleeds past the edges of a fill, paper has texture, strokes have mass, flow fields drag brushwork around. When the model calls brush.fillBleed(0.25) it is deciding how far the ink runs.

Sources indicate that note. The author of p5.brush had been trying to teach a machine to paint long before any of this. In 2022 he made a generative art series that hides a diary about teaching p5.js to draw like a child: "It is barely able to use the crayons [...] It cannot follow simple commands. I'm done for today, very infuriating." The series was meant to have three pieces, and he made two. When Surya's video went viral, he quoted it, sharing that diary and saying this work is the third piece arriving on its own.

In a recent development, p5.brush exposes 47 methods. The prompt allows 10: scaleBrushes, noStroke, fill, noFill, fillBleed, fillTexture, beginShape, vertex, endShape and circle. What the other thirty-seven add, lines, hatching, custom brushes, would break the watercolour look. With these ten the model can only paint filled shapes, and the library adds the bleed to every one of them.

In a recent development, his blog post saved me a lot of time I could have wasted iterating on the prompt. A long API reference makes the model invent methods that do not exist, and his 200 GEPA iterations converged on a strict allowlist with no documentation. I saw the same failures and wrote the allowlist by hand. My only addition to that recipe is one sentence: paint each petal two or three times, a significant pass first and a smaller, more opaque one inside it. This small change made my outputs a lot more colorful.

Sources indicate that note. If it's the first time you hear about GEPA, it is an automatic prompt optimizer. A language model reflects in plain words on where the current prompt failed and proposes a better one, and the loop repeats.

Sources indicate that the gate is the final piece. The sketch has to compile, use the library instead of direct p5 calls, put real pigment on the canvas, and not try to trick the scorer, for example by writing text on the canvas.

Recent findings suggest that the pool consists of 178 paintings divided into two tiers based on my personal preferences, love and okay. All of them are actually generated by a model. Four open-weight models, called through Inference Providers, wrote p5.brush sketches, each one working from a real, openly licensed photo of a hibiscus from iNaturalist. A vision model gave written feedback on every sketch, over three refinement iterations. Every final render was then rated one at a time, by me, and 178 made the cut.

Here I chose four different families of models to test their different styles. These four were the open models that produced a valid sketch every time in a quick reliability check, and two other candidates were dropped for failing it. If you want to produce your own pool, you might choose others.

Sources indicate that the tiers do real work in the reward. When the pairwise judge draws four references, half come from love and half from okay, so the policy always faces some rivals it can sometimes beat, and a win pays the same against either tier. This is one of my few deliberate changes: the original compares against its top tier only, and I kept the easier tier in the draw so a weak early policy still gets signal.

Sources indicate that no human-made painting is in there, which is a real limitation. p5.brush is a niche library, and the human work that exists in it with accessible code is a handful of pieces, nowhere near what a training corpus would need, as his blog also notes.

The interesting idea here, as I've already discussed previously, is that the model will learn to imitate what the pool contains. If we point the environment at a different dataset, the reward would automatically change without touching a single line of code. For the dataset I generated and openly share, I also include the source sketch.

If we look closer at the judges, the two of them answer different questions. HPSv3 decides whether it is a flower, and the pairwise judge decides whether it is well painted in the style I chose.

According to recent reports, before anything worked, there was a long stretch of flat reward curves. If you've tried to reproduce a research paper/blog without open artifacts, you probably can relate. Every run tested what I thought was a reasonable theory about what was wrong. A run takes a lot of time, so I queued the next one while still going through the last one's results. As always, starting from something easier that works and then building on top of that was the answer. A simple control task, with no browser and no judges, was the first attempt that learned, and the reason was that my learning rate was just too low.

Another change that cost me time to find was adjusting the LoRA parameters correctly. The usual target_modules list assumes a dense model, and Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is a mixture of experts that names most of its projections differently, so the adapter was training ten layers out of forty. I solved this by changing it to all-linear, which reaches every linear layer. The routed experts in this architecture are fused tensors that even all-linear leaves frozen, but everything else gets an adapter, and that was enough to learn.

The fix was four changes in TRL's GRPOTrainer:.

These four changes unlocked the first successful run (hps-only), with the reward clearly improving.

In a recent development, with that configuration, all three runs learn. Both judge runs were released for 200 steps and stopped at 110, with the reward still climbing slowly. A step takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, and the comparison between mixes was already stable, so I stopped both to save compute. Mean group reward over the first and final third of each run:.

In a recent development, the three curves line up with how much weight my taste carries. The more the judge weighs, the lower the start and the noisier the climb. judge-led spent its first thirty steps nearly flat before it moved. It is the same move that solved the debugging. Shrink the problem until something learns, then add the hard parts back one at a time.

Sources indicate that the pairwise judge term itself climbed in the two runs that used it. The model wins more comparisons against the pool as training advances, which is the claim hps-only could not make. No group in any run collapsed to identical rewards, the GRPO failure mode that kills the gradient. For the curious, the per-metric curves (HPSv3, paint coverage, entropy) are in the repository as CSV.

The full launch command, the hardware and the two environment variables that turn this into the other two runs are in the recipe.

In a recent development, in every run, the first thing the model learned was to stop producing bad paintings, the near-blank canvases and shapeless washes that score under 0.3 in total reward. In hps-only, three quarters of the rise in the group mean comes from bad paintings becoming rare. In the judge runs the collapse is even steeper: rollouts under 0.3 fall from 99 to 16 across judge-led's thirds, and from 37 to 4 in hps-led.

This is why the obvious visual, the best painting of each step, highlights almost no difference in hps-only. It moves +0.034 across the run while the median moves +0.155. The learning is visible in the middle of the distribution.

It has been revealed that what the pairwise judge changes is the top. In hps-only, paintings got more reliable without getting better. The quality of the good ones added just +0.03 to the group mean, and once HPSv3 saw petals around a centre and a stem, it stopped asking for more pigment. With the judge on, the other half of the story appears. Better here means closer to the pool, so closer to what I rated as "good" or something I liked more. That added +0.12 in judge-led and +0.16 in hps-led, the best of each step rose too, and paint coverage doubled in both runs (0.11 to 0.23, and 0.13 to 0.30) where hps-only barely moved it. With a reference left to beat, a good painting can still get better, and the model starts being rewarded for using more pigment.

In a recent development, one more finding. The model ignores an explicit instruction, and it is right to. The system prompt asks for fifteen to thirty filled shapes. If we look at the real mean, it is between 7 and 9, and n_shapes barely correlates with reward in any run (+0.000, −0.14, +0.07). The policy is not rewarded for obeying that sentence, so it does not obey it.

Recent findings suggest that there is also a ceiling on the hps-only route. If every rollout matched its good ones, that run's mean would sit at 0.771. Whether more steps would break it is an open question.

It has been revealed that the paintings also show something that the tables miss. Within each run, they all look similar. As training advances, the rewards inside each group get closer together, and the median paintings in the opening video look like takes of the same flower. That is GRPO doing what it is designed to do with a pool built from one subject. The pool decides what counts as variety, the same way it decides what counts as quality. If the reward only pays for matching one flower, the model learns to paint that one flower. More diverse output would need a more diverse pool, and building one is more curation work. Surya's newer compositions are an example of this. Alex Yango's animal paintings are the same recipe with different choices in the pool. This is the biggest difference between an aesthetic reward and a maths grader. Behind the number there is a very human job, deciding what belongs in the reward set. Jason Liu's essay on taste says the general version in one line. AI shifted the bottleneck from making to noticing.

It has been revealed that surya closes his blog with some of his favourites. Instead of picking mine, below is a wall with the 178 paintings the reward scored highest across the two judge runs, the same number the reference pool holds, in no particular order. Open it and pick your own.

To choose, you looked at many and kept a few, and that is exactly the job that built the reward of this project. Every painting of every run, with its sketch and its reward, is in the rollouts datasets, and browsable in this gallery.

According to recent reports, since the reward was partly based on my taste, it is fair to close with my verdict as a viewer. To my eye, judge-led is the run that ends up the most diverse and the most artistically interesting. hps-led paints convincing watercolours, but its best ones share a soft, wet-on-wet look that is almost a style of its own. hps-only converges the hardest, and most of its paintings settle on the same colours. You can judge for yourself in the gallery, which has every painting of every run, sortable by step and by reward.

This project is mostly infra. A run needs a trainer, two Spaces, an inference router and a websocket to stay healthy for hours straight, and every piece that fails quietly turns into a wrong number somewhere else. Half the work is checking that the number you read matches what actually happened.

In a recent development, failures of the infrastructure were entering the reward as zeros. A render that timed out or a scorer that did not answer scored the same as a bad painting, 0.0 inside the group. Across all my runs that was about 1.5% of rollouts, and in the worst run it reached 5.2%. That trains the model on noise, so those paths now return None and the rollout is excluded from the group.

I also found a bug in OpenEnv, and sent the fix upstream. The client keeps one persistent websocket, and a socket closed by the far end stayed cached, so every later call failed even though the environment was healthy. It cost me two half-finished runs to find it. The fix is submitted upstream, and the runs launched with it have been running clean since.

The reward of a step depends on which references it drew. The pairwise judge samples four references per step, so every step faces a different set of rivals, and some draws are simply harder. GRPO itself is mostly safe, because advantages are computed inside the group and a hard draw moves the whole group together. The curve I was reading was not safe, and some of what looked like a bad step was just a hard draw. The image above is one example. Step 12 scored half a point below step 11 mostly because it drew the hardest references of the run, while the paintings themselves look close.

Rounded numbers, and only for the runs that finished.

A step is eight rollouts and takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, of which 70 to 80% is rendering. A single render takes 69 to 96 seconds against a 90 second deadline. Part of that is expected, the Space has no GPU, so Chromium renders the WEBGL canvas in software and p5.brush's bleeds and textures are heavy pixel work. Even so, I expected it to be faster, and I have not found the full cause.

A scorer can cost more than the training that uses it: HPSv3 has to be up for the whole run, so pause the Space, or set its sleep timer, when the run ends.

Everything runs on HF Jobs, with the environment as a Docker Space and metrics in trackio.

Industry observers note that the rule of this project was to reproduce the recipe with every resource open, not to improve it, so a list of untried ideas piled up along the way. These are the ones I would actually try, in order of how much evidence there is.

Multi-step, and letting the model see what it paints. This is the first thing I would try. The original blog trains single turn, so I trained single turn, and in this setup the model paints with its eyes closed. No image ever goes in, and the only feedback it gets is one number. The evidence that a feedback loop works is the pool itself. The reference paintings came from models iterating three rounds under a vision critic, and the later rounds are better. The material that defines the reward was made with a loop the policy never gets.

According to recent reports, smaller models. There is evidence that 35B is more than needed. In my side experiments a 4B already wrote valid sketches that passed the gate. If a 4B can learn this, the cost of the experiment drops by an order of magnitude.

Other ideas on the list are SFT on the pool sources before starting RL, rewarding pigment explicitly, moving the judge's reference mix from easy to hard as the run advances until only love remains, widening the ten-method allowlist for more visual range (my attempts on this crashed more sketches and broke the watercolour look), and checking how consistent the pairwise judge really is by scoring the same image twice.

And the method is not specific to flowers. Alex Yango painted animals with the same mechanism, and Brendan Hogan trained canvas animations against a pool of hand-rated clips. I had also played with something similar before using Simon Willison's pelican benchmark, where code is rendered to an image and scored.

Industry observers note that and underneath all of it sits the question this project cannot close. 178 paintings made by models define what this trained model considers beautiful. The pool is the bottleneck, and it is the part of the pipeline with no principled answer.

For anyone reproducing this, there are two deliberate divergences from Narreddi's recipe, both argued earlier in the article:.

The rest, all-linear for the LoRA, infrastructure failures returning None instead of 0.0, stopping the judge runs at step 110, are decisions I had to make along the way because his blog does not specify them. His implementation is not published, so I cannot tell whether they match his choices or diverge from them.

The per-rollout numbers in this article can be recomputed from the published datasets. Nothing here depends on any Space staying switched on.

In a recent development, the method and original idea are Surya Narreddi's. The library is Alejandro Campos Uribe's.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo.
  • I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition.
  • In a recent development, AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt.

I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also new ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

In a recent development, AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS.

HeadlinesTest your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough reveals a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub.

Recent findings suggest that what I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production.

AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs. You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:.

Amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito. The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus prepares in all Cognito Regions.

Claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements: Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use.

It has been revealed that amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

Amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges.

It has been revealed that amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch, with policies covering existing groups or only upcoming ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE).

The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – Newly introduced Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:.

Recent findings suggest that optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock – This guide follows an agent’s cost through repeated calls, reasoning, caching, and human review. I like its emphasis on measuring a completed task and comparing outcomes against a documented baseline. Its worked prices are illustrative; use your own workload and reconcile estimated costs with billing data.

Industry observers note that how Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions – Zillow describes reusable content modules and configuration-driven AWS Step Functions Express Workflows for more than 100 million daily notifications. The useful engineering details include idempotent modules, batching, campaign isolation, and testing expressions with the TestState API before deployment. Those patterns apply well beyond notification systems.

AWS re:Invent – Join the community in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. Browse more than 2,200 sessions, including workshops and deep dives, or register for the free livestream to follow keynotes and selected sessions remotely.

It has been revealed that AWS Community Days – Find community-led technical talks, workshops, and hands-on learning near you. Check each organizer’s page for current dates and registration details.

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

Hera probe finds DART left a stadium-sized dent in asteroid Dimorphos

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Next step is to move in for a closer look at the carnage.
  • The European Space Agency's Hera probe has revealed a stadium-sized crater on Dimorphos, the asteroid NASA struck with its DART spacecraft in 2022.
  • The Double Asteroid Redirection Test was deliberately crashed into the asteroid on September 26, 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Next step is to move in for a closer look at the carnage.

The European Space Agency's Hera probe has revealed a stadium-sized crater on Dimorphos, the asteroid NASA struck with its DART spacecraft in 2022.

The Double Asteroid Redirection Test was deliberately crashed into the asteroid on September 26, 2022. The original strategy called for a European spacecraft – Asteroid Impact Mission (AIM) – to launch first and observe the before and after effects of DART. AIM was canceled, and the Hera mission launched in 2024.

It has been revealed that DART was a success. Scientists were able to determine that the impact had indeed changed the orbit of Dimorphos. The question was what else had happened to the asteroid. Scientists spotted ejecta and debris following the DART impact, but the close-up observations by Hera have revealed the full extent of the collision.

Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, noted: "Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape or stayed the same.

"Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once! The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid's entire width.".

Scientists also noted that the asteroid is now tumbling in its orbit.

Sources indicate that hera is surveying the 151-meter-wide Dimorphos and its larger companion, the 730-meter-wide Didymos, from about 25 to 30 km away. It moves around the pair at roughly 12 cm/s, using thruster firings to trace rectangular paths rather than conventional circular orbits.

Industry observers note that the strategy is to approach closer, to about 13 km, to get higher-resolution snaps. A complicating factor is the discovery that hundreds of orbiting boulders surround the asteroids. Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, remarked: "The team will have to take account of these objects in the coming weeks as the mission moves in closer.".

Hera will deploy two CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, in early 2027. The Italian-led Milani will study surface composition and surrounding dust, while the Luxembourg-led Juventas will use radar to probe Dimorphos's interior before attempting a landing.

Recent findings suggest that scientists also want to measure Dimorphos's mass. Combined with the observed change in its orbit, that will help them assess how effectively DART transferred momentum to the asteroid and improve predictions for future deflection attempts.

Industry observers note that hera mission manager Ian Carnelli remarked: "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet." ®.

According to recent reports, before an agent can answer a question about your PDFs, someone has to build the pipeline: parse every file, split it into chunks, embed each chunk, write the chunks to a vector database, and then learn that database's schema to query it. For video it gets harder: transcode the files, cut them into clips, embed the frames, and keep track of which second of which video each clip came from.

#161304. Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

📅 03 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1567 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task.
  • Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing.
  • While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each new agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

Industry observers note that that is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:.

In a recent development, that one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with fresh runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

According to recent reports, from there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the newly introduced one.

Sources indicate that with funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

recall returns the original text, not a summary, and highlights exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three notable properties:.

According to recent reports, the agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:.

The bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Recent findings suggest that before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

In a recent development, recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:.

Or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:.

funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent claims so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

Recent findings suggest that A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

According to recent reports, claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

This matters in a few different scopes:.

Published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

Industry observers note that A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious.

According to recent reports, your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

It has been revealed that funes is open source too. Open an concern for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Industry observers note that ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Recent findings suggest that full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

Huawei and crew tout homegrown EDA tools to overcome China’s fab deficit

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chip design software leans heavily into 3D packaging and multi-node assemblies.
  • Chinese telecom and IT giant Huawei boasted about its advancements in domestic electronic design automation (EDA) software this week, which it needs to accelerate the adoption of homegrown chip manufacturing.
  • EDA is an umbrella term for software, hardware, and services essential to the planning, design, and production of modern chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chip design software leans heavily into 3D packaging and multi-node assemblies.

Chinese telecom and IT giant Huawei boasted about its advancements in domestic electronic design automation (EDA) software this week, which it needs to accelerate the adoption of homegrown chip manufacturing.

EDA is an umbrella term for software, hardware, and services essential to the planning, design, and production of modern chips.

Today, Cadence Design Systems, Synopsys, and Siemens dominate the industry, but US export controls have restricted Huawei and other blacklisted Chinese businesses' access to their tools.

The US blacklisted Huawei back in 2019 over concerns the telecommunications equipment giant could be forced to inject backdoors into its gear.

Unable to access top EDA tools, Huawei’s chip division, HiSilicon, was forced to develop its own with the help of Phlexing Technology.

This week, Phlexing chairman Qing He detailed the company’s efforts to bring latest EDA tools to support Huawei’s so-called Tau Scaling Law design philosophy.

Sources indicate that “Tau EDA is the domestic EDA tool chain for Tau chips. It comes from a long, close partnership with Huawei,” he stated.

We discussed the tech earlier this year, but in a nutshell, it involves using advanced packaging, specifically 3D hybrid bonding, to achieve higher transistor density for a given area.

It has been revealed that the TSMC of China, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC), is still years behind Taiwan, South Korea, and the US on process technology. It presently has the ability to mass-produce chips on the equivalent of a 7 nm process.

For comparison, TSMC began producing 5 nm-class products in 2020 and commenced mass production of 2 nm-class chips in late 2025.

So, Huawei aims to use 3D packaging to close the gap, but for this to happen, it first needs tools capable of designing such chips, and that’s just what Phlexing claims to have done with its GloryBolt and GloryEX platforms.

According to recent reports, “Traditional EDA has long handled only single processes. Tau EDA needs to integrate and decompose multiple processes,” He noted. “Coupling multi-scale, multi-structure, and multi-physics problems called for new analysis tools.”.

It has been revealed that this, He claims, culminated in the co-development of a process design kit (PDK) with Huawei beginning in 2024. These technologies have now gone live.

The development comes as Huawei looks to bring larger, more capable processors to market.

Recent findings suggest that we previously discussed the tech giant’s latest developments around AI accelerators, near packaged optics, networking, and rack systems. Many of these advancements will depend on multi-die chip packages, enabled by EDA tools, like those built by Phlexing. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

According to recent reports, note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:.

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:.

According to recent reports, the gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it reveals that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

To reproduce or extend this work, see the original IFStruct v1.0 blog post, the Liquid4All/ifstruct benchmark repo, and the LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0 dataset.

Latest Update: Ambiguous Errors Are the Mind Killer

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Prasad

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In which I express frustration at the widespread FUD caused by ambiguous errors in the software we write and consume.
  • In a recent development, I must not fear.
  • It has been revealed that have you ever written or encountered something you think would be an “ambiguous error”?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 26, 2026 / Amit Prasad.

In which I express frustration at the widespread FUD caused by ambiguous errors in the software we write and consume.

In a recent development, I must not fear. Fear is the mind-killer. Fear is the little-death that brings total obliteration. I will face my fear. I will permit it to pass over me and through me. And when it has gone past I will turn the inner eye to see its path. Where the fear has gone there will be nothing. Only I will remain.

It has been revealed that have you ever written or encountered something you think would be an “ambiguous error”? No? How about HTTP 500 Internal Server Error? -EINVAL? Status.INTERNAL? Or even a {"status": "error"}?

Industry observers note that ambiguous errors, that is errors that are represented opaquely, are quite literally everywhere. Compared to happy-path return values, errors have long been second-class citizens across all software. I always felt that this was some abstractly “bad” thing, but it wasn’t until recently that I was able to put substance behind these feelings.

Software has boundaries, whether that be between my application and the libraries it consumes, the operating system it runs atop, or the remote services it calls out to. Boundaries are powerful! They let us hide immense complexity behind simple contracts — AWS S3 being the canonical example. But across a boundary, the only information I have to act on is exactly what you return to me.

So I’m left with two bad options. I can reverse-engineer your errors, in the process becoming a hated Hyrum’s Law perpetuator. Or I can throw up my hands and treat every catch or ? as if I were passing around a bomb. We consume tons of high quality, rigorously tested software, but can’t take advantage of it, because we don’t understand how it fails.

In a recent development, worse, ambiguous errors are viral. Once you’ve consumed one, re-establishing what actually went wrong is far more work than just passing it forward. So you don’t try, and now your callers have the same problem.

Industry observers note that even Rust, with great support for strongly typed errors, isn’t immune. io::Error wraps the OS’s errno, itself a “god error” kept in line by the Linux kernel’s (very good!) docs. A NotFound from fs::remove_file is something most callers would consider a success, yet most code just ?s it upwards alongside everything else.

In a recent development, the usual Rust advice is anyhow for applications and thiserror for libraries, but every application can become somebody else’s library! Typed errors should become part of your API. Adding fresh error variants should be considered breaking changes. How your software fails is part of its contract.

Software can fail in countless ways, but a caller can only do a handful of things about it: retry, fix its input, give up, or blame someone else. Errors should encode enough meaning to fill in those gaps.

Recent findings suggest that more concretely, at Modal we encounter an amusing variation of this. Running rollouts for Reinforcement Learning involves constructing sandboxed working environments, and when one fails, the trainer should be aware of how. Infrastructure failures should be thrown away, lest they bias training. But a reward-hacking model may simply learn to crash its sandbox if it thinks things are going sideways, in an attempt to escape penalization. Adding an error contract to this model allows the trainer to understand and account for these errors.

According to recent reports, writing the contract forces you to answer questions like “How exactly does my software fail?” and “How might someone want to react to those failures?“. You may find that your application can’t fail in a way your interface hinted was possible, or that you yourself can be more resilient to upstream failures. With agentic coding assistants, it’s more and more possible to actually do this exercise. List out every error from the leaves of your execution graph upwards, eliminate the ones that don’t make sense, and add stronger types to the rest.

AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2074 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, GPU support is now available for EC2 G-series GPU instances for Event Functions running on AWS Lambda Managed Instances (LMI).
  • In a recent development, why customers need this Customers keep asking to run GPU workloads with the simplicity of serverless.
  • Sources indicate that cost is the second problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, GPU support is now available for EC2 G-series GPU instances for Event Functions running on AWS Lambda Managed Instances (LMI). You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads, including machine learning inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing, on GPU instances with serverless simplicity. GPU-accelerated functions are deployed as container (Open Container Initiative, OCI) images. You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate. GPU-accelerated functions run on the same Lambda Managed Instances foundation that already gives you Amazon EC2 pricing and specialized compute without managing servers.

In a recent development, why customers need this Customers keep asking to run GPU workloads with the simplicity of serverless. Building on self-managed GPU infrastructure means selecting instances, installing and reconciling GPU drivers and CUDA libraries, planning capacity, writing scaling logic, and hand-building the event integrations that connect the GPU step to the rest of the application. Serverless GPU services that hide that work often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.

Sources indicate that cost is the second problem. GPUs are expensive, and utilization is usually low because a single workload rarely saturates a GPU. A small inference task can leave most of a provisioned GPU idle while you pay for the whole thing.

This feature closes both gaps. You bring a function, and Lambda runs it on a GPU in minutes, triggered by the same AWS events as any other Lambda Event Function, billed and secured the same way. It also maximizes utilization of every GPU you pay for, by consolidating functions onto instances and keeping GPUs busy across concurrent requests.

What you can build You can run both AI/ML inference and non-ML workloads using GPU-accelerated compute on Lambda Managed Instances. This capability is optimized for inference rather than training, and custom models rather than large foundation models already available on services like Amazon Bedrock. Common workloads include:.

Part of the Lambda programming model A GPU-accelerated function is one step in a larger application, and it composes with the rest of Lambda. Lambda durable functions orchestrate multi-step, long-running workflows around the GPU step, with checkpointing and automatic recovery. Lambda MicroVMs run untrusted or model-generated code in isolated, stateful sandboxes. In an agentic workload, a MicroVM executes the tool-use logic on CPU, then calls a GPU-accelerated function running on Lambda Managed Instances for inference.

Recent findings suggest that GPU-accelerated functions also support the extended function timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations, so you can run batch and other long-running GPU jobs, such as media transcoding or multi-step inference, without re-architecting. GPU-accelerated functions support container images up to 32 GB (10 GB per file), up to 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2,048 to 32,768 MB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, up to 48 concurrent requests per execution environment, and up to 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider.

Let’s try it out To show what this looks like in practice, I deployed an open-source large language model (LLM) from Hugging Face as a Lambda function and sent it a prompt. With the vLLM base image from Lambda, I only set the Hugging Face model ID in the MODEL_ID environment variable, without writing any inference code. I used Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, a small instruction-tuned model that suits in-application tasks such as summarization, classification, and extraction. The flow has four steps: create a capacity provider, build and push the container image, create a function from that image, then publish and invoke. Before you begin, request an increase to your G-series instance quota (listed as Running On-Demand G and VT instances), because latest accounts might start with a quota of 0. For more information, see On-Demand Instance quotas.

It has been revealed that first, I created a capacity provider, where I specify the GPU instance types Lambda can use and let it auto-scale. Listing several instance types lets Lambda pick the most cost-effective one that is available and fall back across generations when capacity is tight.

The Lambda console demonstrates the newly introduced capacity provider, lmi-gpu-cp, in the Active state. Note the VPC configuration with its subnets and security group.

Figure 1: The capacity provider is Active, with its VPC configuration.

In a recent development, next, I built the container image. Lambda provides a curated vLLM base image that includes the vLLM inference server, PyTorch, Transformers, and the CUDA toolkit, along with a runtime interface client that supports concurrent invocations. The image serves the model for me, so I don’t write a handler or any inference server code. My entire Dockerfile is one line:.

After pushing the image to Amazon ECR, I created the function. I chose the model with the MODEL_ID environment variable, which accepts a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an Amazon S3 location, or a local path. Lambda downloads the model, manages GPU memory, and serves requests. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct is a public model, so I didn’t need a Hugging Face token. For private or gated models, or to get higher download rate limits, you can also set HF_TOKEN.

Industry observers note that GPU-accelerated functions use AcceleratorConfig to request accelerator memory. AcceleratorMemorySize is the minimum GPU memory the function needs, and Lambda places the execution environment on the smallest available GPU that meets it, so the GPU you get can have more memory than you requested. I set PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency to 4, the default. The vLLM server batches concurrent requests on the GPU, so invocations share one copy of the model and the GPU stays busy. I also set ExecutionEnvironmentMemoryGiBPerVCpu to 4, which gives the function the 16,384 MB of memory and 4 vCPUs it needs while leaving capacity on the 2xlarge instance for Lambda’s management components.

The function overview shows what makes this a GPU-accelerated function: the attached capacity provider that supplies the GPU instances and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR, all wired into the same function model you already use.

Figure 2: The lmi-gpu-inference function overview, showing the attached capacity provider and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR.

Sources indicate that functions on Lambda Managed Instances run from a published version, so I published one. Publishing provisions the execution environments, and each one downloads the model weights and warms up the engine before the version becomes active. The cold start happens during the publish step, so the first caller doesn’t wait for it.

Then I sent the model a prompt. The payload is a standard OpenAI request body: a messages array routes to chat completions, and a prompt field routes to text completions.

The model answered from a GPU inside the Lambda execution environment, and the response is a standard OpenAI completion object, so any OpenAI-compatible client works with it.

Recent findings suggest that four concurrent invocations finished in about the same time as a single one, on one execution environment that shares one copy of the model in GPU memory. From a Hugging Face model ID to a live, OpenAI-compatible GPU endpoint took about 10 minutes, most of it unattended while Lambda provisioned capacity and warmed up the model.

Industry observers note that that’s a working LLM endpoint with no inference server code, no GPU drivers, and no cluster to manage. To try a different model, I update MODEL_ID and publish a new version, with no image rebuild. Each version is an immutable snapshot, so different models can run side by side as separate versions. It is also a Lambda Event Function, so I can trigger it from an Amazon SQS queue to process documents in batches, put Amazon API Gateway in front of it, or call it as the inference step in a Lambda durable functions workflow.

For production, copy the model weights to an S3 bucket in the same Region, point MODEL_ID at that bucket, and set VLLM_LOAD_FORMAT=runai_streamer so the weights stream straight into memory. This gives faster starts and removes the dependency on the Hugging Face Hub. For more guidance, see the best practices for running inference workloads. Beyond LLM inference, you can also run custom ML inference, media processing, and other GPU workloads. See the Lambda documentation for best practices.

The configuration tab demonstrates the settings that matter for a GPU-accelerated function: 16,384 MB of memory, the 15-minute timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage for the downloaded weights, alongside the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency of 4, the 4:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio, and 16 GB of accelerator memory.

Figure 3: The function’s configuration, including memory, timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage, and the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency, the memory-to-vCPU ratio, and accelerator memory.

When you finish testing, delete the function and then the capacity provider so that Lambda stops the GPU instances and you stop paying for them.

How it works The capabilities below are what you get out of the box, each one removing GPU work you would otherwise own.

It has been revealed that skip the GPU software setup. Curated base images ship with the frameworks and tools handled for you, so you do not install or reconcile them: base:cuda (CUDA toolkit and runtime), cupy:cuda (CuPy, NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Numba), pytorch:cuda (PyTorch, torchvision, torchaudio, transformers, FFmpeg), and serving images vllm:cuda and sglang:cuda. Use them directly, extend them, or bring a fully custom image.

No GPU infrastructure to operate. Lambda handles driver compatibility, provisioning, routing, and load balancing, so you ship functions instead of running GPU fleets. Deploy with the same Console, CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, AWS SAM, and Terraform workflow as any Lambda Event Function.

It has been revealed that trigger GPU work from any AWS event. The same 200+ event sources that trigger Event Functions, including Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon EventBridge, trigger GPU-accelerated functions directly, with the same scaling, error handling, and retries. No custom integration code.

Serve concurrent requests on each GPU. Each execution environment can process multiple concurrent invocations on the same GPU, which you control with the per-environment concurrency setting. Raising it packs more requests onto each GPU instance to drive utilization up, so you get more throughput from the capacity you already pay for.

Recent findings suggest that multiple instance types. Specify multiple instance types or generations, and Lambda selects the most cost-effective available option and falls back across your list to reduce Insufficient Capacity Errors.

Capacity options. GPU instances run as Amazon EC2 On-Demand instances, and your existing Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply. For predictable GPU availability, create an EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservation (ODCR) that matches your capacity provider configuration, and Lambda uses that reserved capacity automatically.

Large container images and storage. Container images up to 32 GB are supported, along with up to 32 GB of NVMe ephemeral storage in /tmp. Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading lets your function begin executing before the full image is downloaded, which reduces execution environment startup time by up to 70%.

Sources indicate that see GPU usage without extra setup. GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization appear alongside standard function metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and in the AWS Lambda console.

After invoking the function, the console surfaces the GPU-specific metrics next to the standard ones. Track GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization to see how much of the accelerator each invocation actually uses, which is the signal that drives both auto-scaling and cost.

Figure 4: GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization for the vLLM function under concurrent load.

Industry observers note that pricing and availability This feature is generally available today, supporting the Amazon EC2 G-series (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f, G6e) at launch, with more instance families to come. You pay the underlying EC2 instance fee (eligible for Savings Plans and Reserved Instances), plus a 9.75 percent management fee for GPU instances, and the standard Lambda request fee of $0.20 per million requests. For pricing and Region availability, see AWS Lambda pricing.

You can also build with your AI coding assistants and agents: explore the Builder Center and connect your tools with the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which bundles the AWS MCP Server and curated agent skills.

To get started, visit the AWS Lambda console and see the GPU-accelerated functions documentation.
