NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders.
  • We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach.
  • NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

It has been revealed that neoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:.

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:.

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

According to recent reports, we report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

Recent findings suggest that viDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

It has been revealed that † Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:.

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Industry observers note that before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding fresh documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

It has been revealed that so we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

Sources indicate that neoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

Recent findings suggest that we provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers right now supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:.

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

In a recent development, neoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

It has been revealed that neoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News DoorDash Scales Dispatch 10x While Maintaining 99.99% Peak Availability.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

Sources indicate that doorDash has rebuilt its real-time dispatch platform to handle growing delivery demand, replacing a monolithic optimization engine with a distributed architecture that separates coordination from computation. The redesign delivers 10 times higher throughput and more than 99.99% availability during peak periods, while enabling the company to run machine learning and reinforcement learning models within dispatch workflows.

Sources indicate that the previous dispatch engine tightly coupled business logic, logistics state management, and computationally intensive routing algorithms. As delivery volume increased, its optimization workload became increasingly difficult to process within the time available for dispatch decisions. The underlying algorithms had roughly quadratic time complexity, and during peak periods, demand approached four times the system's processing capacity. The engine consequently relied on fallback heuristics and sometimes made assignment decisions using incomplete information.

As the DoorDash engineering team explained:.

The fatal bottleneck wasn't just raw machine capacity; it was the speed of reality.

In a recent development, rather than address the bottleneck through conventional horizontal scaling, DoorDash redesigned the execution model around two independently scalable tiers. The engineering team described the motivation:.

To scale into the future, the system didn't just need more capacity; it demanded a fundamentally new execution model.

The new platform separates execution into two independently scalable tiers. A stateful coordinator manages dispatch lifecycles, maintains global logistics state, and validates business rules. Stateless compute workers handle mathematical optimization, vehicle-routing heuristics, and model inference.

According to recent reports, the coordinator distributes localized portions of logistics data to workers using payload sharding over gRPC. This avoids broadcasting the entire global state to every worker and reduces network overhead. Workers process their assigned optimization tasks independently, while the coordinator manages orchestration and result aggregation.

Evolution from DoorDash's monolithic dispatch engine to its distributed architecture (Source: DoorDash Blog Post).

According to recent reports, the redesign addresses computational complexity through hierarchical decomposition. Rather than solving one global optimization problem, the coordinator partitions logistics data into geographic clusters and delivery trajectories. Workers process smaller problems in parallel, and a reconciliation layer combines results across partitions.

Industry observers note that doorDash used shadow testing before directing live dispatch decisions to the latest platform. Production requests were duplicated, with the legacy engine determining assignments while the new platform's outputs were logged for comparison. Teams evaluated matching quality, delivery times, and resilience under load. After establishing parity, they used controlled switchback experiments and fallback mechanisms during rollout.

Shadow testing compares legacy and latest dispatch outputs (Source: DoorDash Blog Post).

DoorDash reports a tenfold increase in dispatch throughput, with more than 99.96% of runs completing within 20 seconds. During Super Bowl Sunday, the platform maintained more than 99.99% availability despite a 10% week-over-week increase in peak volume.

It has been revealed that the architecture also introduces a hybrid L1/L2 model serving. Latency-sensitive inference runs locally within compute workers using ONNX Runtime, avoiding remote procedure call overhead. More complex evaluations use isolated remote model-serving clusters, keeping heavier workloads away from the coordinator's state-management path.

According to recent reports, doorDash has also deployed multi-agent reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust dispatch objective weights based on localized marketplace feedback, including merchant congestion and courier utilization. The agents adapt the trade-off between delivery speed and batching efficiency at individual stores. The approach was evaluated through production switchback experiments and accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Reinforcement Learning from World Feedback.

UK Home Office waved through border system without a working fix for bad data

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ICO reprimand follows failings that risked wrongful detention, with a temporary correction process taking more than a year to arrive.
  • The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded the UK Home Office over a border watchlist system released without an effective way to correct inaccurate personal information.
  • The regulator noted the failings risked people being wrongly detained for additional checks at the UK border, potentially causing distress and other harm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ICO reprimand follows failings that risked wrongful detention, with a temporary correction process taking more than a year to arrive.

The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded the UK Home Office over a border watchlist system released without an effective way to correct inaccurate personal information.

The regulator noted the failings risked people being wrongly detained for additional checks at the UK border, potentially causing distress and other harm.

The platform in question, Helios, was slated to replace its predecessor, Warnings Index, in September 2024 and despite an initial delay due to concerns over data quality, went live the following month.

Both Helios and Warnings Index are watch-listing systems, designed to allow law enforcement officials – mainly but not exclusively Border Force – to check people's data against official records at the UK border.

Helios's federated operating model, whereby the data sources are not centrally managed, yielded quicker results than Warnings Index, but contained a critical flaw in that operational staff could not alter incorrect records.

Platform operators, such as Border Force officers, could not amend the data that feeds into it, neither after the fact nor in real time. This was not the case with Warnings Index, which had a dedicated team responsible for correcting data entries in real time.

Under Helios, staff were supposed to report inaccuracies to the organization responsible for the relevant source data, which would make the correction.

One slight problem: there was no established reporting system at the time Helios was launched on October 2.

The platform went live anyway, as officials deemed the data integrity and security risks presented by Warnings Index to be greater than those of Helios.

Just nine days passed before the Home Office's data protection officer had to submit a breach report after Helios operational staff stated they didn't know how to request data corrections.

During the time, Helios operators sent 87 data rectification requests to the Warnings Index correction team, despite it having no capability to make the required changes to the data.

The Home Office later said that many other requests likely weren't logged as the proper processes were not in place, and that staff should have logged the matter through a ServiceNow IT ticket, as any other departmental civil servant with any kind of IT issue would have.

But the Home Office also noted that including personal data in those helpdesk tickets would itself constitute a data breach.

The ICO mentioned in its reprimand document [PDF] that it is "unclear" how such a reporting arrangement could realistically work in practice, given that a report would require details from a subject's record that required rectification as well as the fresh, accurate information that should be used to replace it.

The Home Office's proposed workaround was to get operational staff to verbally read out said personal data over a phone call with the IT helpdesk – a procedure it described as possible "but cumbersome.".

It took the Home Office more than a year to implement a temporary data-rectification method, which involved a BX Data Query tile on the IT Now platform, allowing Helios operators to securely report data accuracy concerns.

The latest method went live on October 25, 2025.

By March 18, 2026, the Home Office remarked the latest process had received more than 6,500 correction requests and around 5,000 records had been removed.

The ICO mentioned it "remains concerned" about the efficacy of this method, given that operators cannot include personal data in the tile report, but the regulator is satisfied the problem is at least in part fixed.

The Home Office also remarked it was aware of an increase in customer complaints following Helios's launch, and around 800 cases in which people were delayed at the UK border pending additional checks.

It was unable to attribute a specific number of these to Helios's technical problems, however.

"The Home Office further stated that it was not aware of any data subjects suffering distress as a result of using its services at the UK border," the ICO's report stated.

Industry observers note that A Home Office spokesperson told us: "We take data protection extremely seriously. That is why we have co-operated fully with the Information Commissioner's Office. "We immediately removed all outdated records to minimize delays to passenger journeys and strengthened mechanisms to speed up updates."Our processes will continue to be kept under review, ensuring we meet data protection obligations while protecting border security.".

Joanne Stones, investigations manager at the ICO, remarked: "People must be able to trust that decisions about their immigration status at the UK border are made with accurate, up to date information." She added: "They also have the right to expect that when information is inaccurate, there is a swift and efficient way for it to be corrected.

According to recent reports, "We recognize that federated systems like Helios present unique challenges and welcome the steps the Home Office has taken since this matter was identified. However, the Home Office must ensure that its permanent solution provides a robust and effective way to identify and correct inaccurate information without delay.".

Recent findings suggest that the ICO's public sector enforcement policy favors guidance, reprimands, and other interventions, reserving fines for the most egregious cases. Its rationale is to avoid diverting money from public services and effectively punishing those affected twice.

According to recent reports, fines have included £350,000 for a 2021 MoD email that exposed details of Afghan evacuation applicants, and £750,000 for the PSNI's 2023 disclosure of workforce information, including surnames, initials, ranks, and roles. The PSNI penalty was reduced from £5.6 million under the public sector approach. ®.

Tech Report: Why optimistic updates are corrosive

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I was having an X conversation with @ben_codez, and they asked: why is showing an update as succeeded, before the underlying operation has actually succeeded, corrosive?
  • According to recent reports, it's corrosive because it normalizes software that is plainly broken and doesn't respect our users.
  • I made a chart of what I understand to be Ben's position on communicating with their people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I was having an X conversation with @ben_codez, and they asked: why is showing an update as succeeded, before the underlying operation has actually succeeded, corrosive?

According to recent reports, it's corrosive because it normalizes software that is plainly broken and doesn't respect our users. If a user flips a switch, and sees it flip, and then comes back, and the switch is unflipped, the software is broken. How can you operate software that doesn't do what you request it to do? It erodes trust.

I made a chart of what I understand to be Ben's position on communicating with their people.

"Booking confirmed" shown before the server checks the seat.

No self respect Ben: "No self respecting dev would show the user a booking had succeeded before server verification.".

Your like demonstrates as done before the server notes "ok".

Ben: "liking a post", "(It can retry silently).".

If the user closes the tab before the server has it, their like is lost and the user is never told.

Your post demonstrates greyed out until the server states "ok".

Ben: "Right!", to a post shown "greyed out maybe, to indicate it wasn't committed".

Sources indicate that but in addition to that, it's actually easier to make software that doesn't lie to your people. You can skip all the reconciliation machinery that's required to create UI that communicates to users that the change they thought had gone through had indeed not gone through.

It has been revealed that here's a quick demo of using instant intent to communicate the state toggling a switch e.g. a like button.

It has been revealed that when you click the switch, the client shows the button as pressed straight away and sends the click to the server. The switch takes no more clicks while it's pressed, and if there's no answer within half a second, it starts to blink. The client then won't enhancement until the server answers with the reconciled HTML view, which Datastar morphs in place.

Experiment with different latencies and taking it offline, to see how the interaction feels under different scenarios.

The pressed and blinking look is the same CSS the seats use, on the main page.

AWS Weekly Roundup: Local Zone in Bogotá, 30-minute Lambda timeout, and more (November 24, 2026)

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1408 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some limits shape architecture more than any feature does.
  • Two other threads ran through the week.
  • HeadlinesAWS Local Zone in Bogotá, Colombia – AWS opened a upcoming Local Zone in Bogotá, so you can now run applications that need single-digit millisecond latency closer to users in Colombia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some limits shape architecture more than any feature does. AWS Lambda released in 2014 with a 60-second timeout, moved to 5 minutes in 2015 and to 15 minutes in 2018, and then stayed there for eight years. Last week the limit doubled, and in the same week Lambda learned to run on GPUs and gave platform teams their own runtimes. That is a lot of Lambda for one week.

Two other threads ran through the week. A new AWS Local Zone in Bogotá brought AWS infrastructure closer to people in Colombia. And AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS), Amazon Cognito, and Amazon CloudFront each shipped a piece of identity for agents: who an agent is when it highlights up at your door, and how little it should be allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

HeadlinesAWS Local Zone in Bogotá, Colombia – AWS opened a upcoming Local Zone in Bogotá, so you can now run applications that need single-digit millisecond latency closer to users in Colombia. AWS Local Zones place compute, storage, and networking near large metropolitan areas with the same APIs and tools as a Region, for workloads like real-time gaming, live streaming, and financial transactions. The Bogotá Local Zone supports Amazon EC2 C7i, M7i, and R7i instances, Amazon EBS gp3, gp2, and io1 volumes with local snapshots, Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, AWS Direct Connect, and Application Load Balancer. To start, enable us-east-1-bog-1a in AWS Global View.

AWS Lambda now supports a 30-minute timeout for on-demand Event Functions – You can now configure any Event Function with a timeout of up to 30 minutes (1,800 seconds), double the previous limit, for synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping invocations. On Lambda Managed Instances, synchronous invocations also go to 30 minutes, while asynchronous and event source mapping invocations keep the 90-minute timeout from September. Standard Lambda pricing applies, in all commercial Regions. Agentic requests that chain model and tool calls, media transcoding, and file conversion are the workloads AWS calls out. Before raising the value, read the considerations in the Compute blog post: a service that invokes your function synchronously applies its own timeout, client read and socket timeouts need to be longer, and a NAT gateway drops idle connections after 350 seconds, so long calls need keep-alives. For longer work, durable functions still run for up to a year, and now emit OpenTelemetry traces.

AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances – You can now run GPU-accelerated inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing as Lambda functions, packaged as OCI container images, with no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile. In the walkthrough, four concurrent requests shared one copy of the model on a single GPU and finished in about the same time as one. It’s optimized for inference with custom models, on G-series instances from G4dn to G6e. You pay the EC2 instance fee (Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply), a 9.75% management fee for GPU instances, and $0.20 per million requests.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:.

Amazon Polly now supports voice cloning – You can now create a custom voice in Amazon Polly from a few minutes of recordings of a consenting speaker, running on the Polly generative engine. It launches in seven languages, including English, Spanish, and Portuguese, and each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. Polly doesn’t keep the recordings or train on them. Creating a voice is free, and you pay for the speech you synthesize. It’s a gated release, so request access through your account team. The ML blog post covers brand-voice use cases for contact centers, voice agents, and content.

AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes – You can now manage a Lambda runtime as its own resource, separate from function deployment. Platform teams package approved SDKs, certificates, and security or monitoring agents as an OCI image in Amazon ECR, and functions pick up updates as Lambda recycles execution environments, with no per-function redeploys. Updates can be staged, with health metrics and rollback. There’s no additional charge, and the Compute blog walkthrough shows the platform-team workflow.

In a recent development, AWS STS introduces GetScopedCredentials to scope down permissions at runtime – You can now take the temporary credentials a workload already holds and derive narrower ones, cutting permissions, session duration, or both. The result keeps the caller’s original identity, and permissions only ever narrow, so a sub-agent can never end up with more access than whoever created it. Access to the API is controlled with IAM policies, and every call lands in AWS CloudTrail. It’s available in all commercial Regions and beyond, including GovCloud (US) and China.

It has been revealed that amazon Cognito now supports dynamic client registration – You can now let MCP clients and AI agents register themselves at runtime (RFC 7591) instead of creating an app client in advance for each one. You choose between requiring an access token with a registration scope or opening registration to any client, and dynamically registered clients carry a client ID prefix so you can filter and manage them with the rest. It’s available on the Essentials and Plus plans, and client ID metadata documents arrived the same week.

It has been revealed that amazon CloudFront Functions now supports network calls – You can now call your own APIs from a function with cf.fetch() and act on the response, so authorization, personalization, or fraud checks that used to need Lambda@Edge or a trip to the origin can run at the edge. AWS’s own example: check an AI agent’s permissions and usage budget before the request reaches your API or MCP server. Network calls cost $0.10 per million on top of invocation charges and are included in the Pro flat-rate proposal and above. The Networking blog post also covers cf.beacon() for background analytics.

Amazon Aurora DSQL now supports multi-Region peering across continents – You can now build a multi-Region Amazon Aurora DSQL cluster with peers on different continents, such as US East (N. Virginia) and Europe (Ireland), and read and write to one strongly consistent database from both. It was a busy week for DSQL: PL/pgSQL functions and procedures arrived, and storage upgrades brought up to 50% higher write throughput at no additional cost.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:.

How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers – With more than 12,500 developers in R&D, BMW treats governance as deterministic code outside the agent’s reasoning loop, mostly in the CI/CD pipeline, so neither the agent nor its prompts can override it.

Sources indicate that AI coding agents on Amazon EC2 Mac: How Cognition scales Devin for macOS – Cognition starts a fresh macOS VM for each Devin session in under a minute on Amazon EC2 Mac hosts across six Regions. The detail worth stealing: sessions are decoupled from hosts, and Cognition reports that about 90% release their VM when idle and resume from a snapshot in seconds.

How Klaviyo processes 3 billion daily events at scale with Amazon MSK Express – Timely reading for Black Friday week. Klaviyo moved from RabbitMQ to Amazon MSK Express brokers to absorb roughly 7 times normal event volume during Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Running one set of processors across three priority topics, instead of separate infrastructure per level, cut costs by roughly 30%, according to the team.

AWS re:Invent – It’s next week: join the community in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, or register for the free livestream to follow the keynotes and selected sessions remotely.

AWS Community Days – Find community-led technical talks, workshops, and hands-on learning near you. Check each organizer’s page for current dates and registration details.

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

It has been revealed that that’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui.
  • Recent findings suggest that workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes.
  • It has been revealed that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Recent findings suggest that workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

It has been revealed that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

Sources indicate that all the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

This is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

Industry observers note that in Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

That same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

Recent findings suggest that there's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

Recent findings suggest that this is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

The drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

Industry observers note that gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

This is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

Industry observers note that there are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

It has been revealed that AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

The image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

Sources indicate that so far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

Sources indicate that A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:.

ZeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

According to recent reports, this isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

Every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node highlights up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:.

Now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:.

bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

It has been revealed that if you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

Sources indicate that really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes.

Recent findings suggest that analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?

Breaking: 45°C inlets just killed the chiller. Most people haven't noticed yet

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In my mind and in my car, we can't rewind, we've gone too far.
  • Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall.
  • Recent findings suggest that if anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In my mind and in my car, we can't rewind, we've gone too far.

SC25 in St. Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall. Pipes, pumps, manifolds, quick-disconnects, and a lot of people who clearly spend more time thinking about pressure drop than floating-point. I kept expecting to see a booth selling industrial fire hoses. Chicago is a much bigger building – McCormick has roughly four times the exhibit space St. Louis had – so the pre-show question was whether SC26 will still look like that or whether the hall is large enough to dilute the effect.

Recent findings suggest that if anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago. The heat problem didn't get smaller just because the building got bigger.

Sources indicate that we also saw a lot of new companies displaying their cooling wares at SC26. I follow this stuff closely and see two broad trends. First: consolidation with big industrial suppliers buying up the liquid cooling pioneers. Second: anyone with an angle is heading into the market. Both trends were visible on the floor in Chicago, and everyone had something to say about higher inlet temperatures, whether they have a real story or not.

The real news, though, is a number Nvidia dropped earlier this year: 45°C (113°F) liquid inlet temperature for their parts. That's not a small tweak. Most liquid-cooled systems have been living in the 30-35°C (86-95°F) world because that's what the chips would tolerate. Jump to 45°C (113°F) and a whole bunch of datacenters that presently need chillers suddenly don't.

If AMD, Intel, and the Arm folks can match it – and we’d be shocked if they aren't already working on exactly that – then free cooling stops being a cool climate thing and becomes the default for a lot of places.

Rooftop dry coolers can reject nearly any incoming fluid temperature and bring it below 45°C (113°F). There are few places in the world where ambient temperatures approach 113°F, and for the hours when outside temps spike, adiabatic assist is available. This is where water is trickled through a mesh surrounding the dry coolers, which drops the effective temperature another 10–20 percent.

So, in our fresh cooling world, there are two closed loops: one taking heat from the server gear and then passing it to a second, different loop that takes the hot water to the roof, cools it, then brings it back again.

Sources indicate that what's missing here? It's the chillers. You won't need them anymore. These are essentially huge rooftop refrigerators that cool water even more after the dry cooling. They're expensive, need a lot of maintenance, gulp electricity and are thankfully unnecessary now for upcoming datacenter builds.

The power and water savings are not trivial. Legacy designs that rely on chillers and open evaporative towers commonly put 20 percent to 40 percent of total facility energy into cooling. A large share of that is the chiller plant itself – compressors, pumps, and cooling-tower fans. Move to dry coolers running at 45°C (113°F) inlet and that slice collapses.

Published estimates and vendor modeling for high-temperature liquid loops put the reduction in cooling energy in the 50 percent to 70 percent range versus a conventional chiller-plus-tower plant, which translates into a 10 percent to 20 percent drop in total datacenter power  – depending on the starting PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) and climate.

In a recent development, water use falls even harder. Traditional evaporative towers can consume millions of gallons a year at a mid-size site. Dry coolers use essentially no outside water in normal operation; adiabatic assist only wets the mesh during the hottest hours, cutting annual water consumption by 80 percent to 95 percent in most climates. Those are the numbers that make the 45°C (113°F) inlet such a significant deal.

Sources indicate that the same shift also changes the economics of the mechanical plant itself. A chiller plant is not just an operating cost; it is capital equipment that has to be sized, installed, maintained, and eventually replaced. Dry coolers are simpler, cheaper to install, and have far fewer moving parts. When the chips will accept 45°C (113°F) fluid, the business case for putting a mechanical refrigeration plant on the roof of a new build gets hard to defend in most climates. That is the part that has not yet fully registered outside the cooling specialists.

According to recent reports, designing systems around these higher inlet temperatures still takes real engineering work – sizing the loops, choosing the dry coolers, and making sure the facility can run at the fresh set points without surprises. Existing buildings add another layer. Many were built with pipes, pumps, and heat exchangers sized air cooling or lower temperature liquid. Raising liquid inlet temperature means checking flow rates, pressure drops, and making sure the existing set-up delivers.

Recent findings suggest that at SC26 I had meetings with a couple of companies that do this work and buttonholed more in their booths. My top-of-mind questions were: Are the 45°C (113°F) inlet temps for real? Yes, they are, and are being used as a design basis to an extent – they need to leave headroom, of course.

Recent findings suggest that any news on whether the other chipmakers are going to hit the Nvidia number on inlet temperature? Attendees were closed-lipped on this one. Nothing public from the other vendors (AMD/Intel/Arm). But on the cooling vendor side, they are happy to see the increase and will comply.

My instincts are telling me that the other chipsters may have been caught flatfooted by Nvidia's 45°C stake in the ground, but those same instincts also tell me that handfuls of Peanut M&Ms healthy snacks. I’ll nose around more.

In a recent development, there's real money at stake here from a TCO standpoint. One cooling vendor reports that their initial testing shows 3 percent to 4 percent cooling energy cost decrease for every additional 1°C inlet temperature increase. That's a significant number at scale.

We're approaching a point where industry advances are answering many of the objections (the real ones, not the hysterical ones) raised by the anti-data center movement.

Much lower energy use, water consumption down by 85 percent to 90 percent, higher efficiency and lower costs. Not a bad deal, right? ®.

Hackers help themselves to 1Password's source code and customer data

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An intruder planted malicious code in backend services, but the biz insists passwords are safe.
  • 1Password is reassuring customers that their vaults remain secure after an attacker breached its systems and stole account information and private source code.
  • The Canadian security biz disclosed this week that an attacker had compromised an employee's corporate GitHub account, made off with private source code, and deployed malicious code to its backend services to siphon off customer information.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An intruder planted malicious code in backend services, but the biz insists passwords are safe.

1Password is reassuring customers that their vaults remain secure after an attacker breached its systems and stole account information and private source code.

The Canadian security biz disclosed this week that an attacker had compromised an employee's corporate GitHub account, made off with private source code, and deployed malicious code to its backend services to siphon off customer information.

1Password, which began investigating the intrusion on November 19, hasn't said how many customers were affected, but confirmed that the stolen data includes names and email addresses used to sign in to the service, account identifiers, timestamps showing when users created and last accessed their accounts, and various pieces of non-secret account metadata.

The firm insists the information that customers actually pay it to protect was beyond the intruder's reach. "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password stated.

In a recent development, arguably more troubling is the revelation that the intruder gained access to 1Password's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) infrastructure, which houses credentials used to keep its products running. The company says it has rotated or revoked potentially exposed credentials and that neither its apps nor its browser extensions were affected.

1Password hasn't explained how access to an employee's GitHub account enabled the attacker to deploy malicious code to its backend services, nor has it detailed the extent of the attacker's access to its software build and distribution infrastructure. The manufacturer did not respond to The Register's questions.

The miscreant also got their hands on tokens embedded in emails sent to some customers as part of account invitations, provisioning, and recovery processes. These tokens aren't enough to access an account on their own, according to 1Password, as consumers must also authenticate via single sign-on or enter a verification code sent to their registered email address.

It has been revealed that the company claims it specifically notified the small number of users with affected provisioning or recovery processes underway. It found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed provisioning tokens.

Still, the breach has prompted the password management biz to beef up those verification codes, replacing the six-digit numeric variety with ten-character alphanumeric codes to make brute-forcing them considerably more difficult.

1Password has booted the intruder out of its GitHub environment, revoked the stolen token, and rolled back the affected backend services to clean versions of the code. It's since shored up security around its development infrastructure and employees' devices, and brought in outside security specialists to review its handiwork.

The incident recalls the first stage of LastPass's 2022 breach, when an attacker compromised its development environment and stole source code. Information obtained in that intrusion helped enable a second attack that exposed customer vault backups, including encrypted passwords.

The UK Information Commission's Office slapped LastPass with a £1.2 million ($1.6 million) fine last December over the incident, which compromised the personal information of up to 1.6 million UK owners. Among the regulator's gripes was that LastPass had fallen short of the higher standard of security expected of a company entrusted with people's passwords.

Customers aren't being asked to change their account passwords or Secret Keys, neither of which 1Password stores, although the organization is warning users to be on the lookout for phishing attempts.

According to recent reports, A list of email addresses belonging to people known to use a particular password manager is a handy thing for a phisher to have, especially when noted password manager has just given them a plausible pretext for getting in touch. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News GitHub Ditches CSS-in-JS for CSS Modules, Reports 55% Faster SSR after Three-Year Migration.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

GitHub has published an in-depth account of a three-year effort to move github.com off CSS-in-JS and onto CSS Modules, reporting a 55% reduction in server-side rendering time and 25% faster component initialisation across its Primer-powered design system.

It has been revealed that written by Primer engineers Josh Black and Marie Lucca, the post explains how component counts on certain pages began to explode in 2023, exposing scaling problems with the existing styled-components setup. Initial page loads, server render times and style enhancement costs all grew with component count. The team picked CSS Modules because it kept native CSS features and co-location while removing client and server runtime work, letting styles roll up into static stylesheets delivered with the HTML.

Recent findings suggest that for every Primer component the team added a CSS Modules variant, gated it behind a feature flag, verified parity with visual regression tests, then rolled it out from the Primer team to GitHub staff and finally all consumers. By December 2024, Primer itself was fully on CSS Modules. The harder half was the roughly 7,760 sx prop usages scattered across github.com, the de facto styling standard for years. A transitional @primer/styled-react package let sx keep working against migrated components during the crossover.

A typical conversion looks like this:.

A rotation of eight engineers migrated 6,419 props over six months, seeing SSR improvements ranging from 3% up to 22% per page. The final 895 props were cleared in three weeks by two engineers leaning heavily on Copilot coding agents. GitHub also had to decouple theming for its seven themes and high-contrast variants before pulling styled-components out entirely. A VS Code plugin and internal codemod cut the manual burden, and GitHub notes that styled-components entering maintenance mode reinforced the direction.

According to recent reports, on Hacker News one commenter running a similar migration reported a 30% build time speed improvement and much better tree shaking on Next.js across a codebase over 1M lines. Others were sceptical about user impact, with one arguing that the reduction in size was not massive enough to justify making all CSS names unreadable, adding that hashed class names make ad-blockers, custom CSS and browser extensions harder to build. A separate thread noted that CSS-in-JS can be made zero-runtime without moving to Modules at all.

GitHub joins a broader shift away from runtime CSS-in-JS. Linear recently completed its own 1,000-PR move from styled-components to Meta's atomic StyleX library, citing similar render-time concerns after upgrading to React 18's concurrent mode. Others using vanilla-extract or Tailwind have shifted style generation to build time entirely. The common thread is to pay the cost once at build, not on every request.

Industry observers note that the Primer Design System is GitHub's open-source component library, providing the foundational building blocks used across github.com. Teams following the same path can start from the Primer React v38 release notes and the migration guide for CSS variables, which covers the move from sx props to CSS Modules.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

#161289. Industry News: Async GRPO with LoRA across HF Jobs: a bucket, a proxy, and no NCCL

📅 10 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4607 w)
📖 Baca
