📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there’s recently been some discussion about the benefits and downsides of lock (mutex) poisoning in Rust, spurred by a recent proposal to make the default mutex non-poisoned, i.e. silently unlock on panic (see also, recent discussion on Hacker News). As a passionate defender of lock poisoning, I thought I’d gather and write about my thoughts on this matter.

In a recent development, rust, like most multithreaded languages, has mutexes: a construct to ensure that a particular piece of data can only be accessed by one thread at a time. The way mutexes work in Rust is particularly well-considered:.

Sources indicate that this is all quite reasonable! Let’s look at an example that processes incoming messages for a set of tracked operations. Let’s assume that multiple threads could be processing messages, so we have to guard the internal state with a mutex. (We’ll discuss alternative approaches to this problem later.).

It has been revealed that this is a very typical use of mutexes: to guard one or more invariants or properties of some kind. These invariants are upheld while the mutex is unlocked. In this case, the invariant being guarded is that Operations::ops has complete and up-to-date tracking of all in-progress and completed operations.

According to recent reports, of equal importance is the fact that, while the mutex is held, the invariant is temporarily violated. In order to process the message, we have to remove the state from the map, create a upcoming state, then put it back into the map. During this period, Operations::ops is missing this one operation, so it no longer tracks all operations. But this temporary violation is okay, because no other threads see this in-between state. Before the mutex is released, this code is responsible for putting the operation back into the map.

Recent findings suggest that is it always true that the operation is put back into the map? Unfortunately not always, in the presence of what I think of as unexpected errors. Many practitioners draw a separation between two different kinds of errors that a system can have. The terms recoverable and unrecoverable are sometimes used for them, but I tend to prefer the following terms (see also some discussion by Andrew Gallant):.

Sources indicate that generally, in Rust, expected errors are handled via the Result type, and unexpected errors are handled by panicking. Now, there isn’t a firm requirement that things be this way.

But in typical production-grade Rust, expected errors are Results while unexpected errors (and only unexpected errors) are panics. Lock poisoning is built around this assumption.

In a recent development, consider what happens if a panic occurs in OperationState::process_message. This depends in part on the build flags and surrounding code, so let’s look closely at all the possibilities. In Rust, there are two ways to configure build flags on panic:.

Industry observers note that some real-world applications (such as most of what we ship at Oxide) abort on panic, but most of this post is actually moot for aborts. So in the rest of this post, we’re going to focus on the default unwind behavior.

If a panic is invoked in the context of a catch_unwind, an Err(E) is returned, where the value E is whatever message or other payload the panic occurred with.

If there’s no catch_unwind, and the panic occurs on the main thread, then a message is printed out and the program exits with an error.

and the program exits with a non-success exit code.

If there’s no catch_unwind, and the panic occurs on a different thread, then a message is printed out, and the panic message is returned as the result of JoinHandle::join.

If you run this slightly more complex program:.

and the program exits with a non-success exit code.

Industry observers note that an interesting thing to note here is that there were two panics: one in the spawned child thread with the panic! message, and one in the main thread when the expect was called. The panic responsible for producing the non-success exit code was the one that occurred in the main thread, not the child thread.

This raises the question: what if a non-main thread panics and the thread is not joined? With this program:.

And the program exits with a successful exit code! There’s no indication that a panic occurred other than the message printed out, which can easily be missed.

The upshot of all this is that panics in non-main threads are not magic. In order for the system to make decisions based on whether a panic occurred, it must process that, either with catch_unwind or via JoinHandle::join, and it’s all too easy to just ignore panics.

Coming back to our Operations example above, what does that mean for our mutex’s critical section?

This might look like a lot of ifs, but they’re more common than you might think: they’re all either the default in Rust or a very common way to write code.

Sources indicate that rust’s designers had the foresight to see this problem, and introduce lock poisoning as a detection mechanism for this failure mode. The way poisoning works is that:.

In a recent development, almost all code immediately panics on seeing a PoisonError via .lock().unwrap(): this is often called propagating panics. But PoisonError can be handled more explicitly than that. Note that PoisonError, and poisoning more generally, is purely advisory: you can retrieve the data underneath, and even clear the poison bit in Rust 1.77 and above.

The fact is, though, that anything other than .lock().unwrap() is rare in practice. This is emphatically not a reason to remove poisoning, and in fact is a strong argument to retain poisoning while making the ergonomics better (see below). What is notable is detection, not recovery.

Industry observers note that so, putting it all together: if a child thread panics in a critical section, then it is quite possible that the data is in an inconsistent or logically corrupt state. To indicate this, the mutex is marked poisoned. If the child thread is not waited on by the parent, this might be the only indication that a panic previously occurred in a critical section!

It is precisely this confluence of factors that makes lock poisoning such an crucial feature.

In a recent development, is the problem of inconsistent mutex-guarded state limited to panic unwinding? I’d argue that it is a property of unexpected cancellations more generally: you start executing a critical section thinking that it will be run to completion, but something causes that process to be interrupted.

In Rust, there are two sources of unexpected cancellations, with strong parallels between them:.

As documented in Oxide RFD 397 and RFD 400, unexpected future cancellations have resulted in so many mutex invariant violations that we now avoid Tokio mutexes entirely1. My perspective here comes from much pain dealing with this matter in async Rust, and wanting very much for this footgun to not make its way to synchronous Rust.

See the appendix for more details.

In other words, is poisoning often too conservative? My answer to this is that panics do not always cause invariant violations, but they’re so common, and the downsides of corrupt state so unbounded, that it is still valuable to have lock poisoning as a strong heuristic.

According to recent reports, firstly, if all you’re doing is reading data that just happens to be guarded by a mutex (maybe because some other function writes to that data), a panic in the critical section can’t cause invariant violations. (But also, you may wish to use an RwLock.).

Sources indicate that secondly, some simple kinds of writes can also avoid causing invariant violations. For example if all you’re doing is updating some counters2:.

Finally, it is sometimes possible to carefully architect code to be unwind safe, such that if a panic occurs, either:.

Recent findings suggest that for example, the standard library’s HashMap and BTreeMap are architected this way. In our Operations example, we could, rather than removing the operation from the map entirely, replace it with an Invalid sentinel state.

Recent findings suggest that in these cases, it is true that a panic in a critical section is not harmful, and that the typical .lock().unwrap() approach will reduce system availability. But the notable thing to keep in mind is that code changes over time. One of the things I like about Rust is how resilient it is to changes over time: by encoding properties like mutable access into the type system, Rust makes it that much harder for new team members (or even yourself six months from now) to screw up. However, like async cancel safety, unwind safety is not encoded in Rust’s type system3, so it’s easy for code that’s fine today to be wrong tomorrow.

Industry observers note that the main downside to a .lock().unwrap() that misfires is reduced availability and denial of service. But the downsides to an undetected panic are unbounded, and can range from denial of service all the way to “(part of) an HTTP request ending up sent to a party it should not have been sent to,” or in other words personal information leakage.

A downside that (while potentially serious) is bounded, versus the kind of flaw that can kill an organization—I know which default I want.

Recent findings suggest that what about writing panic-free code? You can carefully write your critical sections to not have panics. But that is a property that’s especially hard to maintain as code changes over time. Even something as simple as a println! can panic. Also, if the critical section can’t panic, then it doesn’t matter whether the mutex poisons or not.

It has been revealed that A bit of history here: in Rust 1.0, panics could only be detected at thread boundaries via JoinHandle::join. This meant that back then, the only way for panics to cause invariant violations was for:.

Since then, two Rust features were added:.

With both of these, you can operate on arbitrary data (i.e. not just data guarded by a mutex) and leave it in an inconsistent state. To see how, let’s rewrite the Operations example above to not have a mutex inside of it, and to require exclusive access to make any modifications to it.

Since there are no mutexes involved any more, this is no longer a critical section in the classical sense. But note that we still have the invariant that ops tracks all operations. This invariant is temporarily violated, with the idea that it’ll be restored before the function returns. Since &mut means nothing else has any kind of access (read or write) to this data, we know that this in-between state is not seen by anybody else.

But just like with mutexes, this breaks down with unwinding. With catch_unwind, you can do:.

And with scoped threads, you can do:.

If a panic occurs in process_message, Operations is logically corrupted. This failure mode has resulted in a proposal to have a Poison wrapper that poisons on panicking. That absolutely makes sense and is worth pursuing.

But, along with the Poison wrapper, there are some suggestions to go further and suggest that the current std::sync::Mutex type should be changed in the next Rust edition to, instead of poisoning on panic, silently unlock. (And also, as a followup, that the current Mutex should instead become Mutex>.).

According to recent reports, (It’s worth noting that there’s another non-poisoning option: the mutex stays locked forever, as C programmers might expect. This option is somewhat appealing because it is safe by default, in a sense. But once a thread is stuck waiting on the mutex, there’s no easy way to recover. So it’s not panics that propagate, it’s stuck threads. This seems strictly worse than a poisoning mutex to me, so I’ll assume the proposal means silent unlocking.).

I first want to give credit to this proposal: it is quite beautiful.

Recent findings suggest that while all of these are true, I keep coming back to how unbounded the downside of an undetected panic is, and how easy it is to get wedged in this state. Mutexes and poisoning have value separate from each other, but I don’t think they are as independent as they seem at first. My understanding from writing Rust code over many years is that almost all uses of mutexes benefit from poisoning, and almost all instances of poisoning one needs to care about are with mutex-guarded data.

In a recent development, why are mutexes special? As we’ve established above, poisoning can make sense in non-mutex contexts too. What makes mutexes a particularly valuable place to have it? The reason has to do with what I like to call the cancellation blast radius. Corrupted data only matters if it is shared mutable state: changed in a way that resulted in an invariant violation, and visible outside of where the failure occurred. If a typical &mut reference panics in the middle of an operation, it’s likely that the data it is referring to will also be torn down, in which case those invariant violations don’t matter4. But the whole point of mutexes is that they’re shared across threads! So data corruption is almost certain to be externally visible.

There are some use cases that would benefit from non-poisoning mutexes, like metrics and best-effort logging, but those cases shouldn’t drive the default.

According to recent reports, more specifically, I am worried that a common complaint about lock poisoning (see below) is that it has too much friction. Having to use Mutex> instead of Mutex adds even more friction, so people are going to opt for non-poisoning mutexes more of the time. This is going to lead to grave mistakes in production.

This is a spot where zero-cost abstractions and safety by default are seemingly at odds with each other. I would like to see performance numbers to quantify this better, but if I may hazard a guess, the incremental cost of checking the poison flag (a single atomic load with relaxed ordering) is minimal compared to the cost of acquiring the lock in the first place.

I mentioned earlier that parking_lot’s mutexes silently unlock on panic. A large chunk of the Rust ecosystem uses parking_lot today, often for performance reasons. Does that mean that code using parking_lot has these unbounded downsides?

According to recent reports, the answer depends on a bunch of things, but in general (and especially in library code) that is indeed what I’m suggesting. For instance, this critical section in parity-db is quite large. Reasoning about whether it’s unwind-safe seems very difficult to me; this is exactly the kind of code that mutex poisoning does well to guard against.

Industry observers note that in this case, the binary is configured to abort on panic, so it’s fine. But reusable Rust libraries cannot require panic = 'abort', and if this code were in a library on crates.io, it would be a real cause for concern.

According to recent reports, A common response to this class of matter is to not bother with any of this unwinding stuff, and always abort on panic. This comes back to the idea of the cancellation blast radius described above: aborting the process on panic guarantees that in-memory state is torn down.

According to recent reports, I have a lot of sympathy for this idea! This is what we do at Oxide. (Why am I writing this post if it doesn’t affect my workplace? Well, first, I care about the health of Rust more generally. Second, libraries must work with unwinds. But most importantly, we have seen the pain of unexpected async cancellations at Oxide, so we know how bad it can be.).

Industry observers note that but also, that works fine with the current approach: .lock().unwrap() always succeeds. Whether mutexes poison or not only matters with panic = 'unwind'.

This leads to what I think is driving a lot of discussion here:.

I get this complaint. I really do. Having to write .lock().unwrap() everywhere sucks. It’s extra characters in a language already filled with syntax noise. It can cause rustfmt to format your line of code across multiple lines.

In a recent development, these are all valid points. But there is a much better solution for them, one that doesn’t give up the very important benefits of poisoning: in the next Rust edition, make lock() automatically panic if the mutex is poisoned! (And add a lock_or_poison method for the current behavior5).

It’s worth comparing the different options here:.

Based on this table, I believe the answer is clear: if a breaking change is going to happen, it’s much better to make lock automatically panic than to make panics silently unlock.

Sources indicate that concurrent programming is very difficult. Rust makes it easier than most other languages, and lock poisoning is an important part of the story. Let’s avoid introducing any regressions here.

Providing a Poison wrapper makes a lot of sense. Making the default std::sync::Mutex silently unlock on panic would, however, be a mistake.

According to recent reports, should Rust’s standard library even provide non-poisoning mutexes? That’s a harder question. I’m worried that their mere presence in the standard library will lower the barrier to people doing the wrong thing, particularly in libraries where panic = 'abort' cannot be assumed. But I think non-poisoning mutexes have some legitimate uses, so I don’t object too strenuously if the tradeoffs are carefully documented.

Writing all this out was very helpful to me in getting my thoughts straight, and I hope it’s helpful to you too.

Cover photo by Karen Rustad Tolva, used with permission. Thanks to Fiona and several of my colleagues at Oxide for reviewing drafts of this post. Any errors in it are my own.

Discuss on Hacker News, Lobsters, and /r/rust.

Updated 2025-12-06: Added a section to Separating mutexes from poisoning on what makes poisoning particularly valuable for mutexes, more than in other contexts.

Unlike panics, the standard library’s mutex does not poison on future cancellations. (I believe it’s not possible to poison on future cancellations with the RAII pattern.).

But wait! Tokio provides its own Mutex type, which is sendable to another thread. This means that it is possible to put an await point in a critical section, and so the issue of unexpected cancellations within a critical section rears its ugly head with Tokio mutexes.

In a recent development, tokio mutexes also do not poison if the critical section panics. At Oxide we abort on panic so this matters less as a reason to avoid them, but is yet another asterisk that pushes me away from them. ↩︎.

A more typical way to manage simple counters is with an atomic, but if the data is more complex than just an integer, a mutex may be necessary. ↩︎.

Rust does have some rudimentary support for unwind safety in the type system, but it is more of a suggestion that most users ignore, and because of that there’s a proposal to remove it from Rust. ↩︎.

In a recent development, the exception is Drop implementations, which may have to be written robustly to guard against temporary invariant violations. ↩︎.

It has been revealed that the more obvious try_lock is already taken. ↩︎.

GitHub availability report: October 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.
  • The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate.
  • As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

Recent findings suggest that that capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

Recent findings suggest that we also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in people. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind strategy. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to revision, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

According to recent reports, actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

In a recent development, A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Industry observers note that customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

According to recent reports, web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, latest commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

In a recent development, audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

According to recent reports, some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, upcoming connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the glitch.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

It has been revealed that copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 9 minutes.

It has been revealed that customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Issues, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

Sources indicate that A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. New requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

The pool was already running near capacity when some revision requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

According to recent reports, follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

According to recent reports, now that code ships faster than ever, you have more time to spend on projects just for the fun of it. Here’s what we can learn through that process as developers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 Aims to Make Robots Safer, More Dexterous, and Faster Learners.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5, a vision-language-action (VLA) model designed to improve robots' dexterity, reliability, and learning speed, while enabling safer operation in unstructured real-world environments.

In a recent development, according to DeepMind's vice president and head of robotics Carolina Parada, the model "marks a leap forward in three key areas": dexterity, reliability, and safety. She claims its performance has been evaluated across more than 200 tasks, with reported improvements of 30% to 100% in success rates and 20% to 30% in task completion compared with prior versions. Demonstrated capabilities include serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box, and pipetting liquids.

These tasks represent a step toward human-level dexterity by combining a number of skills, including advanced tool use, complex manipulation of deformables, and handling delicate objects with finesse.

The model is designed to work natively with different types of robots, including humanoid platforms such as Apptronik's Apollo 2 and tabletop pick & place systems such as Franka Duo platform.

In a recent development, parada highlights the industrial trials conducted with Mercedes Benz, in which Apollo 2 humanoid robots were deployed on an existing industrial line, achieving a 96% success rate in tasks involving automotive kitting and sorting mixed metal brackets. In the trial, the Gemini Robotics ER embodied reasoning model enabled the robot to keep track of the workflow over multiple steps and adapt to changeing conditions, while Gemini Robotics 2.5 controlled the robot's hands and arms.

Another key aspect highlighted by Parada is Gemini Robotics 2.5's safety features, which include using reasoning guidance to identify and manage physical hazards:.

Much like safety classifiers add a protective layer around Gemini’s responses, this guidance allows the robot to navigate complex environments securely. In our evaluations, this capability boosted safe task completion around obstacles by 33% and around nearby people by 43%.

DeepMind also open-sourced the latest safety benchmark ASIMOV-jailbreak, containing hundreds of unsafe prompts across dozens of scenes.

Commenting on the announcement on LinkedIn, GEICO director of software Sean P. observed that "the combination of simulation, learning from mistakes, and real-world testing is what will make robots more capable and reliable in everyday tasks".

LightSpeed founder and CEO Biju Kulathakal emphasized that 96% accuracy may not be enough in real contexts involving humans:.

Pausing when a person gets close is what gets robots out from behind the fence. And on a real line, customers live in the 4%. Learning from its own mistakes is how that closes.

Level principal engineer Ariel Franco Ferreira expressed his view that.

Releasing an open benchmark for jailbreaks on a VLA model is the part I find most interesting, because a prompt injection that ends in a physical action is a very different failure from a bad chat answer.

He also raised the question of how to handle situations "when the robot refuses the unsafe step but leaves the task half done in a risky state".

As a final note, Gemini Robotics 2.5's development was accelerated using Gemini 4 Argon as a simulation engine, leveraging its robotics research capabilities to generate simulated environments.

#161278. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1556 w)

tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows.
  • As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift.
  • This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project revealed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

In a recent development, v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

It has been revealed that A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

It has been revealed that the model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Sources indicate that each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:.

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. Newly introduced words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Reproduce the shared-prefix result with:.

Recent findings suggest that caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated newly introduced memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Sources indicate that each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Recent findings suggest that repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on fresh input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

According to recent reports, the overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

It has been revealed that the next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the upcoming merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:.

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Recent findings suggest that every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we initiative to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:.

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

Breaking: Microsoft hotpatches hotpatch that could crash Windows Server 2025

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Expiring IPv6 routes can bring affected systems down, though corrective update doesn't require a restart.
  • Microsoft has released an out-of-band hotpatch to fix a bug in November's Windows Server 2025 security update that could crash some servers when an IPv6 route expires.
  • The patch for the patch, KB5138318, addresses crashes on systems with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Expiring IPv6 routes can bring affected systems down, though corrective update doesn't require a restart.

Microsoft has released an out-of-band hotpatch to fix a bug in November's Windows Server 2025 security update that could crash some servers when an IPv6 route expires.

The patch for the patch, KB5138318, addresses crashes on systems with Router Advertisement (RA) enabled that receive time-bound IPv6 routes. When a route timer expires, affected servers can halt with error 0x139 (KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE).

Issued on November 25, the corrective enhancement takes effect without requiring a restart, according to Microsoft.

Recent findings suggest that KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE means the kernel has detected corruption of a critical data structure and stopped the system. Microsoft has identified route-timer expiry as the trigger but hasn't explained the underlying coding fault.

According to recent reports, good to see the operating system being protected against the impact of the corruption. Less good for administrators wondering why their servers have suddenly misbehaved.

Sources indicate that lansweeper puts Windows Server 2025 at 7 percent of the servers it monitors, compared with 32 percent for Server 2022 and 33 percent for Server 2019. Only systems with the affected hotpatch and networking configuration are implicated.

Industry observers note that microsoft's Windows Server updates have not gone well over the last few months, with out-of-band updates issued in September, October, and November. An out-of-band upgrade to deal with a problem introduced in a hotpatch (in this case, KB5131077) therefore carries with it a certain sense of inevitability.

In a recent development, hotpatches are a way of getting OS security updates on a Windows Server without requiring a restart and so are, in theory, a boon for administrators keen on maximizing uptime. According to Microsoft, in addition to faster installations and better protection, there is "lower workload impact with less need to restart your machine.".

Avoiding a planned restart is less of a selling point when the alternative is an unplanned crash. ®.
