Way back in 2019, I wrote the blog post An Overview of Go's Tooling. It was a popular article and IIRC, ended up being one of the most-read items in the Go Weekly newsletter that year. It's also one that I personally still come back to fairly often, when I want to remind myself of a specific command that I can't remember.

It has been revealed that but a lot has changed in the past 7 years, and some of the information in that original post is now painfully out-of-date. So this is a version 2 of that post... fully updated for the module-enabled, gopls-integrated, token-fuelled world that we now live in 😊.

One of the biggest improvements to Go's tooling has been the introduction of latest ways to run third-party tools. We now have three options — go install, go run, and go tool — each suited to slightly different use cases.

The first option is to install the tool on your local machine using the go install command. You can run this command from anywhere on your machine, and it will download the necessary source code for the tool and create an executable binary in your GOBIN directory. So long as your GOBIN directory is on your system path, you can then run the tool whenever you need it.

For example, to install the latest version of govulncheck, check its install location, and run it, you can do this:.

Using go install tends to be a good option for general-purpose tools that happen to be written in Go, where you don't need to pin a specific version for use within a project or necessarily keep up with the latest release. Personally, I tend to use it for installing tools like hey, which I often use for things outside of Go development.

In a recent development, the second option is to use go run to execute a specific version of a tool without installing it. For example, to run the latest version of govulncheck you can use the following command:.

I've written in detail about using go run to execute tools previously in this post, but this option is really useful when there is a tool you want to quickly run on an ad hoc basis.

Personally, I often use go run in this way during code reviews, when I want to do a one-time run of a specific static analysis tool using the latest version.

Sources indicate that I also find this approach useful in small solo projects where I don't have to worry about tool version differences with other developers. I'll often create a Makefile which uses go run to execute the latest version of code-quality tools — similar to this.

Recent findings suggest that lastly, there is now the option to add a tool as a module tool dependency to your go.mod file. At a very high level, you can use the go get -tool command to add the tool as a module dependency, and the necessary version information and checksums will be added to the go.mod and go.sum files. For example:.

And then you can run the specific version of the tool listed in the go.mod file with the go tool command, like so:.

This is a great option when you are working with a team of people, where for consistency and reproducibility you want to make sure that everyone is using exactly the same version of a tool.

I've previously written a much more detailed tutorial about how to use the go tool functionality, and I recommend checking that out for more information.

Another major development in recent years has been gopls. This is the official language server for Go, which you can use with any text editor or IDE that supports the Language Server Protocol (LSP).

If you're not already familiar with LSP, it's essentially a protocol that allows text editors to communicate with external programs called language servers, which act as the "brain" behind smart editor features.

The Go language server supports a wide range of smart editor features, including:.

To use gopls, the first thing you need to do is install it on your computer using the go install command, like so:.

Once gopls is installed, you then need to configure your editor to use it.

If you're using Zed or Helix, they should automatically detect gopls on your machine and start using it without any additional setup.

Sources indicate that if you're using VS Code, you'll need to install the official Go extension. To do this, open the Extensions Panel, search for golang.go, and install this extension. After you restart and open a .go file, you should see a lightning bolt next to the Go version in the status bar at the bottom of your editor. This indicates that the language server is running.

For other editors, the steps are a little more complicated. Please see the official setup steps for Vim and Neovim, Emacs and Sublime Text.

Recent findings suggest that once your editor is configured, you should see smart editor features become available. For example, here's a screenshot of documentation when hovering over the http.Error() function in VS Code.

Sources indicate that the go doc tool remains the de facto way to view the documentation for standard library packages in your terminal. You can use it to view the documentation for an entire package, or for a specific type, function or method. For example:.

You can also use the -src flag to view the relevant source code:.

Since Go 1.25, you can also use the -http flag to start a documentation server and browse the documentation locally in your web browser. For example, to view documentation for the bytes package in your browser you can run the following command:.

Industry observers note that to display information about your current Go operating environment, you can use the go env command. This can be particularly useful if you're working on an unfamiliar machine.

Industry observers note that if there are specific values that you're interested in, you can pass them as arguments to go env. For example:.

To show documentation for all go env variables and values you can run:.

If you have your text editor setup to use gopls, there is a good chance that your .go files will automatically be formatted according to the Go conventions each time they are saved, as well as having their import lines automatically added, removed and sorted as necessary.

If you're not using gopls, or you want to format files outside of your text editor (for example, as part of a pre-commit hook or CI pipeline), you can use the gofmt tool to format them. For example:.

Industry observers note that in these commands, the -w flag instructs the tool to rewrite files in place, the -s instructs the tool to apply certain simplifications to the code, and the -d flag instructs the tool to output diffs of the changes. If you want to only display the names of changed files, instead of diffs, you can swap this for the -l flag instead. Note that gofmt works recursively, so if you pass it a directory like . or ./cmd/foo it'll format all .go files within that directory tree.

Alternatively, you can run the go fmt command — which is essentially a wrapper around gofmt -l -w — like so:.

Often, as part of a quality audit check in a CI pipeline, I want to check that .go files are formatted correctly, without actually changing anything. To do this, I usually run gofmt -l . and check that the output from this command is empty. There's an example of this in the audit check in this Makefile.

It has been revealed that it's also worth mentioning the goimports tool, which formats your .go files in the same way as gofmt, but also updates your import lines — adding, removing and sorting the lines as necessary. You can run it like so:.

You can use the go mod tidy command to automatically add missing dependencies to, and prune unused dependencies from, your go.mod and go.sum modfiles based on the imports in your .go files.

Sources indicate that it's a good idea to run this periodically to keep your modfiles synchronized with your code. Personally, I try to run this before each commit to make it easier to see exactly which code changes were responsible for adding or removing a dependency when looking through the version control history.

If you want to check if the modfiles are synchronized without actually changing them, you can use the -diff flag like so:.

In a recent development, this is a really useful command to use in audit checks and CI pipelines, because when you run it with -diff it will print out any changes and then exit with a non-zero code. If no changes are needed, it will exit with code 0.

It's also worth mentioning that running go mod tidy ensures your modfiles include the dependencies needed across all possible build tag, OS and architecture combinations. Commands like go run, go test and go build are more selective, and only require dependencies for the current build configuration. This is why you might sometimes see additional lines appear in your modfiles unexpectedly when running go mod tidy.

It has been revealed that for debugging Go applications, the standard tool to use is Delve. It allows you to set breakpoints, step through your code line by line, and do things like inspecting the values of variables and viewing the current call stack.

You can install Delve by running:.

Nowadays, the easiest way to use Delve is generally via the debugger integration in your text editor. For example, in VS Code you set breakpoints by clicking in the gutter next to a line of code, start a debugging session by opening the 'Run and Debug' panel, and use the debugging toolbar to step through your application and inspect what's happening as it runs.

In a recent development, it's also possible to use Delve outside of a text editor and start an interactive debugging session in your terminal. For example, assuming you installed Delve using the go install command above, you could start debugging an application in the ./cmd/web directory by running:.

You can then use Delve's commands to set breakpoints, continue execution, step through your code, and inspect variables, in much the same way as in a text editor.

There is a nice introduction on how to use the terminal-based debugger in this post, and more information about debugging with Delve can be found in the official Delve documentation.

In a recent development, go 1.26 made major changes to the go fix command, updating it so that it now automatically 'modernizes' your code to use the latest Go idioms and standard library APIs. When you run it, it will do things like replacing interface{} with any, and rewrite code to use functions like slices.Contains() rather than manual loops.

You can see a complete list of the analyzers that go fix supports, and what they do, by running go tool fix help:.

At its most basic, you can use go fix like this:.

In a recent development, however, it's vital to be aware that go fix will silently rewrite your .go files in place. If you want to know in advance what changes it will make without actually applying them you can use the -diff flag like so:.

In a recent development, sometimes, when looking at the diff, you might decide that you want to make some, but not all, of the changes. For example, there have been times when I've decided that my original code was clearer without the modernizations applied by the embedlit and mapsloop analyzers. You can disable specific analyzers individually like so:.

Sources indicate that since the release of gopls, the simplest, safest and most flexible way to refactor your code is by using its code transformation features in your text editor. For example, you can inline function calls, extract code into a function, rename identifiers, and move or remove parameters across your codebase, all in a few clicks.

For example, in VS Code you can use the 'Rename' and 'Refactor' options in the right-click menu to refactor code like so:.

More information, including a description of all supported refactoring features, can be found in the official gopls documentation.

Sources indicate that however, if you don't want to use gopls, or are using a text editor that doesn't support it, you can still use gofmt with the -r flag to implement a rewrite rule that can assist with certain refactoring tasks. I've written more about this in my 2019 blog post on Go tooling here.

Recent findings suggest that there are a few live reloading tools available for Go, which you can use to automatically rebuild and restart an application whenever certain files change. These are especially useful when developing web services, because they let you make changes to your code or template markup and then check the results in a browser without having to manually restart the application each time.

In a recent development, the most mature and popular live reloading tool for Go is air-verse/air. You can run it using settings in a TOML configuration file , like so:.

Recent findings suggest that or you can configure it using command-line flags. For example, to watch all directories and rebuild the ./cmd/web application whenever a file with an extension in the set .go, .tmpl, .css, .js or .sql changes, you could use the following command:.

Here's a video illustrating the air live reloading functionality when developing a web application:.

Sources indicate that go's language server, gopls, includes an experimental MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that exposes some of its functionality to AI coding assistants (such as Claude Code or OpenAI Codex). This effectively allows the assistants to leverage the same "smart features" that your text editor has access to, rather than just relying on reading your files.

Assuming that you have gopls installed, you can configure your AI coding assistant to use the gopls MCP server by following the instructions in the official Go MCP documentation.

You can also run the gopls mcp -instructions command to get guidance for using the MCP server, which you can then provide to your coding assistant. For example:.

In a recent development, another MCP server worth mentioning is mrjoshuak/godoc-mcp. This allows AI coding assistants to look up Go package documentation directly, which can be more token-efficient than reading through source files. You may wish to try this if you're using AI assistants heavily and want to reduce token usage.

In late 2022 the Go team released govulncheck, which checks your codebase against the Go vulnerability database to find known vulnerabilities in any standard library packages or third-party dependencies that you're using.

Unlike many other vulnerability scanners, it only flags vulnerabilities that actually affect you... meaning that a vulnerability in a part of a package that your code doesn't use won't be flagged.

It's an excellent tool, and I recommend running it routinely before you deploy a new version of your application to production.

Long term, the plan is for govulncheck to become part of the main go command, but for now you can run it like so:.

Another really helpful tool is gosec, a static analyzer that looks for potential security problems in your code. You can run it like so:.

In my experience it's not uncommon for gosec to flag complications which on further inspection are false positives in the context of your specific codebase, or where you are deliberately using something insecure. When this happens, you can annotate the specific code with a #nosec comment to instruct gosec to omit it from future reports. For example:.

The venerable go vet command should still be your first port of call when it comes to static code analysis. It runs a relatively small set of checks, but the checks have a high signal-to-noise ratio and if go vet reports an glitch, then it's very likely to be a problem you should address.

It's normally best to run go vet with its default settings, like so:.

You can see a complete list of the checks that go vet runs in the 'Registered analyzers' section of the help documentation:.

It has been revealed that and you can also disable specific analyzers if you don't want their checks to run. For example, to disable the composites analyzer, which checks for unkeyed composite literals, you can run go vet like so:.

It has been revealed that the staticcheck tool is kind of like go vet on steroids. It carries out around 160 different checks on your code — the vast majority of which are related to code correctness and performance, although it also includes a handful of checks for for 'stylistic' complications like comment formatting too.

The complete list of checks, along with their respective ID codes and descriptions, can be found here.

It's crucial to note that staticcheck does not run all checks by default — only a subset of them. But you can configure exactly which checks are run using either the -checks command-line flag or a config file. For example:.

The nilaway tool is really useful for finding potential nil-pointer panics in your code. It's similar to the older nilness tool in what it aims to do, but is more comprehensive in its checks.

Recent findings suggest that if you're not worried about nil-pointer panics in your test code, and only want to check your production code, you can also run it with the -exclude-test-files flag enabled. Like so:.

The errcheck tool has been around for a long time (14 years!), and it remains a great way to check for unhandled errors in your code.

You can run it with its default settings like so:.

Sources indicate that it's worth mentioning that, by default, errcheck only reports errors which are completely unhandled. It doesn't report errors that are handled by ignoring them and assigning them to the blank identifier _.

To include these errors in the report, you can run it with the -blank flag enabled, like so:.

It's worth noting that not every error always needs to be handled. For example, it's conventional to ignore errors returned by http.ResponseWriter.Write(), or errors from fmt.Fprint() when writing to standard streams. Or you might deliberately choose to ignore errors from nice-to-have non-critical cleanup operations, where you decide that handling errors would add more complexity to your codebase than it's worth.

So it's possible to exclude specific functions from the errcheck report by creating an exclude file and passing it via the -exclude flag like so:.

It's also worth mentioning the shadow tool, which identifies instances of variable shadowing in your code.

This tool was also built by the Go team and has been around for a very long time, but has never been included in the default go vet analyzers or the go command because it is notoriously noisy and reports a lot of instances of variable shadowing that aren't actually problematic.

It has been revealed that nonetheless, it's still worth knowing that it exists. Personally, I do use shadow occasionally when I'm doing a code review of a large codebase, and skim through the results to see if anything jumps out as looking unexpected or out of place.

The revive tool is a code linter, and is kind of the spiritual successor to the now frozen and deprecated golang/lint package.

There is some overlap between revive and the staticcheck tool that we talked about earlier, but revive focuses more on checking code style and conventions, whereas staticcheck focuses more on finding bugs and performance complications.

Generally, revive is good to use on projects where you have multiple contributors and you want to maintain common standards in terms of code and comment style.

You can run it with its default settings like so:.

Normally though, I prefer to run it using the -formatter=stylish flag, which groups failures by file and includes links to the specific documentation for each failure.

You can also disable and customize specific checks by creating a TOML configuration file and passing it via the -config flag, like so:.

Deadcode is an excellent tool for finding functions in your code that aren't being used, which you can potentially delete or comment out. Similar to govulncheck, the deadcode tool is officially maintained by the Go team, but isn't right now part of the go command.

You can run deadcode with the default settings like this:.

But it's important to note that by default, deadcode does not consider code in _test.go files when checking if something is used or not. This means that functions which are only used by your tests can incorrectly be reported as dead code. So to make sure test files are included in the check, I almost always run deadcode with the -test flag enabled, like so:.

Another neat way to use deadcode is when you are looking at a function and can't figure out why it exists, or you're struggling to fully trace where it is being called from.

According to recent reports, if you run deadcode with the -whylive flag, you'll get a report showing the shortest path from a main() function in your program to the code in question. For example, let's say you have the module example.com, and you wanted to trace where the internal/response.HTMLRenderer.Render() method is being called from, you can run a command like this:.

If you've made the decision in your codebase to wrap errors before returning them to the caller (which is generally a good idea to help with debugging), the wrapcheck tool helps you find any instances where you've forgotten to do this.

If you are running a lot of tools as part of your code quality checks, you might want to consider Golangci-lint to help with this. It acts as a wrapper around many of the tools we've talked about above, running them in parallel and outputting the results in a single consistent format.

Alternatively, and slightly more simply, I often use a Makefile with a single audit task that runs the tools I want, similar to this.

Personally, when I want to upgrade to a upcoming version of Go on my primary development machine, I have a simple Bash script that I run to download and install the new version. The script and instructions are available here if you'd like to take a similar approach. I then run it like:.

Sometimes it's useful to have multiple versions of Go installed on your machine. For example, you might want to test your code against different Go releases, or try out a new version without replacing your existing one.

You can do this using the go install golang.org/dl/... command. For example, to install Go 1.26.0 alongside your existing Go installation, you can run:.

Sources indicate that you can then use this alternative version by running the versioned executable instead of go. For example:.

It has been revealed that it's vital to note, though, that Go 1.21 and newer support automatic toolchain switching. So running a versioned Go command inside a module that requires a newer toolchain may cause Go to automatically download and use that newer version instead. If you want to disable this, you can set the GOTOOLCHAIN environment variable to local, like so:.

To check for dependency updates, the best tool around is probably oligot/go-mod-upgrade. You can run it like so:.

Sources indicate that this launches an interactive tool which lists all dependencies that have upgrades available. You can then select the ones you want, and they'll be upgraded to the latest available version.

In the past, if you want to use a modified version of a dependency (for example, you temporarily want to use a local fork until a patch is merged upstream), you would use the go mod edit command to add a replace rule to your go.mod file pointing to the modified version, as described here.

Although this approach does still work, an alternative option is to create a Go workspace and a go.work file in your module root.

For example, assuming that you are in the root of your module, and the modified dependency you want to use is located in the directory /local/code/mydep, you can create a workspace and a go.work file that references the current module and modified dependency like so:.

The go.work file that is created should then look like this:.

Recent findings suggest that and when you run the code in your module, the modified dependency should be picked up and used, rather than resolving the dependency from the module cache in the normal way. Note that the dependency still needs its own go.mod file, and that the dependency's module path must match the import path your code uses.

Industry observers note that go workspaces are also really useful in the scenario where you are developing two modules at the same time which rely on each other. When you want to do this, you can create a go.work file in the parent directory of the two modules, which points to the two module directories. For example, if you have two modules located at /local/code/a and /local/code/b, you could create a go.work file in /local/code that references them both like so:.

For more information about Go workspaces and go.work files, please see the official tutorial.

Sources indicate that if you ever look at your go.mod or go.sum files and wonder "why is that listed as a dependency?", you can find out by running the go mod why command. This will show you the shortest path from a package in your main module to a given dependency. For example, to see why golang.org/x/sys is listed as a dependency you can run:.

It's also worth knowing about the go mod graph command, which prints a plain-text module requirement graph.

Sources indicate that the output from this tool is just a plain text listing, not a visual graph, but I've had some success with dumping the output from go mod graph into AI tools and asking them to generate a visualization. Alternatively, if you want something more reliable and reproducible, you might want to consider trying the samber/go-mod-graph and bayraktugrul/modview tools, which will generate visualizations for you.

In a recent development, downloaded dependencies are stored in the module cache on your computer. If you're not sure where your module cache is located, you can check by running the go env GOMODCACHE command.

If you ever want to clear the module cache — which can be useful if your cache has become corrupted or want to rule it out as the source of a bug — you can use the go clean tool like so:.

But be aware that this is a blunt instrument — it will remove the downloaded dependencies for all projects on your machine.

You can use the go test tool to run the tests in your project like so:.

It has been revealed that if the code you’re testing leverages concurrency, or you’re running tests in parallel, then you may want to use the -race flag to enable Go's race detector during the tests. This will increase the running time of the tests, but it's an easy tweak that can help find data races that occur while the tests are running.

If any of your tests need access to VCS information in debug.BuildInfo, you should also make sure to use the -buildvcs flag when running tests, like so:.

If you want to only run some specific tests, rather than all the tests in a package, there are a few ways to do this.

If you're using VS Code or GoLand as your text editor, the simplest way is via the testing functionality built into your editor. For example:.

Sources indicate that if you're not using an editor that supports this kind of functionality, you can also use go test with the -run flag to run specific tests. This accepts a regular expression, and only tests which have names that match the regular expression will be run. When using this, I normally also use the -v flag to enable verbose output, so I can make sure that the tests I expect are actually being run 🙂.

It's also worth mentioning that Go caches test results at the package-level. If a package hasn't changed between test runs, then the cached test result will be displayed with a "(cached)" annotation next to it. If you want to force your tests to run in full, you can use the -count=1 flag, or mark cached test results as expired by using the go clean tool.

A final flag that I sometimes use is -failfast, which will stop further tests in a package from running after the first failure.

Note that if you're running tests in multiple packages (for example by using go test ./... ), then the tests in the other packages which didn't have the failure will continue to run.

As an alternative to go test, you may also want to consider using the gotestyourself/gotestsum tool. This is effectively a wrapper around go test which prints the test output in a nice way, similar to this:.

Sources indicate that it's also possible to enable test coverage analysis when running tests by using the -cover flag. This will display the percentage of code covered by the tests in the output for each package, similar to this:.

Alternatively, you can use the -coverprofile flag to generate a coverage profile and view it in your browser by using the go tool cover -html command like so:.

This will give you a navigable listing of all the test files, with code covered by the tests displayed in green, and uncovered code in red.

If you want you can go a step further and set the -covermode=atomic flag to make the coverage profile record the exact number of times that each statement is executed during the tests.

When viewed in the browser, statements which are executed more frequently are shown in a more saturated shade of green, similar to this:.

If you don't have a web browser available to view a coverage profile, you can see a breakdown of test coverage by function/method in your terminal with the command:.

For quick and simple load testing of a web application or API, one of the best tools around is rakyll/hey. For example, if you want to load test the http://localhost:5051 endpoint by sending 10,000 requests with up to 100 concurrently, you can do so like this:.

The output includes useful information such as the number of requests per second, response-time distributions, and summary counts of HTTP response status codes.

hey supports a bunch of configuration options, which you can find by running:.

Alternatively, if you want a more sophisticated general-purpose load testing tool, you may want to consider tsenart/vegeta or grafana/k6, both of which are written in Go (although k6 test scenarios are typically written in JavaScript).

Occasionally you might want to stress test something in your application by running a test multiple times in succession. This can be useful for checking for sporadic or intermittent failures, or when you're trying to reproduce an intermittent bug that you've been seeing.

There are a couple of ways to do this, but the simplest is by using the go test flag -count. For example, to run the TestFooBar test 500 times, you could run:.

It's key to note that -count repeats test executions in serial. Tests containing a t.Parallel() instruction can still run concurrently with other parallel tests within each execution, but the repeated executions themselves won't overlap.

If you want to repeat the same test multiple times in parallel, you can use the stress tool.

To use the stress tool, you'll first need to compile a test binary for the specific package you want to test. You can do this using the go test -c command. For example, to create a test binary for the package in your current directory:.

In this example, the test binary will be output to /tmp/foo.test. You can then use the stress tool to execute a specific test in the test binary like so:.

Sources indicate that note: In the example above I've used the -p flag to restrict the number of parallel processes used by stress to 4. Without this flag, the tool defaults to using a number of processes equal to runtime.NumCPU().

Go 1.18 introduced support for fuzz testing, which makes it possible to run tests with randomly generated inputs in an attempt to find bugs and unhandled edge cases.

For example, let's say that you have a Slugify() function which takes input text like "An example string" and turns it into a slug like "an-example-string".

You could create a FuzzSlugify fuzz test for it like so:.

In this example, the calls to f.Add() provide some seed corpus values for the fuzz test, which give Go a starting point for generating additional inputs. You don't need to provide seed values, but it's generally a good idea to include a few representative examples.

When you run go test ./... in the normal way, the FuzzSlugify test will be run, but only using the seed corpus values.

Recent findings suggest that to actually trigger fuzzing, you need to run it with the -fuzz flag. This takes a regular expression matching the name of the specific fuzz test you want to run. It's only possible to run one fuzz test at a time, and if multiple fuzz tests match the regular expression you'll get an error saying -fuzz matches more than one fuzz test.

You also need to pass in the path to the package that contains the fuzz test — you cannot use ./....

So, for example, to execute the FuzzSlugify fuzz test in the ./cmd/web package, you would run the following command:.

Recent findings suggest that in this example, the fuzz test found a problem with the Slugify() function — specifically, when the input text is "0\t0", the whitespace \t character is not removed. It's also crucial to note that, in this example, a file has been created at testdata/fuzz/FuzzSlugify/dde7a120ccdf11af containing the failing input. This input will be included in the seed corpus every time you run go test in the future (even when not using the -fuzz flag), so that the bug doesn't accidentally get reintroduced.

It has been revealed that fuzzing will continue indefinitely until either a failure is found or you terminate the run manually (e.g. with Ctrl+C). If there are no problems found, you'll see output which looks similar to this:.

Industry observers note that the "fresh interesting" count is the number of inputs discovered that increase the code coverage observed by the fuzzer. When the number of "new interesting" inputs starts to plateau, it can be a sign that you're not getting much additional coverage from continuing the test and you may want to terminate it.

According to recent reports, alternatively, you can set a fixed runtime for the fuzz test using the -fuzztime flag. For example, to run it for 30 seconds:.

For more information, I'd recommend checking out the official Go fuzzing documentation and the getting started tutorial.

Before compiling your application, it's sensible to run go mod verify to check that the dependencies in your module cache haven't been modified since they were downloaded.

Industry observers note that I normally run go mod verify immediately before running go build, as part of an automated build process in a CI workflow or Makefile task. This helps to make sure that builds are reproducible, and you're not using an accidentally modified dependency during compilation.

Recent findings suggest that to compile a main package and create an executable binary you can use the go build tool. Typically I use it in conjunction with the -o flag, which lets you explicitly set the output directory and name of the binary like so:.

In these examples, go build will compile the specified package (and any dependent packages), then invoke the linker to generate an executable binary, then output this to /tmp/foo.

It's notable to note that the go build tool caches build output in the build cache. This cached output will be reused again in future builds where appropriate, which can significantly speed up the overall build time.

Using the build cache comes with one notable caveat — it does not detect changes to C libraries imported with cgo. So if your code imports a C library via cgo and you've made changes to it since the last build, you'll need to use the -a flag which forces all packages to be rebuilt. Alternatively, you could use go clean to purge the cache:.

In a recent development, if you ever want detailed output explaining precisely what go build is doing behind the scenes, you can use the -v flag to print package names as they are being compiled, or the -x flag to print the detailed commands that are being run. You'll probably want to use these in conjunction with the -a flag, because otherwise you might not see much output as Go reuses packages from the build cache rather than recompiling them.

Finally, if you run go build on a non-main package, it will be compiled in a temporary location and again, the result will be stored in the build cache. No executable binary will be produced.

By default, go build will output a binary suitable for use on your current operating system and architecture. But it also supports cross-compilation, so you can generate a binary suitable for use on a different machine. This is particularly useful if you're developing on one operating system and deploying on another.

In a recent development, you can specify the operating system and architecture that you want to create the binary for by setting the GOOS and GOARCH environment variables respectively. For example:.

To see a list of all supported OS/architecture combinations you can run go tool dist list:.

For more information about cross compilation, I recommend reading this post.

When building your executable, you can use the -gcflags and -ldflags flags to change the behavior of the compiler and linker and see more information about what it's doing. You can see a complete list of available compiler and linker flags by running:.

Probably the most well-known and commonly-used of these is the linker -X flag, which allows you to "burn in" a (string) value to a specific variable in your application. For example, to burn in the value "bar" into the main package's global foo variable you can use it like so:.

For more information about the -X flag and some sample code see this Stack Overflow question.

It has been revealed that it's possible to reduce the binary size — typically by around 25% — by instructing the linker to strip symbol tables and DWARF debugging information from the binary. We can do this by using the -s linker flag, like so:.

It's not a Go-specific tool, but you can also use a tool like upx to compress the binary size further if you want. Please see this post for more information.

Sources indicate that once you have generated a binary, you can use the go tool buildid command to inspect its build ID. This is an identifier embedded in the binary by Go, representing the inputs to the build (code, compiler version, flags, etc.) and the resulting output. It acts as a "fingerprint" for the build, and is also used internally by Go's build cache.

For example, to check the build ID for the binary at /tmp/foo, you can run:.

It has been revealed that looking at the build ID can be useful when checking for reproducible builds, as identical builds should produce the same ID. If two builds produce different IDs, it suggests that something about them is different.

For more information about Go build IDs and reproducibility, please see this post.

Another useful tool is the go version -m command, which lets you inspect a binary's build information — including the Go version, the module it was built from, its dependencies and VCS information. To inspect the binary at /tmp/foo, you can use it like so:.

Sources indicate that A nice feature of Go is that it makes it easy to benchmark your code. If you're not familiar with the general process for writing benchmarks there's a good guide here.

In a recent development, to run benchmarks you need to use the go test tool, with the -bench flag set to a regular expression that matches the benchmarks you want to execute. If you don't want to run regular non-benchmark tests, you should omit them by using the -run=^$ flag. For example:.

I almost always run benchmarks using the -benchmem flag, which includes memory allocation statistics in the output.

By default, each benchmark test will be run for a minimum of 1 second, once only. You can control this with the -benchtime and -count flags:.

Industry observers note that if the code that you're benchmarking uses concurrency, you can use the -cpu flag to see the performance impact of changing your GOMAXPROCS value (essentially, the number of OS threads that can execute your Go code simultaneously). For example, to run benchmarks with GOMAXPROCS set to 1, 4 and 8:.

To help analyze the results of the benchmarks, you can use the benchstat tool. This replaces the older benchcmp tool, which is now deprecated.

When you are using the -count flag to run benchmarks multiple times, you can use benchstat to easily see the median value and confidence interval across all the runs. For example:.

It has been revealed that you can also use it to compare benchmarks before and after a specific change. For example:.

Sources indicate that go makes it possible to create diagnostic profiles for CPU use, memory use, goroutine blocking and mutex contention. You can use these to dig a bit deeper and see exactly how your application is using (or waiting on) resources.

There are three ways to generate profiles:.

Using the -***profile flags when running benchmarks or tests will result in a test binary being outputted to your current directory. If you want to output this to an alternative location you should use the -o flag like so:.

Industry observers note that my favourite way to inspect a profile is to use the go tool pprof -http command to open it in a web browser. For example:.

This will default to displaying a flame graph visually showing where your application is spending its resources, with wide boxes being the 'hot spots'.

You can also navigate to other views of the profile including top usage by function and source code:.

And also a graph showing the execution tree for your application, like this:.

According to recent reports, if the amount of information is overwhelming, for CPU profiles you might want to use the -nodefraction flag to ignore nodes that account for less than a certain percentage of samples. For example, to ignore nodes that appear in less than 10% of samples you can run pprof like so:.

According to recent reports, and finally, if you're analyzing profiles for a web application created via net/http/pprof, you can also fetch the profile from the application and open the visualization in one step. For example, if your web application is running on http://localhost:4000 you could generate a 30-second CPU profile and view it like so:.

For more information about profiling and pprof, please see the official README.

Go also supports profile-guided optimization (PGO), which allows the compiler to use information gathered from profiling your application to make better decisions when compiling your code.

Normally, when compiling your code, the compiler has to make educated guesses about which functions are likely to be called frequently, which code paths are more common, and where it should make optimizations. PGO allows you to provide a CPU profile from a representative run of your application so that the compiler can make better-informed decisions.

For example, it may use this information to more aggressively inline frequently called functions, or optimize common code paths.

The good news is that using PGO is relatively straightforward. First you need to generate a CPU profile using one of the techniques described in the previous section. Then you need to pass it to go build via the -pgo flag when building your application. For example, if your CPU profile is saved as /tmp/cpuprofile.out, you can use it like so:.

In a recent development, alternatively, you can rename your profile to default.pgo and place it in the directory containing your main package. Go will automatically detect this file and use it when building your application, so you don't need to specify the -pgo flag explicitly.

In practice, the recommended workflow is to collect a representative profile from your production application, use that profile when building your next release, and periodically collect fresh profiles as your application evolves.

For more information, see the official PGO documentation and the Go blog post introducing PGO.

It has been revealed that sometimes profiling isn't enough to understand what's happening in your application. For example, a CPU profile can show you which functions are consuming the most CPU time, but it won't necessarily help you understand why a goroutine is blocked, why your application isn't making progress, or why a request is taking so long.

For these situations, Go has a built-in execution tracer, which has been improved significantly in recent Go versions. It records runtime events such as goroutine scheduling, system calls, garbage collection, and other activity over a period of time. You can then use the go tool trace command to visualize and explore what happened.

Industry observers note that you can generate a trace from your tests or benchmarks, use net/http/pprof to create and download a trace for your web application, or use the runtime/trace package to generate traces from a running application. You can then use go tool trace to view the output in your web browser. For example:.

This will open an interactive visualization that lets you explore what was happening during the trace.

For more information, please see the Go blog post on tracing, the runtime/trace documentation, as well as this dotGo conference talk by Rhys Hiltner.

I talked earlier about enabling Go's race detector during tests by using go test -race. But you can also enable it for running programs when building an executable, like so:.

It's critical to note that race-detector-enabled binaries will use more CPU and memory than normal, so you shouldn't use the -race flag when building binaries for production under normal circumstances.

But you may want to deploy a race-detector-enabled binary on one server within a pool of many. Or use it to help track down a suspected race condition by using a load-test tool to throw traffic concurrently at a race-detector-enabled binary.

By default, if any races are detected while the binary is running, a report will be written to os.Stderr. You can change this by using the GORACE environment variable if necessary. For example, to run the binary located at /tmp/foo and output any race reports to /tmp/race. you can use:.

Industry observers note that another complementary tool for helping to track down race conditions is amit-davidson/Chronos. This uses static analysis of your code to try to identify race conditions, rather than using real-time detection like Go's race detector. This means it can be a good option to try if there is a suspected race condition that you are struggling to replicate.

If you're confident that you've found an unreported matter with Go's standard library, tooling or documentation, you can use the go bug command to create a upcoming GitHub issue.

This will open a browser window containing a GitHub issue pre-filled with your system information and reporting template.

You might like to check out my other Go tutorials on this site, or if you're after something more structured, my books Let's Go and Let's Go Further cover how to build complete, production-ready, web apps and APIS with Go.

Tech Report: Stale links on UK public sector websites direct visitors to gambling dens

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Consultancy finds 93 routes to casino promotions across 26 orgs, with defunct enterprise partnership domains repurposed.
  • UK public sector websites are directing visitors to gambling promotions through old links to defunct local enterprise partnerships (LEPs), research by digital consultancy Digital Royalty has found.
  • The consultancy identified 93 links across 79 pages on websites belonging to 26 public bodies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Consultancy finds 93 routes to casino promotions across 26 orgs, with defunct enterprise partnership domains repurposed.

UK public sector websites are directing visitors to gambling promotions through old links to defunct local enterprise partnerships (LEPs), research by digital consultancy Digital Royalty has found.

The consultancy identified 93 links across 79 pages on websites belonging to 26 public bodies.

Industry observers note that LEPs brought together councils and businesses to promote economic growth in England under a coalition government initiative launched in 2010. Central government funding ended in April 2024, with their core functions transferred to local and combined authorities.

Recent findings suggest that among other things, Digital Royalty builds and looks after websites, which means chasing down old links. In August, it found that a link on Surrey County Council's website led to a former LEP address now displaying casino content. It went looking for more.

Digital Royalty founder Alex De Sousa stated: "Slow is usually a sign of caution and diligence, but 31 months after the LEPs wound up, it's crossed into inefficient and dangerous.".

In a recent development, the consultancy offered The Register four examples of websites run by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), Hull City Council, Parliament, and the Local Government Association. One example is a government page about the Digital Skills Partnership, originally published under an earlier incarnation of DCMS.

The page includes a link that appears to be for the Humber Digital Skills Partnership within the Humber LEP website, but in fact takes users to a site advertising "Independent Non GamStop Casinos UK – New Casino Sites Outside GamStop." GamStop is the self-exclusion scheme designed to help people restrict their online gambling, which makes the links more concerning than ordinary website clutter.

The same link appears on the Hull City Council website under a list of Joint Committees, Partnerships and Trusts where it appears as Local Economic Partnership (Humber LEP).

An old page for the Parliament website detailing the Department for Business, Energy & Industrial Strategy committee's Industrial Strategy report includes a footnote (135) that appears to be for the Business Central funding finder service, but takes the user to the "Highest RTP Non GamStop Casinos for UK Players.".

The Local Government Association's (LGA) sustainability and waste route map included a link to the former York and North Yorkshire LEP website. The destination initially appeared legitimate but contained links promoting crypto casinos. The LGA now appears to have removed the link.

All the organizations mentioned have been contacted by The Register to offer them the opportunity to comment.

It has been revealed that digital Royalty checked former web addresses associated with about 70 LEPs and growth hubs, then used a backlink index to identify roughly 3,000 incoming links from public sector sites. Most were simply outdated rather than leading to gambling content.

Industry observers note that the findings are not exhaustive: the index may miss pages, and the research did not cover other types of defunct public body whose domains may have been repurposed. ®.

Garage v2.6.0 released with web admin, v1.x EoL & other news

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are glad to announce the release of Garage v2.6.0 that includes a brand-new web administration UI funded by NLnet.
  • The Garage project has been quite active lately, so we thought it would be a good time to write a blog post to present new features and give some information on what's coming next.
  • In a recent development, this is the culmination of almost two years of work by Tixie Salander.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are glad to announce the release of Garage v2.6.0 that includes a brand-new web administration UI funded by NLnet. We also discuss many other small news: Helm chart repository release, Garage v1.x EoL, Garage v3.0.0 beta 1 and an outlook on upcoming work on S3 versioning.

The Garage project has been quite active lately, so we thought it would be a good time to write a blog post to present new features and give some information on what's coming next.

In a recent development, this is the culmination of almost two years of work by Tixie Salander. We started this collaboration in 2024 when it was clear that a user interface was one of the most sorely lacking feature of Garage. We are very grateful that NLnet has again engaged with us and provided funding to make this a reality.

Here's a minimal example to test 2.6.0 right away:.

Running 2.6.0 or above, you can access the web interface on the garage admin API port, by default port 3903, so http://localhost:3903/ if you are running garage on your machine with the example above.

Recent findings suggest that logging in requires a garage admin token. The example above prints it on the command line. If you have set the admin_token configuration variable in your configuration file, you may use that token. Otherwise, you'll need to create a separate token from the command line with garage admin-token create.

One world of caution: administering a remote cluster over plain HTTP is NOT safe, as your admin token is transmitted in plain text with each request. You'll need to setup an HTTPS reverse proxy in front of your Garage node to encrypt the connection, or/and access your node through a VPN such as Wireguard to make sure no one can eavesdrop the credentials.

Once logged in the cluster, you will be greeted by a cluster overview screen that looks like the following (this is a live example from our Deuxfleurs cluster):.

The web interface follows a similar pattern to the CLI: cluster monitoring, layout configuration, bucket and access credential management are all available as you expect. Here are example videos (now included in the Quick Start guide as well) showing the setting up of a new cluster from scratch:.

From a development standpoint, the web UI currently lives in a separate Git repository so please report any issues there and not in Garage's main glitch tracker. Tixie will continue being the maintainer of the UI moving forward.

In a recent development, this has also been one of the longstanding requests from our Kubernetes users, and it's now done! Starting today you can deploy Garage on Kubernetes easily thanks to our self-hosted Helm repository. Both "regular" (tgz+index.yml) helm chart repository as well as OCI artefacts are available. Instructions in the documentation have been updated accordingly. Happy Helming!

Recent findings suggest that thanks to Boris M. and Maximilien for contributing this improvement to Garage, along the many contributors that participated in finding the right way to make this work.

The Garage helm chart follows its own version scheme, with the current version being 0.10.7.

The last release of the 1.x branch was v1.3.1 in January 2026, almost a year ago. Many significant bug fixes, including security fixes, are currently only present on the v2.x branch. At this point, it would be too much work to backport them to 1.x and it didn't seem there was any ask to do so from the community either. So we are officially deprecating Garage v1.x and urging all users still on this branch to enhancement to v2.x as soon as possible. The release note has been updated accordingly.

In a recent development, we have published a first beta release of Garage v3.0.0. This release does not yet include S3 versioning (sorry!). This unfortunately needed to be a major release because of a few breaking changes we wanted to release without waiting for s3 versioning to come though:.

We are looking for testers for this beta so please give it a try and report any findings on our issue tracker!

Recent findings suggest that this beta release also marks the first step toward having a reliable Fjall metadata engine so please report to us not only problems, but also cases of successfully running a Garage cluster on Fjall with significant activity, so that we can gain confidence that it works well and potentially mark it stable soon. This also means we'll take bug report for Fjall challenges, something that we explicitly disregarded so far for the 2.x experimental implementation.

As per the release notes, the most important breaking changes for consumers to be aware of are:.

To finally align with industry standard, most Prometheus metrics have been slighly renamed, we provide an updated Grafana dashboard.

The Fjall major version enhancement breaks compatibility with the Garage 2.x Fjall as data files from older versions are not supported. If you were using Fjall on v2.x, you will need to migrate manually: convert your metadata to another format (LMDB or SQlite) with garage node convert-db before upgrading. You can convert back to Fjall once you successfully upgraded to v3.

The complete list of breaking changes can be found in the changelog linked above. Happy testing!

Finally we want to close this post with an update on S3 versionning.

In 2027 we will start a newly introduced collaboration with Armaël to implement what is certainly the most requested feature in Garage: S3 object versioning.

We understand that there has been growing impatience for this feature to be implemented in Garage, and rightfully so as it would enable new use-cases such as for long-term archiving where compliance is vital, or as a backup target that cannot be tampered with.

In a recent development, we thank the community for their patience, and kindly ask them to understand why this hasn't been done before: while there have been several attempts by community members, this is a deep problem that requires intricate understanding of how Garage stores metadata, and implementing it without taking this into account leads to code that, while it might appear to work on the surface, is in fact incorrect. A correct implementation requires a significant rewrite of core parts of Garage, which we believe can presently be accomplished only by experienced maintainers. We will also take this rewrite as an opportunity to fix some performance problems, such as those arising with extremely major objects.

I would like to make an key note on object locking and WORM: we will provide an implementation of locking primitives/WORM per the S3 API specification, however note that due to Garage's lack of a consensus algorithm, this implementation will not be fully correct. This means that Garage will implement best-effort detection of access requests that would violate locks, but will not be able to guarantee that it upholds locks in all cases. More precisely: using conditional writes (If-Match, If-None-Match) as a substitute for a distributed mutex or to discriminate between concurrent write requests will obviously not work, but ensuring that a successfully uploaded object cannot be overwritten after the fact should work in most cases. We will take care of properly documenting what works and what doesn't, but in practice, this means that locking and WORM will be gated behind a feature flag (a configuration parameter) that requires cluster administrators to acknowledge that they might be running unsafe workloads if they don't understand exactly what the feature does.

Thanks for reading, and for your continued support in our journey to a robust and resilient distributed storage system.

Alex, Maximilien and Tixie, The Garage (and Garage UI!) Maintainers.

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (460 w)

Organization was religious about backups but sinned by leaving them exposed

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (460 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Never put the backup server in the same Windows domain as production.
  • In a recent development, welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account.
  • Recent findings suggest that our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a manufacturer that provides data protection and recovery software.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Never put the backup server in the same Windows domain as production.

In a recent development, welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we’re thankful every time someone leaves a password sticky note on a monitor or fails to delete a terminated employee’s admin account. But neither of those common occurrences is what we’ll be talking about today. Instead, our subject broke the number-one rule of backups: you gotta keep ’em separated.

Recent findings suggest that our story comes courtesy of Da Li, who serves as global alliance manager at Info2Soft, a manufacturer that provides data protection and recovery software. At one point, a partner called him into a case where a Chinese vehicle parts manufacturer fell victim to a ransomware gang. Unfortunately, its backup was compromised too.

In a recent development, the manufacturer had religiously backed up its manufacturing execution system (MES) and SAP orders, inventory, and finance systems every night. There was even a green dashboard that indicated the backup process had succeeded, and someone checked that every morning.

However, one Friday evening, crims broke into the network and found out that the backup server was joined to the same Windows domain as the rest of the network. The hackers found a plaintext password for the backup service account in a maintenance script on a file share and discovered that someone had used the very same password for a domain admin account.

Industry observers note that so the first thing the crooks did was delete every restore point on that backup server. Then they started encrypting the production servers to ransom them.

“Every backup job had succeeded for three years,” Li noted. “The failure was that the thing meant to save them could be reached with the same keys as the thing being attacked.”.

It has been revealed that have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com. Anonymity is available upon request.

The results were devastating. With the MES and SAP data both gone, the plant couldn't schedule production, ship parts, or track them.

By the time Li was called in, the plant had already resolved its ransomware situation. We don’t know whether it paid or not. The manufacturer did ask Li and his company to make sure that this couldn’t happen again.

According to recent reports, li’s fix was not radical, but it was instructive. He made sure that the company now keeps its backup system outside the production domain, uses unique credentials, and requires MFA to reduce the risk of unauthorized access even if a password is compromised. He also made sure that the company keeps at least one offline backup and runs a test restore quarterly to ensure it’s prepared for emergencies.®.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News .NET MAUI 11 Makes CoreCLR the Default Runtime and Adds Incremental XAML Hot Reload.

Nov 26, 2026 3 min read.

Industry observers note that microsoft released .NET 11 on 10 November, and .NET MAUI in .NET 11 changes the default runtime from Mono to CoreCLR on all supported platforms. It also adds incremental XAML hot reload, implicit XAML namespaces and fresh test project templates. The work spanned seven previews and a release candidate, and the documentation describes product quality as the release's focus. Overall, this release consolidates more than it expands.

In a recent development, .NET MAUI (Multi-platform App UI) is Microsoft's cross-platform UI framework for Android, iOS, Mac Catalyst and Windows apps built from one C# and XAML codebase. .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support. Microsoft notes that MAUI follows its own support policy, separate from the runtime's STS and LTS lifecycle.

Industry observers note that the runtime switch is the most significant change. According to Microsoft, CoreCLR puts mobile and desktop apps on the same runtime as the other .NET workloads. Release builds use composite partial ReadyToRun by default. On Apple platforms, which disallow JIT compilation, code that isn't precompiled runs in the CoreCLR interpreter. Native AOT is an opt-in publishing option, and its Android support is still experimental. Microsoft recommends developers to test app libraries before choosing their deployment model.

Sources indicate that XAML gets four main improvements. First, incremental hot reload, still in preview, patches live instances of pages and controls without recreating them. It is on by default in Debug builds, works with dotnet watch, and can be disabled with EnableMauiIncrementalHotReload. Second, implicit namespace declarations are now on by default, so the root xmlns and xmlns:x are optional. Third, lazy ResourceDictionary loading makes large dictionaries initialise up to roughly eight times faster when XAML source generation is used. Finally, RelativeSource bindings with a resolvable AncestorType now compile to trim-safe code.

Industry observers note that handlers keep replacing the legacy renderers with newer implementations. Windows uses the new CollectionView2 handler by default, Android Shell is now handler-based, and iOS and Mac Catalyst now use handlers for NavigationPage, TabbedPage and FlyoutPage. The old renderers remain available as a manual fallback. On iOS, Appearing now fires before a page is pushed rather than after it becomes visible, and secondary toolbar items move into an overflow menu. Developers who depend on the old timing should switch to NavigatedTo.

Controls get smaller additions. Maps gain clustering and custom pin icons, plus an Azure Maps-backed implementation on Windows. TabbedPage gains badges, BoxView a Fill brush, and LongPressGestureRecognizer becomes configurable. Shell also supports route templates such as trip/{tripId}.

In a recent development, animation methods now accept a CancellationToken, and their non-Async variants are obsolete. On the platform side, a new Passkeys class in Microsoft.Maui.Authentication wraps WebAuthn creation and assertion, while the server still has to validate challenges and attestation. Permissions.PostNotifications now works on iOS, and splash screens can have dark-mode variants.

In a recent development, for Android, the minimum API level rises from 21 to 24, and x86 architecture is no longer supported. The release notes report shorter builds: an incremental build after a managed source change dropped from 68.3 to 52.3 seconds. They also report startup gains of 2.4 to 4.5 per cent from partial ReadyToRun, at the cost of a slightly larger package. Apple targets now require iOS, tvOS and Mac Catalyst 18.2 and macOS 15.2, with Xcode 26.4.

It has been revealed that several changes break existing code. The Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships, the Color record is now sealed, Java.Lang.Object.JavaFinalize() is obsolete, and non-font SwipeItem icons are no longer tinted automatically. When upgrading, Microsoft advises to focus on throughly testing navigation, custom handlers and trimmed publishing.

The full list of changes, including per-preview release notes, is in the .NET MAUI documentation. .NET MAUI ships as a workload with NuGet packages, so a project can pin specific versions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a massive part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so owners can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

According to recent reports, GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

According to recent reports, we suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

According to recent reports, no extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

Sources indicate that the model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

In a recent development, transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

In a recent development, our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

Recent findings suggest that the llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Recent findings suggest that transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

In a recent development, when GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

Sources indicate that llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

Industry observers note that transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for fresh architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

In a recent development, that opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

In a recent development, our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

Industry observers note that A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

Sources indicate that to show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Recent findings suggest that faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

Recent findings suggest that the initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peninsula Energy says plant and wellfield control systems were affected, with no restart date yet.

Peninsula Energy has temporarily shut down its Wyoming uranium operation after a "cybersecurity incident" affected plant and wellfield control systems.

The Australian uranium producer said on Wednesday that it had activated its response procedures and brought in outside specialists following the attack on its US subsidiary, Strata Energy, which operates the Lance uranium project.

Peninsula Energy mentioned it believes the attack is "confined to the plant and wellfield operating and control systems," and that back-office functions, such as payroll and other corporate systems, in both the US and Australia, remain unaffected.

"The firm's immediate priorities have been to protect the safety of its employees, secure its operating systems, and work towards the restoration of operations in a safe and controlled manner," it noted in an update to the Australian Securities Exchange.

The notification [PDF] went on to say that Peninsula Energy's investigations into the attack, including whether any data was compromised, remain ongoing.

According to recent reports, peninsula has not given a restart date and says it cannot yet assess the impact on its 2027 production guidance. Operations will remain suspended until recovery and safety checks are complete. "Peninsula will provide further updates to the market as material information becomes available," it said.

The disclosure of additional information came two days after Peninsula secured a short trading halt, which referenced a cybersecurity incident at its Wyoming site.

The November 23 filing [PDF] dated the incident to Friday evening in Western Australia. Wednesday's update clarified that Strata detected it on the morning of November 20, local US time.

Peninsula subsequently requested a voluntary suspension of trading until the earlier of November 30 or an announcement on restarting operations and any resulting change to production guidance.

Peninsula's Lance project is a uranium mining operation, extracting the element from underground deposits and turning it into uranium concentrate, aka yellowcake or U₃O₈.

Uranium concentrate is feedstock for nuclear fuel production, typically undergoing conversion, enrichment, and fabrication into uranium dioxide pellets before use in reactors.

The Lance central processing plant was constructed to produce a maximum of 2.0 million pounds (Mlb) of U₃O₈ annually, and is licensed for 3.0 Mlb.

Recent findings suggest that peninsula previously forecast production of 500,000 to 600,000 pounds in 2027, having withdrawn its 2026 guidance earlier this year following operational problems at Lance. It now claims it will reassess the 2027 outlook once operations resume. ®.

How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible
