AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
  • Recent findings suggest that the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
  • At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

Recent findings suggest that the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many new tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates fresh tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

Recent findings suggest that A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

Recent findings suggest that the specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

Industry observers note that the user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

Feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

According to recent reports, difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little latest training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

Industry observers note that the verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

Sources indicate that consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

Completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

Industry observers note that these properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

In a recent development, autoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into new executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

AutoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

We distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create new tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

According to recent reports, identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

The generator creates new tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

The target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a new target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

The multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

To support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

Together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

In a recent development, generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Industry observers note that each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

Sources indicate that the pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

Industry observers note that for example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

Recent findings suggest that A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

According to recent reports, passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

In a recent development, A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

In a recent development, the controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

The useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

After post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Recent findings suggest that our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We initiative to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

It has been revealed that we use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

Industry observers note that autoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

The synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

The training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

We also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

Industry observers note that the tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates new tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SIMMTECH’s board approved two KRW 150 billion private perpetual bond issues on November 26, 2026 to expand production of AI-oriented SOCAMM module substrates and high-layer MSAP substrates, according to convertible-bond and bond-with-warrants decisions filed through South Korea’s DART corporate-disclosure system.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SIMMTECH’s board approved two KRW 150 billion private perpetual bond issues on November 26, 2026 to expand production of AI-oriented SOCAMM module substrates and high-layer MSAP substrates, according to convertible-bond and bond-with-warrants decisions filed through South Korea’s DART corporate-disclosure system.

The Series 11 securities are unsecured private perpetual convertible bonds; Series 12 comprises unsecured, non-detachable private perpetual bonds with warrants. Each filing designates the full amount as facility funds for the two substrate categories from December 2026 through December 2027, with no allocation to working capital or debt repayment. Subscriptions occurred on the approval date, while cash payment is scheduled for December 4, 2026, so the disclosures cover an approved financing before the proceeds are received.

It has been revealed that SIMMTECH approved KRW 274.2 billion in an August 25, 2026 capacity-investment decision for a dedicated AI-oriented SOCAMM module-substrate factory and additional high-layer MSAP substrate capacity through December 31, 2027. That decision cited increasing demand for both product categories and identified internal resources or external financing, excluding a rights offering, as the funding sources. The November approvals supply a defined external financing structure for the same two substrate categories, rather than marking a change in product direction.

Sources indicate that both series carry an initial 3% coupon and maturity yield and mature on December 4, 2056. Full conversion or warrant exercise for either series would produce 1,409,906 common shares at KRW 106,390 per share, equivalent to 3.54% of SIMMTECH’s existing shares for that series. Conversion and exercise rights open on December 4, 2027 and run through November 4, 2056.

The Series 11 capital-securities terms and corresponding Series 12 terms allow SIMMTECH to defer interest at its discretion, with unpaid amounts accumulating additional interest. The company can also extend maturity on the same issuance conditions, while holders have no right to demand early redemption.

From December 4, 2029, the coupon and maturity yield increase by four percentage points, followed by annual one-percentage-point increases capped at 19%. SIMMTECH may redeem either series quarterly beginning on that date, giving it a scheduled route to retire the securities as their cost rises.

In a recent development, SIMMTECH reported preliminary third-quarter 2026 results showing consolidated revenue of KRW 535.9 billion, up 43.7% from a year earlier, and operating profit of KRW 101.8 billion, up 721.6%. The figures are unaudited and subject to change during accounting review. The resulting operating margin is roughly 19%, calculated from the reported revenue and operating profit.

Microsoft: Hackers in China, N Korea using ARTEX AI tool to break into global tech systems

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agentic offensive framework automates familiar attack techniques, with weak defenses potentially breached in minutes.
  • Chinese and North Korean state-sponsored hacking crews are among the growing number of groups known for using the ARTEX pentesting tool in attacks, Microsoft said this week.
  • ARTEX is an open source, AI-powered penetration testing framework that attackers have adopted to automate reconnaissance, credential attacks, and exploitation since its public release in July.Campaigns that have been linked to ARTEX have targeted cloud environments, IT software like ConnectWise, and financial institutions globally, sometimes reaching privileged access in under three hours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Agentic offensive framework automates familiar attack techniques, with weak defenses potentially breached in minutes.

Chinese and North Korean state-sponsored hacking crews are among the growing number of groups known for using the ARTEX pentesting tool in attacks, Microsoft said this week.

ARTEX is an open source, AI-powered penetration testing framework that attackers have adopted to automate reconnaissance, credential attacks, and exploitation since its public release in July.Campaigns that have been linked to ARTEX have targeted cloud environments, IT software like ConnectWise, and financial institutions globally, sometimes reaching privileged access in under three hours.

Salt Typhoon is arguably the most recognizable name on the list of ARTEX beneficiaries – the group responsible for attacks on telcos AT&T and Verizon, US government systems, UK prime minister's aides, and more.

The lesser-known Crystal Typhoon – the group behind the ArcaneDoor attacks back when Microsoft called it Storm-1849 – was also named alongside it, as were North Korea's Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft also named China-state-aligned Storm-0940, linked to the ConnectWise compromise, and financially motivated, Cambodia-based Storm-3358. It had previously reported both groups' use of ARTEX.

Chinese cybersecurity company ThreatBook claimed ownership of ARTEX in November. GitHub user "Autumn-27" originally published its source code with a Chinese-language interface in July.

Various forks of the repo, which was taken down in October, have meant that the same framework is available in multiple languages.

According to Infrawatch, there are more than 130 variants of ARTEX in circulation, and it is the most widely used agentic offensive framework (AOF) at present.

Like other offensive security tools adopted by criminals, ARTEX can lower the effort required to mount attacks. Experienced groups can also use it to automate repetitive work and pursue multiple avenues at once.

As Microsoft echoed this week, after the FBI and AWS issued their warnings earlier this month, ARTEX is proving to be a useful tool for the more sophisticated groups to streamline and hasten their attacks too.

It's being used to help attackers steal AI and cloud credentials at "industrial scale," as AWS put it, which provide attackers access to advanced models for free.

Microsoft notes ARTEX can progress from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access within minutes, depending on its configuration and the target's defenses.

"In the past few weeks, we've reported several distinct campaigns that abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation," its threat intelligence team blogged. "These campaigns illustrate how threat actors use ARTEX to automate various stages of the attack chain.

"Threat actors define scope and targets for ARTEX, which then uses AI agents to set verifiable goals, define tactical steps for each stage of the operation, use tools to attack targets, create graphs to track discovered systems and results of actions, and report back to the threat actor.".

Sources indicate that notably, ARTEX does not offer any new attack techniques. All of the tool's capabilities were previously known to the cybersecurity world, but its value lies in the automation capabilities it offers people, chaining attacks at machine speed.

In the UK NCSC's warning about AOFs this week, it remarked the key strengths of this technology are its speed, its thoroughness in probing target systems for weaknesses, how it learns from failures instantly, and that it is inexpensive to run at scale.

Sources indicate that AOFs' speed comes at a cost, however. These tools are noisy, the NCSC said, making them easier to detect in network logs and by defensive solutions.

Sources indicate that some examples of the attacks in which the tool has been implicated include Storm-0940's hit on ConnectWise, which enabled attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, various financial institutions in South Korea and India, UK registrar 123 Reg, and the European Commission. ®.

The Agent Remarked It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

📅 03 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row.
  • According to recent reports, figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind.
  • Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

According to recent reports, figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

Industry observers note that then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

Sources indicate that an AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

Sources indicate that you can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

It has been revealed that want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

Sources indicate that the gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

According to recent reports, A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

It has been revealed that starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

Table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

Sources indicate that claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

Sources indicate that one good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

Only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

In a recent development, kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

In a recent development, claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

Recent findings suggest that A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

It has been revealed that capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

Sources indicate that we took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

Recent findings suggest that A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

Figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

The frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

It has been revealed that table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

Sources indicate that we assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

It has been revealed that the practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

Sources indicate that what to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

Sources indicate that classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.

Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

Recent findings suggest that each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

According to recent reports, every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

Sources indicate that at the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

It has been revealed that the trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

Recent findings suggest that thinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

Industry observers note that tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:.

In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):.

Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:.

Recent findings suggest that now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:.

The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

The useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

ST003_006 delegates its pass check to validate_database. Unequal result and golden database hashes fail even when diff is empty. The diff explains a failure; it does not decide the pass.

Industry observers note that this small replay exercises the released function with four authored effect inputs. Run python3 reproduce.py. It verifies the source pin and tests supplied hashes; it does not calculate a database hash, run an agent, or reproduce the full environment.

The useful cut is agent-reported "done" versus backend terminal state.

Recent findings suggest that A green success from the same process that acted is a claim, not a grade. I'd want the eval to score durable side effects (ticket status, refund state, policy-cited fields) against a frozen oracle — and fail when the narrative is green while the database disagrees.

Practical check: can a run be marked done when the terminal-state fixture is red?

The distinction between backend correctness and report faithfulness is particularly interesting here.

Appendix A explicitly acknowledges that, for the 477 backend-only tasks, an agent can execute the correct state transition while misreporting the outcome to the user. Similarly, the completion proxies in Appendix D.2 capture termination and process signals rather than the semantic correctness of a completion claim.

Would a separate report-faithfulness diagnostic be useful alongside the existing deterministic verdict?

For example, a stratified, human-annotated sample could distinguish:.

Responses without a verifiable outcome claim could be tracked separately.

In a recent development, this would preserve the existing deterministic scoring contract while distinguishing execution reliability from reporting reliability. Two agents with identical backend success rates could differ substantially in how accurately they communicate their outcomes.

I'm particularly interested in whether the released trajectories would support such an analysis.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: How to Kill the Code Review.

Nov 26, 2026 2 min read.

Closing the Engineering the Developer Experience track at QCon San Francisco 2026, Ankit Jain, co-founder and CEO of Aviator, argued that line-by-line code review is already quietly dead on most teams, and that the sharper question is "how long until we stop reading the code?" He also flagged his conflict of interest up front, noting that he runs a organization that sells a solution and asking the audience to "be suspicious of me.".

The talk revisited an essay he wrote for Latent Space in March 2026 proposing a five-layer trust model to replace reviews. Eight months on, Jain remarked the mechanics held up but the essay missed human judgment entirely. He began with the data that unseated his original framing. A 2013 Microsoft study found 44% of reviewers cited defect-finding as their motivation, yet only 14% of their comments were actually about defects, and a 2018 Google study of more than nine million reviews reached almost the same split. Code review was never really about bugs, he argued, it was about knowledge sharing, echoing Addy Osmani: "We made writing cheap, and understanding stayed exactly as expensive as it has always been.".

Recent findings suggest that A September Faros study of more than 4,000 teams found that over 75% of PRs now merge without any human review, average PR size has grown, and redo work is up 67% year over year. Earlier research showed review quality drops sharply past 400 lines, yet the median PR today is 640 lines. "We are reviewing the code, but we are rubber stamping it," Jain remarked, pointing to a Reddit post from an experienced developer refusing to review AI-generated PRs that collected over 1,900 upvotes. The result is "review theater," where agents write, another AI reviews, agents revise, and humans skim and merge.

Industry observers note that to replace a single review, Jain proposed six layers: Argue, Capture, Codify, Prove, Debate, Own. Agents should argue about a change locally before the PR exists, surfacing only what they disagreed about. Intent and acceptance criteria, familiar from behaviour-driven development, should be captured during the coding session and attached to the PR rather than discarded. Repeated review comments become invariants, standing rules with scope, provenance, a verification method, and a team owner. Aviator mined 11,000 of its own review comments to produce 64 invariants. Evidence should replace green checks: screenshots, DOM snapshots, recorded requests, latencies, and database logs, because the same agent that wrote the code likely wrote its unit tests. Humans then debate decisions rather than diffs, and ownership shifts from author and reviewer to the teams that own the rules.

Sources indicate that jain reported his nine-engineer team now merges four times the PRs it did a year ago and still approves every one, while reverts have dropped around 40%. He also shared a failure: a change passed every filter and caused an 18-minute outage from an unindexed query, after which the post-mortem asked which rule was missing rather than who approved it. Critical areas such as security, authentication and billing still get line-by-line review.

Recent findings suggest that he closed with a line: You can outsource your thinking. You cannot outsource your understanding.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Huntington Ingalls Industries lands deal despite MoD pledge to buy British wherever possible.
  • Britain's Royal Navy is investing £142 million ($185 million) in underwater drones to tackle sea mines, but the contract has gone to an American defense supplier.
  • The Ministry of Defence (MoD) claims that the UK's ability to protect vital sea routes will be strengthened through the procurement of these Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles (UUVs).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Huntington Ingalls Industries lands deal despite MoD pledge to buy British wherever possible.

Britain's Royal Navy is investing £142 million ($185 million) in underwater drones to tackle sea mines, but the contract has gone to an American defense supplier.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) claims that the UK's ability to protect vital sea routes will be strengthened through the procurement of these Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles (UUVs).

These will form part of the Royal Navy's move toward a "Hybrid Navy" comprising a mix of crewed, uncrewed, and autonomous platforms in order to meet future challenges.

Recent findings suggest that the UUV selected for the job is the REMUS 620, built by Huntington Ingalls Industries (HII), the largest military shipbuilding company in the United States. HII has a facility at Portchester, on the south coast of England, but is still a US-owned company.

We asked the MoD how the award fits its pledge to prioritize buying British wherever possible, and what share of the contract's value will support UK industry.

Industry observers note that the contract includes HII's Sea Launcher automated launch and recovery systems and will bring support services previously delivered overseas to the UK. HII claims it will support 15 jobs, while the MoD identifies Portchester among the locations benefiting.

HII says this is the largest international order in its 25-year history of supplying uncrewed systems. The MoD has previously acquired REMUS 100, REMUS 300, and REMUS 600 vehicles for mine countermeasure operations.

The new vehicles will locate sea mines to support clearance operations and help keep shipping routes open.

By using drones to comb a body of water for explosive devices, the Royal Navy's crews can be kept a safe distance from any potential immediate threat. Traditionally, this work has been conducted by specialist crewed ships such as the Hunt class or Sandown class, but these are being retired from service in favor of uncrewed systems.

The Royal Navy also operates SWEEP, an uncrewed boat towing equipment that mimics a ship's magnetic, acoustic, and electric signatures to trigger mines from a safe distance.

The fresh REMUS underwater vehicles can be sent ahead of other vessels to search beneath the surface, making minehunting operations safer, faster and more flexible, according to the MoD.

"This investment strengthens our ability to protect freedom of navigation, which is critical to our security and our economy," said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP.

In a recent development, like others in the portfolio, REMUS 620 resembles a naval torpedo. It is capable of operating at depths of 600 meters and has an endurance of up to 110 hours on a single mission. The drones will be integrated with SeeTrack and Neptune software developed by SeeByte in the UK, which is already used by the Royal Navy.

In trials announced in October 2025, a REMUS 620 demonstrated launch and recovery using a submerged test fixture replicating a Virginia-class submarine's torpedo tube. The work could enable submarines to deploy and retrieve underwater drones on future missions. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A product team can ship the same model to two customers and inherit two different compliance problems.
  • Recent findings suggest that that is what makes AI regulation an operating challenge in 2027.
  • Industry observers note that the timetable itself requires care.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A product team can ship the same model to two customers and inherit two different compliance problems. One customer uses it to draft internal notes; another uses it in a consequential decision. The technology may look similar while the legal role, evidence requirements and affected people change.

Recent findings suggest that that is what makes AI regulation an operating challenge in 2027. Businesses will need a usable account of where the product may go, what it may do there and which obligations travel with the use case.

Industry observers note that the timetable itself requires care. The European Commission states the AI Omnibus entered into force in July 2026. Its current AI Act FAQ distinguishes high-risk application dates, including December 2, 2027 for Annex III systems and August 2, 2028 for certain product-related systems. Older summaries can therefore mislead planning. These forecasts use the position available on November 3, 2026; subsequent legal changes could alter the calendar.

Sources indicate that the promise of one global product will increasingly require a more detailed release package. In 2027, suppliers will publish market-specific configurations or documents that distinguish the customer's role and intended use. The underlying model can remain shared. What changes is the precision with which the company explains the conditions under which the finished service can be offered.

According to recent reports, one underlying model can support many products, and one product can create different obligations depending on its purpose, consumers and deployment location. A general writing assistant and an employment-screening system do not become equivalent simply because they share model infrastructure.

The Commission's explanation of AI Act scope distinguishes providers, deployers and general-purpose model suppliers, including some actors outside the EU whose products enter its market. That role-based structure makes a single undifferentiated global compliance statement increasingly difficult to use.

My expectation is practical differentiation: market-specific documentation, transparency settings, intended-use boundaries and enterprise support. This need not require separate models for every country. Over-separating the technical stack can itself create maintenance and testing problems. The more likely architecture is a shared product with explicit regional conditions and a controlled process for deciding which configurations may be sold where.

In a recent development, look for documentation that identifies the jurisdiction, product role and applicable use case. Regional server hosting by itself would not establish this forecast. A meaningful compliance package should explain which obligations it supports and what the customer still needs to do.

Map market access requirements onto the release process before promising worldwide availability. Buyers should ask whether the supplier's documentation covers their actual use case. A generic claim that a model is compliant can obscure obligations that arise only when the buyer deploys it.

Sources indicate that A procurement team cannot wait until a deadline to discover that the purchased system lacks the oversight or records its deployment requires. In 2027, buyers of EU high-risk applications will ask earlier for operational evidence. That will move compliance discussion into demonstrations, acceptance criteria and contracts, where the customer can still influence what is delivered.

It has been revealed that A legal deadline does not coincide neatly with an enterprise buying cycle. Contracts, integration work and staff training can begin months before deployment. Buyers therefore have a reason to ask for the evidence needed to operate the system while they still have negotiating leverage.

The Commission's enforcement overview distinguishes the responsibilities of authorities and the timing of obligations. The Council's AI Act timeline also records the evolving implementation sequence. These official materials describe the legal framework; they do not prove that every supplier is ready.

Who receives an alert? What can a supervisor override? Which logs can the customer inspect? The weakness will be performative documentation that describes capabilities the actual product configuration does not provide.

Look for assurance documents tied to a named version and deployment context. Public tenders and completed supplier packages will be stronger evidence than statements of intention. Repeated postponements of implementation dates would reduce the immediate pressure behind this prediction.

Prepare a reusable evidence package, then adapt it to the customer's role and deployment. Buyers should connect contractual promises with acceptance tests. Oversight and logging obligations need operational owners and budgets, rather than being left entirely to legal review at signature.

Recent findings suggest that A sandbox is most valuable when it resolves a specific uncertainty. Participation can become misleading if it is presented as unrestricted approval. In 2027, public sandbox outputs will make testing boundaries and practical lessons more visible. The useful result may be a narrower product scope or a clearer obligation—an outcome less promotional than endorsement, but far more actionable.

Testing under supervision can help a developer understand how an emerging product fits a legal framework. It does not automatically establish that every later configuration, customer or use case is acceptable. The value of a sandbox lies partly in making those boundaries explicit.

The Council's implementation timeline identifies the revised timetable for national sandboxes. The Commission FAQ explains their role in supporting innovation. My forecast is about published practical outputs during the year, not an assumption that every member state will produce comparable results on the same schedule.

Sources indicate that publication may be limited by confidentiality and the resources of participating authorities. That is why the forecast does not require a comprehensive public register of every experiment. Still, examples of specific lessons would help smaller suppliers more than promotional announcements saying that a manufacturer has joined a program.

Look for identified use cases, test conditions and the distinction between advice, experimentation and authorization. A participant describing sandbox admission as a general government endorsement would be weak evidence of mature implementation. Guidance that changes a product's scope would be much more informative.

Use a sandbox to resolve specific uncertainties and preserve the resulting conditions. Strategy for obligations outside the test environment. Investors and customers should inspect the actual output before treating participation as evidence that a product can be deployed at scale.

A legal change matters to a customer when somebody explains what it changes in the product. In 2027, more suppliers will connect regulatory updates to configurations, documentation or intended-use limits. That will require legal interpretation and product management to share a working process, so customers receive a specific action rather than another broad announcement about the importance of compliance.

Compliance cannot remain a one-time launch assessment when both the legal framework and the product are changing. A fresh downstream use, a revised model or a changed implementation date can invalidate assumptions used in an earlier sales process.

In a recent development, the difference between the 2026 Omnibus change and earlier implementation summaries illustrates the operational problem. Separately, the Commission's One Europe, One Market roadmap includes further policy initiatives; proposed legislation must be distinguished from enacted obligations. A roadmap target should never be presented as a current legal duty.

In a recent development, the practical capability will be a controlled link between legal interpretation and product behavior. Suppliers will need to explain what changed, which customers are affected and whether action is required. Too many undifferentiated notices can create alert fatigue, while silent changes can leave customers operating under obsolete assumptions.

Look for dated notices with an identified legal trigger and a specific customer action or configuration change. A generic regulatory newsletter would not qualify. Clear separation of proposals, adopted rules and effective obligations will be a useful sign of quality.

In a recent development, give product, legal and customer-success teams a shared change process. Customers need notification rights that fit their deployment cycle. Maintain a dated record of the assumptions behind market access decisions so that a change can be assessed without reconstructing the entire product history.

In a recent development, the businesses best placed to navigate AI regulation will be able to explain their products with unusual precision. Which role, which use, which market and which date are operational questions. Answering them well can make expansion more predictable even while the surrounding rules continue to evolve.

Tech Report: Introducing Falcon ASR

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.
  • Industry observers note that we’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect.
  • In a recent development, in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.

Industry observers note that we’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In a recent development, in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Industry observers note that arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

According to recent reports, we trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

Recent findings suggest that WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

In a recent development, we evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:.

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

According to recent reports, falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

Industry observers note that the model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Sources indicate that our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

Industry observers note that قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

Recent findings suggest that تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:.

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

Recent findings suggest that يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

It has been revealed that يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

Improving Human Impersonation, as the Web Closes Up Against AI

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Web scraping used to be a more casual affair: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) routines created on a write-once, run-many basis – humans recording their browsing actions, refining them through various automation processes, and setting them to run at intervals, unattended, in order to obtain data from websites that only want real humans (or paying clients) accessing them and their data – and which take measures to repel automated browsing of this kind.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Web scraping used to be a more casual affair: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) routines created on a write-once, run-many basis – humans recording their browsing actions, refining them through various automation processes, and setting them to run at intervals, unattended, in order to obtain data from websites that only want real humans (or paying clients) accessing them and their data – and which take measures to repel automated browsing of this kind.

Of course, domains subject to this treatment often considered RPA to be more akin to ‘data exfiltration’ and/or ‘hacking’ than any definition of ‘browsing’. Prior to the current era of AI, web scraping emerged from obscurity quite rarely, as a marginal form of pest; until LinkedIn launched an ultimately-doomed lawsuit against HiQ Labs, an ‘intelligent automation’ provider, and one of many corporate concerns that challenged LinkedIn’s right to harvest publicly, profit privately.

Since publicly-available data has become a truly valuable resource for AI companies (rather than the insipid ‘Data is the upcoming gold’ rhetoric of ten years ago), at least 60% of reputable sites have been found to be repelling an AI crawler – a rise (in 2025) from 23%, two years earlier.

In practical terms, defending against any kind of web scraper is about pattern-matching, and looking for evidence of algorithmic access, such as screenshotting non-selectable text, or polling the CSS stylesheets, or the other underlying structures of a page.

These actions in themselves, no matter who or what executes them, are often considered evidence of automated processes rather than human interaction; personally – and especially at Yandex – I often have to complete CAPTCHAs because I make ‘uncommon’ or technical queries; and the more protective and protected domains are generally intolerant of anything but ‘mom ‘n pop’ baseline browsing behavior.

However, that’s still a relatively rare and heavy-handed experience. For the most part, anti-scraper logic and algorithms are looking not so much at the actions as for the way they are enacted – and especially for repetitive usage patterns for keyboard and mouse interaction. This could mean that a played-back RPA human interaction that works at first will shortly become blacklisted, because its lack of variation reveals it over time as a routine, and not a person.

Because of the growth of AI scraping, the tools of the RPA industry have suddenly become of great interest both to AI and intelligence companies that consider publicly available data ‘fair game’ in spite of any interstitial defenses (a stance theoretically supported by LinkedIn’s defeat in the aforementioned lawsuit – at least in the US); and the defending domains that in most (but not all) cases don’t have quite enough market capture to retain their profitable user base behind a login-wall, and would prefer to keep access open.

In the latter case, the companies have hardened themselves against the customary dedicated ‘headless’ browsers common in RPA, and against dedicated RPA frameworks such as Microsoft’s Playwright, and its derivatives and forks.

According to recent reports, the security sector has taken an interest lately in whether AI-powered web agents can actually still be recognized by sites that are on the defensive against such activities. After all, these incursions may not be running on a CRON job, but neither are they ‘human’.

In this regard, a fresh paper† from Canada proposes an AI-powered web agent designed to test the effectiveness of current anti-bot defenses. By combining a modified version of Chromium with AI models trained to reproduce human mouse and keyboard activity, the new system achieved access (non-rejection of browsing) in 89% of tests on a benchmark of protected websites – 12 percentage points above the best previously-published result:.

Comparative test results for bypassing eleven categories of web bot protection. Figures indicate successful page access as percentages, with test counts in parentheses. The upcoming paper’s system, DarkAgent, achieved the highest overall score across 80 tests, compared with previously published results for nine other browser configurations. Source.

The system, dubbed DarkAgent, consists of Browsium, a customized Chromium browser engineered to conceal evidence of automated control; and Behavium, a framework incorporating two machine learning models: MouseGen, and KeyboardGen, which, together, simulate human interaction with the browser:.

The DarkAgent workflow. Browsing decisions are translated into simulated human interactions, executed through Browsium’s native input mechanisms. The resulting page changes are fed back to the planning agent to determine its next action.

The architecture, shown above, addresses four categories of evidence available to bot detection systems, namely interaction patterns; browser and device characteristics; evidence of automated browser control; and network protocol characteristics.

The aforementioned KeyboardGen was trained on the Aalto keyboard dataset, derived from a study of 136 million keystrokes, to reproduce typing rhythms, errors and corrections. MouseGen was trained on the Boğaziçi Mouse Dynamics dataset, with additional scrolling data sourced from the Attentive Cursor dataset:.

It has been revealed that examples of mouse movements, in coordinate and interpreted form, from the Attentive Cursor Dataset. Source.

Both generators use Transformer architectures, while the browser modifications were implemented through conventional programming. OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 was used to decide which actions to perform during the benchmark tests.

The browser’s reported identity and the simulated user behavior are coordinated throughout each session, so that the various signals presented to a website remain consistent with one another. To support this, a separate JavaScript-based environment within Chromium allows the agent to inspect web pages without exposing its presence to the website’s own scripts:.

Comparison of conventional browser automation (top), using the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) to inspect and control web pages, and the latest paper’s approach (bottom), where a private communication channel reduces the evidence of automated activity visible to websites.

The simulated mouse movements and keystrokes are then processed by the browser as genuine user input, with the same trusted status granted to physical mouse and keyboard activity. Variations in mouse trajectories and typing patterns, learned from recorded human activity, facilitate different sequences of movements and actin timings, reflecting the natural inconsistencies of human interaction.

DarkAgent was evaluated using Stealth Bench V1, a benchmark developed by Browser Use, comprising 80 short mouse and keyboard tasks on live websites, requiring no login and covering eleven categories of protection: Cloudflare; PerimeterX; DataDome; Akamai; reCAPTCHA; Kasada; Shape; GeeTest; hCaptcha; Temu; and (unspecified) site-specific anti-bot systems.

The tests were conducted in August 2026*, using geographically-matched residential proxies, with success measured solely by whether page access was obtained, and discounting task completion. Comparative results were drawn from earlier baseline tests conducted by the benchmark’s authors.

To establish the individual contributions of DarkAgent’s components, 30 browsing sessions were scheduled for each of 18 configurations on a website hosted by the researchers, with identical prompts, tasks, planning models, and limits on the number of actions.

For this, standard Chromium and Browsium were tested with and without Behavium, and with MouseGen and KeyboardGen enabled independently.

Additional comparisons were made with Firefox; Camoufox; the Playwright derivative Patchright; CloakBrowser; and publicly-available human behavior simulators Ghost Cursor; HumanTyping; and CloakBrowser’s Humanize.

The browsing sessions were evaluated using FP-Agent (an existing bot-detection system); additionally, JA4DB (a database of network connection fingerprints) was used to check whether the browser’s reported identity was consistent with its network activity.

Beyond the initial Stealth Bench V1 results presented earlier, all browsing sessions conducted without behavioral simulation were identified as automated by FP-Agent, while every session conducted with Behavium enabled in either Chromium or Browsium was classified as human:.

Sources indicate that bot detection results across 18 browser configurations, based on 30 sessions per configuration. P(Human) indicates the average probability of human activity assigned by FP-Agent, Verdict indicates the most frequent classification, and the final column identifies the browser engine inferred from the network connection.

Similar results were obtained with Ghost Cursor and CloakBrowser’s Humanize, indicative of a weakness in FP-Agent (which doesn’t examine how fast the mouse moves, or how its speed changes).

In AgentShield tests, all 139 form-filling sessions from the benchmark’s existing automated agents were flagged as bot activity, as were all ten sessions conducted with Browsium using standard automated input. With DarkAgent and CloakBrowser + Humanize, all ten trials per configuration were completed successfully without detection:.

Results of the AgentShield form-completion tests, showing successful submissions, bot detection rates, detection scores, mouse movements and keypress durations. DarkAgent and CloakBrowser + Humanize escaped detection, though DarkAgent’s keypress durations were considerably closer to those of human users.

When new fields appeared in the form, they were attended to by DarkAgent within an average of 3.74 seconds, compared to 4.72 seconds for human consumers. The greater variation in human response times suggests, the authors contend, that bots could still be identified by the length and consistency of the pauses between actions.

Although this almost-impenetrable paper is not likely to gather many adherents to the cause, web scraping is one of the most interesting challenges for the dataset-builder and proponent of agentic AI.

However, it’s fast-becoming a Quixotic pursuit; even sites that may be indifferent to data acquisition routines are now likely to become defended against RPA and agentic AI in the very near future, simply because it is becoming a default position.

While data of the kind dealt with in this research can be extracted from human engagement farms in Asia, such data will inevitably form recognizable patterns in the aggregate, so that the routines that are part of them can be specifically blocked – a familiar pattern in a latest cold war that’s starting to heat up.

Projecting the scenario to an extreme, truly effective RPA countermeasures could signal the wholesale revival of the crowdsourced worker – lately an eclipsed figure.

* Relevant only because GPT4.1 was available then.

Pensioners assured their funds will arrive as normal.

The UK's Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has taken some services offline after detecting a "cyber incident," but states regular benefit and pension payments are unaffected.

The department unveiled the precautionary shutdown on Friday morning. "We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems," it remarked.

"We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) to investigate and to bring services back online as rapidly as possible and to minimize any disruption.

In a recent development, "Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal. If an online service you need is unavailable, please try again later. As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links.".

The Register contacted both the DWP and NCSC for more information. The DWP declined to comment beyond the statement issued publicly.

According to recent reports, GC3 coordinates responses to incidents affecting government. The Government Cyber Unit leads the wider Government Cyber Action Plan, backed by more than £210 million. It is led by the government CISO, Bella Powell.

Officials have not commented on any of the usual details one would expect from a cyber incident disclosure, including the specific services that were downed, when they are expected to return, or whether any data is thought to be compromised, even at this early stage.

The UK government has also been criticized recently for investing heavily in AI cyber defenses, while the concern of legacy and aging IT continues to be neglected in the background.

It confirmed at the end of October that it was throwing £130 million at AI cyber defense technology, as part of a wider £600 million cross-government AI spending spree announced by the Treasury.

ExfilSquad recently claimed to have stolen around 607,000 records from the Department for Education and another 114,000 from the Police National Legal Database. ®.
