#161231. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📅 08 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1547 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1547 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1.
  • Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way.
  • The first message is where I spend my effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

Industry observers note that at the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

It has been revealed that you don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

It has been revealed that A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

It has been revealed that on the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App.

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

According to recent reports, the agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App.

Industry observers note that ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App.

In a recent development, no dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App.

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena.

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

Recent findings suggest that I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE.

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

According to recent reports, if you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, choose Slack when your biggest need is communication across departments and the tools you already use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unite.AI may receive compensation when you use links to products we review. This does not influence our editorial evaluations. Read our affiliate disclosure.

It has been revealed that A busy channel is good at surfacing a request and much less reliable as a delivery proposal. Slack and ClickUp overlap more than a simple chat-versus-tasks comparison suggests: Slack has Lists and workflows, while ClickUp includes Chat and collaborative Docs. The decision is which environment should organize the team’s daily work.

According to recent reports, choose Slack when your biggest need is communication across departments and the tools you already use. Choose ClickUp when tasks, dependencies, time, and reporting need one accountable home. We prefer ClickUp as the delivery system for a project-heavy team, with Slack retained when its wider communication network already has value.

Both products appear in our best AI collaboration tools guide. This comparison evaluates where each belongs in a real team workflow, including where using them together is more useful than replacing one with the other.

Consider a product team preparing a website launch. Design must finish before development, copy needs approval, and analytics must be ready before release. A marketing lead needs a quick answer about launch risk, while individual contributors need to know what to do next.

It has been revealed that slack is a natural place to create the launch channel, bring design and engineering into the same thread, and capture the decision behind a change. A Slack list can assign small follow-ups with dates and status. A canvas can keep the brief and key links visible, reducing the time new participants spend asking for context.

According to recent reports, clickUp gives the launch a more explicit delivery structure. Tasks can carry an assignee, due date, status, and custom fields; subtasks separate work that belongs under a larger deliverable. Dependencies make the relationship between design, development, and approval more visible. A manager can move between a task list and a schedule view without reconstructing the plan from messages.

For a small, straightforward launch, Slack Lists may be enough. Our recommendation moves toward ClickUp when there are repeated handoffs, several rolls out, or a need to track effort and report progress consistently. ClickUp’s flexibility brings setup work of its own: too many statuses and custom fields make a simple project harder to use.

In Slack, a useful AI request starts with work the team has already discussed: summarize the open questions, explain a decision, or prepare a brief for someone joining the project. Slackbot’s value comes from the relevant context it can access, not from replacing an accountable owner. The official example below shows research being organized into a canvas; it is a vendor product example, not a result from our own test.

In a recent development, clickUp Brain can work with project context, and the action-item menu shown below illustrates the connection between writing and follow-up work. The useful result is a proposed set of actions that a team can assign and refine. For the launch example, we would keep those actions in the project so that a summary and the delivery record do not drift apart.

Slack is the stronger choice when the question is who said what, why a decision changed, or which colleague needs to join the discussion. ClickUp is the stronger starting point when the output needs to become managed project work. Neither AI output settles a dependency or commits a deadline on its own; a project owner still needs to approve the change.

In a recent development, plan choice matters for this workflow. Slack Free and Pro provide a limited Slackbot preview; Business+ includes 15 messages per member each week, with additional usage available through the applicable credit arrangement. Permission and connected-app scope determine what the assistant can use. A paid communication plan and unrestricted AI usage are different purchases.

Slack’s official overview below reveals how AI fits into the communication workspace. Use it to understand the product’s approach alongside the concrete work examples above.

Recent findings suggest that slack AI | AI that works where you do. Video: Slack.

The ClickUp overview provides a second view of the decision: how AI can support project follow-through rather than just summarize discussion.

According to recent reports, how to Streamline Project Management With ClickUp Brain. Video: ClickUp.

Sources indicate that clickUp’s Slack integration can create tasks from messages, show rich previews, and post activity updates to chosen channels. That supports a practical handoff: a customer issue arrives in Slack, someone turns it into a ClickUp task, and the channel receives meaningful progress changes rather than a second manually maintained task list.

In a recent development, use one authoritative task record. If the same deliverable lives independently in a Slack list and a ClickUp task, somebody will eventually patch only one. ClickUp documents the integration as available across plans, but particular automation and connected-search capabilities have their own blueprint requirements. An integration is also not permission for every user to see every private task.

The examples below use standard USD annual-billing rates, expressed as a monthly equivalent. They exclude tax, temporary promotions, and additional AI usage. Annual billing means paying the annual commitment, rather than buying a month at the displayed equivalent.

For ten people, Slack Pro plus ClickUp Core comes to a $162.50 monthly equivalent, or $1,950 billed annually, before tax and optional usage. Slack Pro plus ClickUp Business is $242.50 per month equivalent, or $2,910 per year. The combined stack is easier to justify when Slack already connects departments or external collaborators beyond the project team.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • RETN notes that network operators and telcos are now directly competing with AI datacenters for chips and other components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Optical equipment prices up around 50% this year as telcos compete with datacenters for components, indicates RETN.

The AI building boom is driving up optical networking equipment prices and stretching delivery times to as much as 18 months, according to network operator RETN.

RETN notes that network operators and telcos are now directly competing with AI datacenters for chips and other components.

Sources indicate that as Reg readers will be aware, memory prices have soared by four or five times over the past year or so, but RETN indicates optical networking equipment prices have risen by around 50 percent since the start of 2026. Worse are the extended delivery times, with optical network kit that used to arrive within three months now taking 12 to 15, and some orders taking up to 18 months.

Recent findings suggest that this is as bad as, if not worse than, the shortages during the pandemic, when chip supply problems left network vendors unable to fulfill orders. The problem now is that because of the AI boom, demand is outpacing supplies.

In its report, "AI, Connected," RETN claims developers building outside established datacenter hubs may need to involve network carriers two to five years before opening.

In a recent development, the sudden demand for network kit from hyperscalers and AI campuses is only one factor, RETN states. Raw material shortages, skilled labor shortages, energy constraints, geopolitical tensions, and logistical challenges are also compounding the glitch.

Industry observers note that however, it concedes that many carriers didn't help themselves by previously postponing network upgrades to cut expenditure. That work has now become unavoidable at the worst possible time.

Industry observers note that network diversity is now seen as a must-have, the report indicates. Where customers were once satisfied with two routes to long-haul destinations, they expect operators to provide four or more redundant routes now.

According to recent reports, the aim is to prevent a single failure from taking down critical services. Multiple connections are only useful protection if they avoid shared physical failure points, such as the same ducts or cable routes. A diverse circuit might cost €1,800 ($1,975) a month instead of €600 ($658), it claims, but an outage could prove far more costly.

RETN also indicates AI datacenters are moving away from populated areas to remote locations, where access to suitable land, power and water may be easier to come by. Hyperscalers are building in the Nordics, where land is affordable, the climate is cooler, and plenty of renewable energy is available.

Remote sites may lack the fiber infrastructure needed to connect them to other datacenters and customers. The Register reported on this issue earlier this year.

In a recent development, for sites close to cities, developers often fund the fiber themselves, which adds just a few percent to the total project cost. But over longer distances, the case becomes harder to make, and carriers are understandably reluctant to build a long-haul route to serve a single remote site.

Some developers are prepared to swallow the cost: RETN says a major cloud provider is exploring converting an abandoned factory in Central Europe into a large-scale server farm, despite little existing fiber in the area.

However, RETN's warning is that connectivity must be planned alongside power and construction, not left until the datacenter is nearly ready to open. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reuters reported on November 26, 2026 that Z.ai had fallen behind schedule on GLM-5.5, its next flagship designed with roughly 3 trillion parameters, a measure of model size, while Moonshot AI had begun distilling from Google and Meta models as training data from OpenAI and Anthropic models became harder to obtain.

Industry observers note that distillation uses answers generated by a more capable model to train another system. A person familiar with Moonshot’s operations stated anti-distillation safeguards had also slowed its development, and that Google’s and Meta’s latest releases had made their models attractive alternative data sources. Moonshot is also seeking substitute computing: a separate source said it had intensified efforts to rent capacity in Europe, corroborating earlier CNBC reporting, and planned to approach Chinese chipmakers about training on their processors.

Two people familiar with the matter noted Z.ai had planned to release GLM-5.5 in November 2026. One of them said increasingly effective anti-distillation safeguards were partly responsible for the hold-up and that latest US computing restrictions could push the launch into the first quarter of 2027 or later, despite the earlier goal of finishing training and releasing it by the end of 2026. Z.ai, Moonshot, Google and Meta did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The disclosures put simultaneous pressure on the resources behind Chinese developers’ low-cost challenge to US rivals: outputs from more capable models and overseas access to advanced chips. Anti-distillation measures constrain unauthorized extraction of model outputs, while the newly introduced licensing rule targets overseas arrangements that let developers use Nvidia processors without importing them.

Moonshot is particularly exposed to the new US Commerce Department rule because it rents computing power to train its models and prioritizes overseas providers, a person with knowledge of its operations said. The rule took effect on November 19, 2026 and imposes licensing requirements for covered computing arrangements at data centers outside the US above a threshold roughly equivalent to 750 Nvidia H100 chips. Operators already providing covered services before the rule took effect have 90 days to obtain licenses.

According to recent reports, A person with knowledge of Moonshot’s operations said domestic computing capacity could not fully replace its overseas supply if access were cut off entirely, a scenario that could stretch its usual six-month interval between major releases to 12 months or longer and push Kimi K4 to around mid-2027. Moonshot released Kimi K2 in July 2025, K2.5 in January 2026, and K3 in July 2026.

Z.ai confirmed GLM-5.4 on November 23, 2026, describing it in the model’s technical release as its first flagship built on a Loop Transformer. The architecture reruns a shared block of layers to refine internal states without adding parameters. The 750-billion-parameter model loops 28 layers from the GLM-5 base for two iterations; Z.ai adapted an already pretrained base through continued training rather than starting from scratch.

Z.ai states the design reaches intelligence comparable to models with 2 trillion to 3 trillion parameters. To control deployment costs, the second pass reuses the first pass’s attention indices and combines shared and sliding-window key-value caches, which store prior context, rather than creating another full-context cache.

The company also acknowledged that GLM-5.4 can enter excessively long reasoning loops, although it stated the resulting reflection and self-correction improve accuracy beyond the model’s parameter count. The model is available through Z.ai’s chat and coding products; API access is listed as coming soon, and open weights are planned after safety hardening.

In Anthropic’s September 2026 threat-intelligence report, the firm defines illicit distillation as industrial-scale, covert extraction without authorization and attributes more than 23 million exchanges to Moonshot between May and July 2026 and more than 3.4 million to Zhipu, branded outside China as Z.ai, over 17 days in June and July 2026.

Anthropic said Moonshot silently relayed customer requests to Claude and used fraudulent proxy accounts and cross-session replay techniques to extract reasoning transcripts for training, while Zhipu used Claude to clean and normalize harvested transcripts, judge model outputs, filter training data, and support other post-training work. Anthropic’s layered defenses combine proxy-network attribution, extraction classifiers, account bans, identity checks, and summarized or encrypted reasoning intended to make stolen transcripts less useful.

Moonshot previously told China’s National Business Daily in July 2026 that Kimi K3’s gains came from original architectural changes, rejecting suggestions that they resulted from distillation.

It has been revealed that GLM-5.4 shows how architectural efficiency can extend an existing model, but it does not resolve the constraints around the next generation. The reported GLM-5.5 and Kimi K4 schedules are exposed to tightening access to large-scale computing and training data drawn from rival models, pressures that reusing a pretrained base cannot fully address.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

Industry observers note that LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Recent findings suggest that pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Sources indicate that edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

  • Datacenter spending is booming but the models, the chips, and the clout all live in US and Asia.

  • Sources indicate that gartner forecasts European IT spending of $1.57 trillion in 2027, up 9.9 percent from 2026, compared with worldwide growth of 15 percent to $7.35 trillion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Datacenter spending is booming but the models, the chips, and the clout all live in US and Asia.

Europe's IT spending is growing more slowly than the global average, according to Gartner, whose analysts warn that the region's push for tech sovereignty faces commercial and technological obstacles.

Sources indicate that gartner forecasts European IT spending of $1.57 trillion in 2027, up 9.9 percent from 2026, compared with worldwide growth of 15 percent to $7.35 trillion. For 2026, it estimates spending growth of 20.7 percent in North America and 13.7 percent in China.

"The world seems to be racing towards this AI goal of where the large language model provider is going to be, and the race seems to be between North American-based providers and some Asia Pacific providers," John-David Lovelock, Distinguished VP Analyst at Gartner, told The Register.

He remarked Europe had traditionally trailed in IT uptake. "We saw that happen when global sourcing, cloud, and software as a service all came along. It's down to the pushback against the idea of creative destruction," where fresh technologies replace old ones.

Europe's fastest growing categories are datacenter systems, forecast to grow 29.7 percent in 2027, and infrastructure as a service, at 26.7 percent.

Even so, Lovelock does not expect Europe to compete with North America and China on AI investment.

Industry observers note that "For AI provision, Europe is going to be behind, and there won't be a way to catch up," he said. "The AI datacenters, the large language models, the foundational models, the tools and techniques for building out AI are all being centered outside of Europe, but enterprises don't need to do that. So the question becomes: regardless of where the source of the AI is coming from, can the enterprises actually adopt and use it? In one sense, Europe will be behind in the provision of AI, but it need not be behind in the use.".

The gap nonetheless complicates Europe's push to reduce its dependence on US technology suppliers. The European Union has introduced fresh rules to encourage tech buyers to favor sovereign tech over the dominant tech vendors, but Lovelock doubts they will move spending much.

In a recent development, "Sovereignty is a wonderful flag that we fly on the front of a building. IT is running in the basement. CIOs are not going to buy a second-best solution that costs more simply because it's sovereign.

"They are not going to break any laws, but they are not going to make a decision that puts their firm in a worse position at a higher cost. While sovereignty gets [vendors] on the list, it doesn't assure that they get purchased," he told us.

Earlier this month, Gartner predicted that by 2029, more than 90 percent of EU organizations will have a digital sovereignty strategy, but argued that a fully sovereign technology stack remains out of reach.

In a recent development, "The global technology supply chain is too interconnected, and many critical dependencies cannot be replaced at a commercially viable scale," said Bettina Tratz-Ryan, VP analyst at Gartner. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CNBC reported on November 26, 2026 that Nvidia chip sellers have told neocloud operators, which rent out accelerated computing capacity, they will not supply GPUs if any of the resulting computing capacity will be rented to Chinese companies, citing two people familiar with the private communications.

It has been revealed that the condition is broader than Nvidia’s earlier position, according to the report: the company had remarked it would not sell to customers renting more than 50% of their GPUs to Chinese companies, whereas the seller messages reject any Chinese rental capacity. That moves tenant screening directly into hardware procurement across a supply chain running from chip sellers to neoclouds.

Recent findings suggest that the disclosure follows a related development on November 25, 2026, when some Nvidia GPU sellers were seeking replacement buyers for chips apparently intended for data centers where Chinese companies would rent access. The earlier development concerned resale; the new one is an explicit condition on purchases.

Industry observers note that the seller messages followed the Bureau of Industry and Security’s November 16, 2026 announcement of an interim final rule that took effect November 19, 2026. BIS noted the measure is designed to prevent remote-computing arrangements at third-country data centers from circumventing existing restrictions on sensitive U.S. technology, bringing remote-access controls into closer alignment with controls on physical shipments.

The rule requires a license when there is knowledge that covered advanced-computing items being exported, reexported or transferred within a country are destined for data centers worldwide that provide, or will provide, access to more than 12 million aggregate TPP to companies headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination, including China, or to companies whose ultimate parent is headquartered in those locations.

According to recent reports, aggregate TPP is the sum of the covered integrated circuits’ or commodities’ total processing performance. Digitally or physically linked data centers can be combined toward that threshold when they share resources as a unified whole. Applications are reviewed case by case.

In a recent development, exporters and foreign data centers are expected to check customers for direct or indirect ownership or control by persons located or headquartered in those destinations, including through an ultimate parent. A data center’s refusal or inability to provide sufficient compliance information is a red flag that must be resolved before proceeding.

A later change from a permitted end use to a prohibited one can require BIS authorization. Data centers already providing covered compute before publication must obtain a license within 90 days of the effective date to continue without facing future export restrictions.

Computing used exclusively for commercial recommender systems is excepted when required information is submitted; systems generating novel text, images, audio, video, software or other content do not qualify. Separate destination-based license requirements apply to covered items sent to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, with an exclusion for end consumers that are headquartered in the United States or have a U.S.-headquartered ultimate parent, provided reporting requirements are met.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC’s Squawk Box on November 25, 2026 that the Commerce rules were intended to close loopholes involving indirect access. He described both smuggling through places such as Southeast Asia and remote access from data centers in third countries.

Industry observers note that the reported condition and the rule move compliance in the same direction: tenant screening at the point of GPU purchase, backed by ownership checks and authorization obligations that continue after deployment. Under the reported condition, a neocloud’s hardware access depends on the customers its capacity will serve, wherever the data center is located.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one.
  • Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.
  • You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something latest, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):.

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:.

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Sources indicate that pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Recent findings suggest that boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Industry observers note that black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

It has been revealed that FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

Sources indicate that A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

Sources indicate that let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

According to recent reports, FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

Recent findings suggest that the text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

Recent findings suggest that this gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

Industry observers note that in stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

According to recent reports, at the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

According to recent reports, the distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:.

It has been revealed that the fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are fresh to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

AI Could Soon Edit Live Videos in Real Time

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Live video gives viewers a direct connection to events as they unfold, which helps audiences follow developments and hear speakers in context.
  • Sources indicate that for example, Microsoft’s recently published patent application proposes replacing spoken words and adjusting lip movements to match in near real time.
  • Microsoft filed application US20260341309A1 in 2025, describing a proposed approach to AI-assisted video editing, rather than announcing a confirmed product launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Live video gives viewers a direct connection to events as they unfold, which helps audiences follow developments and hear speakers in context. Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered editing could reshape that connection by changing speech before it reaches viewers.

Sources indicate that for example, Microsoft’s recently published patent application proposes replacing spoken words and adjusting lip movements to match in near real time. Such capabilities could support clearer communication, but they also raise questions about whose words audiences actually hear. Understanding the differences between original and AI-edited video can help explain what editable video could mean for viewer trust.

Microsoft filed application US20260341309A1 in 2025, describing a proposed approach to AI-assisted video editing, rather than announcing a confirmed product launch. Its scope covers both recorded presentations and near-real-time changes to live events. The proposed system could remove filler words, correct mispronunciations and replace other speech, including colloquial expressions or words it identifies as inappropriate. It would also adjust the speaker’s lip movements to match the replacement audio.

Recent findings suggest that audience profiles could influence those choices. The filing describes profiles containing details such as age, language, cultural background and education level, which could guide speech replacements. Viewers could therefore receive different versions of the same event, with wording tailored to their profiles.

The proposed process begins with capturing a speaker’s audio and video during a live event. An AI agent identifies words to change, guided by editing settings or audience profiles. Generative AI then creates replacement speech and adjusts the corresponding video frames, including lip movements, to match.

It has been revealed that these changes would happen within a short broadcast buffer. The filing describes a roughly one-to-10-second delay, giving the system time to process speech before presenting the modified stream. To keep the result flowing naturally, the system would smooth audio and visual transitions around each replacement. Some implementations could also enhancement captions to reflect the edited speech and retain original recordings for later reference.

Sources indicate that multilingual presentations could let viewers hear speech in their preferred language while seeing lip movements that match the translation. Educational broadcasts and training sessions could use this approach to reach audiences across language barriers. Audience-based adjustments could also help explain unfamiliar terms in language suited to viewers’ knowledge.

In a recent development, speakers who stutter could choose to use optional editing support during presentations or live broadcasts. That choice should remain with the speaker, including control over which speech patterns the system changes. Removing a hesitation can make speech easier to follow while preserving the message, although pauses sometimes convey uncertainty or emphasis. Meanwhile, replacing a factual claim changes the substance of the statement and requires a different level of scrutiny and speaker approval.

Industry observers note that existing AI tools already offer parts of the proposed system’s capabilities, including translated speech, synchronized lip movements and live voice modification. Their uses and limitations help show how Microsoft’s proposal compares with available products and research demonstrations.

Sources indicate that heyGen’s Video Translation tool works with uploaded footage, translating speech into a selected language and synchronizing the speaker’s lips with the new audio. Its Dynamic Duration option lets individual segments stretch or compress by up to 20%, allowing more natural pacing when translations are longer or shorter. This flexibility helps accommodate differences in phrasing between languages.

According to recent reports, the workflow processes an existing recording before the creator shares the translated version. Microsoft’s proposed system would instead modify an incoming live broadcast within a short delay, making changes while the event continues.

Krisp’s AI Accent Conversion processes speech during live conversations, adjusting pronunciation to help listeners understand the speaker more easily. It aims to preserve the person’s voice and tone while modifying how words sound. This could support communication in customer service calls and meetings where unfamiliar accents create listening challenges.

The distinction lies in what changes. Accent conversion focuses on pronunciation while preserving the words and their meanings. Microsoft’s proposed system goes further by allowing word replacements and corresponding video edits, potentially changing the statement itself.

It has been revealed that microsoft’s VASA-1 explores how AI can turn a still portrait into a moving, speaking face using an accompanying audio clip. Beyond matching mouth movements to speech, it generates changes in expression and head position that make the face appear more lifelike. It offers another example of how AI can create convincing footage from limited source material.

Its ability to animate a portrait also creates opportunities for impersonation, particularly when someone pairs a recognizable face with fabricated speech. Those concerns led Microsoft to withhold public access, with no full release planned until it has confidence in its ability to ensure regulation-compliant use. This position reflects the challenge of making useful avatar technology available while limiting applications that could falsely portray someone saying something.

In a recent development, when AI changes speech while preserving a speaker’s appearance, viewers could attribute the replacement words to that person. A speaker might approve pronunciation corrections without agreeing to changes that reshape an opinion or factual claim. Consent therefore needs to cover the scope of editing, especially when the finished video presents generated words as the speaker’s own.

Recent findings suggest that generated talking faces and synthetic voices extend this concern beyond alterations to existing footage. They could make someone appear to deliver a statement without participating in the recording. Some people already struggle to recognize sarcasm or identify a skit. When staged content already confuses, the prospect of widespread deepfake misinformation becomes a reasonable concern. Research shows that all age groups are susceptible to digital manipulation.

Convincing impersonations could damage reputations or distort public debate. Their growing plausibility could also give people an excuse to dismiss authentic recordings as AI fabrications, making genuine evidence harder to establish.

In a recent development, broadcasters and creators should clearly disclose AI edits and provide access to original recordings, especially when changes affect meaning. These steps help audiences understand what changed and give speakers control over statements presented in their name. Independent platforms like C2PA Content Credentials can support transparency by documenting media origins and editing history. They function like a nutrition label for digital content, allowing anyone to inspect the available history using compatible tools.

For consequential clips, viewers should compare the footage with sources and independent reporting. Realistic faces, matching lip movements and familiar voices alone offer limited grounds for trust.

Sources indicate that AI video editing could improve cross-language communication and give speakers more control over how they present themselves. Microsoft’s proposed system and research demonstrations represent different stages of development. As audiovisual edits become more convincing, disclosure and verifiable original recordings will become more crucial for maintaining trust.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black horse down (again), this time on Black Friday.

Lloyds Bank and Bank of Scotland customers reported problems accessing online banking and transferring money on Friday morning.

In a recent development, reports on Downdetector began rising around 1000 UTC. Lloyds also acknowledged problems on its service status page. A reader who supplied the screenshot below noted the particularly awkward timing: the last Friday of the month is payday for many workers.

It's also retail silly season: while Brits don't celebrate Thanksgiving, many UK outlets nonetheless participate in Black Friday sales, meaning storefronts are losing out.Others are concerned with more practical purchases. One customer tweeted that she had "no food at home and cannot shop because I cannot transfer funds from my secondary Lloyds account to my main one. At this point I'm just going to withdraw every penny the moment I'm paid, so much for Internet banking. Never had this years ago.".

Bank of Scotland, another Lloyds Banking Group brand, reported similar problems on its service status page: "We're aware some customers are having challenges with our app and online banking at the moment. We're sorry about this and are working hard to fix it.".

Earlier this year, a botched overnight software upgrade at Lloyds Banking Group potentially exposed other customers' transaction information to almost 448,000 app users. In a letter to Parliament's Treasury Committee, consumer relationships CEO Jasjyot Singh blamed a defect in the API handling transaction data. The incident affected Lloyds, Halifax, and Bank of Scotland, and prompted goodwill payments to thousands of customers.

Lloyds Banking Group remarked late last year that it had more than 21 million mobile app people and over 23 million digitally active customers.

A spokesperson for Lloyds Banking Group told The Register: "We're aware some customers are having difficulty accessing the app this morning. We’re sorry for the inconvenience and are working to get things back to normal as promptly as possible." ®.

Latest Update: Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • Sources indicate that meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Sources indicate that meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Industry observers note that meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Industry observers note that muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the fresh modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

It has been revealed that the language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Recent findings suggest that muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Sources indicate that only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Sources indicate that muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

Industry observers note that the context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

In a recent development, grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Sources indicate that video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

Recent findings suggest that as a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

In a recent development, muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:.

The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.

From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:.

Industry observers note that muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

It has been revealed that we tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

In a recent development, once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning highlights up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:.

Sources indicate that this is a substantial model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:.

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

Sources indicate that you can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

According to recent reports, first, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Recent findings suggest that now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

In a recent development, we trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

It has been revealed that we tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

According to recent reports, hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

In a recent development, finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Sources indicate that muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

Industry News: Canada Invests $700 Million More to Expand AI Compute Access Fund

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Canadian government expanded the AI Compute Access Fund with an additional $700 million on November 26, 2026, bringing it to $1 billion and opening a sector-specific call for health and life sciences projects.
  • Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon announced the next phase in Toronto.
  • Solomon also announced more than $52 million for 45 companies under the fund’s initial phase, lifting cumulative commitments to more than $118 million across 89 Canadian companies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Canadian government expanded the AI Compute Access Fund with an additional $700 million on November 26, 2026, bringing it to $1 billion and opening a sector-specific call for health and life sciences projects.

Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon announced the next phase in Toronto. The expansion adds to the fund’s initial $300 million and is intended to help Canadian organizations develop, test and commercialize AI products by offsetting cloud-compute costs. Eligible work includes model training, inference and fine-tuning.

Solomon also announced more than $52 million for 45 companies under the fund’s initial phase, lifting cumulative commitments to more than $118 million across 89 Canadian companies. Those earlier-phase awards are distinct from the expansion and cover health care, agriculture, manufacturing, finance and transportation projects.

The updated program guide covers up to 80% of eligible cloud-compute costs from sovereign providers and up to 50% from Canadian-based providers. Sovereign suppliers must operate infrastructure in Canada, process and store data there, be incorporated and registered in Canada, be Canadian-owned, and keep governance and decision-making authority in the country.

Recent findings suggest that canadian-based providers must meet the infrastructure, data and incorporation requirements. The ownership and governance tests do not apply to that category. Multinational companies with Canadian-registered entities can therefore qualify when the infrastructure and data remain in Canada. The rate structure offers a larger potential subsidy for choosing a provider with Canadian ownership and control without excluding multinational suppliers’ Canadian operations.

Eligible proposals must include $100,000 to $5 million in compute costs and end no later than March 31, 2030. Applicants can be Canadian-registered for-profit companies, nonprofit corporations or charities, including qualifying postsecondary institutions; they generally need fewer than 500 full-time-equivalent employees, Canada-based research and development teams and a commercialization plan. Contributions may be non-repayable, conditionally repayable or repayable, depending on the project’s assessed benefits and risk.

Health and life sciences applicants must submit a statement of interest by 11:59 p.m. ET on December 17, 2026. Those invited to proceed must file full applications by 11:59 p.m. ET on January 4, 2027, with compute contracts, invoices or other documentation in place or in progress. A selected applicant whose agreement is still in progress must finalize it before signing a contribution agreement.

Assessment covers market potential, organizational and financial capacity, technology readiness, expected economic and public benefits, and alignment with government priorities. Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada claims it will endeavour to make funding decisions within 90 business days after the call closes. The department will also use AI tools to support analysis of application information, conduct risk-related research and assist with program administration, while retaining final authority over recipient selection.

An official recipient backgrounder shows the range of supported work. Vancouver-based Apera AI is developing 4D vision and simulation-driven models for factory robots, while Toronto-based RetiSpec is working on a non-invasive retinal-imaging tool intended to detect early Alzheimer’s disease. Gotcare, also in Toronto, is building an AI-enabled home-healthcare management system focused on rural and underserved populations.

The sector calls sit within the government’s AI for All strategy, which names five priority areas: health and life sciences, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, and manufacturing and robotics. The strategy describes Canada’s sovereign compute capacity as nascent and notes most Canadian small and medium-sized businesses lack an affordable domestic option, leaving them reliant on foreign cloud platforms for training, testing and deployment.

According to recent reports, the government is also connecting the renewed fund to its commitment to bring 500 megawatts of sovereign AI compute online. The expanded program is intended to create demand for Canadian providers and support investment in domestic AI infrastructure, linking commercialization assistance to a broader infrastructure objective.

That makes the reimbursement gap central to the policy: companies receive the strongest support when their computing is owned, operated and governed in Canada. The open question is whether the demand created by these subsidies can support enough affordable domestic capacity while helping Canadian AI products reach the market.
