UK government rejects national consultation on AI datacenters

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ministers point to project-level environmental checks as petition passes 39,000 signatures.
  • The UK government has rejected calls for a UK-wide public consultation on the environmental impacts of AI datacenters, despite a petition attracting more than 39,000 signatures.
  • Campaign group Protect the Wild launched the petition last month, calling for a national consultation that would consider whether further expansion should be restricted, paused, or halted until those impacts are properly understood and addressed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ministers point to project-level environmental checks as petition passes 39,000 signatures.

The UK government has rejected calls for a UK-wide public consultation on the environmental impacts of AI datacenters, despite a petition attracting more than 39,000 signatures.

Campaign group Protect the Wild launched the petition last month, calling for a national consultation that would consider whether further expansion should be restricted, paused, or halted until those impacts are properly understood and addressed.

The nonprofit says the petition smashed the 10,000 signature threshold above which a government response is required in just three days, and the total stood at over 39,000 as this article was being prepared.

According to recent reports, in its response, published on November 23, the government ruled out the requested UK-wide environmental consultation, saying individual projects' impacts should be addressed through the planning process. It pointed instead to a separate consultation on its draft datacenter planning policy, open until January 8, 2027.

"Datacenters are vital to the UK's digital economy. They underpin the digital services that people rely on every day, including public services, healthcare and the way people work. They also provide the infrastructure needed to develop and use AI," the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) indicates.

"Building more capacity in the UK will support economic growth and innovation, while strengthening national resilience and ensuring the UK is well placed to realize the opportunities presented by AI.".

But it adds that the government recognizes the environmental impacts of bit barns are real and must be understood and mitigated, and this is one of the reasons why it established the Data Centre Covenant tests.

This Covenant, published last month, sets out tests all compute sheds "are encouraged to meet," while "strategic datacenters" are required to meet them to qualify for additional government assistance.

Sources indicate that the government has yet to define which datacenters qualify as "strategic," saying it will publish further details and eligibility criteria in due course. Qualifying projects could receive help securing power and accelerating planning.

Briefly, the Covenant tests are that operators cover any energy costs they create, so that communities do not have to pick up the bill; that they invest in local communities; adhere to the highest environmental standards; create jobs and drive reindustrialization; and provide secure and reliable access to their compute resources.

According to recent reports, if this has a ring of familiarity, it is because President Trump earlier this year introduced a Ratepayer Protection Pledge, under which hyperscalers and AI companies agreed to protect US consumers from any bill shocks due to the energy and infrastructure requirements of their datacenter projects. It seems that where the US leads, the UK still often follows.

The Covenant sets out efficiency targets and reporting expectations, but does not explain how compliance will be enforced or specify penalties for failing to meet its tests.

Protect the Wild notes that it "barely acknowledges wildlife, habitats or biodiversity. In fact, it doesn't mention any of those things at all.".

The Covenant does, however, call on operators to "protect nature," without spelling out specific safeguards for wildlife, habitats, or biodiversity.

Industry observers note that while the government encourages all server farms to meet the tests, only those it considers "strategic" are required to do so, as we noted above. And even that is only in order to qualify for extra government support, not in order to gain approval for a project.

Further, the campaign group contends that having environmental concerns addressed on a project-by-project basis at the planning level is a major barrier to tackling greenhouse gas emissions at a national level.

It cites the draft National Policy Statement for Data Centres, under which operational emissions from nationally significant projects in England, including those from on-site power generation, would be managed against national climate commitments at an economy-wide level rather than assessing each application's contribution to those targets.

Protect the Wild also argues that project-level assessments do not adequately capture nationwide habitat loss, even though the planning process requires consideration of cumulative environmental effects.

Datacenters have become a growing public concern in the UK, although opposition has not reached the level it has in the US, where anti-datacenter sentiment played a major part in political campaigns for the recent midterm elections.

But there were protests around the country at the start of November, such as in London and at Great Torrington, a town in Devon where a proposed 1.5 GW data campus and battery energy storage facility would cover 850 acres of nearby farmland.

Celebrity TV cook Delia Smith recently joined protests over a proposed datacenter on the edge of Norwich in Norfolk over concerns it may threaten a nearby nature reserve.

In a recent development, protesters are unlikely to find much sympathy in Westminster. The government has already pinned its hopes for growing the economy on AI, as detailed in its AI Opportunities Action Strategy last year, and it sees building more datacenters as key to achieving this.

The Guardian reports that Natural England, the government's own advisory body for the natural environment, is being threatened with abolition weeks after raising objections to a large AI campus near Bristol because of the threat it poses to protected wildlife and habitats.

According to recent reports, A separate report found that the government met with 137 different businesses to discuss datacenters between July 2024 and June 2026, but did not meet a single community group or environmental organization during the same period. ®.

Article: Engineering Reliable Telematics from Smartphone Sensors

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Articles Engineering Reliable Telematics from Smartphone Sensors.

Nov 27, 2026 21 min read.

In a recent development, A smartphone can provide a surprising amount of information about a journey, including GPS estimates location and speed, accelerometers measure motion along the device's axes, gyroscopes capture rotation, and others. A connected vehicle may expose additional signals, such as speed, engine state, or diagnostic information.

Combining these sources creates opportunities for fleet monitoring, usage-based insurance, driving-behavior analysis, trip reconstruction, and connected mobility services.

However, having more sensors does not automatically produce better telemetry.

Microsoft Ignite 2026; Explore What's Next in AI and Software Engineering - Learn how to architect agentic systems, modernize cloud infrastructure, and tackle emerging engineering challenges. Get practical insights from Microsoft experts and industry leaders. Watch on demand.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, a GPS patch may arrive after a vehicle has already slowed down. A phone may rotate in its mount, changing how its accelerometer readings relate to the vehicle's movement. An application may pause collection when the operating system restricts background activity. A backend service may receive observations out of order after a device reconnects.

Each observation may look reasonable in isolation, but the problem appears when the system combines observations that do not describe the same moment, coordinate frame, or physical event.

Industry observers note that I would approach this as an architectural problem before treating it as a sensor-processing problem. The goal is not to make every sensor perfect. It is to build a system that understands the limitations of its inputs and prevents unsuitable evidence from silently becoming a business decision.

This distinction matters because a misleading telemetry event can have consequences beyond an inaccurate chart. It may influence a driver's score, trigger a fleet alert, affect an insurance calculation, or lead an operations team to investigate an event that never happened as represented.

For architects, the challenge is deciding where sensor collection, normalization, quality evaluation, and event detection belong and what contracts connect those stages.

For mobile engineers, the concern is preserving useful observations despite changing device orientation, sampling gaps, intermittent connectivity, and operating-system lifecycle behavior.

For streaming and data engineers, the problem includes delayed events, out-of-order delivery, duplicate observations, and reconciling streams that operate at different sampling rates.

For product and operations teams, the question is how to distinguish a confident event from one that needs further evidence or should not be reported at all.

The practical outcome is a design approach that makes data limitations visible, keeps event logic separate from data-quality decisions, and provides evidence that can be inspected when a result is challenged.

I arrived at this architecture by tracing the journey of a telemetry observation from the moment it is captured to the point at which an application uses it to make a decision. Rather than starting with a sensor-fusion algorithm, I considered what could go wrong at each step. A speed measurement could be delayed, two observations could represent different moments, a phone's orientation could change, or an operating system interruption could leave gaps in the collected data. Each problem affects a different part of the processing flow, but all can ultimately influence the same business decision.

This led me to identify the responsibilities that a reliable pipeline needs to address independently: preserving the original measurements, establishing their temporal relationship, interpreting them in a consistent reference frame, evaluating their quality, detecting events, and retaining the evidence behind the resulting decisions. These responsibilities form the six logical stages described below. The intent is not to prescribe a particular deployment topology, but to establish clear architectural boundaries so that uncertainty introduced at one stage does not silently propagate into the next.

I prefer to separate raw measurement collection from interpretation. Requirements such as detecting harsh braking, classifying trips, or calculating a driving score should not dictate how raw observations are represented.

Sources indicate that A practical architecture has six logical stages, as the following image reveals. They do not need to be six separately deployed services, as several can run within the same mobile application. The separation into six stages matters because each stage has a distinct responsibility, failure modes, and validation requirements. In the next sections, we are going to review all these stages in detail.

Sources indicate that figure 1. A quality-aware mobile telematics pipeline (Source: created by the author).

Start by retaining the original observation before applying transformations.

Recent findings suggest that A record should carry the value and its unit, source or sensor type, measurement timestamp, available arrival timestamp, and relevant metadata. Depending on the source, that metadata might include accuracy estimates, sensor sampling information, device identifiers, or the vehicle association.

Industry observers note that why preserve the original? Because a later transformation may be incorrect, an assumption may change, or an event may be disputed. If the system retains only its normalized output, engineers may be unable to determine whether the original observation was poor or the transformation introduced the error.

It has been revealed that for example, suppose an application converts a GPS speed reading into a standardized unit and later combines it with vehicle speed. If an event looks implausible, the engineering team should be able to inspect the original value, its timestamp, and the conversion applied to it.

Preservation does not mean keeping every field forever, since retention, privacy, security, and storage policies still apply. It means defining which evidence is needed for diagnosis and traceability before transformations discard it.

According to recent reports, sensor streams do not necessarily report at the same frequency or on the same schedule. A vehicle interface may produce frequent speed updates while GPS observations arrive less often. Mobile and backend components may also introduce different buffering and delivery delays.

The first distinction I make is between measurement time and arrival time.

Recent findings suggest that measurement time describes when the observation was captured, according to its source clock. Arrival time describes when a component received it. Arrival time is useful for understanding latency, but it is not a safe substitute for measurement time when reconstructing physical events.

A stream processor that compares the latest values received from two sources can accidentally compare different moments. This becomes especially problematic during rapid acceleration, braking, or turning, when the underlying state changes rapidly.

The architecture should therefore define an alignment policy. It needs to specify how observations are matched, how much temporal separation is acceptable for each use case, and what happens when the system cannot find a suitable match.

In a recent development, interpolation may be appropriate for some continuous signals, but it should not be applied indiscriminately. It can create a plausible-looking value where the evidence is sparse, and it may obscure a sharp change. The system should retain whether a value was directly measured, interpolated, or otherwise estimated.

When alignment cannot be established within the required tolerance, the right result may be lower confidence or no event at all.

A measurement's value is only part of its meaning. Its unit, coordinate frame, source, and interpretation matter just as much.

A phone's accelerometer reports motion in device coordinates. Those axes are attached to the phone, not inherently to the vehicle. If the phone rotates in a mount, the relationship between the phone's axes and the vehicle's forward, lateral, and vertical directions changes.

Recent findings suggest that A system that assumes the phone is always mounted in the same orientation can interpret device movement as vehicle movement. That can distort acceleration, braking, and turning estimates.

Industry observers note that normalization should make these assumptions explicit. It may include unit conversion, coordinate transformation, sensor calibration, and checks on the validity of orientation estimates. A transformed observation should retain enough information to identify the transformation and its assumptions.

In a recent development, the system must also distinguish coordinate normalization from measurement quality. A transformation can be mathematically correct but based on an uncertain orientation estimate. The result may therefore remain unsuitable for a particular event calculation.

At this stage, the system asks a different question: not simply whether a value exists, but whether it is fit for the intended use.

Useful checks include freshness, timestamp alignment, missing samples, source consistency, measurement uncertainty, and the reliability of any required coordinate transformation.

These checks should not be buried inside individual event rules. A shared quality stage gives different event detectors a consistent view of the evidence and makes quality decisions easier to monitor and test.

I would use three broad outcomes:.

Industry observers note that these are not universal labels with fixed thresholds. A GPS observation might be adequate for a coarse trip map but unsuitable for calculating a short, sharp braking event. Quality must be evaluated in context.

Event detection should consume measurements that have already passed through the relevant quality checks.

It has been revealed that this does not mean every event requires every sensor. A trip-start detector and a harsh-braking detector have different evidence requirements. The architecture should allow each detector to declare what it needs and how it handles missing or uncertain inputs.

Consider a braking detector that combines vehicle speed and GPS speed. If the two values refer to different moments, the detector may infer a rate of deceleration that is not supported by the underlying movement. A quality-aware design prevents the detector from treating a poor match as equivalent to aligned observations.

The detector should also distinguish the event's classification from the quality of its evidence. An event may be a candidate for further review rather than a definitive result. Keeping these concepts separate makes the system easier to tune without changing the meaning of quality checks throughout the pipeline.

The final stage produces more than an event label.

A useful event record can include the event type, event time or interval, relevant vehicle or trip association, quality status, supporting observations, and the processing-rule version. Where a confidence estimate is used, its meaning and limitations should be documented rather than treating it as a universal probability of correctness.

Industry observers note that this information makes a decision inspectable. An engineer can trace an event to the observations that supported it, see whether any measurements were downgraded, and understand which processing logic was applied.

It also helps separate two questions that are often conflated: "What did the system decide?" and "What evidence justified that decision?".

These six stages form one continuous data path. Raw preservation protects the evidence; temporal alignment and normalization make observations comparable; the quality gate determines their suitability; event detection applies the domain logic; and the final record explains the result.

The value of this architecture comes from the boundaries between stages.

According to recent reports, this is deliberately more than a sensor-fusion algorithm. It is a contract for how imperfect physical observations become software decisions.

The principle is straightforward: preserve what was measured, establish what it means, evaluate whether it is fit for use, and only then act on it.

Sources indicate that imagine a fleet operator whose mobile application scores driving behavior. Drivers receive alerts for harsh braking, and fleet managers use the events to identify potentially risky patterns.

According to recent reports, one morning, a driver approaches a traffic light and brakes normally. The smartphone collects GPS-derived speed while the vehicle interface reports speed independently. The backend later records a harsh-braking event.

The driver disputes the alert. The vehicle did slow down, but not as abruptly as the application claims.

The engineering team examines the processing flow and discovers that the phone and vehicle streams were paired by arrival order. GPS updates were less frequent, and one observation represented an earlier point in the journey. During deceleration, the system compared that older speed estimate with a more recent vehicle measurement.

The discrepancy looked like physical behavior. Part of it was actually a timing problem.

The pipeline had accepted both values because they were syntactically valid. It had no mechanism to establish whether they were temporally comparable.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. How a timing mismatch can create a misleading event (Source: created by the author).

In a recent development, the team introduces a temporal-alignment stage before event detection. Each observation retains its measurement timestamp, while arrival time is tracked separately. The pipeline evaluates the freshness of each observation and avoids comparing streams when timing uncertainty exceeds the application's defined tolerance.

The detector also stops treating every speed discrepancy as equivalent. When the measurements are not sufficiently aligned, it lowers confidence or abstains from generating a definitive event.

The team adds monitoring for timestamp offsets, stale observations, alignment failures, and event reclassification. These metrics help distinguish a change in driving behavior from a change in data quality.

It has been revealed that this approach does not guarantee that every braking event will be classified correctly. It gives engineers a way to identify a measurement-comparison problem before treating it as driver behavior.

The same pattern applies to fleet diagnostics, trip reconstruction, usage-based insurance, and connected-vehicle analytics.

The lesson: before interpreting disagreement between sensors as physical behavior, establish whether the measurements are temporally comparable.

Time alignment does not solve the second major problem: orientation.

Recent findings suggest that an accelerometer measures along the device's axes. A vehicle-relative interpretation assumes that the system knows how those axes relate to the vehicle. If the phone rotates, that relationship changes.

The gyroscope can help estimate rotation, and sensor-fusion algorithms can estimate orientation. Neither eliminates uncertainty automatically. Estimates may drift, the initial orientation may be unknown, and the phone can move independently of the vehicle.

A field named longitudinalAcceleration can therefore be misleading if it was calculated from device-relative measurements while the phone's orientation was uncertain.

The architecture should distinguish raw device-frame measurements from transformed estimates and preserve the assumptions behind each transformation.

Consider a mobile telematics application that detects cornering and sudden lateral movement using the phone's accelerometer and gyroscope.

Industry observers note that A driver starts a journey with the phone secured in a horizontal dashboard mount. The application estimates orientation and interprets motion relative to the vehicle. Later, the mount loosens on a rough road, and the phone rotates. The driver continues straight.

The application detects apparent lateral movement and records an aggressive-turning event.

According to recent reports, the sensor values changed, but the physical interpretation was wrong. The device's orientation changed, so the relationship between its axes and the vehicle's direction of travel was no longer the same.

This problem is easy to miss when testing only with a phone mounted in a fixed position. The algorithm may perform well in a controlled setup and fail when users reposition the phone, adjust the mount, or carry it during a trip.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. The device frame is not automatically the vehicle frame (Source: created by the author).

Recent findings suggest that the team makes orientation confidence an explicit input to event detection. Raw accelerometer and gyroscope observations are preserved, while transformed measurements carry metadata describing the estimated reference frame and the confidence in that transformation.

The detector no longer assumes that one phone orientation remains valid for the entire journey. It monitors orientation changes and identifies periods when the relationship between the device and vehicle is uncertain.

When orientation is reliable, the application can use transformed measurements according to its validated detection policy. When confidence falls, it can rely on other trustworthy evidence, reduce the confidence of the event, or abstain from making a definitive classification.

According to recent reports, the team tests deliberate phone rotations, loose mounts, different mounting positions, and periods when orientation cannot be estimated reliably. It measures false positives and false negatives against a defined reference rather than assuming that a more sophisticated algorithm automatically improves accuracy.

This also improves the user experience. Instead of penalizing a driver for an uncertain observation, the application can indicate that it could not classify the event reliably.

The lesson: sensor accuracy and interpretation accuracy are different things. A sensor can report its measurement correctly while the application assigns that measurement the wrong physical meaning.

The same principle applies to phone-based activity recognition, wearable devices, robotics, and industrial IoT.

The quality gate is the fourth stage in the architecture, but its responsibility extends beyond checking whether sensor values look reasonable. It determines whether the available measurements are reliable enough for the specific decision an application intends to make.

The preceding stages preserve observations, establish temporal relationships, and normalize their measurement semantics. However, even after these steps, the resulting measurements may still contain uncertainty, missing samples, or inconsistencies. Without an explicit quality evaluation, individual event detectors must handle these conditions independently, often using different assumptions and fallback rules. This can lead to inconsistent decisions across the application.

Industry observers note that I consider the quality gate a contract between the telemetry pipeline and the business logic that consumes its output. It makes the limitations of the available evidence explicit and defines what downstream components are permitted to do with it.

This section explores three aspects of that contract: why measurement quality must be evaluated in the context of the intended decision, how the system should distinguish between accepting, degrading, and abstaining from a result, and why abstention should be treated as a legitimate outcome rather than a processing failure.

Suppose a fleet application supports two functions: displaying the approximate route of a trip and identifying a short, aggressive braking maneuver.

Recent findings suggest that the route display may tolerate a less frequent location patch. The braking detector needs evidence that is sufficiently aligned in time and suitable for estimating a rapid change in speed.

Using the same universal threshold for both functions can be unnecessarily restrictive for one and dangerously permissive for the other.

In a recent development, instead, each consumer should declare its requirements. The quality gate evaluates the observation against those requirements and communicates the outcome.

Sources indicate that this approach also makes product trade-offs explicit. If a team wants more events at the expense of accepting weaker evidence, that decision becomes a documented policy choice that can be evaluated—not an accidental consequence of a permissive fallback in a detector.

Recent findings suggest that engineering teams often focus on maximizing the number of events detected. But a system that always returns an answer can create a false sense of certainty.

Industry observers note that abstention is useful when the evidence does not support the intended decision. It should not be treated as an exception that disappears into a log file.

The system should record why it abstained, whether additional data could resolve the uncertainty, and whether the decision needs to be revisited. For some use cases, waiting briefly for a delayed observation is reasonable. For others, the system may need to return an explicit "insufficient evidence" outcome.

It has been revealed that this is especially important when events influence human decisions, scores, or downstream automation. A clearly identified lack of evidence is often more useful than a precise-looking result that cannot be defended.

A quality-aware architecture is only as good as the team's ability to see it working. If the system records only the number of events generated, it becomes difficult to distinguish a genuine change in driving behavior from a change in sensor availability, application lifecycle, or processing logic.

I would monitor the quality pipeline alongside the business outcomes.

Useful operational signals include:.

Sources indicate that these measurements should be segmented where useful by device type, operating-system version, sensor source, application version, and collection conditions. Otherwise, a system-wide average may conceal a failure affecting a particular group of devices.

I would also connect quality metrics to event outcomes. If the number of harsh-braking events suddenly rises, the team should be able to investigate whether driving behavior changed, timestamp skew increased, or a new application version altered sampling behavior.

This requires a distinction between technical metrics and business metrics. Event counts and driver scores tell us what the application concluded. Freshness, alignment, and rejection metrics help explain whether the evidence behind those conclusions changed.

Recent findings suggest that observability should support investigation, not just dashboards. Logs and event records need enough structured context to reconstruct a decision while respecting data-retention and privacy requirements.

A smartphone sensor pipeline does not run in a perfectly controlled environment. Applications can move into the background, devices can enter power-saving modes, connectivity can disappear, and operating systems can constrain background execution.

The architecture should not assume that a requested sampling rate guarantees a continuous stream.

In a recent development, on the device, collection code should handle sensor unavailability, sampling gaps, lifecycle transitions, and local buffering. When connectivity returns, queued observations may arrive in a burst or out of order. The backend should therefore apply its temporal-alignment and duplicate-handling policies even when the data originated from a single phone.

Recent findings suggest that the system should preserve the distinction between the time an observation was measured and the time it was uploaded. It should also make gaps visible rather than filling them silently with fabricated continuity.

According to recent reports, offline operation introduces another design decision: how much data to buffer and for how long. That depends on the product's latency, privacy, storage, and battery constraints. Not every observation needs to be retained indefinitely, but the policy should be deliberate.

Sources indicate that these concerns are not separate from sensor reliability. They determine whether the system has enough timely evidence to make a defensible decision.

I would not attempt to perfect every sensor or event detector at once. I would start with one high-impact event and establish a reliable path through the architecture.

In a recent development, the goal is not to add complexity for its own sake. It is to discover where the system's assumptions are hidden and make them explicit before those assumptions affect a business decision.

Sources indicate that A quality-aware architecture makes sensor limitations and processing uncertainty explicit, but it does not eliminate them. Architects and developers should consider several limitations when applying this model.

The architecture can identify missing samples, stale observations, and unreliable measurements, but it cannot reconstruct physical events when evidence was never captured. Interpolation and estimation may help, but introduce assumptions and should not be treated as direct measurements. When evidence is insufficient, the system should communicate that limitation rather than manufacture continuity.

According to recent reports, the six stages define architectural responsibilities, not specific sensor-fusion, calibration, or event-detection algorithms. Developers must validate these techniques against appropriate reference measurements and real-world conditions. A well-structured pipeline cannot compensate for an inaccurate orientation estimate or an incorrectly designed detection algorithm.

Freshness, timestamp tolerance, measurement uncertainty, and orientation confidence must be evaluated against the intended decision. Requirements for displaying a trip route differ from those for detecting harsh braking. Thresholds should be validated for each use case, and confidence scores should not be treated as universal probabilities of correctness.

Background execution restrictions, battery consumption, connectivity, device diversity, and privacy influence what can be collected and processed. Teams must balance these constraints with evidence requirements and processing latency. They must also define how uncertain outcomes and abstentions are communicated and when additional data or manual review is appropriate.

Ultimately, this architecture is a framework for managing uncertainty, not a guarantee of perfect telemetry. Its effectiveness depends on sensor quality, validated algorithms, appropriate quality requirements, and continuous testing under real-world conditions.

Smartphones make telematics more accessible by combining location, motion sensors, computing power, and connectivity in a single device. But the convenience comes with a trade-off: device placement varies, sampling behavior is managed by the mobile platform, and measurements have different timing and coordinate semantics.

The architectural response is to separate observation from interpretation. Preserve what the phone measured. Establish when and in what frame it was measured. Evaluate whether the evidence is suitable for the decision. Only then should business logic act on the result.

According to recent reports, the phantom braking scenario indicates why measurements from different sources must be temporally comparable. The rotated-phone scenario shows why device orientation must be treated as a variable rather than an assumption. Both demonstrate why a technically healthy pipeline can still produce an unreliable conclusion.

The distinction is simple: collecting telemetry produces data. Engineering reliable telemetry produces evidence that downstream systems can evaluate, qualify, and use responsibly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

Sources indicate that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

Sources indicate that the multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the latest release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

In a recent development, we also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Industry observers note that apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

Sources indicate that the results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

According to recent reports, all recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

Sources indicate that the report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

In a recent development, access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been declared by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Industry observers note that thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team unveiled the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

Recent findings suggest that in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

Recent findings suggest that if you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

In a recent development, project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

The Prototype Paradox: What to Do When AI-Built Apps Outgrow the People Who Made Them

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that picture a Friday afternoon in a mid-sized manufacturer’s planning team.
  • The barrier to building software has nearly disappeared, and the evidence indicates how fast people are taking advantage of it.
  • Recent findings suggest that I don’t think that’s something to be alarmed about.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that picture a Friday afternoon in a mid-sized manufacturer’s planning team. A supply planner is tired of pulling three exports, cleaning them by hand and pasting them into a tracker. She opens an AI coding assistant and describes what she wants. Two hours later she has a small web app that pulls the data, flags late purchase orders and suggests which ones to expedite. It works. On Monday she highlights it to two colleagues. By the end of the month, a dozen people across planning and procurement use it every morning. Nobody in IT knows it exists.

That story is now ordinary. The barrier to building software has nearly disappeared, and the evidence indicates how fast people are taking advantage of it. According to Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, 45% of employees now regularly use AI tools on work devices, three times the 15% recorded in 2025. Much of that use happens outside official channels. Gartner’s Q1 2026 Global Labor Market Survey of more than 12,000 employees and managers in 40 countries found that 88% of workers who have an employer-provided AI tool also use a personal one for work.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t think that’s something to be alarmed about. It’s mostly a sign of real demand. But it creates a problem that most organizations haven’t named yet. The difficult question is no longer whether people can build useful software with AI. It’s what happens after they do.

Enterprise software usually enters an organization through a door: a procurement process, a security review, an architecture decision. AI-built tools come in through a different route. They begin as personal conveniences and become shared infrastructure gradually, without anyone deciding that they should.

I think of this as an invisible graduation. A personal tool becomes a team tool when the first colleague bookmarks it. It becomes an operational tool when someone gives it a live database connection instead of a spreadsheet export. It becomes critical when a process starts to depend on it, and the old manual workaround is forgotten.

Industry observers note that each step seems minor. Taken together, they turn a weekend project into something the business runs on, with none of the controls that would normally come with that role. Survey data indicates this is already widespread. In BlackFog’s survey of 2,000 UK and US employees, 51% remarked they had connected or integrated AI tools with other work systems or apps without IT approval or oversight. The same research found 60% were willing to accept security risks with unsanctioned AI tools in order to work faster or meet deadlines.

We have seen this pattern before. In the 1990s and 2000s, spreadsheets and desktop databases built by business owners became the hidden backbone of finance, risk and operations at many companies. Some of the most expensive operational failures of that period came from those end-user tools: models nobody had reviewed, formulas nobody could trace, and files whose authors had long since moved on. AI-built apps are the same phenomenon with more power. A spreadsheet can only do what its formulas allow. An AI-built app can call APIs, write to databases and send emails.

In a recent development, in most business functions, an ungoverned tool is mainly a governance and audit problem. In supply chain operations, it’s a continuity risk, because supply chain sits underneath almost everything else the business does.

Sources indicate that think about where the planner’s expedite tool ends up being used. During a port disruption or a supplier shortfall, it’s the first thing the team opens. Its recommendations shape which orders are pushed, which customers are told to expect delays and how inventory moves between locations. If it breaks at that point, or quietly produces wrong answers, the effects don’t stay within planning. They reach customer service, finance, manufacturing and eventually the customer.

Recent findings suggest that the blast radius of a tool depends on how many decisions downstream of it rely on its outputs, not on how sophisticated it is. In supply chain, that number tends to be large and to grow without anyone noticing.

When AI-built tools fail to make the transition into enterprise operations, it’s usually because of two kinds of debt that the original builder never had a reason to pay down.

The first is security and compliance debt. Apps generated from a handful of prompts often have weak or absent access control, have never had a security review, and were never assessed against frameworks such as SOC 2 that the rest of the stack must meet. This isn’t simply a matter of careless builders. The underlying models have well-documented weaknesses. In its 2025 GenAI Code Security Report, Veracode tested more than 100 large language models on 80 curated coding tasks and found that, although the code worked, it introduced security vulnerabilities in 45% of cases. More worrying for anyone expecting the problem to disappear by itself, Veracode found that even as models got better at producing syntactically correct code, their security performance stayed flat over time.

It has been revealed that the second is knowledge debt, and it gets far less attention. All software needs maintenance. When a tool is built by one person through a conversation with an AI, the only real documentation is in that person’s head, and often not even there, since they may never have read the generated code closely. The tool becomes tribal knowledge. When its builder changes roles, goes on leave or leaves the tech giant, nobody can fix it, extend it or say with confidence what it does. Knowledge debt grows with adoption: each new user increases the cost of the day the tool stops working.

For this reason, I expect a large share of the vibe-coding activity inside enterprises today to end up as throwaway work. That doesn’t make it a waste. Many of these tools are excellent prototypes. They prove a need exists, define requirements more clearly than any workshop could, and show what users actually value. But a prototype that proves a need is a different thing from a system built to meet it.

Recent findings suggest that banning these tools would be a mistake, and it probably wouldn’t work. TrustedTech’s Shadow AI in the Workplace report found that almost one-third of employees noted they would keep using AI tools even if workplace rules banned them and disciplinary action was possible. A ban pushes the activity out of sight. It doesn’t stop it.

A more useful approach is to treat AI-built tools as positions on a ladder, where each rung has a clear set of expectations:.

Recent findings suggest that rung 1: Personal sandbox. One user, read-only access to data that user already owns, such as a personal export. The tool informs; it doesn’t act. Here the right policy is to leave it alone. These tools are where experimentation happens, and the cost of failure is one person’s afternoon.

Rung 2: Shared insight. A few users, still read-only, still informing rather than acting. The risk is no longer a security breach. It’s a wrong answer spreading across a team. Minimum expectations: a named owner, a short description of what the tool does and where its data comes from, and a check that someone other than the builder can run it.

Rung 3: Connected. The tool has a live connection to systems such as ERP, planning or customer data, even if it only reads. That changes the security picture entirely. The tool now needs proper access control, credentials management and a security review equivalent to what you would require of any third-party software holding the same data.

Rung 4: Acting. The tool writes back to systems of record, changes dates or quantities, or sends messages to suppliers or customers. That makes it production software in every sense, and it belongs on a governed platform with auditability, change control and a team responsible for supporting it.

Two questions determine where a tool sits and when it needs to move up: Who depends on it? and What can it touch? The number of customers is the clearest indicator of what a failure would cost. Data access and the ability to act determine how bad that failure could be. One additional test overrides the rest: if nobody other than the builder could maintain the tool tomorrow, it’s already a liability on any rung above the first.

Recent findings suggest that the aim isn’t to stop tools from climbing the ladder. Tools that climb are the ones proving their value. The aim is to ensure the controls keep up with the climb, rather than finding out after an incident that a Rung 1 tool has been operating at Rung 4 for six months.

In a recent development, for a long time, enterprise software decisions followed a reasonably settled rule. Building was slow and expensive, so you bought anything that didn’t differentiate your business. AI has unsettled that rule because building has become fast and cheap.

But this reasoning confuses the cost of creating software with the cost of owning it. AI has sharply reduced the cost of the first version of an application. It has done much less to reduce the cost of securing it, scaling it, supporting users, responding to audits and continuing to develop it over years as requirements change. Those are the costs that make software ownership expensive, and generating code quickly doesn’t make them smaller.

Industry observers note that so the question should change. “Can we build this?” now almost always has the answer yes. The more useful question is: “Do we want to own this permanently?”.

In a recent development, if a capability genuinely distinguishes your business, owning it may well be worth it, and AI makes building it more feasible than it has ever been. If it’s operational plumbing that many other companies also need, such as demand sensing, inventory reconciliation or supplier collaboration, your engineers’ time is probably better used elsewhere. In those areas, it makes sense to work with providers who carry the security, compliance and maintenance burden every day and can respond to your requirements promptly. The economics of AI favor building in more cases than before. They don’t make every build a good idea.

Sources indicate that my own engineering team learned a version of this firsthand. When we’ve given AI a loose prompt and accepted the result at face value, we’ve sometimes spent longer understanding and fixing the code than it would have taken to write it carefully from the start.

According to recent reports, we aren’t the only ones. In a randomized controlled trial run by the research nonprofit METR, 16 experienced developers worked on real tasks in projects they knew well. When they were allowed to use AI tools, they took 19% longer on average, even though beforehand they had predicted AI would speed them up by 24%. The researchers were careful to say the result doesn’t mean AI tools are useless, and the tools have improved since. But the difference between perceived and actual productivity is the key lesson, and it matches what we’ve seen.

It has been revealed that I think the cause is a shortcut in the design process. Building software used to mean writing a detailed specification and handing it to a developer. Now AI can produce the specification itself, and because it looks polished, people often don’t read it closely. It looks fine at a glance. The problems are in the details, and detail skipped at design time comes back later as rework.

Industry observers note that the same is true for business processes. AI can produce workflows that look very convincing. Humans still have to do the due diligence: get into the details, check the logic and settle the design with a person involved. Once that’s done, AI can run the process reliably every day. The design step is the one part you can’t yet hand over to AI.

According to recent reports, the same discipline applies to the AI automation that does reach production. Start with tasks that are repetitive and deterministic, where the correct output follows reliably from the inputs. These can still be complex. What matters is that they don’t depend on judgment. Aim for automation that is right almost all the time, close to 99%, so that consumers come to trust it.

Over-ambition has a cost that’s easy to underestimate. Imagine an automated process that’s right 60% of the time. It’s tempting to describe that as “automating 60% of the work.” In practice, people can’t tell which 60% is right without checking all of it. They end up reviewing every output, investigating the 40% that’s wrong and correcting it, often with less context than if they’d done the task themselves. An automation at that accuracy can easily generate more work than it eliminates, and it damages users’ willingness to trust the next automation you introduce.

Production AI should run inside explicit policies: guardrails that keep outputs within predefined ranges, and clear rules about which actions can run automatically and which need human review. An AI that proposes reorder quantities might be allowed to act alone on changes within a narrow tolerance and be required to send anything outside that range to a planner. As models get better and a track record builds up, those guardrails can be relaxed. Autonomy should be earned through demonstrated reliability, not granted in advance.

For organizations that want to move from reacting to these tools to managing them deliberately, here is a practical sequence:.

Recent findings suggest that vibe coding isn’t the problem. It’s one of the fastest ways an organization has ever had to discover what its people actually need. The mistake is treating a fast prototype as a finished enterprise system or letting it become one by default because no one stopped to decide.

Sources indicate that the organizations that scale AI well will be the ones that spot the difference early. They’ll keep personal tools personal, move shared and operational tools onto governed foundations before something breaks, and decide what to build or buy based on what they’re prepared to own for the long term, not on how promptly something can be built. In supply chain, where every function depends on the strategy being right, that discipline is what separates innovation from fragility.

Build your own Paint

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Buildyourownpaint

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This tutorial shows you how to write a small drawing app in Rust, in the spirit of Paint.
  • Sources indicate that we start from an empty cargo new.
  • The tutorial is split into 12 chapters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome! This tutorial shows you how to write a small drawing app in Rust, in the spirit of Paint. We open a window, draw rectangles, circles and lines with the mouse, move them around, pick a color, and export the drawing as an image.

Sources indicate that we start from an empty cargo new. By the end, you have about 800 lines of Rust spread over fifteen or so files, with a single dependency: minifb, which opens the window and gives us the keyboard and the mouse. Everything else we write ourselves: filling pixels, drawing a line, checking whether the mouse is on a circle, converting an HSV color to RGB.

The tutorial is split into 12 chapters. Each one ends with a program that compiles and does something you can see, even if at first it's just an image file with a red square in it.

Sources indicate that I'm a developer and I've been doing data science for several years. But in my free time, I've always been drawn to low-level things: bare metal, and how a computer works at the very bottom of the stack.

I wrote this tutorial with someone in mind who is starting out, or simply curious, and who wonders how a program ends up showing something on the screen. It covers the basics of rasterization, that is, how a rectangle or a circle turns into pixels, starting from nothing and in small pieces you can understand one at a time.

It has been revealed that that's mostly what I'd like to show: by moving forward step by step, in a language close to the machine, you end up with something that works and that you wrote entirely yourself. It takes time, but there's nothing magic about it. If this tutorial takes away a bit of that mystery and makes a few beginners want to look further down, it will have done its job.

Industry observers note that this tutorial is a way to learn Rust by building something. I assume you've read the first chapters of the Rust Book (variables, functions, if, loops) but haven't written a real program with it yet. The heavier concepts, like enums, traits, borrowing, modules or error handling, come along chapter by chapter, when we need them.

You don't need to know anything about graphics. As for math, you need Pythagoras for circles and a projection to tell whether the mouse is on a line. I explain it when we get there.

Each chapter has boxes that explain why Rust does things the way it does. If you already know, skip them. Same for the exercises at the end of each chapter: they're there if you want practice, but nothing that follows depends on them.

I'd still recommend typing the code rather than copy-pasting it. It's slower, but typing is how you make mistakes, and fixing them is how you end up understanding what the compiler is trying to tell you.

According to recent reports, let's be upfront: at the end, you won't have GIMP. There's no brush, no layers, no undo. And technically, our app isn't even really a Paint. Paint paints pixels that can't be moved once they're down, whereas we keep a list of shapes that can be selected and moved. We come back to this in chapter 11, and the Going further page has ideas for adding a brush, a paint bucket or undo.

After that, Going further suggests ideas to keep going on your own, from freehand drawing to a version that runs in the browser.

All the code is in the pages, you don't need anything else. But if you prefer, the GitHub repo has one tag per chapter: git checkout ch05-mouse gives you the exact code at the end of chapter 5, and git diff ch04-window ch05-mouse highlights everything it adds. It's also handy to start again from a clean state if you get lost. The Following along with git page explains all of this.

If you find a mistake, an unclear explanation or a piece of code that doesn't compile, open an concern on GitHub. It really helps.

If you're ready, start here: chapter 0.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • True cost may be much higher for delayed SAP replacement that helped bankrupt the city.
  • Birmingham City Council faces a £128.1 million bill for its disastrous transition from SAP to Oracle – more than six times the original estimate for a project that contributed to its financial collapse.
  • Papers presented to its Audit Committee this week put the combined cost of the original implementation, which went live in 2022, and this year's reimplementation at £128.1 million, against £19.96 million forecast in the 2019 business case [PDF].
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

True cost may be much higher for delayed SAP replacement that helped bankrupt the city.

Birmingham City Council faces a £128.1 million bill for its disastrous transition from SAP to Oracle – more than six times the original estimate for a project that contributed to its financial collapse.

Papers presented to its Audit Committee this week put the combined cost of the original implementation, which went live in 2022, and this year's reimplementation at £128.1 million, against £19.96 million forecast in the 2019 business case [PDF].

The report, from program director Philip Macpherson, remarked the project's funding allocation had previously reached £157 million.

The report remarked the upcoming Oracle Fusion system went live in August without any priority-one or "showstopper" issues.

"The program has now moved into the Post Go Live Support phase where [it] continues to provide extra support but slowly transitions towards 'Business As Usual' operating procedures," the report said.

It is an understatement to say the same was not true of the first attempt to move the council's finance, HR, and payroll systems off its legacy R/3 SAP system to more modern software.

Industry observers note that the first project started in 2019 and was supposed to go live in April 2021, but was delayed by a year. After the council started to use the system in April 2022, it soon became beset by a series of serious problems.

It has been revealed that although the council had planned to implement Oracle "out-of-the-box," it created several customizations, including a bank reconciliation system that failed to function properly. The council struggled to understand its cash position and was unable to produce auditable accounts. It has spent more than £5 million on manual workaround labor. The system move also contributed to it becoming effectively bankrupt, an event it failed to foresee due to the malfunctioning finance system.

Industry observers note that it later emerged that officials ignored a "red" warning prior to the go-live date. They were explicitly told the system could cause late payments, a failure to collect debt, and incorrect accounting if it went live. Officials gave the go-ahead regardless.

The council decided to reimplement Oracle from scratch, while running the current system as best it could and implementing off-the-shelf software CivicaPay, now rebranded as Civica Income Management.

Despite the apparently trouble-free relaunch, the true cost to the council is likely higher than the projected £128.1 million implementation bill.

For a start, the original £19 million budget was supposed to support the software implementation for schools, but that was excluded from the reimplementation.

It has been revealed that secondly, the council expected significant savings from moving to Oracle in 2022 through greater efficiency. The 2019 business case booked £27 million in savings from 2019 to 2031, for example.

A 2024 analysis by Audit Reform Lab, based at the University of Sheffield, estimated that the disaster's direct and indirect financial impact, including lost savings and deteriorating tax collection, would reach £216.5 million by April 2026.

Council taxpayers can be assured the new system has gone live without major problems, but that is hardly cause for celebration. ®.

Industry News: The Scaling Problem No One Talks About in Education: Who Checks the Teacher?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I remember when we started discussing a major venture round to open up 30 latest children’s clubs a year, one investor’s question stuck with me: “How will you keep the quality of teaching the same in location number 30 as in location number one?”.
  • Sources indicate that frankly, he asked me the right question.
  • Most education networks control quality the way they did 30 years ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I remember when we started discussing a major venture round to open up 30 latest children’s clubs a year, one investor’s question stuck with me: “How will you keep the quality of teaching the same in location number 30 as in location number one?”.

Sources indicate that frankly, he asked me the right question. In education, scale is rarely limited by capital, real estate, or demand. It’s instead limited by the one thing that is hardest to copy: what actually happens between a teacher and a group of children when no one is checking?

Most education networks control quality the way they did 30 years ago. A supervisor visits the site, sits in on a class, and takes notes. Then, someone else watches a recording later. It works at three locations, but this could be broken at the last branch.

In a recent development, let me explain this using GMNSM as an example. Take 10 locations, with four groups a day at each, six days a week. At 30 minutes of review per session, that adds up to 480 review hours over four weeks. Using our own staffing costs for manual reviews, I estimate that would cost about US$6,100. The estimated workload grows with every club you add. Sampling keeps that workload down, but it leaves most lessons unseen.

The lesson for education is straightforward: if you can only inspect a sliver of what happens, you are not managing quality, but guessing at it.

In a recent development, speech AI has become good enough, and cheap enough, to turn a lesson recording into something a manager can act on. The research is also catching up. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial with 224 Utah mathematics and science teachers, automated feedback on classroom audio increased teachers’ use of focusing questions by 20% compared with a control group.

Commercial tools are following now as well. Coverage in Education Next describes apps that separate teacher and student speech, and reports talk time and wait time, “like a Fitbit for instruction.” However, the same piece also raises the hard question: what happens when this data moves from private reflection into a formal evaluation?

At GMNSM, we built Allim AI, an internal system to automate this quality loop, and the process was more instructive than the technology.

The idea is simple. You give the model your methodology – values, annual programme, lesson structure, and expected outcomes. The system reviews the coach’s speech in the discussion after practice, not the training session itself. It checks which questions the coach asked against the lesson blueprint and flags moments that may warrant human review. If the lesson is about building confidence, we ask: “did the coach discuss the assigned video, ask the required questions, summarize the takeaways, and help children apply them to real life?”.

The output is a score and practical coaching notes: fewer filler words, less judgemental language, and more room for different perspectives instead of one “correct” answer.

Three design decisions mattered more to us than the model itself.

According to recent reports, not everyone welcomed this in GMNSM. Some colleagues left because mandatory microphones felt like we didn’t trust them. I understand their reaction, and I would even be suspicious of any founder who dismisses it.

It has been revealed that the wider data states this is not an edge case. Gallup research found that only 20% of employees who work on a computer or digital device have a great deal of trust in their leaders to use employee data responsibly. A 2025 ExpressVPN survey found that one in six employees had considered quitting over monitoring they considered invasive. As one expert put it in a recent HR Daily Advisor-style analysis of AI that detects toxic managers, the same tool can look like support in a high-trust organization and “Big Brother” in a low-trust one.

So, my practical advice to other operators is this: treat it as a development tool first. If staff only ever see it as a scoreboard, they’ll either game it or leave. If it gives them specific, private, useful feedback, many will start using it the way it’s intended to be used. Tell people what gets recorded, why, and who sees it before it goes out. Also, accept that some people will opt out. When we did this, we explained the purpose to some colleagues and parted ways with others, which we respect.

Recording children’s classes raises obvious data-protection questions, and in Europe, the rulebook is tightening. Under the EU AI Act, certain uses of AI in education and employment can be classified as high-risk, depending on the system’s intended purpose. Not every use falls into that category, but the direction of travel is clear: the more an AI system influences decisions about people, the more scrutiny it should expect.

Industry observers note that whatever the legal classification, the practical principles are the same. Disclose what is recorded and who can access it. Minimize the data you collect. Keep people, not algorithms, responsible for decisions. These practices help earn the trust that makes feedback at scale possible.

Sources indicate that finally, AI will not fix a weak methodology, and it cannot replace a coach who genuinely cares about children. What it can do is make quality visible, consistently and affordably, so the lesson in location number 30 is no more of an accident than the lesson in location number one.

Andrej Kuprejev is the founder and CEO of GMNSM, a Dubai-based martial arts and holistic education network, and the founder of Allim.AI, the AI platform that supports coaching quality across its academies. A Lithuania-born former competitive judo and jiu-jitsu athlete, he founded GMNSM in 2022 to combine physical training with soft-skills development for children. It now runs 11 academies across the UAE, Qatar and Cyprus.
