Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3319 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the fresh US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Recent findings suggest that beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

It has been revealed that the decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

According to recent reports, the first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

According to recent reports, the residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Industry observers note that beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Recent findings suggest that every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Recent findings suggest that hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

According to recent reports, the most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

Industry observers note that A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

It has been revealed that the pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Industry observers note that beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Sources indicate that beam's config defines an expert-parallel blueprint. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

According to recent reports, beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

In a recent development, for faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Sources indicate that beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

It has been revealed that we are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

In a recent development, below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

According to recent reports, the quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

Sources indicate that after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Industry observers note that training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Recent findings suggest that reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can upgrade the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

It has been revealed that the recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Sources indicate that upgrade: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Industry observers note that evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

According to recent reports, the next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

Industry observers note that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Sources indicate that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

Sources indicate that we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

Recent findings suggest that you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

It has been revealed that we wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

In a recent development, first, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

Recent findings suggest that that’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

Industry observers note that this is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Industry observers note that also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Citing several media reports, Greenpeace Belgium stated on November 27, 2026 that the Walloon Region had ordered construction stopped at Google’s Aiseau-Presles data-center site on November 26, 2026, after the group sought an emergency halt over work continuing despite the amended permit’s revocation.

The reported order followed Greenpeace’s November 23, 2026 letter to the Walloon administration requesting an immediate stop. Residents had alerted the group that work was continuing, and its emergency-procedure release says satellite imagery supported the request. Spokesperson Nadia Cornejo welcomed the reported stoppage and said Greenpeace would continue monitoring activity at Aiseau-Presles.

Google’s original permit, granted in 2024, covered three data centers. A revised application in 2025 merged two of them into a single larger building and replaced the planned air-cooling system with water cooling drawn from the Sambre, making water use central to the subsequent permit dispute.

Industry observers note that the Walloon administration approved the amended permit in April 2026, and residents appealed a month later. Walloon minister François Desquesnes revoked it in August 2026 following that appeal. Greenpeace connected the decision with what it described as a historic drought in Belgium and said the minister had highlighted the data center’s water needs in his reasoning.

In a recent development, the satellite document supporting the suspension request contains five observation dates between August 13, 2026 and November 14, 2026. As a comparison for the cooling demands at issue, Greenpeace indicates Google’s existing Saint-Ghislain project withdraws 1 billion liters of water annually for cooling, returns one-quarter of it and evaporates the remainder.

The site is part of the Écopole business park, which covers more than 150 hectares across Farciennes and Aiseau-Presles on rehabilitated industrial land. The municipality records the first-stone ceremony for the Google data center on April 5, 2024.

Sources indicate that greenpeace’s account of the Council of State proceedings indicates Google sought annulment and suspension of the revocation on October 17, 2026. Greenpeace and several residents sought to intervene on November 16, 2026 to present their arguments, and a public hearing is scheduled for January 7, 2027.

Separately, a Walloon government framework published on November 12, 2026 presents data centers as support for AI and cloud development while identifying electricity, land and water as strategic constraints. The framework makes a prior partnership contract with the region a condition for covered projects with capacity of at least 25 megawatts, excluding infrastructure exclusively for an organization’s own needs.

Sources indicate that the framework relies on existing authorization procedures rather than creating a fresh one. It also bars data centers from sites meeting regional strategic-location criteria, subject to stated exceptions, and calls for projects to document electricity demand and ramp-up plans while setting expectations for water efficiency and recovery of waste heat.

According to recent reports, the immediate question is whether construction remains stopped while Google’s legal challenge proceeds. Wallonia’s wider framework makes the underlying trade-off explicit: attracting AI and cloud investment while preserving electricity, strategic industrial land and water for residents and other businesses.

These details. These are all publicly available. It's ok to cache it. What about internal data? Some of those unique IDs. You have UUID. Do you want to expose it outside? What about your item ID? Do you want to expose it outside? These are things that need to be determined. This is something that you need to work with your InfoSec team to understand what is the organization's level of classification, and how much they want to expose it, add it to a cache, and things like that.

Sources indicate that what about confidential data, like name, address, phone number, things like this? Definitely, we need to encrypt it or tokenize it. Whatever is the best fit or recommendation from the InfoSec team. Now this is a time where we need to think, does it make sense to add it in cache? We are going to cache because we want to reduce the time. Now if you're adding a confidential data in the cache, be mindful that you need to pay for decrypting it or de-tokenizing it. Are you ready to accept that? Is your system ok to do that? Then, about classified information. Your SSN number, your passport number, all of this information, a strict no. You cannot cache this data.

Industry observers note that next, we'll move on to circuit breakers. Circuit breakers are very helpful. It helps you contain your problem area to a specific region. It doesn't allow the entire system to be brought down. Instead, it contains the problem in one specific area. In that way, circuit breaker is very important. If you take a mental model. What happens, let's say when a downstream fails, and you have 10 downstream calling, and one of the downstream suddenly starts failing, the queue starts to build up, your thread pool queue is also high, your backup queue is also high. Now, as per your system logic, you try to retry and you also have incoming requests. There is a complete possibility of system being down. You are actually having a self-inflicted failure. Even if there is a request which does not need this downstream A, the request could fail for them. A circuit breaker helps in that.

Recent findings suggest that it helps you contain that. It is crucial to use this. When the circuit breaker is open, it's not going to allow any request. It's going to allow time for the particular downstream to prepare itself, to come back up. When it partially opens up to send a few requests is to see whether it succeeds. Once it succeeds, it sends the remaining requests. This is very helpful.

Then, what about fallbacks? Maybe we could take this example. When you're viewing an item on a search, you actually see this hottest item trigger, or you see this, five people are viewing onto this item. I have 10 purchased this item two hours back, or an hour back. All of these are hot information which are available. You need to be more accurate to give this information, or maybe nearly accurate. What if we don't have this? What if the service which returns this information are failing? Then you probably go and use your fallback text, which is like, maybe, yes, this is a hot item. Many people are viewing. We had more transactions. Don't give the exact number. This is the use of fallback. Consciously decide based on what your service is doing. Check if there are any places where you could use this tactic of a fallback.

It doesn't have to be a static text. It could also be defaulting to certain numbers based on the situation. The other one is data partitioning, which is mostly underrated. The main theme is to avoid hotspots. Why do we want to avoid hotspots? Because we want to distribute the traffic to all the shards possible. When you're deciding about partitions, make sure you choose a key which will give you a unique distribution across. Don't choose something like, I'm going to put all my hot sellers into one shard, like the top sellers into one shard. When there is a specific season, for example, Thanksgiving in the U.S., it's going to make all the requests go into that shard. It does not make sense to divide your sharding based on this theme. Rather use a key which is very generic: maybe the ID of the user itself, maybe his login name.

Use things which are generic, and make sure that gives a default distribution or a common distribution into all the shards. Sometimes due to regulations, it is also required that you need to split your data based on the region. Like EU region, you need to have a separate shard. U.S. region, you need to have a separate shard. This does not solve the problem because, again, if you have a seasonal event, it's going to go into that particular shard. That is why it is crucial to subdivide it based on the other keys that you have.

Now that we have seen a quick recap, we started with why is latency key, why is being fast important. We saw a request journey. We saw a list of tradeoffs. Now, until we measure, we don't know how good we are performing. That is why measuring things is really important. A measure could tell you how long things went well, or did not go well. Tracing will tell you why something happened. If you're not having tracing, you are missing out on something, on identifying why the problem even happened. Tracing is very important. If you haven't built it, it's time to actually build this. There could be themes, with the teams coming up saying, "My Redis is failing. My DB looks fine, but my cache calls are failing." How are we figuring out all of these things? Only because we have tracing built. You are able to take just the unique ID, look through the complete request, and see where exactly the problem has happened.

Sources indicate that if you are able to identify, that's because you have tracing built in. Let's move on to having SLOs. Before maybe going into SLOs, I want to touch base on SLIs, service level indicators. They are like direct metric information. Let's say you are getting 100k requests per second. Then let's say around 95k requests have succeeded, and the remaining 5k were not successful. This 95% is your success rate, or your application's availability is just 95%. The same thing, you could track for your error rates, you could track for a specific error also. You have that specific downstream, you can tie it based on the feedback system, what is the availability of the feedback system. All of those things could be done. You could also have measures like, how many of my requests is responding well within 200 milliseconds? If the number was 99.8, then that is the time that you have done it.

How do we tie this to a goal? That's where SLO comes in, service level objective. Let's say you want to make sure in a 30-day period, I want the availability of my system to be 99.9. Then that is your SLO. What happens when you set this up? You are going to be alerted. The team is going to be alerted. The leaders are going to know, when an SLO, the buffer, the time that you had, if you're utilizing that buffer in a week, which you had set for a month, then it is time to pause on all your velocity works that you're doing, and first fix the system. Did I make a wrong judgment about the SLO? My SLO number itself, did I do a mistake in configuring that, or should I go back and check my application service? Check the path, where is it going wrong?

Has it been happening consistently? Then there is something to do about it. Then there is some refactoring which needs to be done. There is no one solution which can fix it. You have to do small things at every journey to make sure that you're getting it right. This is where SLO is very helpful. Thread pool observability. We saw about thread pools and the importance of thread pool. Now, if we don't have an observability dashboard, you are not going to know whether your queue is getting built up. Am I getting an alert for it? Setting up alerts, before that, you need a dashboard. We need dashboards for active threads. What is my queue size? What is a completed task count? Then, what is my rejection rate? If I have information for all of these, then it's helpful for me to fine-tune during the next iteration.

Now that we have seen about how we could measure, how we could fix it, we have seen a lot about technical things going wrong, technical aspects going wrong. Now it is time to look at the human side of things. What is within our control? What can we do as a team to get this done? That's where culture comes into picture. During planning, are we talking about SLA? Are we talking about latency? Are we talking about what is our goal? During retrospective, did we talk about the last incident which happened? What was the last issue where you had to come back online and check things on a weekend? Did you have to spend your night over it? What was that incident? Are we discussing it as a team? Are we trying to fix our dashboards? Are we trying to fix our alerts? I know that teams set up alerts only in Slack, and your Slack thread is filled up with all these alert messages, nobody is looking into it.

Sources indicate that are we looking into that? These are things collectively which a team needs to take up, like during your planning session, during your retrospective. This is nothing but performance and review. What are some of the anti-patterns which we need to avoid? Considering staging data. Let's say you're doing a load test in staging and taking that number for your production. That's no way the same. Your environment in your lower region is not the same as what you're doing in production. Do not take that as a benchmark. If you're going live, maybe start with 1%, 2% traffic. Or even better, start it with traffic mirroring, if that is allowed. You mirror your traffic and see whether your fresh flow that you've added is performing at the same level as earlier in production. Is it delaying your latency? Is there something that you need to restructure? The other things could be synchronous logging, where you're logging too much information.

What is the future holding for us? There are a lot of things, like capabilities around adaptive routing where routing could be done to regions which are having less traffic. AI-assisted predictions, you can have models to predict, this is the hot cache. Make sure you can warm it up beforehand. You can use predictive warming. Edge-native executions, all of these are in the future.

Let me give you some information which you could try before the weekend. When you go back, what could you do? Choose a simple flow in your application, from end to end. Note it down. Work with your lead. Is there any journey that could be removed? Is there any duplicate logic? I've also seen these patterns when I'm reviewing code between the teams. If there is a dependency X, and you have three flows, like A is calling B, B is calling C. You always have this X which is getting called in all the flows. You tend to have that one service which everybody wants. What do we go about it? Is there anything that you can do about changing it? These are all things that you can check. Now, instrument it, and budget. You'll note down what is the graph. If you don't have a p99 dashboard, create one.

Note down what was the current latency. If it is at 500, yes, note it down. Look at the different junctions, your paths. Note down what each path has taken up. Now, where do you want to go from here? What is your budget? Cap it. Make improvements. Remove that unnecessary call. Rephrase it. Add thread pools. Parallelize it, if it's possible. Add cache if it's not there. Do all of these things, and take a result out of it. Run an L&P and take a result out of it. Now you can check the before and after metrics. I would like to leave with one quote. We are what we repeatedly do, so excellence is not an act, but a habit. I hope we inculcate that as a habit.

Participant 1: With regards to p95 and p99, what are they? Is it percentile?

Participant 2: I have one question around serialization and that you mentioned that we should clear up if it is not required. How do we measure the cost between clearing up the data before it gets serialized and to be returned versus just sending the entire data and then hoping that it will work?

According to recent reports, saranya Vedagiri: This is where your logging is helpful. Let's say you're calling x downstream service and you have the log from your application level and you also have the logging from your downstream. They will tell you, I received the request at 10, I returned back at 10, 10, or whatever, that milliseconds. In your logging, you would have not got the time that they had mentioned, so look at that. There is a buffer in between. Is that adding up, between what they say as they have sent to what you have received? There can be only a certain buffer for your network. If you are seeing a 50 milliseconds difference, then there is something going wrong. Is it your queue or is it your size? There is no one direct indicator, but it could be either of these two things.

Smartphone shipments face another bleak year before modest 2028 comeback

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Counterpoint forecasts another 6% shipment drop in 2027, with volumes still below 2025 levels by decade's end.
  • Global smartphone shipments are forecast to fall 14 percent this year and another 6 percent in 2027, with a recovery not expected until 2028.
  • That's the outlook from Counterpoint Research's latest Smartphone Market Outlook Tracker, which points to rising memory costs and constrained supplies as continuing pressure on handset makers and buyers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Counterpoint forecasts another 6% shipment drop in 2027, with volumes still below 2025 levels by decade's end.

Global smartphone shipments are forecast to fall 14 percent this year and another 6 percent in 2027, with a recovery not expected until 2028.

That's the outlook from Counterpoint Research's latest Smartphone Market Outlook Tracker, which points to rising memory costs and constrained supplies as continuing pressure on handset makers and buyers.

The downturn was particularly sharp in the third quarter: IDC and Omdia estimated year-on-year shipment declines of 22 percent and 20 percent respectively, as rising prices and component shortages squeezed the market.

Don't expect things to get better in the short term, as Counterpoint forecasts another 6 percent drop during 2027. But it believes that the market may see a 6 percent rebound in 2028, as memory supplies improve, pricing begins to stabilize, and pent-up demand for replacement phones returns.

The 2026 outlook has been shaped by sharply rising component costs, particularly for DRAM and NAND flash. According to IDC, memory costs have risen approximately 350 percent since last year and are still climbing.

As Reg readers will be well aware by now, this has been blamed on the memory manufacturers prioritizing output of high-margin chips to go into AI servers and GPU accelerators, creating a shortage of the mainstream components that are needed for devices like PCs and phones.

Vendors have responded by raising prices, reducing memory configurations, and withdrawing lower-cost models. As The Register previously reported, memory costs accounted for almost 60 percent of the total bill of materials in sub-$400 smartphones during Q1 of 2026.

For 2027, Counterpoint warns the outlook is for continued tight mobile DRAM supply, further price increases for low-power DDR (LPDDR) memory, and limited evidence to suggest short-term capacity increases.

"The 2026 decline was initially expected to mark the low point of the cycle, but the memory situation has remained more restrictive than anticipated," noted principal analyst Yang Wang.

"Mobile memory allocation is still being displaced by AI and server demand, while higher costs are taking longer to move through handset portfolios and retail channels. The result is a much weaker 2027, particularly for lower priced devices and price sensitive markets.".

Global shipments are forecast to rebound by 6 percent in 2028, but that would bring shipments only roughly back to this year's already shrunken level, rather than hitting the peak of previous years.

Counterpoint cautions that the scale of the rebound will depend on how promptly lower component costs translate into retail pricing.

A speedy improvement in mobile memory allocation during the second half of 2027 could bring replacement demand forward and swell shipments, but continued competition from the AI market or another round of handset price increases would hinder recovery.

Recent findings suggest that "The unusually low 2027 base creates the potential for a robust rebound in 2028 once the memory bottleneck begins to ease. But this should not be interpreted as a return to the old market trajectory," Wang said.

"Some low-end demand has been permanently lost, and the 2028 market will still be about 14 percent below 2025 shipments.".

Potential availability of 6G-capable smartphones toward the end of the decade could give the market a boost, but Counterpoint does not expect it to regain its 2025 shipment levels by 2030. ®.

#161198. Taking Email Back

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1633 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Linux-magazine ↗ Open Full Page

Taking Email Back

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Linux-magazine

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The fourth in a five-part series on European-funded open source projects in hardware and software.
  • In a recent development, deuxfleurs, a French nonprofit, keeps its servers in members' homes in Lille, Nantes, and Massy: two or three second-hand Lenovo ThinkCentre mini PCs each, with a copy of the same data so its websites stay up when one of them loses power or fiber line.
  • The software for self-hosting email in this manner is called Aerogramme, and it isn't finished.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The fourth in a five-part series on European-funded open source projects in hardware and software.

In a recent development, deuxfleurs, a French nonprofit, keeps its servers in members' homes in Lille, Nantes, and Massy: two or three second-hand Lenovo ThinkCentre mini PCs each, with a copy of the same data so its websites stay up when one of them loses power or fiber line. Quentin Dufour, one of the founders, indicates some major French websites already serve their pages from this setup. Next, the collective wants its email to work the same way.

The software for self-hosting email in this manner is called Aerogramme, and it isn't finished. Deuxfleurs still runs its own mail on Dovecot, a long-established open source mail server, and aims to move to Aerogramme around January 2027.

It has been revealed that the collective is heading the opposite way from almost everyone else. According to the independent daily DNS measurements published by RIPE Labs, email for the million busiest domains on the web has consolidated dramatically: In 2016, 44.6 percent of these domains used small or self-hosted servers, and that share halved to 22.4 percent by July 2026. Small regional hosting companies and independents are losing accounts to corporate providers like Google and Microsoft, who together handled 38.6 percent of these busy domains.

Industry observers note that email is older than the Internet itself, and it still runs on open standards anyone can implement. Any server can deliver to any other, and any standards-compliant client can read any mailbox. It’s the hosting that has concentrated into a very few hands, eroding autonomy and giving hosting providers power over the data that travels through digital correspondence.

Two cases illustrate how this can limit operational independence. In May 2025, staff at the International Criminal Court (ICC) told the Associated Press that the court's chief prosecutor lost access to his Microsoft email account after he was named in US sanctions; Microsoft denies suspending services but hasn’t explained what happened to his account. In February 2026, the Dutch government told its parliament that the tax administration was moving about 40,000 workplaces to Microsoft 365 for lack of a short-term alternative, while acknowledging that Microsoft could be forced under state pressure to stop delivering services.

In a recent development, the Dutch government reversed course in October: The tax administration, customs, and the benefits agency will run mail and calendar on their own servers from 2027, with European open source tools for storage and collaboration to follow. The question now: How are developers working to decentralize email hosting on a wider scale? Each obstacle pushing organizations off of small or self-hosted email servers has open source projects working on a solution. Three of them show how the pieces fit; all of them supported by NGI Zero, the EU-funded programs that enable open source research and development.

In the 1990s, running your own mail server was ordinary. Universities and small companies did it, and so did Mauro De Gennaro. In 1993, as a teenager, he fetched mail for owners of his bulletin board over UUCP: the dial-up protocol Unix machines used to exchange mail. He has worked on mail software for most of the three decades since. When he looked at the open source stack again about six years ago, he saw "it's the same software that companies and servers have been using for over 20 years.".

Industry observers note that he counts 12 separate programs to run a conventional self-hosted setup. Each has its own configuration format and logs, written by different people in different styles. The software works well, he claims, but was "designed and documented for other developers." Bundles such as Mailcow and Mail-in-a-Box install the whole set at once: “They abstract the complexity," De Gennaro says, "but they do not remove it." Since all of it was designed for a single machine, running it as a cluster server is possible in the same way it's possible to take a Fiat Cinquecento and turn it electric: "It was not designed for that." Google debuted Gmail into that friction in 2004, with a gigabyte of free storage, and let companies run their own domain's mail on it. "Then they started billing," De Gennaro says. The users were captive, and moving email is disruptive enough that few of them left.

It has been revealed that ben Bucksch joined the Mozilla mail team in the late 1990s, where his first contribution made email links clickable; he also served in leadership for the Thunderbird Council and invented AutoConfig, which lets a mail client set up an account from nothing but an email address. In his telling, the lock-in started within the client.

IT departments think about email as servers; “what users want is to keep their workflow," Bucksch says. Microsoft shaped those workflows with Outlook's calendar and corporate features: Outlook works properly only with Microsoft Exchange, and Microsoft is pushing Exchange customers into its cloud. By some estimates, about 75 percent of professional mailboxes are on Office 365. "If we want to free the lock-in," he says, "we need to start with the client.".

Dufour and Armaël Guéneau of Deuxfleurs locate the problem in operations. IMAP is the protocol most clients use to read mail. An IMAP server has to serve webmail that queries the server for every view, desktop clients such as Thunderbird that synchronize whole mailboxes, and phones that do some of each. Implementing it is hard; the reliability people expect is harder. When the tax office sends you an email, Dufour notes, "it must work." The expertise to run mail at that level, Guéneau says, "tends to be captured by hyperscalers.".

According to recent reports, as Dufour tells it, Google didn't adapt existing mail software; it built Gmail on top of its distributed storage. Open source mail software was designed for one machine first, so adding distribution later, he notes, requires "really huge trade-offs.".

Recent findings suggest that reclaiming email is more complex than deciding to run your own server and navigating the software. Your service has to fluently speak with the large providers and support migration without disrupting service. And, of course, it needs sustainable funding.

Today, publicly funded teams are working on solving each of those three problems.

In a recent development, stalwart, the server from De Gennaro’s team, focuses on streamlining the software to replace 12 programs with one: Installation takes two commands and a six-screen web wizard. It speaks every common mail and collaboration protocol: SMTP for sending, IMAP and POP3 for reading, JMAP for web-based mail, and CalDAV and CardDAV for calendars and contacts. Spam filtering, sender authentication, and TLS encryption are built in. Give it a token for a DNS provider such as Cloudflare or Route 53, and the server publishes its own mail records. Behind the wizard are nearly 3,000 settings across 176 screens, which most operators never touch. De Gennaro calls Stalwart "the software at the other end of your email client or calendar client.".

According to recent reports, stalwart 1.0 was released in October 2026 after five and a half years of development. NGI Zero funded the project with two grants: one for the mail server, and one for calendars, contacts, and file storage.

For users who can’t leave Outlook features behind, there’s Parula. Keeping the application logic strictly separate from a thin interface layer, and a well thought-out common logic, so a upcoming protocol takes “just a few thousand lines of code,” Bucksch and his team at Beonex GmbH built an Outlook-like interface alongside a modern interface, a chat-style view and a classic three-pane view. It runs on a JMAP server or any other mail server and offers shared team mailboxes, delegated access so an assistant can run a manager’s calendar, and free/busy lookups for team meetings. It speaks IMAP, JMAP, and POP3, plus four from Microsoft: Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync, Microsoft Graph, and Outlook Web Access.

Recent findings suggest that aerogramme, an IMAP server that doesn't keep any state of its own, answers the operations problem in the storage. It doesn’t send or receive mail, so it needs a separate mail transfer agent such as Postfix; then it encrypts each mailbox on Garage, compatible with Amazon’s S3 interface. Garage replicates every piece of data in three locations, so customers can still read and write their mail if a site goes offline. This design for power cuts and residential Internet connections gave up perfect synchronization, but it spreads maintenance work among five to ten members rather than requiring one significant server host to give up all his weekends.

The research problem, Dufour says, is mapping the mail, calendar, and contact protocols cleanly onto object storage. Aerogramme is still on the way, with internal deployment planned for January 2027 and a public beta a few months later. To get there, a second grant funded through NGI Zero is supporting a hunt for edge cases where a network delay or a failure halfway through writing could lose a message.

The three projects already interoperate with each other and with other email programs on the NLnet list funded by NGI Zero. Parula lists Stalwart as a supported server; Stalwart can keep its messages in Garage. Bucksch and De Gennaro both name Mox as another server built as a single package. Different teams, working separately, have split the email problem and built solutions that fit back together.

Improvements to SMTP will provide better guarantee of confidentiality.

Version 1.0.0 of the Tarmail mail server has just been released. The developers claim that their software is particularly resilient against exploits, spam and email worms.

New mail protocol will shut out the NSA and prevent snooping on metadata.

IndiMail, an email solution made of open source components, now includes greylisting spam filtering in version 1.6.

#161197. TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

📅 19 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (938 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that torchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • Recent findings suggest that torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that torchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

Recent findings suggest that torchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Sources indicate that starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

In a recent development, to date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

According to recent reports, for the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron consumers use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Industry observers note that text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

Sources indicate that the following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

In a recent development, now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Recent findings suggest that parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

It has been revealed that nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

According to recent reports, training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Recent findings suggest that many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

It has been revealed that make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, people can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that trueLayer announced on November 27, 2026, that a Papa John’s AI agent had completed what it described as the first agentic Pay by Bank payment to a named UK retailer. The pilot involved UK retail banks including Lloyds and NatWest and ran through the Financial Conduct Authority’s Supercharged Sandbox.

According to recent reports, the agent helped with the customer’s order and then paid directly from the bank account linked to the customer’s Papa John’s account. Pay by Bank uses open-banking technology to link a bank account rather than a card, bringing the payment step into the AI-assisted ordering process. At a showcase on November 26, 2026, TrueLayer presented its findings to the FCA and industry participants.

A customer creates one mandate with the bank, setting limits for a particular merchant or over a chosen period that the agent cannot exceed. Each attempted payment is checked against those limits, so an instruction above them is declined by the bank rather than relying on the agent to police itself. Payment approval remains inside the bank app, keeping banking credentials and passwords away from the agent. Customers can revoke the arrangement through either the merchant or their banking app at any time.

According to recent reports, this separates the agent’s ability to initiate a purchase from the bank’s enforcement of the customer’s payment authority. TrueLayer also described the pilot as the first agentic use of the variable recurring payment APIs at Lloyds and NatWest, bank interfaces for payments authorized under an ongoing customer mandate.

Sources indicate that trueLayer argues that bank mandates let consumers delegate purchases without sharing card details, that non-card payments can preserve competition in payment acceptance as agents handle more shopping, and that the showcase can inform the conditions and standards needed for safe adoption at scale. The work remains a sandbox pilot rather than a general consumer launch.

Industry observers note that the retailer pilot followed TrueLayer’s July 22, 2026 announcement of its selection for the sandbox. The FCA received 199 applications and selected 21 companies for a cohort running from July 13, 2026, through December 31, 2026, with a particular focus on agentic payments. The sandbox, part of the FCA’s AI Lab, provides a controlled setting and regulatory support for moving advanced AI use cases toward commercial deployment.

Recent findings suggest that an earlier prototype kept a person in the loop while completing a transaction inside an AI shopping agent. It supported a one-off immediate payment and Bank on File, which establishes a recurring mandate for future purchases. The Papa John’s work extends those mechanics into a named retailer’s ordering flow with participating UK banks.

In a recent development, the FCA’s expectations for agentic AI in financial services, published on November 24, 2026, add regulatory context to the demonstration. The regulator mentioned firms must identify which agent activities require authorization and which rules apply, particularly when software can initiate transactions, move money, arrange borrowing or make investment decisions.

Using an external AI provider does not transfer compliance responsibility away from a regulated firm or its senior managers. They are expected to understand how autonomously their systems act, the risks created and the controls needed in real time and under stress. When customers’ agents approach a firm, it should have processes to recognize the agent, verify consent and permitted actions, and provide help if something goes wrong.

Payments are a specific case. Before accepting an agent’s instructions, firms should assess their systems, controls and potential liabilities, including whether to accept a payment initiated by an AI agent or from a wallet under its control. The pilot’s bank-held mandate and in-app approval address the spending-control portion of that assessment; they do not by themselves settle broader questions of regulatory authorization, liability and senior-management oversight.

Sources indicate that the pilot establishes a concrete division of authority between agent and bank. Wider adoption depends on pairing that payment mechanism with the FCA’s broader expectations for accountability, consent, liability and customer support, which extend beyond whether an individual transaction stays within its limit.

MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1364 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • It has been revealed that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and latest Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

It has been revealed that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

It has been revealed that you'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

In a recent development, you can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

It has been revealed that every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Industry observers note that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

Industry observers note that the decoding kernel demonstrates up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Industry observers note that small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

Industry observers note that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Industry observers note that several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

It has been revealed that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Recent findings suggest that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Sources indicate that bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

Sources indicate that pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aditya Infotech Limited stated in a stock-exchange filing on November 27, 2026 that it had completed a ₹45.39 crore cash purchase of 30% of KGraph AI Solutions Private Limited on a fully diluted basis. KGraph becomes an associate organization, with its BLUE video-analytics technology slated for integration into CP PLUS surveillance products.

The company’s November 5, 2026 announcement described the consideration as a mix of fresh equity and purchases from existing shareholders, with an implied post-money valuation of approximately ₹151 crore. Managing Director Aditya Khemka noted: “Video compression is foundational to the next phase of surveillance. As cameras multiply and resolutions rise, the cost of storing and moving video becomes the real constraint.”.

The price was based on a registered valuer’s report. The transaction was not a related-party deal, none of Aditya Infotech’s promoters, promoter group or group companies had an interest in KGraph, and no governmental or regulatory approvals were required.

KGraph’s Semantic Codec adds a perception-aware compression layer to the standard H.264 video codec, identifying redundant visual information while retaining essential details. Based on deployment data, Aditya Infotech mentioned the technology could reduce video storage and bandwidth requirements by up to 90%.

The codec is designed for cost-efficient edge hardware without GPU infrastructure and works with existing cameras and recording systems. The firm said this could extend video retention and lower deployment costs without replacing installed infrastructure, giving CP PLUS a potential upgrade path for customers already running surveillance equipment.

Sources indicate that KGraph’s broader BLUE platform turns continuous video streams into searchable enterprise data. The investment is part of CP PLUS 2.0, Aditya Infotech’s move from hardware-led surveillance toward integrated security covering data management, edge computing, AI analytics and cloud integration.

KGraph will continue to operate independently while collaborating with Aditya Infotech’s R&D and engineering teams in Noida, Ahmedabad and Taiwan. The collaboration pairs KGraph’s computer-vision, embedded-systems and compression expertise with Aditya Infotech’s engineering, manufacturing and customer reach.

KGraph’s six co-founders bring 15 to more than 20 years of experience and academic backgrounds from IIT Bombay and IIM Bangalore. The firm has a 10-patent pipeline, with three applications filed and seven in progress.

Incorporated on August 16, 2023, KGraph develops AI-powered software for compliance, automation, safety, monitoring and regulatory reporting across industrial and commercial sectors. It operates in India, and BLUE is its principal product. The completion filing reported audited turnover of approximately ₹80 lakh in FY2025-26, compared with approximately ₹36 lakh in FY2024-25 and no turnover in FY2023-24.

Aditya Infotech’s board approved the investment on November 5, when the parties executed a share subscription and purchase agreement and a shareholders’ agreement. The original transaction filing allowed 30 days from execution, or a later mutually agreed date, for completion. Closing on November 27 therefore fell within the initial timetable.

It has been revealed that the completed stake gives CP PLUS access to KGraph’s compression and analytics expertise while leaving the startup independent. The commercial question now is whether joint engineering can turn the manufacturer-reported efficiency gains into deployed CP PLUS products and a larger revenue base for KGraph.

AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses.
  • Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps.
  • A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

In a recent development, the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Industry observers note that support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

It has been revealed that reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the newly introduced provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

According to recent reports, the first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

In a recent development, language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.
