Industry News: The State of Allocators in 2026 - Finally Stabilised

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it's only been a couple of months since the last article, and I am pleased to see that, after 10 years of limbo, allocators have finally been stabilised!
  • So, now we have an MVP of the allocator API, what can we do with it?
  • In this article I'll step through a few use cases that might be handy to the layman rust programmer, so hopefully you can see the benefit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it's only been a couple of months since the last article, and I am pleased to see that, after 10 years of limbo, allocators have finally been stabilised! While it feels like the never type did steal a bit of thunder, rust 1.100 was nonetheless a monumental release. Congratulations on the team that shepherded this through.

So, now we have an MVP of the allocator API, what can we do with it? What does it get us besides closer feature parity with other system languages like C++ & Zig?

In this article I'll step through a few use cases that might be handy to the layman rust programmer, so hopefully you can see the benefit.

This was one of the leading cases for custom allocation. Dropping in rust is not free. There has been prior art in actually moving memory to a dedicated thread to Drop highly nested structures. This is actually only half a solution. You're still paying for the deallocation call costs, just it's not in the hot path anymore.

In a recent development, instead, what if we knew that we would have a period of time in our code, where we're going to allocate a lot of stuff, do something with it, and then free everything? A good example of this is a web request, or a database query.

Industry observers note that A request comes in, fills in some data structures, and then when the request finishes, the memory isn't needed anymore so it's dropped. This sort of "burst" pattern of allocation, where you allocate a lot up front, and then tear things down all at once at the end, is quite common.

According to recent reports, for this we can use a bump allocator: reserve a substantial block of memory, and allocate from that, rather than paying the cost of talking to the system allocator for every allocation. Think of it like the BufReader and BufWriter of std io, rather than make repeated syscalls to fetch data, we can buffer that data in a big block, so that we can reduce the overhead considerably.

Industry observers note that you want more memory? Just check if the size fits in our block, return that slice, increment our counter (bump!), and we're done. We can add more blocks as well, if we run out. This makes allocations very cheap, we don't need to keep much state around besides from a counter.

It has been revealed that the downsides of this approach is when we come to deallocate memory. We don't keep track around where individual allocations are made. However, this actually solves our drop takes a long time problem, since we can just deallocate everything all at once.

Essentially if the impl of the bump allocator is:.

There are a few tradeoffs for doing things like this in a bump allocator, and not every allocation is going to benefit. Hence why it's important to be able to adjust our allocation strategy locally rather than just globally. However, an astute reader might notice that, if we are bumping large swathes of memory, this is going to possibly cause our memory usage to increase considerably. Well, that brings us to our next section: memory accounting.

Recent findings suggest that the next challenge that can be solved by custom allocators is knowing how much memory particular sections of code is being used. I.e, memory accounting. The key here is that, we can use existing allocators, and sprinkle in some extra bookkeeping to keep a pretty accurate ledger.

There are a number of use cases that accounting can shape the behaviour of code. Say you have a cache of objects, and you want to set a threshold above which, we start evicting entries. Or say you want to do an external sort, but you don't know how big your data structures are at the start, but you want to use up as much memory as possible. Or maybe you are wanting to place a limit on a code sandbox, because it's sharing resources with other sandboxes.

Industry observers note that what you can do is wrap an allocator, with a custom accounting layer, and use this to drive your decisions. I.e, here is a very trivial example:.

Then we can wrap the global allocator, and see how much our cache is using:.

In a recent development, now, a single atomic, while is great for an example, does have some perf overhead. So, one of the crates that I have created, while keeping in mind performance, is thresher: an accounting allocator with a callback on threshold. It uses a combined "local" task/thread and "global" counter to avoid atomic contention, feeding back in every 64KiB of allocation.

thresher gets its name from the cutest shark: the Thresher Shark.

Now, what you can do with thresher is, use it to trigger callbacks when allocations are hit:.

This prints out what you'd expect:.

In a recent development, one production use case, is that we're using thresher on logfire to provide us heap profiles of our rust services when memory hits a configured threshold. I did a deep dive into heap profiles and why they are extremely useful in an older blog: a tale of two lengths. In thresher you can find a jemalloc example where you can instrument this yourself!

OK so we can control memory when it is dropped, we can use memory accounting to know how much memory we're using, what's left? How about where it goes?

Recent findings suggest that this is probably the more esoteric of the 3 examples I wanted to give. There are some situations where you actually need to control where the memory lives, and sometimes by doing some allocation tricks you can get better performance out.

Sources indicate that one example would be what smallvec and friends do. Instead of going straight to the heap to allocate things, they have a small amount that lives on the stack, and only if allocations go above a certain size, then do they write to the heap.

While smallvec is more battle tested, here is some example code about how you could do this with the allocator API:.

Then we can use our toy stack first allocator:.

Recent findings suggest that et voila! We have smaller allocations on the stack and then push to the heap as needed. This can give some good performance boosts.

Normally when you align memory allocations, this is based upon the thing that is being allocated for. I.e, is it a u64? align to 8 bytes or a u32? align to 4. If it's not correctly aligned, this can cause undefined behaviour and all sorts. You notice in both the bump and small stack example I had to do some shenanigans to find the next appropriately aligned address. However, there is some scenarios where the alignment of memory is external to what is being allocated.

In linux, when you read anything from disk via standard syscalls, you are usually reading from the kernel's page cache. I.e, the spare memory the kernel has around to make things transparently fast. Most of the time that is fine, but there are some times when you want to bypass it.

I.e, there is a long standing bug in kubernetes that can cause pod eviction if you are using the page cache. Or: if you are doing your own caching layer, sometimes it doesn't make sense to double up on memory devoted to caching files.

It has been revealed that so, there is a bailout provided, in the guise of O_DIRECT that allows you to directly access files from the file system. However: one of the requirements of using this flag is that you are reading or writing into memory that is aligned to the device's logical block size. This is usually a multiple of 512, but can be less or more depending on the hardware.

The implementation of a block aligned allocator is pretty simple, here's one where we just hardset it to 4096:.

With this, we can now write simple code to read directly using O_DIRECT:.

Here, the read_exact call can fail on some devices if we're not using block size aligned allocations.

Like with the stack first allocation, there are libraries that allow you do this already, such as the aligned-vec crate, with their own data types to work nicely.

But here's the rub: say you had an application where you wanted to blend and mix in different allocation strategies: some vecs you want to be block aligned, some you want allocated on the stack, but you want to be able to use shared methods for both. Do we want to use smallvec and aligned-vec in order to deal with a data structure that is essentially the same thing, just allocated differently?

std allocators allows you to be generic over the collections, regardless of allocator used:.

And I think that's pretty powerful.

It has been revealed that it's going to take a bit of time for the ecosystem to catch up to custom allocators. A lot of popular crates have an MSRV policy that precludes them from using even latest standard features, and some existing crates, which I would think are a shoe in for the new allocator API, as of writing do not yet have support.

The libs team isn't done yet. This is the MVP of allocators, and, like I mentiond in the the last article, this is the beginning of custom allocator support. There is still work to go to support other collection types like maps etc.. so much to be done. I think that what we have is useful enough to start using it now, and also to start adapting and allowing library consumers the ability to provide their own allocators with their API.

I'm excited to see what people build, and what other use cases are unlocked with it!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A device does not get a larger battery because the model needs more tokens.
  • Industry observers note that in 2027, that discipline will become a selling point.
  • MLPerf Mobile v6 and MLPerf Inference v6.1 show how benchmark coverage is evolving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A device does not get a larger battery because the model needs more tokens. It does not get a second memory pool when another application is running. And when connectivity disappears, the customer still expects the product to do its job. Edge AI lives inside those physical limits.

Industry observers note that in 2027, that discipline will become a selling point. The most revealing demonstrations will show what remains useful after the device warms up, the network drops and the ideal test conditions are gone.

MLPerf Mobile v6 and MLPerf Inference v6.1 show how benchmark coverage is evolving. Apple's Foundation Models framework also makes local inference more accessible to application developers. My 2027 forecasts focus on products outside the data center: what they can do offline, how they divide work with the cloud, and whether they sustain their advertised performance.

It has been revealed that turning off the internet is a remarkably clarifying product test. It reveals which parts of a supposedly local workflow still depend on a remote service. In 2027, more edge products will document useful tasks that survive that test. Offline availability will become a specific capability to inspect, rather than a reassuring adjective attached to a chip.

An application can contain an on-device model while still requiring a remote service for retrieval, authentication or a critical planning step. Calling the product local does not establish that its principal workflow survives disconnection.

Gemini Robotics On-Device illustrates the effort to bring embodied inference closer to the machine. Apple's third-generation foundation-model research likewise describes work across local and server models. These are different systems, but both make the boundary between device and cloud a practical engineering choice.

The hardest part may be dependency management rather than model size. A local language model cannot summarize a document that the application has never cached, and a robot cannot assume its remote task database remains current.

Recent findings suggest that look for deliberate network-disconnection tests and a list of remaining dependencies. A useful demonstration should show startup, ordinary execution and recovery after reconnection. A cached prerecorded answer or an offline label without a documented task would be weak evidence.

Test the actual workflow in the locations where connectivity is unreliable. Specify which tasks must remain available and how stale data are handled. Local inference is valuable when it improves continuity or control of data, even if its raw model quality is lower than a cloud alternative.

Peak performance is a moment; a product has to keep working. In 2027, more evaluations will pair task quality with sustained latency or throughput under disclosed memory and power conditions. That will expose the difference between a model that runs briefly on a development board and a service that remains useful inside the customer's finished device.

A brief benchmark can run before thermal limits reduce clock speeds. A larger model can fit in theory while leaving too little memory for the rest of the application. These effects determine whether the device delivers a useful service after the first minute.

Industry observers note that MLCommons' mobile benchmark work provides a structured starting point for comparisons. Qualcomm's developer resources show the importance suppliers place on deployment optimization. Vendor materials explain intended capabilities; they should be distinguished from independent tests of a finished device.

The forecast is that more evaluations will connect hardware measurements to a task a customer recognizes. Tokens per second without a quality threshold can reward an unusably compressed model. Battery life without workload frequency can conceal a test that barely exercises the AI system. A serious comparison fixes both the service being provided and the conditions under which it must run.

Sources indicate that look for warm-device results, concurrent application load and output-quality checks. Explicit enclosure and power settings will make comparisons easier. A peak TOPS figure alone would not qualify, and desktop development-board results should not be presented as finished handheld performance.

Run acceptance tests on production hardware with the intended enclosure and workload. Include memory headroom and battery or power limits in the specification. Hardware startups can differentiate through transparent sustained results, especially when they cannot compete with the largest vendors' marketing budgets.

Industry observers note that sometimes the cloud is the right place for a task. Sometimes sending it there defeats the reason the device exists. In 2027, developer controls will make that choice more visible, including what happens when the remote path fails. The useful hybrid system will let its owner decide which trade-offs are acceptable instead of hiding them behind automatic routing.

In a recent development, the sensible architecture is often mixed. Local models can handle familiar, private or latency-sensitive tasks, while a larger remote model handles work that exceeds the device's capability. The risk is a hidden switch that changes privacy, cost or availability without the developer understanding it.

In a recent development, the Apple Foundation Models framework spans model access options, while Gemini Robotics On-Device 2's model card describes the scope of a particular local model. These sources do not imply that all tasks can move interchangeably between environments.

Automatic routing can still be useful, but its policy should be inspectable. Otherwise the product may satisfy a quality test in the lab while violating an operating requirement in the field.

Look for explicit developer settings, task-level telemetry and a documented failure mode. Tests should distinguish model fallback from retrieval or storage access. An application that silently sends difficult requests to the cloud would offer less evidence of controllable hybrid operation.

In a recent development, set routing policy around data sensitivity and service requirements. Budget for remote usage where it remains necessary. Buyers should know whether the quoted device performance includes cloud assistance, because that changes both cost and the meaning of offline availability.

A model update can improve one device and exhaust another's memory. It can also change behavior in a language or sensor condition the rollout team barely tested. In 2027, commercial platforms will describe staged deployment and rollback around device-level task performance. Maintaining a fleet will mean managing changing behavior as well as distributing fresh files.

Updating a model is not identical to updating an ordinary software component. A smaller model can use less memory while producing worse outputs for a particular language or sensor. A upcoming runtime can accelerate one workload while increasing power use in another.

MLPerf Inference v6.1 reflects the growing range of deployment workloads that need measurement. The implication for fleet management is that a model update should be evaluated on representative devices and tasks, rather than accepted because it has a newer version number.

Sources indicate that this will be harder for hardware with long service lives and uneven connectivity. Some devices may remain on old models for months. The platform needs to know which version produced an output and whether a rollback restores a compatible application state. A central dashboard alone does not resolve those field conditions.

Look for staged releases, device-class performance checks and an actual rollback path. Documented failures caught before broad release would strengthen confidence. A platform that updates model files but cannot track quality differences across devices would address only part of the problem.

Include model maintenance in the lifetime cost of the device. Specify support periods, version visibility and recovery procedures. Hardware companies should preserve enough telemetry to diagnose failures while respecting the privacy advantage that motivated local processing in the first place.

The best edge products will be defined by the work they can sustain inside their constraints. Local processing can offer privacy, availability and a predictable response, but each benefit has to survive the complete device. In 2027, the engineering details will increasingly become the product story.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch people had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

Industry observers note that to make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

It has been revealed that torchTPU adds TPU as a latest backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

It has been revealed that the extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

Sources indicate that TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Recent findings suggest that models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

In a recent development, the Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

According to recent reports, TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

In a recent development, the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

Recent findings suggest that it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an matter on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 complications, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch consumers. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

Industry observers note that we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an matter and tell us about it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after Automattic's confirmation that they would switch their .vibe application to the replacement string of .php1, ICANN has started to publish various objections on the Application Comment Forum (ACF) section of their newly introduced gTLD program site2. They mostly relate to the confusion and security risk posed by a common filetype (especially in web development) becoming a TLD, similar to the outcry over Google's application for .zip (which was eventually successfully delegated). The other common theme is the objection to a private company effectively trying to claim what is an open-source project.

The first is by PHP developer Larry Garfield who accused the WordPress parent of "Inappropriate Squatting":3.

WordPress contributor Jamie VanRaalte objected on the grounds of "Part of a pattern - .php should not go to one company" and also said the .wordpress application was a similarly inappropriate power grab of another open-source project:4.

Web developer Ryan Maietta highlighted the "File Extension Confusion and Security Risks" of using an established filetype as a TLD and the risk of people confusing websites using this domain as being officially endorsed by the PHP project:5.

Forensic analyst Herbert Bärschneider also objected simply on the grounds of confusing the TLD with the filetype:6.

And finally, the ICANN-affiliated Mark William Datysgeld described .php as being "Not viable from a technical perspective"7 highlighting that he has already had complications creating the page for it on the PHP-based ICANN Wiki site, causing it to return a 404 error response8:.
